papers.abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/
authors: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Jiayuan Yan, Bohan Fang, Wisdom Oluchi Ikezogwo, Ainaz Eftekhar, Max Argus, Jason Ren, Jiafei Duan, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting one manipulation policy to robots with different morphologies and capabilities.

Trained with procedurally generated, physically feasible embodiments and simulated trajectories across diverse tasks.
Achieves 63.0% success on held-out simulated evaluations and nearly twice the success of the next-best method on an unseen real-world robot.

papers.abstract: The appearance of a scene is determined by the albedo, roughness, metallicity and normal of every point on its surface, and by the light that reaches it, its irradiance. Recovering these intrinsics from images is ambiguous, and methods that predict them per pixel give the same surface point a different decomposition in every view. We introduce PointX, a simple feed-forward model that predicts intrinsics per 3D surface point instead. A multi-view transformer encodes a set of unposed images, and for any queried surface point, PointX pools the point's tokens across the views in which it appears and decodes the point's intrinsics once. Each point of a 3D reconstruction of the scene, such as a point cloud or a mesh, thus receives a single prediction, which is exactly consistent across views by construction and enables view-consistent relighting and editing. The same model also predicts per-view maps, from one image or many, by querying the point seen at every pixel. These maps agree across views up to the precision of the estimated geometry and correspondences. PointX is significantly more consistent than existing methods, while remaining competitive in accuracy from a single image and improving as views are added. Project page: https://pointx-paper.github.io/
authors: Miguel Farinha, Sam Sartor, Iliyan Georgiev, Giuseppe Vecchio, Ronald Clark, Michael Fischer
bullets: Per-pixel intrinsic prediction can assign inconsistent decompositions to the same surface point across views.
A multi-view transformer encodes unposed images and aggregates tokens from views observing each queried 3D point.
The model predicts one intrinsic decomposition per point, making results exactly view-consistent by construction.
It can also produce per-view maps by querying the 3D point at each pixel, with consistency limited by geometry and correspondence accuracy.
PointX is more consistent than existing methods, competitive from a single image, and improves as more views are added.

papers.abstract: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
authors: Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman, Shuo Yang, Ratheesh Kalarot, Yingyan Celine Lin, Mingze Xu
bullets: Addresses the tight coupling between utterance timing and audiovisual diarization in video captioning.
Uses a two-stage approach: synthetic-caption training on 225K clips, followed by reinforcement learning from 2.9K human-corrected clips.
Generates transcripts, utterance timestamps, speaker grouping, and visual descriptions for each utterance.
On DiaDemBench, achieves strong diarization and substantially better timestamp accuracy than Gemini 4 Argon (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME).
Maintains performance on multilingual and minute-long videos and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with similar-looking speakers. Each track shows one model’s predicted utterances over time, colored by the ground-truth speaker that its description depicts, with wrong speakers outlined in dark red.

Figure 11. A one-word turn right before another speaker (Mandarin). The young man answers with a single syllable lasting 0.3s (first frame), and the man in the gray suit continues immediately (second frame). DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E keep the short turn as a separate line with the correct speaker. Gemini 4 Argon and DiaDem merge it into the next speaker’s line, so turn A is lost. Gemini’s timestamps also miss every boundary (TIME 0), and DiaDem predicts none. This example shows that accurate timestamps and diarization are tightly coupled, as a model without precise turn boundaries tends to absorb a short turn into a longer neighboring one.

Figure 2. Overview of DiaCap. A speech recognizer Ψ transcribes the audio, and an audiovisual LLM Θ takes the transcript T together with the video and audio to predict the timestamps and speaker of every utterance. DiaCap-E2E predicts Y directly without a recognizer.

Figure 7. Failure case: off-screen speaker merged with the on-screen one. In a handheld phone video, a girl (A) asks her mother where she is going, and the mother (B) answers from off-screen. DiaCap describes a single speaker, gives the mother’s reply (“I’ll go wherever I want”) to the girl, and drops the mother’s cut-off last words. Since only the girl is ever on screen, the model does not infer that a second person is speaking.

Figure 9. Off-screen speakers in a multi-shot scene. The first and last turns are spoken while the camera shows someone else. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and describe these speakers as off-screen voices. Gemini 4 Argon gives the woman’s “Uh, Nal-what?” to the man in the blue lab coat and truncates it. DiaDem describes both men only as “man in a lab coat”, so the second man’s two turns go to the first man.

Figure 8. One speaker who goes off-screen. In this typical shot/reverse-shot conversation, a single woman speaks both lines. During the second line, the camera cuts to the listener and the speaker is off-screen. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute both lines to the same speaker. Gemini 4 Argon gives the second line to the visible listener (short reddish-brown hair). DiaDem’s description (“woman with shoulder-length brown hair”) is too generic to identify the speaker, so neither of its lines is credited.

Figure 10. A speaker seen only from behind. The last line is spoken by the man with his back to the camera. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute it to him. Gemini 4 Argon gives it to the man in the gray suit and DiaDem to the man with the mustache, the two people whose faces are visible.

Figure 12. A short interjection from a third speaker. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and place every boundary within the collar. Gemini 4 Argon merges the woman’s two turns into one line, so when scoring Gemini, we merge consecutive groundtruth utterances from the same speaker, which leaves three ground-truth turns. Gemini’s timestamps miss most boundaries (TIME 33). DiaDem describes the speaker of the final interjection only as “man’s voice”, which depicts none of the people in the scene.

Figure 13. Four speakers in one room. DiaCap, DiaCap-E2E, and Gemini 4 Argon attribute all five turns correctly. DiaDem gets three of the five turns wrong. It gives “Are you serious?” (C) and “Me too.” (D) to the young woman, and gives her own “I’m okay with that.” to a young man. Gemini’s timestamps drift by about 0.7s on the last three turns (TIME 40), whereas both DiaCap variants place every boundary within the collar (TIME 100).

Figure 3. Training data curation and annotation. (1) Audio, audiovisual, and visual experts tag each clip. We remove clips with unrelated or out-of-sync audio, deduplicate and resample the rest to balance language, speaker count, and visual scenes, and add no-speech clips with empty targets. (2) An audiovisual LLM annotates who says what, and a speech aligner timestamps each utterance. (3) Human annotators correct hard clips mined from the SFT corpus, plus fewer single-speaker clips, to form the RL corpus.

papers.abstract: The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.
authors: Yuwei Yang, Xiaoxiao Sun, Alejandro Lozano, Yuan-Sen Ting, Yuhui Yuan, Liang Zheng, Serena Yeung-Levy
bullets: Scientific articles provide richer supervision than treating each image-text pair independently.
The method preserves exact matches, adds weaker positives for structurally related pairs, and emphasizes same-type cross-article negatives.
Loom52M combines panel- and figure-level images with enriched descriptions and captions, totaling 52.4 million image-text pairs.
BioLoom reports stronger zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval performance than the evaluated baselines across biomedical benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.
authors: Dawid J. Kopiczko, Tijmen Blankevoort, Yuki M. Asano
bullets: Addresses the challenge of distilling capable closed-model teachers whose chain-of-thought is inaccessible.
Trains students on teacher action trajectories with an empty reasoning block, plus a replay-buffer KL loss to limit policy drift.
Finds cross-format transfer: policies learned without reasoning transfer to inference with reasoning enabled.
Short CoT-proxies improve performance beyond action-only distillation, including gains on AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified.
The approach works with visible outputs and API-provided reasoning summaries from closed teachers.

papers.abstract: Creating a dialogue scene typically requires cutting between multiple views (e.g., close-ups, medium shots, and over-the-shoulder shots) of the actors. Yet capturing such coverage is costly and in many settings unavailable. We study dialogue re-cinematography: synthesizing additional shots from a single wide-angle dialogue video. Existing video generators can synthesize new shots, but rely on visual cues alone, so when the source video barely shows the lips, the generated lip motion fails to match the speech. Our key observation is that the speech audio is view-invariant: it constrains lip motion in any target view. Building on this insight, we adapt a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model to generate the new shot from a target frame that specifies the view, a source video that contains the performance, and the speech audio that drives lip motion. In multi-person scenes, however, pretrained audio-visual models drive every visible face with the same speech, causing speech leakage, where silent listeners mouth the speaker's words. We therefore introduce speaker-aware audio gating, a training-free module that lets the audio drive only the faces that speak in the target shot. On a cinematic paired-view benchmark spanning diverse viewpoints and framings, our method lowers perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% relative to the strongest baseline, Wan 3.0. Our method also remains robust on in-the-wild scenes, highlighting its potential for film post-production.
authors: Anthony Chen, Naomi Ken Korem, Matan Ben-Yosef, Tavi Halperin, Urska Jelercic, Ofir Bibi, Daniel Cohen-Or, Or Patashnik, Maneesh Agrawala
bullets: Addresses the costly or unavailable multi-camera coverage needed for dialogue scenes.

Introduces training-free speaker-aware audio gating to prevent speech leakage onto silent listeners.
On a paired-view cinematic benchmark, reduces perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% versus Wan 3.0.
Also shows robustness on in-the-wild scenes, supporting potential film post-production use.

papers.abstract: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.
authors: Zehan Zheng, Yanyuan Chen, Deming Li, Yutao Tang, Jianwen Xie, Alan Yuille, Jieneng Chen, Cheng Peng
bullets: Evaluates VLMs in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting.
Combines diagnostic question answering with closed-loop interactive navigation under multimodal instructions.
Measures six capabilities: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency.
Finds outdoor environments are substantially more demanding than indoor settings, with poor performance from existing models.
Highlights multimodal interaction and long-term spatial reasoning as key directions for embodied intelligence.

papers.abstract: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.
authors: Feixiang Ruan, Guodong Lv, Kewei Zhang, Wenbo Huang, Yintianrun Zhang, Qiang Wang, Ruiyang Si, Shunyu Yang, Shulong Jiang, Weicheng Duan, Rui Ni, Jianxin Bi, Lekai Wang, Yuze Fan, Haobo Li, Zeliang Fu, Jiankun Zhang, Duomin Wang, Enze Xie, Daquan Zhou

Reports leading simulated benchmark performance, including a 72.9 Bench2Dex score and 81.0% DexJoCo success under full randomization.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of PyRUA-Dex. All learning takes place in simulation. Stage 2 (refinement): one agent finds the program’s bottleneck stage by a stage-wise failure analysis, refines it on randomized layouts and selects the version with the best held-out record. The resulting program runs frozen, without a language model. For the real world, the simulation is built from the real scene (real-to-sim), the frozen program is transferred (sim-to-real), and real-world feedback updates the simulation for the next round of refinement.

papers.abstract: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.
authors: Yueh-Cheng Liu, Snehal Jauhri, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner, Angela Dai
bullets: Covers household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces with detailed geometry, physically based materials, and curated layouts.
Provides object- and part-level semantic annotations for joint visual and embodied learning.
Supports inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation, improving state-of-the-art methods over alternative synthetic datasets.
Introduces a mobile manipulation benchmark for vision-language-action models, scoring both pick-and-place success and grasp location.
The dataset is intended for public release to support research in visual and embodied AI.

papers.abstract: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.
authors: Hussamuddin Syed
bullets: The unedited model almost never completes its thinking block within 4,096 tokens and achieves 15.4% on MATH-500.
Fine-tuning only 140–139,750 high-gradient weights on as few as 50 correct training examples raises 4k-token accuracy to 39.0–45.5%.
The gradient concentrates on near-constant channels in the first three layers, behaving like fixed vectors added to the residual stream.
Under the 32k-token evaluation protocol, the reproduced Astra edit reaches 52.1%, while the authors’ edits perform better at budgets up to 16k tokens.
Combining the Astra edit with a half-strength authors’ edit reaches 62.2% at 32k tokens, outperforming Astra alone and using half as many tokens.

papers.title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
papers.tldr: Tiny, gradient-selected edits largely stop Qwen3.5-0.8B’s reasoning loops, and combining them with a frontier-model weight edit substantially improves math performance.

papers.abstract: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $\beta$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.
authors: Kshitiz, Zheyuan Hu, Robyn Wu, Yizhou Li, Yunchu Zhang, Vattanary Tevy, Kavya Tayal, Shawn Yin, Aykut Onol, Kushal Arora, Dhruv Shah, Abhishek Gupta, Zackory Erickson, Aviral Kumar
bullets: Standard human demonstrations emphasize competent behavior but underrepresent low-level behaviors needed for autonomous improvement.
The authors define “connected behavioral coverage” as behaviors linking challenging robot-environment states to states that enable further progress.
They introduce β-Data, collected through adversarial teleoperation with reversible perturbations and no resets, then relabel trajectory segments with local natural-language outcomes.
A pretrained policy is finetuned on these trajectories while conditioning on recent action history.

In simulation and across three real-robot platforms, the approach shows better zero-shot generalization, more favorable data scaling, and more effective online finetuning than standard demonstrations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces midtraining to build behavioral coverage for robot policies, directly relevant to robot learning and manipulation, with novel data collection and finetuning approach.
papers.title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
papers.tldr: Adversarially collected midtraining data helps robot policies learn diverse low-level recovery behaviors, improving generalization, scaling with data and rollout time, and online adaptation.

papers.abstract: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.
authors: Yuchao Wu, XingCheng Liang, Xuanze Wang, Yini Huang, Yue Wu
bullets: Addresses retrieval of complementary facts scattered across sessions, including evidence with limited query similarity.
Stores complete messages in non-overlapping chunks and builds a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or relation construction.
Uses BM25 for initial retrieval, evidence evaluation, and a second retrieval round guided by lexical cues from selected evidence.
Annotates supported relative-time expressions with calendar interpretations while preserving original wording and temporal granularity.
Achieves the highest reported scores among evaluated methods on LoCoMo (83.08) and LongMemEval (80.20); SAG-Mem-Lite offers lower operational cost with scores of 77.09 and 77.20.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.
authors: Scott Piersall, Yang Gao, Shenyang Liu, Liqiang Wang
bullets: Targets the strong dependence of LLM-generated parallel code on generation guidance.
Combines correctness tests, compiler and static-analysis feedback, runtime data, and load-imbalance profiles into a reward for textual refinement.
Uses external memory to retrieve and accumulate optimization knowledge across runs.
Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, improves runtime, static-analysis quality, and load balance over zero-shot generation and generally over TextGrad.
Ablations and leakage-controlled tests indicate benefits persist with a matched refinement model and transferred knowledge in both skills and memory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: MetaFORGE: An automated meta-learning skill-refinement architecture. MetaFORGE optimizes LLM coding skills through execution-grounded feedback. Generated MPI C code is compiled, statically analyzed, executed, and scored using Eq. (1). Diagnostics and reward trends are converted into a textual gradient for skillprompt rewriting, while iteration artifacts are stored, distilled, indexed, and retrieved as long-term memory, enabling future updates to reuse prior reward-improving strategies.

Figure 8: Held-out cross-task transfer protocol. For each leave-one-task-out fold, METAFORGE is trained sequentially on the two non-held-out tasks across all workload sizes. The resulting transferred skill and cross-task memory are frozen before evaluation. The held-out task is excluded from all Phase 1 skill updates and memory construction.

papers.abstract: Bathymetry measurement and estimation is critical for understanding the structure of underwater environments. While multibeam echosounders (MBES) provide accurate depth measurements, their deployment on surface vessels limits spatial resolution in deep water. Sidescan sonar (SSS), in contrast, can be deployed on autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) to operate closer to the seafloor, enabling high-resolution acoustic imaging. However, the inherent ambiguity in measurements and the limited observation coverage of sonar datasets degrade the performance of state-of-the-art methods for underwater bathymetry estimation from SSS. In this paper, we propose a differentiable neural rendering framework for SSS that enables effective estimation of bathymetry from SSS measurements. Our approach incorporates a measurement model based on SSS geometry, explicitly accounting for its wide elevation aperture and associated ambiguities. We evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating improved robustness and accuracy compared to alternative approaches.
authors: Tianxiang Lin, Sacchin Sundar, Fenghao Liu, Onur Bagoren, Katherine A. Skinner
bullets: Addresses limited-resolution MBES deployment in deep water and ambiguity in SSS-based bathymetry estimation.
Models SSS measurements with geometry-aware rendering, including the wide elevation aperture and related ambiguities.
Evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets.
Reports improved robustness and accuracy compared with alternative approaches.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Pipeline overview. Our proposed method optimizes the sonar neural implicit bathymetry networks and renderer by the total rendering loss. The network takes an input set of SSS images with known poses (T = {R, t}). The sampled 3D points x and viewing directions D(x) are encoded by the multi-resolution hash encoder and spherical harmonics encoder. The neural renderer then estimates the acoustic radiance, which is used for the final SSS image formation model. The networks are supervised by the reference SSS images and other constraints included in the reconstruction loss.

Fig. 7: Visualization of bathymetry estimation results for real-world datasets. The axes x and y are expressed in meters in the WGS 84 / UTM Zone 17N coordinate system. Despite the presence of pose errors and noisy SSS measurements, our method produces more accurate reconstructions of the shipwrecks and achieves lower errors compared to both variants of Xie et al. [14].

Fig. 5: Visualization of bathymetry estimation results for synthetic datasets. The axes x and y are expressed in meters in the world coordinate frame. From all the reconstructed maps and the corresponding error maps, our method produces more consistent estimations and achieves lower reconstruction errors relative to the reference maps compared to Xie et al. [14] and the modified version with sparse altimetry priors.

Fig. 1: Overview of the sensing modality and an example bathymetry estimation task. We present example sidescan sonar (SSS) surveys of the D.M. Wilson shipwreck located in the Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary, together with reference bathymetry using a multibeam echosounder (MBES). Each sonar ping (highlighted by the green and red boxes) is associated with a sensor pose from the AUV. Following the SSS imaging geometry, we sample 3D points and directional vectors as inputs to the neural networks, which render SSS images and estimate the bathymetry.

Fig. 4: Process of bathymetry map generation. The bathymetry matrix is constructed by populating each grid with the height estimated from the neural implicit height representation evaluated at its corresponding geographic location. Grid coordinates of the bathymetry map are in one-to-one correspondence with geographic positions.

Fig. 2: Geometry of a single SSS ping. Under the SSS right-handed coordinate convention, the x-axis aligns with the direction of sensor motion and the y-axis points toward the starboard side. A 3D point P within the SSS field of view is represented by slant range r, azimuth angle θ, and elevation angle ϕ. The SSS emits acoustic signals to both the port (left) and starboard (right) sides, so the azimuth angle of an object is −π 2 or π 2 . rmin, rmax, ϕmin, and ϕmax are the minimum and maximum slant ranges and elevation angles of the SSS. For illustration, only five bins are shown on each side. Point P is projected onto the bin r3 on the starboard side.
Fig. 8: Survey trajectories and example SSS images of the D.M. Wilson and Montana datasets. Both datasets contain 8 survey legs following an OID pattern.

Fig. 6: Survey trajectories and example SSS images of the simulated Terrain and Submarine datasets. The Terrain dataset consists of 20 training survey legs and 1 northeast-oriented survey leg for validation. The Submarine dataset contains 8 survey legs following an OID pattern.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.
authors: Yuxing Liu, Wei Zuo, Walid Krichene, Tong Zhang, Li Zhang
bullets: Speculative decoding speed depends on how closely the draft distribution matches the target distribution.
Open-source draft models often identify the top token correctly but are systematically underconfident.
The paper evaluates post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration.
Standard temperature scaling improves acceptance length by up to approximately 10% across tasks with almost no added cost.
Broader calibration methods may provide further improvements, though their potential is not fully realized here.

papers.abstract: We present RenGen, a latent diffusion model that generates simple scenes from a few tokens and busy scenes from many, saving time and compute on simple scenes without losing realism. Most latent generators represent every image as a fixed grid of patch tokens, so a simple image costs as much to generate as a complex one. Prior methods that vary the token count through content-adaptive tokenization lose image quality as the count shrinks. RenGen instead trades scene complexity, rather than image quality, for fewer tokens. It does so by generating in the latent space of a pretrained region encoder, where each token represents one region of the image, and a decoder renders these region tokens back into pixels. Unlike patch tokens, region tokens cover areas of varying shape and position, so each token must capture both what its region contains and where it lies on the image canvas. We encode this spatial extent by adding positional embeddings to the encoder features before pooling, and we generate it by anchoring each token to a single randomly sampled point, from which the generator infers the region's shape, size, and content. At sampling time, the number of anchor points sets the trade-off between scene complexity and compute. On ImageNet $256{\times}256$, RenGen reaches a gFID of 1.34 with 88 tokens per image on average, the best among methods that vary their token count. It approaches the quality of RAEv2, a state-of-the-art patch-based model, at $2.5{\times}$ lower latency, advancing the Pareto frontier of generation quality versus compute. RenGen's gFID stays flat across scene complexity while latency varies by $2.4{\times}$ between simplest and busiest scenes, and its autoencoder reconstructs nearly as well as RAEv2 (rFID 0.32 vs. 0.30) with $2.9{\times}$ fewer tokens.
authors: Savya Khosla, Jay Mahajan, Akin Tuna Sakalli, Derek Hoiem, David Forsyth, Alex Schwing
bullets: Fixed-grid latent diffusion models spend similar compute on simple and busy images; prior adaptive tokenization can degrade quality.
RenGen represents images with variable-sized, spatially grounded region tokens from a pretrained region encoder.
The number of randomly sampled anchor points controls token count, scene complexity, and sampling latency.
On ImageNet 256×256, it achieves gFID 1.34 with 88 tokens on average and approaches RAEv2 quality at 2.5× lower latency.
Latency varies 2.4× by scene complexity, while gFID remains flat; reconstruction quality is close to RAEv2 with 2.9× fewer tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 2. RenGen overview. (a) The region encoder partitions an image into N regions with Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher (FH) segmentation and pools frozen DINOv3 patch features within each region into region tokens, which the decoder renders back into an image. (b) For generation, P random anchor points fix the region positions. A DiT denoises one region token per anchor point, using the anchor coordinates as 2D RoPE positions, and the shared decoder renders the generated tokens into an image.

Figure 6. RenGen sets a new quality–compute trade-off. Left: gFID versus total TFLOPs per image on ImageNet 256×256. RenGen lies below the Pareto frontier of prior methods (dashed). Right: The source of this gain. At matched model size, RenGen generates 2.9× fewer tokens than RAEv2, which translates directly into 2.6× fewer TFLOPs and 2.5× less wall-clock time per image.

Figure 7. RenGen reconstructs fine detail as faithfully as RAEv2 with far fewer tokens. Each tile shows its token count; RenGen’s follows image complexity, from 31 tokens for the hairpin on a plain background to 103 for the crowded scene.

Figure 1. RenGen’s generation cost follows image content. Top: Wall-clock time and TFLOPs per image for end-to-end generation at different token counts for RenGen. Green values give the speedup over RAEv2, which always uses a fixed grid of 256 patch tokens (dashed line). Bottom: 256×256 samples from a single RenGen model. Each row uses the same class label, and each column uses the token count of the point above it, so fewer tokens yield simpler scenes at lower cost.

Figure 3. Image complexity varies, but patch tokenizers spend the same budget on every image. Top: ImageNet images of increasing complexity, overlaid with the 16×16 patch grid of patchbased latent diffusion models and with their region partitions. The simplest of the four scenes has only 22 regions, while the busiest has 130. Bottom: Regions per image across ImageNet validation set. The mean of 88 is 2.9× fewer than the 256 tokens of a patch grid (dashed line).

Figure 5. RenGen adapts its compute to scene complexity without losing quality. gFID stays flat across four complexity buckets, so in low-resource settings RenGen can generate simple, realistic scenes 2.4× faster and with 2.5× less compute than complex ones. Samples of the same class (bottom; anchor points in white) grow busier as the token budget increases.

Figure 4. Constructing DiT targets. During training, we place P anchor points on the image canvas, partition the canvas into their Voronoi cells, compute each cell’s coverage mask on the patch grid, and encode the image with the region encoder to obtain one target region token per anchor.

Table 3. RenGen achieves the best rFID and gFID among methods that vary their token count. It also reconstructs and generates nearly as well as RAEv2 with 2.6× fewer TFLOPs and 2.5× less wall-clock time (Fig. 6). The checkmark columns indicate whether a method’s token count varies with image content (content adaptive), whether a user can choose the token budget of a single model at inference (controllable complexity), and whether its latents come from a frozen pretrained representation encoder (frozen enc.). §Included as the closest prior generator that adapts its compute to image content; it operates in pixel space, so reconstruction metrics do not apply.

Table 4. RenGen scales to higher resolutions more efficiently than RAEv2. At 512×512, RenGen reconstructs slightly better than RAEv2 while using about a third of the tokens and DiT compute. Because its token count depends on image content rather than resolution, RenGen can also encode the full 512×512 image into the same 88 tokens, improving reconstruction further at no extra cost. A single RenGen model handles both 256×256 and 512×512 inputs here.

Table 2. Randomly fixing region positions with anchor points enables strong generation at low cost. Without any spatial prior, the DiT trains poorly. Conditioning on real layouts separately leads to memorization and requires real images at sampling time, while generating layouts roughly doubles sampling time and still degrades quality. Random anchor points avoid both and outperform held-out real layouts with a single DiT. At sampling, the DiT receives only the points; the training regions determine how the targets are partitioned around them. Sampling time is measured per image at batch size 64 on one NVIDIA GH200.

Table 1. Adding positional embeddings to patch features before pooling them into region tokens gives the best reconstruction and generation. REN tokens reconstruct poorly because their regions overlap and their features encode little position. Fine-tuning REN makes the number of tokens grow during training (∗mean token count at the start→end of training). Pooling patch features within fixed FH regions keeps the token count stable, but the tokens still encode little position. Adding an explicit mask code to each token improves reconstruction but hurts generation, because the DiT must generate these codes precisely.

papers.selection_reason: Content-adaptive token count in latent diffusion reduces compute for simple scenes; relevant to token-level efficiency.
papers.title: RenGen: Generating Images with as Many Tokens as the Scene Needs
papers.tldr: RenGen adaptively uses more tokens for complex scenes and fewer for simple ones, reducing generation cost while preserving image quality.

papers.abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent
authors: Lingwei Gu, Jimmy Lin
bullets: Targets the high cost of frontier agents repeatedly processing context and handling every subtask.
Keeps the frontier model in charge while SLM subagents investigate code, run tests, or search corpora.
Unlike cascades and routers, it delegates subtasks rather than selecting one model for the entire task; no model training is required.
A 27B FP8 SLM reduces frontier cost by 67% for long-horizon coding and 59% for agentic search without performance loss.
A laptop-sized 2B SLM achieves a 66% coding-cost reduction; savings increase with delegated legwork.

papers.abstract: Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. We also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric combining event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity. Across all datasets, EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of SOTA methods and demonstrates robustness across different cameras at any resolution.
authors: Karthik Sundar Senthilkumar, Christopher Thirgood, Simon Hadfield
bullets: Sparse RGB frames cannot uniquely recover the intervening events’ activity, polarity, and timing.
Event Activity Diffusion models discrete event counts, Event Spatial Allocation assigns them to pixels, and Event Timing Diffusion predicts continuous timestamps.
CEFS evaluates realism using activity, polarity, multiscale space-time structure, and temporal fidelity.
The method reportedly achieves twice the accuracy of prior state-of-the-art methods and remains robust across cameras and resolutions.

papers.abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.
authors: Yufeng Huang
bullets: Addresses the loss of efficient full-dot-product integer MMA caused by groupwise quantization.
Reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits; SHI adapts the approach to INT4 kernels.
SQ and SHI improve projection error and KL divergence while increasing decoding and prefill speed over standard baselines.
Reported gains span 2–8-bit settings, including higher prefill throughput and lower KL divergence than the compared systems.
Scope is evaluated across tested models, prompt lengths, and precision levels; the abstract does not establish broader generalization beyond these settings.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.
authors: Yisrael Clark, Guy Katz
bullets: Addresses the risk that semantically incorrect LLM-to-FOL translations corrupt downstream reasoning.
Generates candidate readings with tools such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics.
Uses an SMT solver to test logical equivalence between candidate interpretations and the LLM’s formula.
Rejects or optionally repairs unfaithful translations, while abstaining when analysis or checking is inconclusive.
Evaluated on ProofWriter, RuleTaker, PrOntoQA, and the adversarial LongFaithCheck benchmark, achieving near-perfect selective accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Semantic verification of LLM text-to-logic translations, relevant to LLM reasoning reliability.
papers.title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
papers.tldr: FOL-Proof uses deterministic semantic analysis and SMT-based equivalence checks to verify or conservatively reject LLM-generated first-order logic translations.

papers.abstract: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.
authors: Shijin Gong, Kai Ye, Victor Chernozhukov, Xinyu Zhang, Chengchun Shi
bullets: GRPO group size is important but is typically chosen by trial and error.
The authors formulate group-size selection as estimating a variance ratio from GRPO’s U-statistic policy gradient.
A pessimistic ratio estimator handles instability when the denominator is small by accounting for estimation uncertainty.
A jackknife-based rule is evaluated on synthetic reasoning tasks plus math and code-generation benchmarks.
The method reduces policy-gradient mean squared error and improves optimization over fixed group sizes with modest extra computation.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a resource-efficient alternative to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when fine-tuning LLMs, thanks to the inherent low dimensionality of the loss landscape. It relies on a two-point estimate of the gradient that only accesses the function value and not the gradient, bypassing the resource-heavy backpropagation. Recently, it was accidentally discovered that per-sample clipping can improve the performance of the trained model, while running a differentially private version of zeroth-order optimization \cite{zhang2024dpzero} with a very large privacy parameter $\epsilon$ (corresponding to very little privacy). In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and demonstrate that ($i$) the optimal choice of learning rate $\eta$ is inversely proportional to the clipping threshold $c$, satisfying $\eta c =$ constant; ($ii$) clipping drives the zeroth-order optimization to a different solution with higher test accuracy; and ($iii$) this phenomenon is only observed with per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization and not other zeroth-order alternatives that also provide robust estimates of the gradient. Further analyses with artificially injected label noise reveals that clipping leads to more robust predictions, which stems from the implicit down weighting of hard-to-fit training examples. Our code is available at https://github.com/SewoongLab/ClipZero
authors: Saket Gollapudi, Elisa Bertino, Sewoong Oh
bullets: The optimal learning rate scales inversely with the clipping threshold, keeping ηc constant.
Clipping leads zeroth-order optimization toward a different solution with higher test accuracy.
The effect is specific to per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization, not other robust zeroth-order gradient estimators.
Under label noise, clipping produces more robust predictions by reducing the influence of difficult training examples.
The study focuses on explaining clipping behavior in zeroth-order fine-tuning of LLMs.

papers.abstract: Progress in embodied foundation models is largely measured by task success, while the physical safety of their decisions remains underexamined. Safety evaluations centered on rule following and binary judgments do not adequately assess whether embodied models understand environmental hazards and make safe decisions. We introduce EmbodiSafety, comprising 1,092 snapshot tasks and 540 trajectory tasks across 844 visual scenarios to assess safety over short and long horizons. Six response modes cover direct execution, refusal, clarification, constrained execution, autonomous recovery, and human escalation. Distinguishing recovery from human intervention makes the boundary of safe autonomy an explicit evaluation target. Our protocol assesses mode correctness, risk identification, and actionable handling, with complete decision accuracy requiring all applicable checks to pass. Claude-Opus-5.5 achieves the highest complete decision accuracy among reference models, reaching 56.1% on snapshots and 61.5% on trajectories. We further develop a data construction pipeline and curate 40k examples for safety alignment. Supervised training on this corpus raises the complete decision accuracy of Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B.

papers.abstract: Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.

papers.abstract: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.

papers.abstract: RGB-based video object segmentation (VOS) remains brittle under fast motion and adverse illumination. Event cameras preserve signal under blur and challenging exposure, but provide little evidence when motion slows. Interaction can restore object state for subsequent propagation, yet promptable event methods merely address single windows. We formalize event-based Promptable Video Segmentation (ePVS), where prompts at arbitrary windows initialize, correct, or introduce objects and predictions. We present Event Memory-As-Prompt Segmentation (E-MAPS), which transfers a pretrained promptable segmenter to event streams and learns propagation and correction. Event-to-Token (E2T) aligns recurrent event features with pretrained representations while preserving prompt-conditioning priors. Memory-Aware Prompting (MAP) converts object-conditioned history into sparse prompts, allowing memory and user inputs to share one decoder pathway efficiently. We construct Event-View Masklets (EViM) from 206K aligned RGB-event pairs and 620K masks for two-stage representation transfer and native event-video learning, and establish three training-disjoint benchmarks. E-MAPS leads prompt-once and interactive ePVS across all three benchmarks while being more efficient. It further demonstrates strong performance on zero-shot object tracking benchmarks. papers.abstract: Multi-frame video frame interpolation (VFI) aims to reconstruct dense video from sparse keyframes, requiring accurate intermediate motion and faithful appearance. As temporal gaps grow, flow-based methods can retain observed textures but misplace them under ambiguous motion, whereas iterative latent-diffusion models can synthesize plausible content but incur substantial sampling costs and may alter details during reconstruction with a variational autoencoder (VAE). We present RePix-VFI, named for Re-rendering observed Pixels, a multi-frame VFI framework that couples draft-conditioned one-step video diffusion with reconstruction from observed keyframes. A pretrained video diffusion model refines a flow-rendered draft of the whole window in a single forward pass. For each target frame, our generative readback matches its two bounding keyframes to the generated prediction using an optical-flow estimator. The resulting correspondences guide re-rendering of original keyframe RGB pixels outside the VAE. A lightweight appearance fusion head combines these renderings with generated appearance. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction and perceptual quality. On SNU-FILM at $\times$8 and $\times$16, RePix-VFI achieves the highest PSNR and the lowest LPIPS, FloLPIPS, and tOF among the compared methods, exceeding the best evaluated diffusion-based baseline by 1.71 and 1.48dB in PSNR, respectively. It also runs 32--42$\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art multi-frame VFI diffusion model.
authors: Dayeon Kim, Jeonghyeok Do, Munchurl Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving keyframe details while estimating ambiguous motion across large temporal gaps.
Refines a flow-rendered draft of the full video window with a pretrained one-step video diffusion model.
Matches generated frames to bounding keyframes via optical flow, then re-renders original RGB pixels outside the VAE.
Uses a lightweight fusion head to combine re-rendered keyframe appearance with generated content.

papers.abstract: Model-generated labels offer a scalable route to training lightweight vision models, but what makes a model a good teacher, and can we tell before training a student? We study this in gaze target estimation, where interactive robots need models that are both accurate and efficient. In a controlled comparison of eleven supervision conditions, we vary only the source of gaze-point labels, keeping the student, training protocol and 361k training samples fixed, across three video datasets, two student sizes and three seeds; every student is evaluated against human annotation. Three findings emerge. First, imperfect model-generated labels can replace human annotation: Gaze-LLE, never trained on the target datasets' gaze annotation, trains students that match annotation-trained ones on ViT-Tiny and are significantly more accurate on ViT-Small (average distance error 0.187 vs 0.196), and the ViT-Tiny student runs 32$\times$ faster than its teacher on a laptop CPU. Second, apparent competence can conceal unreliable supervision: given another person's face centre in the prompt, InternVL3 and Qwen3-VL return it on 93.4% and 81.1% of test samples, and a copy-the-coordinate baseline matches InternVL3's labels and students. Without that coordinate, both models fall far behind the specialist. Third, good teachers can be identified before training: validation label error ranks student test error (Spearman's $\rho = 0.91$), and ten annotated clips single out the two specialist teachers in 95% of draws. These findings give practical principles for assessing supervision, exposing shortcuts and selecting teachers for lightweight models.
authors: Scott J. Lewis, Di Fu
bullets: Imperfect model-generated gaze labels can replace human annotations: Gaze-LLE matches annotation-trained students on ViT-Tiny and improves accuracy on ViT-Small.
The ViT-Tiny student runs 32× faster than its Gaze-LLE teacher on a laptop CPU.
Vision-language models may appear competent because they copy face-center coordinates; removing this shortcut causes their performance to fall substantially.
Teacher quality can be screened before student training: validation label error strongly predicts student test error (Spearman’s ρ = 0.91).
Just ten annotated clips identify the two specialist teachers in 95% of sampling trials.

papers.abstract: Scaling embodied simulation requires diverse objects with executable physical representations. We present RFW-W, a physical asset universe connecting rigid, articulated, and deformable asset sources to task-conditioned scene composition. Its reported inventories comprise 1,010,386 asset records: 524,611 rigid assets in 1,212 categories (RFW-R), 402,410 articulated assets in 531 categories (RFW-A), and 83,365 jointly verified deformables in 485 categories (RFW-S). These taxonomies contribute 2,228 dataset--category entries. RFW-R couples category-guided generation with collision geometry, composed physical properties, and interaction annotations; RFW-A uses reusable agent-authored procedural generators with explicit part and joint structure; RFW-S uses structure-aware simulation representations, calibration, and independent testing. A common interface preserves physical requirements specific to each asset type for retrieval and scene assembly. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that RFW-R provides broader asset coverage and stronger scene-fulfillment capabilities than existing datasets. Across five RoboTwin tasks, using 100 demonstrations per task for each asset source, policies trained on RFW-R achieve macro success rates of 71.2% in clean settings and 41.8% under randomization, exceeding the strongest baseline by 15.8 and 10.6 percentage points, respectively. RFW-W provides a scalable and unified asset foundation for generating physically grounded, task-conditioned embodied worlds.

papers.abstract: Physics-based soccer characters must perform diverse motor skills and transition smoothly between them, such as dribbling into a shot. However, skills that perform well in isolation may fail when executed sequentially, as preceding behaviors can leave the character and ball in unfamiliar states. We present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework that enables multiple soccer skill transitions through shared adaptation while preserving the original skill policy outside transitions. MESSI first trains eight task-competent experts using motion priors and task rewards, then distills them into a unified, skill-conditioned Transformer. Rather than retraining individual experts for different transitions, we train a shared, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student through online reinforcement learning. Activated upon skill switching, the adapter helps the target skill handle unfamiliar entry states, while a learned exit mechanism determines when to return control to the original student. By disabling the adapter during native skill execution, MESSI preserves the original student policy by construction. Experiments across individual skills, skill transitions, and continuous skill chains demonstrate substantial improvements over direct switching, including an increase in dribbling-to-shooting success from 19.8% to 61.8%.

papers.abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $\pi_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.

Matched non-reflective panels show that collisions alone do not explain failures: 50–88% of mirror-specific failures involve no recorded robot–panel contact.
Analyses indicate phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real objects, with additional diagnostics for grasping, pushing, and occlusion.
Real-robot tests with π₀.₅ and FastWAM also show reduced success, motivating reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence.
