papers.abstract: Recent advances in low-precision representation have introduced several microscaling numerical formats for LLM quantization. By sharing a scale factor across groups of 16 or 32 elements, these formats enable aggressive low-precision quantization with minimal accuracy degradation, particularly when combined with modern PTQ algorithms. Their accuracy depends on how the numerical format interacts with rotation, PTQ, and scale selection. We study the composability of PTQ configurations across six LLMs and three microscaling formats: MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4, systematically varying Hadamard rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale-selection strategy. Our central finding is that effective quantization recipes are format dependent: both MXFP4 and NVFP4 support accurate 4-bit inference, but techniques that benefit one do not necessarily transfer to the other. MXFP4 benefits substantially from rotation and error-correcting PTQ, whereas NVFP4 gains less from rotation, consistent with its finer-grained scales capturing more within-block variation. Building on these findings, we introduce Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection strategy that mitigates clipping error in power-of-two block scales and improves accuracy across a majority of the evaluated MXFP4 configurations. We show that pairing MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most of the accuracy lost at 4-bit and, on Llama-3.1-8B, matches or exceeds our in-house BF16 baseline. An additional study finds that augmenting MXFP4 with a per-tensor macroscale, a mechanism intrinsic to NVFP4, does not improve average accuracy, suggesting that global rescaling alone does not address the limitations of E8M0 block scales for MXFP4 quantization. Together, these results provide practical guidance for combining numerical formats, rotation, PTQ, and scale selection for accurate low-precision LLM inference.
authors: Natalia Frumkin, Alireza Khodamoradi, Kristof Denolf, Eric Dellinger, Stuart Biles
bullets: The study evaluates MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4 across six LLMs while varying rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale selection.
MXFP4 benefits substantially from Hadamard rotation and error-correcting PTQ, while NVFP4 benefits less from rotation due to finer-grained scaling.
Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection method, reduces clipping from power-of-two block scales and improves most tested MXFP4 configurations.
Using MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most 4-bit accuracy loss and matches or exceeds an in-house BF16 baseline on Llama-3.1-8B.
Adding a per-tensor macroscale does not improve average MXFP4 accuracy, indicating global rescaling does not resolve block-scale limitations.

papers.abstract: Training Transformers requires careful hyperparameter tuning, which becomes increasingly costly for large models. We introduce UDV-Rebalance (UDVR), a reparameterization that inserts an auxiliary diagonal matrix $D$ between naturally paired weight matrices $(U,V)$ appearing throughout Transformer architectures. UDVR periodically rebalances the factors to maintain unit-norm columns in $U$ and unit-norm rows in $V$, with $D$ absorbing the corresponding scales. With rebalancing, a single hyperparameter setting of UDVR remains effective across model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This yields a tuning-free rule that adapts to each weight matrix using only its dimensions. We fit this rule once on ViT models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and it remains valid when the activation function or the optimizer is changed. The same rule transfers to new image domains in DomainNet, to ViT, Swin, and MaxViT on ImageNet, and to language-model pretraining with up to 1.3B parameters. UDVR consistently outperforms Weight Normalization and $\sigma$Reparam and matches a vanilla baseline whose hyperparameters are swept on each target model.
authors: Yikun Hou, Naomi Graham, Alp Yurtsever
bullets: Introduces UDVR, which inserts a diagonal scale matrix between paired weight matrices and periodically rebalances their factor norms.
Uses matrix dimensions to set a single transferable hyperparameter rule, reducing per-model tuning.
A rule fit on CIFAR-trained ViTs transfers to new image domains, multiple vision architectures, and language models up to 1.3B parameters.
Outperforms Weight Normalization and σReparam, while matching a vanilla baseline with target-specific hyperparameter sweeps.

papers.abstract: Satellite-based 3D reconstruction is limited by sparse observations and changes across acquisition dates. Existing methods use generative priors to recover missing visual detail, but ghosting, streaking, and blur persist in their Gaussian scenes. These artifacts become particularly apparent in low-elevation renderings. We introduce CityRecast to suppress these artifacts through Gaussian scene repair and supervision calibration. To correct the Gaussian distributions that produce these artifacts, we first use multi-angle warm-up to constrain their spatial extent. This reduces the initial ghosting carried into progressive refinement. Surface-guided replacement then continues to repair the Gaussian distribution while preserving existing appearance. To provide more reliable supervision for this process, observation calibration mitigates interference from multi-temporal observations. Joint refinement further reduces conflicts among generated views. Experiments on DFC2019 and IARPA demonstrate reduced artifacts in low-elevation renderings while maintaining satellite-view fidelity. Compared with Skyfall-GS, CityRecast reduces FID-CLIP by 25.3% on DFC2019 and 51.8% on IARPA. MUSIQ increases by 14.54 and 24.95 points, respectively.
authors: Shuo Cui, Yingyan Hou, Wanxuan Lu, Hongfeng Yu, Daobing Zhang, Xian Sun
bullets: Addresses artifacts caused by sparse observations and changes across acquisition dates.
Uses multi-angle warm-up to constrain problematic Gaussian spatial extents before refinement.
Applies surface-guided replacement and joint refinement to repair Gaussians while preserving appearance and reducing view conflicts.
Observation calibration mitigates interference from multi-temporal observations during supervision.
On DFC2019 and IARPA, it improves low-elevation rendering quality while maintaining satellite-view fidelity, outperforming Skyfall-GS on reported FID-CLIP and MUSIQ metrics.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models make different trade-offs between prediction accuracy and latency. We study whether a compact ensemble can deliver higher accuracy in less time. Across 816 TabArena splits, our blend of four-estimator Kumo and one LimiX pipeline reaches 2063.8 Elo, 45.4 points above the top published entry in the same fit. Its normalized fit + predict time is 15% lower than Kumo-16's and 98% lower than full LimiX's. We find that greater prediction diversity between the two models helps explain the reduction in error.
authors: Jing Jia, Guanyang Wang
bullets: Targets the accuracy–latency trade-off of tabular foundation models.
Blends four-estimator Kumo with one LimiX pipeline.
Achieves 2063.8 Elo, 45.4 points above the top published entry in the same fit.
Uses 15% less normalized fit-plus-predict time than Kumo-16 and 98% less than full LimiX.
Greater prediction diversity between the models appears to explain the error reduction.

papers.abstract: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.
authors: Maximilian Xiling Li, Nils Blank, Paul Mattes, Pankhuri Vanjani, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Discrete skill policies can fail because of their vocabulary, selector, or execution, but joint training makes these causes hard to separate.
MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with a nearest demonstrated motion, then boundedly corrects it toward the prediction without training new parameters.
Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped reference policy is statistically equivalent to the original.
On LIBERO-90, quantization has no measurable cost and skill choice costs at most 2 points; selector placement and correction explain nearly all remaining gaps, up to 12 points.
Offline reconstruction fails to predict these effects or reliably assess library size, design, and transfer across benchmark suites.

The chunk Cπ of a frozen policy is matched to its nearest movement prototype Pz , placed in the chunk’s frame and corrected toward Cπ within the deviation bound (Eq. 5). Blue: demonstrated. Red: predicted. Black: executed. (c) Decomposition. A reference policy executed through the library (SRref , dashed) sets the baseline. Substituting a selector’s choice, then its placement and correction, splits the selector’s shortfall into selection and execution (LIBERO-90, Table 3).

papers.abstract: We present DOPER, an RGB pose estimation framework that shares a visual backbone across object detection, segmentation, and keypoint prediction to recover the 6D pose of known objects through Perspective-n-Point. Starting from synthetic training, DOPER adapts to real observations using partial supervision while retaining synthetic keypoint labels. Calibrated multi-view observations provide geometric constraints for keypoint supervision. During inference, optional heatmap refinement fits a rigid pose directly to the predicted keypoint distributions, resolving ambiguous correspondences without depth input or a learned pose refiner. Starting from underspecified CAD models, DOPER progressively refines the object representation and pose estimator. Results on SPEED+ and SHIRT further demonstrate effective adaptation to illumination changes and accurate temporal pose estimation. Across the evaluated single-view and multi-view configurations, DOPER achieves state-of-the-art detection AP results on HANDAL, HOPEv2, HOT3D, and T-LESS while using only RGB and running in real time (35 Hz per object model on one GB300). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of jointly learning detection and pose keypoints, with real observations and geometric constraints.

bullets: Addresses 6D pose estimation for known objects using only RGB, without depth or a learned pose refiner.

papers.abstract: Recovering editable computer-aided design (CAD) models from underwater stereo images requires accurate and complete geometry, yet stereo reconstruction produces displaced points and missing regions. The original views retain cross-view disagreement and ray evidence lost during point-cloud fusion. Aqua2CAD exploits this evidence in two stages: view-conditioned correction and quality filtering establish reliable geometric support, while multi-view observations condition a learned shape prior to infer missing surfaces in the original metric frame. The recovered points support surface fitting and solid assembly with manually revised face groups. On an OceanSim-based synthetic benchmark, Aqua2CAD reduces point-cloud Chamfer distance by 60% relative to the stereo reconstruction. Compared with a matched point-only completion backbone, it improves missing-region recovery at 5,mm from 16.27% to 24.16%. With a shared CAD backend, exterior acceptance increases from 6/19 to 14/19. Qualitative results on selected real underwater captures demonstrate recovery of the main structures of six 3D-printed objects.

papers.abstract: Independently pretrained vision and language models may learn shared structures of the same underlying world, providing a foundation for combining them to build multimodal capabilities. However, a key challenge remains in aligning cross-modal feature representations while preserving access to visual information before and after language adaptation. To this end, we propose sparse alignment with visual evidence-guided residual adaptation (SAVERA), a framework that combines frozen vision and language models through bidirectional alignment in a shared sparse space and prompt-guided residual fusion. Specifically, we first present shared-space projection, activation reconstruction and encoding (SPARE), which represents original visual, adapted visual, and textual features through shared soft-gated sparse encoding, with branch-specific reconstruction to preserve their respective information. Second, we devise bridge--text embedding and activation matching (BEAM), a bidirectional cross-modal alignment module that aligns adapted visual and textual features at both the sample and neuron levels, establishing fine-grained cross-modal correspondence. Finally, we introduce prompt-conditioned residual integration of vision and adapted features (PRIVA), a prompt-guided residual fusion module that models vision--language interactions through gating and attention and integrates complementary information from original and adapted representations through residual fusion. Extensive experiments show that SAVERA achieves competitive performance on image captioning and visual question answering while reducing object hallucination.

papers.title: SAVERA: Bridging Frozen Vision and Language Models via Sparse Alignment and Visual Evidence Reuse
papers.tldr: SAVERA connects frozen vision and language models using sparse bidirectional alignment and prompt-guided visual residual fusion, improving multimodal performance while reducing object hallucination.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.
authors: Sezgin Er, Utku Turkbey, Alperen Gur, Omer Faruk Durugol, Suprosanna Shit, Murong Xu, Julia Wolleb, Jiayi Wang, Xiaoliang Wang, Hadrien Reynaud, Teodora Spasojevic, Dong Yang, Andriy Myronenko, Pengfei Guo, Yufan He, Can Zhao, Marc Edgar, Andreas Maier, Michael Moor, Mehmet Kemal Ozdemir, Daguang Xu, Bernhard Kainz, Bjoern Menze, Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci
bullets: Addresses the limited anatomical and abnormality coverage of existing CT AI systems.
Recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts across 28 CT protocols.
Uses multiple-instance learning and an interpretable concept bottleneck linking spatial evidence, findings, and report generation.
Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations without manually annotated lesions.
Achieved strong concept recognition, localization, benchmark, and report-generation performance on held-out and independent evaluations.

figures.caption: Figure 1 FORA links CT findings to spatial evidence and report text. a, Model overview. CT images are encoded across available clinical intensity windows (Hounsfield-unit ranges that display specific tissues, such as lung, soft tissue or bone), and concept-specific attention identifies findings and their locations to guide report generation. b, Example CT examination showing spatial evidence for multiple findings. c, Image regions supporting selected findings, paired with the corresponding generated report sentences.

Figure 2 CT finding recognition and localization. a, FORA and 18 comparison models on held-out CT examinations. b, AUPRC versus the strongest alternative across 2,132 finding-CT-type pairs. c, Public benchmarks; NV-ReasonCT’s CT-RATE AUROC is from its preprint. d, Performance across 12 CT types. e, AUROC advantage over the strongest alternative by CT type. f, Localization on four datasets; hollow points indicate chance. Error bars, 95% confidence intervals. Significance from two-sided paired tests with Holm correction is marked ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01 and ∗∗∗P < 0.001.

Figure 3 Grounded CT report generation. a, Reference and FORA reports for a validation chest CT with matched statements numbered, and FORA’s evidence. Dots mark the reference findings that each model’s report recovered, with column numbers matching the statements. b, Finding-level metrics and LLM-judge score of FORA and seven other report generators on the FORA validation set. c, The 12 most frequent report protocols. d, Performance by number of reference findings per report. e, FORA validation set, CT-RATE and Merlin. Error bars, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Stars, two-sided paired tests with Holm correction (∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001).

Figure 4 FORA cohort and report-derived supervision across 341,581 CT examinations from 238,469 patients. a, Examination counts by CT type. b, Finding co-occurrence network. c, Scanner manufacturers and models. d-f, Slice spacing, positive labels per examination and model-input extent by CT type. g, Patient age. h, Report length by CT type. i, Label frequencies across the 1,459 concepts in the finding hierarchy. j, Asserted, uncertain and denied labels per report. k,l, Tube voltage and volume CT dose index (CTDIvol).

Figure 5 FORA learns finding recognition, spatial localization and report generation from routine CT examinations and reports. a, Self-supervised teacher–student distillation across clinical intensity windows. b, Contrastive alignment of CT features with report sentences. c, Concept-specific attention learns finding recognition and spatial evidence from report-derived labels. d, Concept-guided report generation trained through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces FORA, a general-purpose CT model that performs spatially grounded reporting and localization of radiological concepts, combining 3D perception with multimodal generation.
papers.title: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA
papers.tldr: FORA is a general-purpose CT model that recognizes, localizes, and reports a broad range of radiological findings across multiple examination types using only routine report supervision.

papers.abstract: Video generative models synthesize realistic scenes, yet their interactions often violate physics. A ball dropped onto sand should displace grains and settle into a crater, whereas a generated video may show it passing through the surface or leaving the sand flat. Post-hoc methods typically score generated videos with a vision-language model (VLM), but such scores offer limited guidance on which object or parameter to modify, and each correction costs another synthesis. Simulation-based pipelines instead run fixed stages before synthesis, so simulation errors reach the video. To address these limitations, we present PhysMend, a training-free framework for verification-guided program refinement. PhysMend describes the target event as an editable physical program of grounded objects, events, and required relations, paired with tunable execution parameters. Our key insight is to verify and repair the event on its simulated rollout and on the depth video that conditions the generator (depth control) rather than on generated videos, enabling quantitative violation measurement, targeted editing, and fast re-verification before synthesis. A hybrid verifier evaluates semantic event consistency, physical plausibility, solver stability, and visibility in the depth control. VLM judgments are confined to event semantics and cannot override failed physical measurements, which limits the impact of VLM hallucinations. Each failed check localizes the program fields eligible for repair, and its measured violation scales a bounded update of their parameters. Only accepted depth control reaches the generator, which runs once per input. Experiments on the commonly used benchmarks Physics-IQ, PhyGenBench, and VBench-2.0 demonstrate substantial gains across different generator backbones; for example, PhysMend raises the overall Physics-IQ score of Wan-VACE from 27.33 to 39.40.
authors: Meilong Xu, Ziyi Zhao, Bhagyashree Puranik, Shayda Moezzi, Yixiao Zhang, Kushan Thakkar
bullets: Targets physics violations in generated video interactions, such as objects passing through surfaces or failing to deform them.
Represents events as grounded objects, relations, execution parameters, and editable program fields.
Uses hybrid checks for semantic consistency, physical plausibility, solver stability, and depth-control visibility.
Localizes failed checks and applies bounded, violation-scaled parameter updates; only accepted depth control is synthesized.
Improves Physics-IQ for Wan-VACE from 27.33 to 39.40 and gains across Physics-IQ, PhyGenBench, and VBench-2.0.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PhysMend. Masks, depth, and the VLM turn the input into an editable physical program Π, compiled with parameters θ and executed in Genesis [3]. For the ball released onto sand, Π lists the grabber, ball, sand, and table, and it chains release, fall, and collision, where the collision must contact and deform the sand. Its parameters θ include the release time, initial motion, and sand material. Inside the shaded loop, checks examine the rollout and its depth control. Accepted depth control conditions a frozen generator once, whereas a failed check’s record Rj routes the loop (dashed) to replan Π or repair θ. Frame indices are local to each sequence.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparisons on Physics-IQ. We compare PhysMend with VLIPP [67], NEWTON [13], and VideoCoCo [33] on four cases. The cases are (a) silk covering a teapot, (b) a plastic domino rotating past a magnet, (c) a paper towel released onto liquid, and (d) a knife cutting a tangerine. Each panel shows the input image, an expanded-prompt excerpt, and five chronological frames per method. Ellipses indicate omitted prompt text. PhysMend occupies the first row. Frames keep their original aspect ratios.

Figure 6. Generation calls, time, and Physics-IQ score of PhysMend (blue) and NEWTON [13] (hatched). (a) Mean time per sample on the full Physics-IQ benchmark. For PhysMend, it is the recorded pipeline time with inference on a single 80 GB H100 GPU; for NEWTON, it is a generation-only estimate, 3.4 calls times the measured time of one generation call. (b) Mean RGB generation calls per sample over the full Physics-IQ benchmark, including NEWTON’s regenerations. (c) Overall Physics-IQ score on the full benchmark.

Figure 3. Quantified verification and repair on one representative example from Physics-IQ [43]. Each rollout is simulated, and the VLM and the physical measurements check every event. At k = 0, the simulation is numerically unstable, so no other check is evaluated, and parameter repair raises the solver substeps. At k = 1, the program treats the hanging block as a static fixture. The VLM and the physical measurements fail on the block’s events, and replanning makes the block a moving object. At k = 2, every check passes, and the frozen generator runs once.

Figure 5. From check record to bounded repair. A failed check reports its decision, residual, evidence, affected objects, checked interval, and editable fields. Measured violations scale bounded edits of the reported parameters, structural errors trigger replanning, and construction failures return to their stage. Every revision is re-executed against all required checks and is accepted, retained as a new starting point, or rolled back.

Table 2. PhyGenBench results. T2V and I2V denote input protocols. NEWTON [13] uses a trained planner; VideoCoCo [33] uses a LoRA-tuned editor [21]. Parentheses give each method’s generator backbone. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values in each column; ties share a color.

Table 1. Physics-IQ results. Components and domain scores use the Original protocol. The Verified column gives the overall score on Physics-IQ Verified [50]. Domain headers give scenario counts, with three views each; Therm. and Mag. denote thermodynamics and magnetism. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values; ties share a color. Each backbone is followed by PhysMend with that backbone. OmniWeaving uses I2V for the baseline and tiv2v with PhysMend.
Table 5. Recorded program of the ball-in-sand example. Identifiers and required checks are listed as recorded.

Table 4. Ablations on Physics-IQ. Original scores with WanVACE [26, 57] and a fixed rollout budget. The first row is WanVACE alone, with the expanded prompt p̃ and no depth control. The first three failure-handling variants return simulated depth even if no rollout passes. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values per group.

Table 3. VBench-2.0 physics results. Mech., Therm., and Mat. denote Mechanics, Thermotics, and Material. Scores are percentages; AVG is their unweighted mean. Higher is better. Red and blue mark the best and second-best scores.
Table 6. Physical type to Genesis [3] representation.
Table 7. System components on Physics-IQ. All variants use frozen Wan-VACE [26, 57] and the Original score. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values.

Table 11. Motion guidance for Seedance 2.5. All rows use the same ten-scene Physics-IQ subset. I2V uses the switch frame and prompt; R2V adds a motion video. Scores are on the percentage scale, and gains are percentage points relative to I2V. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values.
Table 9. Repair and routing by domain on Physics-IQ. The first three variants always use simulation; full routing permits the fallback. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values.

Table 8. Verification evidence by domain on Physics-IQ. Original scores with frozen Wan-VACE [26, 57] and the same rollout budget. The hybrid combines VLM judgments with physical measurements. Red and blue mark the best and second-best values.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free verification-guided refinement for physics-aware video generation; directly relevant to video generation.
papers.title: PhysMend: Verification-Guided Program Refinement for Physics-Aware Video Generation
papers.tldr: PhysMend refines editable physical programs through simulation and depth-control verification before video synthesis, producing more physically consistent videos with only one generator run.

papers.abstract: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.
authors: NaHyeon Park, Kyeong-Hwan Moon, Youjin Jeon, Hyunjung Shim
bullets: Streaming models exhibit context inertia: previous video chunks can overpower newly changed prompts.
Discarding or editing cached context risks breaking visual continuity, even when only the previous chunk is retained.
RG measures a cache-free residual by denoising the re-noised previous chunk under the new prompt, then applies it early in generation of the next chunk.
The training-free method improves prompt switching across single- and multi-switch settings while largely preserving visual quality.
It adds one forward pass per chunk and requires no per-model tuning, enabling integration into existing pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Qualitative results on multi-event generation. In each example, the top row is the base model and the bottom row is the same model with RG. Dashed lines mark prompt switches. (a) Three-event stories (10 s). The base models remain in the first event throughout, whereas RG advances to each event as it is prompted. (b) A 60 s interactive sequence with six prompts. RG follows each instruction in turn, including the appearance and interaction of a new subject.

Figure 4. Qualitative results on T2V-CompBench. The white-to-black bar marks the prompt switch. Without RG, the video keeps the initial state after the switch, whereas RG enables the new state to appear while the subject and scene layout remain consistent. SF: Self Forcing, CF: Causal Forcing, MF: MemFlow, IR: Infinity-RoPE, LL: LongLive, AF: Anchor Forcing.
Figure 12. Qualitative results on StoryEval. Each example shows a base model (top) and the same model with RG (bottom) over three events. The white-to-black bars mark the two prompt switches.

Figure 10. Frames of the switch chunk. LongLive (top) and Anchor Forcing (bottom). In each example, the first row is the base model, which continues the previous state. The second row empties the cache at the switch, as in the no-context condition of Sec. 3, and follows the new prompt but loses the scene in the switch chunk. The third row is RG, which realizes the new state within the switch chunk while preserving the subject and background.
Figure 11. Qualitative results on T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute. Each example shows a base model (top) and the same model with RG (bottom). The white-to-black bar marks the prompt switch.

Figure 7. Context inertia by category. Fraction of pairs that switch to the new prompt when the switch chunk is regenerated with part of the cache hidden, on Self Forcing (left) and LongLive (right). Naive denotes the base model. The number of pairs per category is in parentheses. Hiding the whole context recovers most switches, whereas a single cached chunk or the sink alone recovers little.

Figure 13. Qualitative results on InteractiveBench. Each example shows a base model (top) and the same model with RG (bottom) over six prompts in 60 s, one frame per prompt. The white-to-black bars mark the five prompt switches.

Figure 9. VBench Quality penalizes the requested change. In each example, the top row is the base model and the bottom row is RG, and the dashed bar marks the prompt switch. The examples are from LongLive (top), Causal Forcing (middle) and Infinity-RoPE (bottom). The gray numbers give the VBench dimension scores of the base model and of RG. RG follows the new prompt while the base model keeps the old state, yet RG scores lower on aesthetic quality, subject consistency and imaging quality, respectively.

Figure 21. Failure cases. In each example, the top row is the base model and the bottom row is RG. The first frame is the last frame before the switch, and the dashed bar marks the prompt switch. Left: insufficient prompt response. The requested removal of an object (LongLive), change of illumination (SWIFT) or change of pose (MemFlow, InteractiveBench) is not realized. Right: unintended changes. The switch is realized, but a spoon and a hand appear (Anchor Forcing), the glass acquires a handle (Self Forcing), or the cup itself turns into a planet (Anchor Forcing, StoryEval).

Figure 17. Classifier-free guidance on the switch chunk. Applying CFG on (a) Self Forcing and (b) LongLive. Naive denotes the base model. For both models, CFG partially enables the switch but causes artifacts while Residual guidance realizes the switch without artifacts.

Figure 2. Prompt switching under context inertia. (a) Outcomes of 100 prompt switches, most of which are never realized. (b) Relative prompt response ρ under different visible contexts. Even a single cached chunk suppresses it. (c) Chunks generated under each context (columns) for the same switch. The white bear persists with the full or previous-chunk context, partially darkens with the oldest chunk only, and turns black without context at the cost of identity and background.

Figure 6. Noise level and step schedule. Top: noise level τ with our schedule λ = (1, 0.5, 0, 0). Bottom: residual added in full (λi = 1) at the listed steps, with τ = 850. The frame before the switch (yellow neon sign) is shown on the top.

Figure 8. Step-wise prompt sensitivity under visible context. At each denoising step i of the switch chunk, the noisy input is fixed and the prompt sensitivity Si(C) is measured under each visible context C on 100 pairs (log scale, shaded bands show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals). Numbers next to the step-1 points give ρ1, the values of Fig. 2b. “Oldest chunk only” keeps only the oldest chunk still cached, which is chunk 1 for Self Forcing, whose rolling window has dropped chunk 0, and the sink (chunk 0) for LongLive.

Figure 14. On the choice of noise level τ . Achievement (left) and imaging quality relative to the base model (right) on 100 pairs. Dashed lines mark the base models. Achievement rises with τ throughout, whereas imaging quality holds up to τ = 850 (circled) and drops sharply beyond, which is where the restored chunk no longer preserves the subject (Fig. 6).

Figure 15. Qualitative results on T2V-CompBench action binding. The white-to-black bar marks the prompt switch, at which a second subject is added to the prompt. Without RG the video keeps the initial scene, whereas with RG the new subject appears within the first chunks after the switch while the original subject and background are preserved.

Figure 18. Alternatives to residual guidance. Achievement, Quality and scene change (object-masked DreamSim) across the switch for the base model, residual guidance (shaded) and alternatives that weaken the context, strengthen the prompt, change the erase strength, or use the cache-free reconstruction in other ways (prompt-difference (B−A) residual, direct reconstruction, samechunk correction, pure substitution, redraw initialization), on 100 dynamic attribute pairs with Self Forcing (circles) and LongLive (squares). Vertical lines mark residual guidance. Scene change was not measured for the variants without a marker in the right panel. Naive denotes the base model.

Figure 19. Qualitative comparison of the alternatives. For each switch, the top row shows a frame before the switch and the bottom row a frame from the last chunk after it, on Self Forcing (top) and LongLive (bottom). Only RG shows the new prompt while keeping the scene. Removing the context or reconstructing the chunk directly redraws the whole scene, previous chunk only changes the scene or the wrong attribute, cross-attention scaling and same-chunk correction add artifacts, and cache logit, CFG and redraw initialization keep the old state. See Fig. 18 for the quantitative comparison.

Figure 20. Scene cuts on Infinity-RoPE. Each panel shows three consecutive prompts that keep the subject and replace the scene. The top row is Infinity-RoPE and the bottom row is Infinity-RoPE with RG, generated from the same seed. Dashed lines mark the prompt switches. Infinity-RoPE often remains in the first scene or partially updates the scene, whereas RG moves to each new scene at the switch while retaining the subject.

Figure 16. Qualitative results on Rolling Forcing. T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute. In each example, the top row is Rolling Forcing and the bottom row is Rolling Forcing with RG. The white-to-black bar marks the prompt switch.

Table 2. Multi-prompt and longer settings. StoryEval: 100 three-event prompts over 10 s with switches. InteractiveBench: 100 scripts of six 10 s prompts over 60 s, following MemFlow [22] and LongLive [56]. Rows marked + RG apply residual guidance to the model above.
Table 5. VBench dimensions on T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute. Each cell gives the base model → the same model with residual guidance, computed on the post-switch segment as in Tab. 1.

Table 3. Alternatives to residual guidance. Evaluated on 100 random dynamic attribute pairs with Self Forcing and LongLive. Unint.: unintended change, measured as the DreamSim [12] distance across the switch with the changed object masked out.

Table 7. VBench-Long dimensions on InteractiveBench. Computed on the full 60 s video (100 videos). Quality is the VBench score over all seven dimensions. Temporal flickering, motion smoothness and aesthetic quality change by less than 0.005 on every model and are omitted.
Table 4. Prompt pairs of the context inertia set. Examples of one pair per category.
Table 11. Residual guidance on Rolling Forcing. 100 random prompt pairs of T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute. Metrics follow Tab. 1.

Table 13. Comparison with existing guidance-based methods. Classifier-free guidance (CFG), History guidance (HG) and the guidance of MAGI-1 contrast predictions of the same noisy sample at every step. Our Residual guidance (RG) contrasts a context-free prediction against the previous clean chunk, once per chunk, and needs no unconditional branch or training.

Table 9. Ablations. 100 random pairs from the T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute set on Self Forcing (SF) and LongLive (LL). Default: τ = 850, λ = (1, 0.5, 0, 0), and one ϵ shared within the prompt interval. (a) Noise level τ . (b) Step schedule λ. (c) Noise sharing.
Table 12. 240 s generation on LongLive. CLIP and VBench quality per minute for LongLive with and without residual guidance, averaged over 50 scripts.

Table 6. Scene preservation on T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute. Distance between the last pre-switch frame and the postswitch frames over all 200 prompt pairs, at the switch chunk (Switch) and averaged over the four post-switch chunks (Mean). Lower is closer to the pre-switch scene. Structure is the DINO self-similarity distance [50] on the whole frame. DreamSim [12] is computed with the changed object masked out (OWLv2 [37] and SAM [25]). The reference rows report the same distances between a pre-switch frame and a transformed copy of it, on the whole frame. Reference values do not depend on the chunk and span both columns.

Table 14. The context shrinks the classifier-free direction. ∥x̂(C, ynew)− x̂(C, y∅)∥/∥sk−1∥ at the first denoising step of the switch chunk, without context (C = ∅) and with the full context, on the 100 switch pairs of Sec. 3 (mean, 95% bootstrap CI). LongLive is measured after re-caching.
Table 8. Throughput and responsiveness. Measured at batch size 1 with 5 s videos and one switch. RG adds one forward pass per chunk, reducing throughput by around 6%.

Table 10. Prompt switching on T2V-CompBench action binding. These prompts involve adding a second subject at the switch. Metrics follow Tab. 1, with the official action binding score of T2V-CompBench (normalized to [0, 1]) in place of the dynamic attribute score.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the problem of context inertia in real-time interactive video generation by proposing Residual Guidance, a training-free method to improve prompt switching.
papers.title: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation
papers.tldr: Residual Guidance improves prompt switching in real-time streaming video generation without training or modifying the model cache.

papers.abstract: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.
authors: Yu Chen, Haosen Yang, Su Ee Tan, Zhensong Zhang, Jifei Song, Jiankang Deng
bullets: Existing results are difficult to compare because papers use different sampling, resolutions, test splits, and alignment procedures.
The arena evaluates five tasks—including monocular depth, 3D/4D reconstruction, and SLAM—on 23 public datasets plus new captures spanning indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes.
Its deterministic alignment and common metrics address evaluation failures that can substantially distort reported errors.
Across 52 models, single-image depth is near saturation on public benchmarks but remains challenging in large, uncontrolled scenes.
Progress increasingly depends on cross-frame and cross-view consistency: feed-forward 3D/4D models match or exceed monocular specialists and outperform video depth models.

(a) VideoDepth AbsRel of the Spatial Arena pixels in bins of ground-truth depth (every fourth frame of all 15 clips, with each model’s sequence alignment). (b) Mean VideoDepth AbsRel on the six front-camera and nine side-camera Spatial Arena clips, for the 15 models without auxiliary inputs that cover all clips. (c) SfM AUC@5◦ on the seven Spatial Arena scenes, computed separately for image pairs from two front images, from a front and a side image, from the same side camera, and from different side cameras. (d) Drift of every model on every short-range SLAM sequence (7-Scenes, TUM RGB-D, Oxford Spires, and Spatial Arena) against the ground-truth path length per input frame. (e) Drift on every long-range sequence (7-Scenes, TUM RGB-D, and the two Spatial Arena walks, shaded) against the path length. (f) Drift of four long-sequence systems on every large-range sequence against the path length; open markers are Spatial Arena.

Figure 3. Overview of the Spatial Arena dataset. Top left: RGB images with sparse LiDAR depth, dense depth rendered from the 3DGS [47] reconstruction, for forward- and upward-looking cameras indoors and outdoors; the dense depth fills the gaps between LiDAR returns, and masked regions such as the sky stay invalid. Right and bottom left: LiDAR maps of indoor and outdoor scenes with camera trajectories drawn as colored curves. Bottom right: a reconstructed 3DGS scene (RGB, depth, and normal) with its trajectory.

Figure 7. What makes Spatial Arena difficult. (a) Images from 14 scenes, taken by the front camera (upright views along the walking direction) and the two side cameras (rolled views looking up and sideways): dim museum halls with specular floors, a tiled underground platform, close-ups of floors and signs, graffiti, foliage, stairs, and facades seen from below. (b) Depth range within one image (d95/d5 of the valid ground truth; box: quartiles, whiskers: 10th and 90th percentiles) on the 1,688 Spatial Arena MonoDepth images and a sample of the real public MonoDepth datasets (Marigold suite without ETH3D). (c) Absolute camera roll of the same images, from the ground-truth poses (world z is vertical): the front camera is nearly upright (median 5◦), whereas the side cameras are rolled by a median of 50◦. (d) Mean MonoDepth AbsRel of four models in bins of camera roll.

Figure 2. Datasets of SpatialArena. (a) Evaluation cases by environment, static or dynamic scenes, and scene type (inner rings), and per dataset, stacked by task. (b) Unique images per dataset; the 23 public datasets hold 418,929 images. (c) Conditions each dataset tests and the tasks that use it. All five tasks test indoor and outdoor scenes, whereas aerial views, internet photos, and recordings of more than 10k frames are tested by one task each. Spatial Arena adds large-scale scenes with accurate poses and depth to all five tasks.
Figure 4. MonoDepth score vs. paper date. Lines: per-family least-squares fits; legend: slope and score. Other tasks in Figs. 9 and 10.
Figure 5. MonoDepth predictions on AerialMetric, aligned and colored on the ground-truth scale (black: masked region); each tag gives the frame’s AbsRel as a fraction.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to translate task intent into physical interactions as the scene changes. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer semantic and spatial reasoning, while visuomotor policies provide fine-grained control. Yet ambiguous goals and dependencies between actions make their integration challenging. We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework that composes learned manipulation skills through grounded steering and execution feedback. A VLM estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver constructs a skill plan. An agentic harness steers each skill through language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies its outcome to guide phase transitions and replanning. A common phase-level interface supports specialized policies and generalist action models. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot show how Atomic Policy improves task following and supports recovery in complex, long-horizon manipulation. Project page: https://aaronzkd.github.io/atomic-policy/
authors: Kaidi Zhang, Pengyuan Guo, Zhengtong Xu, Caiyi Zhang, Huayi Gou, Guanlin Huang, Aaron Lim, Anas Rafei, Yu She
bullets: Targets the challenge of translating ambiguous task goals into changing physical interactions.
Uses a VLM for symbolic state and goal estimation, followed by PDDL-based skill planning.
Steers atomic manipulation skills with language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies outcomes for replanning.
Provides a common phase-level interface for specialized policies and generalist action models.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show improved task following and recovery in complex long-horizon tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Atomic Policy architecture, shown with point-steered skills for Tabletop Manipulation. The planner combines VLM state and goal estimation with PDDL planning. For the active pick blue cube phase, the grounder (MolmoPoint) supplies a 2D image point pk. The selected skill generates an action chunk At using a diffusion U-Net conditioned on images, proprioception qt, and pk. The VLM checker evaluates the outcome against a phase-specific checklist: done advances the plan, not_done continues the phase, and replan requests a new plan. Blue arrows indicate execution and phase transitions; the red arrow indicates replanning.

Figure 5. Real-robot trial outcomes. Top: in-distribution (ID); bottom: out-of-distribution (OOD). Boxes show the interquartile range (IQR), dark lines mark medians, and whiskers extend to the outermost observations within 1.5 IQR of the box edges. White diamonds mark means, and dots show individual trials (n = 10 per method, task, and condition). Tasks are arranged by increasing language-grounding and compositional demands, from Multi-drawer to Stacking to Crossword. The language-only end-to-end baselines show wide trial-to-trial variation on Stacking and poor performance on Crossword, suggesting limited steerability as language-conditioning demands increase. Atomic + MolmoBot improves over fine-tuned MolmoBot on OOD Stacking and Crossword, supporting the combined benefit of point guidance and atomic-phase execution. Atomic + π0.5 also improves on these tasks without point inputs, showing that high-level planning and checker-controlled execution can improve OOD performance through language-based phase guidance alone.

Figure 6. Completion time of successful real-robot trials. Top: ID; bottom: OOD. Only trials with a task score of 1 are included. Large dots show the mean completion time, vertical lines show ± one sample standard deviation, and faint dots show individual trials; n is the number of successful trials for each method. Fine-tuned MolmoBot completes no Crossword trial, and fine-tuned π0.5 completes a single ID Crossword trial. Completion time for Atomic Policy includes planning, verification, and replanning by the VLM, so successful Atomic Policy trials take longer than successful end-to-end trials; for example, Atomic + π0.5 averages 128.6 s on ID Stacking versus 61.6 s for fine-tuned π0.5. Means based on few successes, such as n ≤ 2, should be interpreted with caution.

Figure 3. Task instructions and phase execution. Each row pairs an instruction with selected observations from execution. Bold labels name atomic phases, and the text after each colon identifies the point target; n/a denotes a phase without point conditioning. Blue boxes mark replanning after a detected failure or uncertain task state, such as a fallen cube in Stacking. The checker uses phase-specific completion criteria to continue execution, advance the phase, or request a new plan. Ellipses omit repeated or previously illustrated phases.

Figure 7. Failure modes on Multi-drawer. Each panel traces the 20 trials of one method (10 ID and 10 OOD) from execution to outcome. Trials either proceed without a recorded failure or encounter an error that is recovered through replanning or remains unresolved. Outcomes are SUCCESS (task score 1), PARTIAL (0 < task score < 1), and FAIL (task score 0). Failure types are wrong object or order (incorrect object, sequence, word, target recognition, or plan), reach or stuck (target or receptacle not reached, drawer not opened, or robot motion stalls), grasp, and place. Recovery is counted only when explicitly recorded in the evaluation notes. No method produces a zero-score trial on Multi-drawer. The Atomic Policy variants fail mainly through grasp and place errors, with one planning error for Atomic + MolmoBot. For fine-tuned MolmoBot, 7 of its 11 unsuccessful trials involve failure to reach the OOD receptacle during placement: the policy fails to guide the grasped object to the white bowl, suggesting difficulty grounding the unfamiliar receptacle’s location.

Figure 4. Learning curves on MolmoSpaces PnP Next-To. MolmoBot and π0.5 are evaluated during task-specific fine-tuning. Solid curves show success averaged over the ten most recent checkpoint evaluations. For the first nine checkpoints, the average uses all checkpoints evaluated so far. Dashed horizontal lines indicate each model’s zero-shot success rate.

Figure 8. Failure modes on Stacking. Panels and failure types follow Fig. 7. All 17 unrecovered failures of Atomic + DP and 9 of 10 of Atomic + MolmoBot are grasp or place errors, while Atomic + π0.5 fails in only 3 of 20 trials. Atomic + DP struggles with the fine-grained alignment required for stacking, suggesting that its low-level visuomotor policy has not learned sufficient placement precision from the available demonstrations. High-level replanning can retry these actions but cannot ensure accurate execution. In contrast, wrong object or order accounts for 8 of 11 failed trials of fine-tuned MolmoBot and 3 of 4 of fine-tuned π0.5, which together produce 11 zero-score trials.

Figure 9. Failure modes on Crossword. Panels and failure types follow Fig. 7. Wrong object, order, or place accounts for 36 of 39 unsuccessful trials of the fine-tuned baselines, whose rollouts often follow the training word or misorder letters. In contrast, 25 of 31 unrecovered failures across the Atomic Policy variants are grasp or place errors, and four trials succeed after recovery. Together with Tab. 4, these results support the benefit of explicit guidance and closed-loop planning for both ID execution and OOD generalization: Atomic + MolmoBot raises task score from 30.0 to 82.5 on ID trials and from 0.0 to 72.5 on OOD trials. Atomic + DP achieves the highest task scores in both conditions (91.3 ID and 90.0 OOD), showing that a point-guided policy can perform well on a task with strong language-grounding and sequencing demands.

Task scores report mean ± sample standard deviation across 10 trials per method, task, and condition. Crossword OOD pools the two evaluated words. VLM experiments use the same prompts and a fully fine-tuned CLIP vision encoder. Grey marks the reference configuration in each group; bold marks the best mean within each group. Metrics follow Tab. 1.

Success and score are reported as mean ± std (%) across five 10-episode blocks from the same 50 episodes. Grey denotes Atomic Policy; bold marks the higher mean. Both methods achieve high task scores on Push 5 Blocks; Atomic Policy achieves higher mean success and score with lower variation on simulated Tabletop manipulation.

papers.abstract: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.
authors: Ross Murphy, Marcel Hedman, Gabriel Brostow
bullets: Addresses fixed interfaces by exploring computers that adapt through generative screen prediction.
Uses three end-to-end pixel-and-action modules: surprise-gated slot memory, a VLM query bridge, and residual rendering.
Recalls occluded files in 64.2% of long closed-loop trials, versus at most 56.0% for recurrent or sliding-window baselines.
Improves terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%.
Explicit memory can be transplanted at test time to causally alter rendered content.

papers.abstract: Grammar-constrained decoding enables large language models to generate outputs that satisfy formal constraints, but in code and domain-specific language generation, the relevant constraints are not always fully available before decoding and may emerge progressively from new declarations, inferred type information, or runtime analysis feedback. Existing structured-decoding engines efficiently handle fixed, predeclared, or previously seen constraint structures; however, when a first-seen grammar update changes the parser state induced by an already committed prefix, the straightforward solution reconstructs the constraint state under the updated grammar, repeating parsing work already performed over the prefix. We introduce GramDelta, an incremental framework for constrained decoding with append-only runtime grammar updates. GramDelta maintains parse state over the committed prefix and propagates only changes induced by newly added grammar rules through historical dependencies, avoiding prefix replay. It then maps the updated parse state to exact next-token masks via compilation-free factorized projection over shared historical charts, avoiding per-update mask-cache recompilation. GramDelta therefore preserves the result of full reconstruction while making update cost sensitive to the actual impact of a grammar change. Experiments across four model configurations show that GramDelta adds negligible overhead without updates; under sustained runtime grammar evolution, it reduces median first-seen grammar-update latency by 10.7--11.5x and reduces the additional TPOT overhead over unconstrained decoding by 53.1--81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline. These results enable efficient constrained decoding when constraints progressively emerge and evolve with the generated prefix.
authors: Hantao Hua, Jiming Su, Yonggang Che, Feng Zhu
bullets: Targets append-only grammar updates caused by new declarations, inferred types, or runtime feedback.
Propagates only grammar-induced changes through historical parse dependencies instead of replaying the prefix.
Projects updated parse states into exact next-token masks without recompiling per-update mask caches.
Across four model configurations, it achieves 10.7–11.5× lower median first-seen update latency under sustained grammar evolution.
It also reduces added TPOT overhead versus unconstrained decoding by 53.1–81.9% relative to reconstruction-based decoding.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-robot manipulation have shown how robots can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. However, successful coordination does not reveal which robots are actually needed. The same task may require different teams as robot capabilities change, resources become unavailable, or objects replace robotic support. We argue that reliable multi-robot manipulation requires physical necessity reasoning: understanding what a task demands, which resources can fulfill those demands, and which are truly necessary. We introduce MRBench, a benchmark for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation. It comprises eight tasks with distinct concurrency and reach constraints, each evaluated under five configurations that change the required resources while preserving the task goal. Our evaluation reveals that existing coordination agents perform well with reference teams but struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support. To address this gap, we propose MRScissors, which separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities and identifies minimal feasible teams through constrained search. Across two model backbones, MRScissors achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points, respectively. Together, these findings expose a critical gap between coordinating robots and understanding their physical necessity.
authors: Yanzhe Chen, Zhijun Cao, Ruihe An, Chang Gong, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Existing coordination success with a reference team does not ensure agents understand which robots are necessary.
MRBench covers eight tasks with varying concurrency and reach constraints across five resource configurations.
Agents struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support.
MRScissors separates task requirements from measured capabilities and searches for minimal feasible teams.
It achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy across two backbones, outperforming baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points.

papers.abstract: The ability to learn and generalize from limited experience, or sample efficiency, is a cornerstone of intelligence. How can we build language models that turn a few user interactions, a few snippets of unfamiliar code, or a handful of experimental results provided in context into knowledge that generalizes? Prior work has found that sleep, a process where the model performs $N$ recurrent forward passes to refine its representations of a chunk of context, can improve long-context reasoning (specifically, within SSM-attention hybrid models). We study whether this method also improves in-context adaptation on general, non-synthetic tasks for transformer language models. To this end, we pre-train language models up to 1.2B-parameters on up to 100B tokens with sleep mechanisms. Notably, longer sleep (i.e., using a larger number of recurrent forward passes $N$) enables the model to learn faster in-context on multiple few-shot algorithmic, question-answering tasks, while also achieving lower next-token prediction loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. On held-out code, models with $N=2$ and $N=4$ match the no-sleep baseline's loss using $2.10\times$ and $2.39\times$ fewer tokens in-context, respectively. More broadly, we view our work as a step toward building models that have better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.
authors: Sangyun Lee, Zhang Enyan, Michael Xu, Hao Tang, Zinan Lin, Weijia Xu, Chris Quirk, Jianfeng Gao, Giulia Fanti, Xiaodong Liu
bullets: Studies whether recurrent “sleep” passes improve in-context adaptation beyond prior long-context reasoning settings.
Pre-trains transformers up to 1.2B parameters with varying numbers of recurrent forward passes over context.
Longer sleep improves few-shot algorithmic and question-answering adaptation and lowers out-of-distribution next-token loss.
On held-out code, 2 and 4 sleep passes match the no-sleep baseline with 2.10× and 2.39× fewer in-context tokens.
The approach targets a better tradeoff between adaptation efficiency and decoding latency.

papers.abstract: Many use cases for large language models (LLMs)---from AI safety to exploration and human interaction---can benefit from epistemic uncertainty estimates. We argue that existing Bayesian Deep Learning solutions, which are often restricted to a fixed model family, fail to capture the full epistemic uncertainty at practical LLM scales. This is because the error due to the bounded capacity of the model family remains invisible to disagreement among models supported by the prior. We relate this error to the well-known power-law scaling of LLM loss with model size. We then show that a second power law quantifies the shrinking disagreement within ensembles as model size increases. Its slower decay relative to the capacity law above suggests that ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and become more competitive as an axis for scaling, compared to a single larger model. Finally, a third power law quantifies the loss of ensemble diversity as members share a larger fraction of training before branching, and therefore identifies a further limitation, beyond the capacity error, for LoRA ensembles and optimization-based or second-order methods that approximate uncertainty around a single training solution. At a high level, these findings suggest diverse ensembles can be a promising axis, both for scaling and uncertainty quantification at larger scales.
authors: Siamak Ravanbakhsh, David Nitchi, Khang Ngo
bullets: Fixed model-family Bayesian methods miss uncertainty from models’ limited capacity.
Ensemble disagreement shrinks with model size according to a power law, but more slowly than capacity-related error.
This slower decay suggests ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and may be a viable scaling axis.
A third power law shows that sharing more training before ensemble branching reduces diversity.
The findings highlight limitations of LoRA and optimization-based ensembles that approximate uncertainty around one solution.

Vector and MLP cells give point gains and conditional 95% intervals from whole-source bootstrap resampling with fitted maps fixed, excluding fitting and selection uncertainty; intervals are not simultaneous across models. N counts total parameters in millions. Percentages reported in the text divide the same gains by original total log loss. Small achieved gains lower-bound full-distribution calibration error.

papers.selection_reason: Presents scaling laws for ensemble uncertainty in LLMs, identifying a new axis for scaling and uncertainty quantification that complements single-model approaches.
papers.title: Scaling Laws of Ensemble Uncertainty in Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper identifies power laws governing model-capacity error, ensemble disagreement, and ensemble diversity, suggesting diverse ensembles increasingly improve epistemic uncertainty estimation as LLMs scale.

papers.abstract: We present the Screw Attention Policy, a geometry-centric manipulation framework that supplies task geometry explicitly and learns only execution. The policy operates on object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes provided by perception and robot models. The policy requires only 30K learned parameters. Trained entirely in simulation on a single robot arm, the policy generalises to new scene layouts, transfers zero-shot across robot embodiments, and deploys directly on a real robot, without adaptation or fine-tuning. It achieves 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen robot arms, and 21 of 24 trials on a real robot. These results suggest that much of what manipulation policies learn at scale is geometric structure that can instead be supplied.
authors: Aly Magassouba
bullets: Uses object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes as explicit geometric inputs.
Learns execution rather than reconstructing task geometry from data.
Trained on a single simulated robot arm with no adaptation or fine-tuning for transfer.
Reports 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen arms, and 21/24 real-robot trials.
Scope: performance depends on accurate perception and robot-model geometry supplied to the policy.

papers.selection_reason: Novel geometry-centric manipulation policy with zero-shot transfer.
papers.title: Supply Geometry, Learn Execution: Screw Attention for Zero-Shot Policy Transfer in Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: Screw Attention supplies manipulation geometry explicitly, enabling a 30K-parameter policy trained in simulation to transfer zero-shot across layouts, robot arms, and to a real robot.

papers.abstract: Most imitation policies that predict chunks of future actions use the dense action representation, in which the chunk holds one control target per step. In stage-structured manipulation, where a task can be divided into stages with definable endpoints, the keypose action representation instead sets each step of the chunk to the endpoint of the stage that step belongs to, and a speed-capped servo supplies the motion. We compare the two in several simulated manipulation tasks and on a real robot, with the same chunk length and matched demonstrations, observations, policy architectures and update budgets; in simulation, each one's execution rule is selected on tuning scenes. When the simulated demonstrations are slowed, paused and rerouted, dense success falls sharply while keypose stays roughly level, across three policy architectures and with endpoints extracted from the recorded demonstrations; keypose also leads under object-size and position shift. With clean demonstrations, keypose leads only when they are scarce and is otherwise close to or behind dense across the simulated tasks, provided that the demonstrations and execution rule suit its executor; when they do not, it falls far below dense. The same dependence on the executor appeared on a real robot learning to open a drawer from human demonstrations: dense succeeded more often, and keypose improved substantially only after its executor's rotation and forward speed were adjusted to the demonstrations. These results suggest that keypose trades sensitivity to such variation in the demonstrations for sensitivity to execution that departs from them.
authors: Haizhou Ge, Mengshuo Wang, Zhixing Chen, Lei Han, Chen Wang, Lu Shi, Guyue Zhou, Ruqi Huang
bullets: The study compares dense action chunks with stage-endpoint-based keypose chunks for stage-structured manipulation.
Experiments use matched policies, demonstrations, observations, chunk lengths, and update budgets in simulation and on a real robot.
With slowed, paused, or rerouted demonstrations, dense performance drops sharply while keypose remains roughly stable; keypose also handles object and position shifts better.
With clean demonstrations, keypose helps mainly when demonstrations are scarce and can perform much worse when its executor is mismatched.
In a real drawer-opening task, dense succeeds more often, while tuning keypose's executor substantially improves it.

The dashed box is one 50-slot chunk; it spans the lift and place stages, so its keypose slots hold two endpoints. The gripper channel is the same in both. Both are trained with the same demonstrations, policy architecture and update budget and execute the first eight of 50 slots before querying again; the keypose command toward a stage endpoint is capped at the 95th percentile of the demonstrations’ per-step motion. papers.selection_reason: Compares action representations for manipulation, directly relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: Keypose or Dense? A Controlled Comparison of Action Representations for Stage-Structured Manipulation
papers.tldr: Keypose representations are more robust to timing and path variation in demonstrations, but their success depends strongly on a well-matched execution controller.

papers.abstract: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
authors: Tingting Liao, Mingjia Huo, Hao Li, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Represents the robot with a 3D model and potentially contacted objects as 3D points from the first frame and calibrated camera.
A parameter-free rule-based simulator applies actions, while a video model renders realistic video alongside the simulated state.
Across unseen DROID setups, robot motion follows the proxy more closely than end-to-end models, while rendering the robot alone is often sufficient.
Adding simulated objects reduces missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%; object-state adherence varies substantially by base video model.
Rigid-object lift behavior is more sensitive to freezing simulated objects for MiniMax-H3 than LTX-2.3, while rigidly modeling cloth and rope remains a limitation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Following the simulated state. Under the recorded actions (top), both base models lift the cup as the proxy does. With the gripper held open (middle) or the simulated objects frozen while the arm moves as recorded (bottom), the proxy leaves the cup in place; SimPWM-H3-C does too, whereas SimPWM-LTX-2.3-C still lifts it.

papers.selection_reason: Simulator-as-proxy video world model for robot manipulation, probing whether video follows simulated state.
papers.title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: SimPWM uses an explicit simulator as a proxy for robot video generation and shows that video models reliably follow simulated robot motion but only inconsistently follow simulated object states.

papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call $\sigma_{99}$), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.
authors: Daehee Kim
bullets: Across 58 open-weight LLMs from 14 families, FFN intrinsic dimensionality consistently follows a middle-heavy layer profile.
The profile is robust across calibration corpora and languages and remains largely preserved after post-training fine-tuning.
PCA-guided width pruning improves distilled students over uniform widths on four teachers, with gains depending on how unevenly dimensionality is distributed.
An inverted allocation performs worst, supporting the structural relevance of the measured dimensionality signal.
The advantage also persists after downstream supervised fine-tuning.

Horizontal axis is normalized layer index; vertical axis is dθ,l/Dl at θ = 0.99. The middle-heavy profile recurs across architecture, training corpus, and scale. How strongly middle-heavy it is varies by family (Qwen2.5/Qwen3 most pronounced, LLaMA-3.x, Mistral, and Yi-1.5 [Young et al., 2024] flatter); checkpoints that are visibly not middle-heavy are concentrated in the ≤ 1.7B-parameter regime and the low-σ99 families flagged in the body.
