papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise intrinsic dimensionality analysis guides width pruning in LLMs, relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
papers.tldr: PCA reveals that LLM FFN capacity needs are typically highest in middle layers, enabling better width allocation than uniform designs under matched parameter budgets.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.
authors: Guowei Guan, Yurong Hao, Jiaming Zhang, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
bullets: Multimodal compression and cross-modal agreement can unintentionally amplify salient, consistently supported signals.
This creates a vulnerability in ranking decisions that content manipulation can exploit.
C3H is an inference-time attack that aligns a target item’s multimodal content with implicit recommendation criteria.
Unlike noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, it manipulates content without changing model training.
Experiments show increased target-item exposure while preserving overall recommendation utility.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The schematic overview of C3H. Under a strict zero-query setting, the framework operates in two stages: (1) Cue Scoring (Stage I) ranks candidate cues from (t0, v0) by compressionsurvivability κ̂ and cross-modal consensus χ̂, selecting a hero cue fh and a secondary cue fs by joint score S = κ̃ · χ̃. (2) Stealthy Editing (Stage II) amplifies fh, fs via text shaping and a low-distortion image transform, gated against the stealthiness set B.
Table 7: Cross-architecture transferability on Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct [43] for MicroLens (N=9) and Beauty (N=14) at K=20.
Table 8: Cross-architecture transferability on Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct [43] for Sports (N=6) at K=20.
Table 2: Main results of attack effectiveness and recommendation utility on MicroLens and Beauty under Few-Shot and Zero-Shot prompts. Best ER per cell is bolded and underlined.
Table 5: Defence robustness on MicroLens (N=9) under Few-Shot and Zero-Shot prompts. Each defence is calibrated to 5–10% rejection on clean items.
Table 4: Leave-one-out ablation on MicroLens (N=9) and Beauty (N=14) at K=20. ∆ER is the drop relative to full C3H.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates a security vulnerability (C2C bias) in Multimodal LLM recommender systems, offering a novel attack vector and analysis of multimodal compression and fusion.
papers.title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
papers.tldr: C3H exploits compression-to-consensus bias in multimodal LLM recommenders to increase a target item’s exposure through tailored multimodal content.

papers.abstract: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.
authors: Hayeong Lee, Youngjun Suh. Byung-Jun Lee
bullets: Problem: Prediction alone does not ensure representations retain the action distinctions needed for planning.
Method: Identify the executed action against alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal.
Key insight: CIA captures action information beyond the conditional action mean, including information invisible to squared-error regression.
Evidence: A controlled example verifies this distinction, and CIA improves planner-averaged mean success over both a base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline.
Scope: Results are evaluated on five visual control benchmarks without changing the planner.

papers.abstract: In Minecraft, a common testbed for embodied agents, semantic tools such as mineBlock pick targets from the simulator's loaded world state without a visibility test, so a buried ore the agent has never seen is one call away, and scores cannot show whether the agent searched. We formalize the missing requirement as evidence closure: every decision of an agent system, including those inside its tools, may depend on the world only through facts for which the agent holds evidence. EviCraft is a runtime and benchmark that enforces closure below the agent and makes the admission rule an experimental variable: a perception-grounded regime (G) admits only what is in line of sight or returned by the agent's own actions, and a loaded-state regime (L) reproduces standard tool stacks, with agents, tools, and worlds held fixed. On Survival, the regime effect exceeds the strongest agent's lead: under G, three mid-sized agents reach the diamond in 32%-40% of runs, against 76%-94% under L, and the strongest agent under G scores below each of them under L. In two models, removing only the line-of-sight test closes 93%-96% of the score gap, and loading state only inside tools recovers 70%-98%, so safeguards on observations and queries leave most of the leak open. In open-ended acquisition, the gain from L concentrates in items that depend on buried resources or mobs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/AllenReder/EviCraft
authors: Wenyou Yi, Lantian Zhang, Guanlin Chen, Xingqiu Xu, Haiyang Sun, Minrui Huang, Tianle Liang, Hao Chen, Haorui Xu, Zhou Zhao
bullets: The paper formalizes evidence closure: agent decisions and tool calls may depend only on facts supported by the agent’s evidence.
EviCraft compares perception-grounded access (G) with standard loaded-state tools (L), holding agents, tools, and worlds fixed.
On Survival, three mid-sized agents reached diamond in 32%–40% of runs under G versus 76%–94% under L.
Removing only line-of-sight checks closed 93%–96% of the score gap in two models; tool-only state loading recovered 70%–98%.
Loaded-state advantages were concentrated on tasks involving buried resources or mobs.

papers.selection_reason: Studies embodied agents in Minecraft with perception-grounded evidence closure, directly relevant to embodied AI.
papers.title: EviCraft: Can Minecraft Agents Find What They Cannot See?
papers.tldr: EviCraft shows that Minecraft agents’ apparent capabilities can be strongly inflated when tools access unseen world state, and enforces evidence-based decisions to measure genuine search.

papers.abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.
authors: Konstantinos Emmanouilidis, Ziqing Xu, Salma Tarmoun, Lachlan MacDonald, Rene Vidal
bullets: Challenges the classical view that SGD stepsizes must remain below a curvature-dependent stability threshold.
Analyzes the dynamics of SGD with large stepsizes under stochastic gradient noise.
Proves accelerated O(T⁻²) convergence for linear predictors and two-layer neural networks.
Also improves convergence guarantees in the stable stepsize regime, including for deterministic optimization.
Numerical experiments show practical benefits from using large learning rates.

Dashed lines indicate the T−2 reference rate which is derived in Corollary 4.2 and Corollary 5.4. Averages are over independent minibatch-sampling streams with the data and features held fixed.

papers.title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
papers.tldr: Large learning rates can accelerate stochastic gradient descent, achieving an O(T⁻²) convergence rate for cross-entropy with linear and two-layer neural-network predictors.

papers.abstract: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.
authors: Wonjune Seo, Minkyung Park, Saerom Park
bullets: Targets quantization-conditioned backdoors that emerge after quantization despite benign high-precision behavior.
Compares full-precision and quantized modules on identical states from the quantized trajectory to isolate local discrepancies.
Repairs dominant discrepancy directions using a closed-form factorized residual adapter, with full-span or low-rank options.
Across four LLMs, three attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats, it substantially mitigates backdoors while largely retaining utility.
Also remains effective against a non-PGD outlier-injection attack; low-rank repair reduces deployment memory overhead.

papers.abstract: Sparse world models for 4D semantic occupancy forecasting represent scenes with a small set of evolving queries to efficiently predict future geometry and semantics for autonomous driving. However, existing sparse world models face a bottleneck in using historical temporal evidence for long-horizon forecasting. They rely on scene states to carry historical information implicitly, allowing errors to propagate and accumulate across successive forecasting steps and causing geometric and semantic deviations. To address this limitation, we present MemAnchorWorld, a sparse occupancy world model that explicitly retrieves relevant historical geometric and semantic evidence for 4D semantic occupancy forecasting. Inspired by the von Restorff effect, we introduce a forecast-time-conditioned hierarchical dual-path memory-anchor retrieval mechanism. Guided by the effective age and semantic compatibility of historical information, it combines query-level candidate selection with point-level memory-anchor retrieval to provide historical evidence for sparse points at different forecast times. To better use memory anchors and existing features, a point-level residual adapter jointly gated by the task and forecast time separately controls residual corrections to semantics, occupancy confidence, and spatial positions. On Occ3D-nuScenes, MemAnchorWorld achieves an average mIoU of 13.55% and an average IoU of 22.84% across the 1-3 s forecasting horizons, attaining state-of-the-art performance on both metrics.Project page: https://memanchorworld.github.io/
authors: Xinyang Jia, Yuqi Zhang, Jiakai Wang, Yahu Yang, Guandong Pan, Chao Tong, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Addresses error accumulation in sparse world models that store temporal information only implicitly in scene states.
Uses forecast-conditioned hierarchical dual-path memory-anchor retrieval based on information age and semantic compatibility.
Combines query-level candidate selection with point-level retrieval for sparse points at different forecast horizons.
Applies a task- and forecast-time-gated point-level residual adapter to refine semantics, occupancy confidence, and spatial positions.
On Occ3D-nuScenes, reports 13.55% average mIoU and 22.84% average IoU over 1–3 s horizons, with state-of-the-art performance on both metrics.

papers.abstract: Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines reconstruct a scene from images in a single forward pass, representing it as real-time-renderable 3D Gaussians. However, the resulting representations contain far more Gaussians than are needed to render the scene faithfully, especially when there are many input views. This drastically increases memory and storage requirements. Existing pruning methods either require costly re-optimization, which defeats the purpose of a single forward pass, or rely on simple strategies that do not exploit all the available information. We present AnyPrune, a transformer-based, optimization-free pruning module designed to work on top of any feedforward 3DGS pipeline. To remove unnecessary Gaussians, AnyPrune learns and exploits pipeline-specific redundancy patterns through a short single-GPU training on the frozen target feedforward pipeline. AnyPrune achieves better rendering quality than existing optimization-free pruning methods in most settings and generalizes to unseen datasets, as shown through extensive experiments across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input view counts. It prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about $5\,\mathrm{s}$ on a consumer GPU, faster than every method that merges Gaussians or re-optimizes the field. It can also be combined with the pruning built into feedforward pipelines, pruning further at moderate ratios while preserving or improving rendering quality. Finally, it can even suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that retains most of the quality.
authors: Nicola Leonetti, Federico Stella, Aoxiang Fan, Saqib Javed, Pascal Fua, Luigi Di Stefano
bullets: Addresses excessive Gaussian counts that increase memory and storage, particularly with many input views.
Uses a transformer-based pruning module trained briefly on a frozen target pipeline to learn pipeline-specific redundancy.
Works across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input-view counts, including unseen datasets.
Prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about 5 seconds on a consumer GPU.
Can complement built-in pruning and suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that preserves most quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of AnyPrune. A frozen feedforward 3DGS pipeline predicts the Gaussians G from the input views. G is rendered from the input poses and the render error Ev is used to compute a per-Gaussian feature vector fi which is encoded by an MLP and processed by the transformer together with the other features. As in SplatFormer, every head reads the per-Gaussian features computed by the backbone and, via a residual connection, the attributes of the input Gaussians. The residual heads predict adjustments to refine G into G′; the mask head predicts a log-space adjustment hi to be added to the Speedy-Splat sensitivity score Si to obtain each Gaussian’s keep logit zi (Eq. (3)). zi is used at training time to compute a factor mi = σ(zi/τ) by which to multiply the refined opacities of the Gaussians before rendering them. The masked field is rendered from the input and held-out views and supervised with Eq. (4), whose photometric term is denoted Lphoto. A sparsity term in the loss pushes the network to prune the redundant Gaussians. At inference, instead of using the soft mask, the user can either keep the k Gaussians with the highest zi to meet a budget, or those with zi > 0 for the model’s own budget.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at medical question answering yet are rarely evaluated on the stepwise diagnostic reasoning that defines real clinical workflows, where impressions are revised as information accumulates. We build Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis (ASCENT), a clinician-annotated benchmark and training resource of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from MedQA-USMLE that decomposes each vignette into EMR-aligned steps (Findings, Impression, supporting Rationale), enabling evaluation of intermediate reasoning under incomplete information. Experiments and training with ASCENT revealed insights into how current LLMs handle stepwise diagnostic reasoning. Even strong reasoning models that perform well on MedQA-USMLE leave substantial headroom on ASCENT, and general-purpose frontier models trail further, exposing a persistent gap between fully informed and stepwise diagnosis. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B on ASCENT yields measurable F1 gains over both pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, with gains driven primarily by precision. Complementary robustness analyses (counterfactual perturbation, format-vs-content control, judge agreement, and rollout) further show that ASCENT-fine-tuned models rely on the diagnostic content of prior impressions rather than imitating their output format, while error propagation under rollout remains a key challenge for clinical deployment.
authors: Yera Choi, Yeong Hwa Kim, Jaedeok Lee, Taekang Kim, Sangdoo Yun, Seong-Eun Moon
bullets: Introduces 3,078 clinician-annotated, EMR-aligned diagnostic problems derived from MedQA-USMLE.
Decomposes cases into Findings, Impression, and supporting Rationale to evaluate reasoning under incomplete information.
Strong reasoning models still lag on stepwise diagnosis compared with fully informed question answering.
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B improves F1 over pretrained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT baselines, mainly through higher precision.
Robustness tests suggest models use prior diagnostic content, but rollout error propagation remains a deployment challenge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: a. Data construction workflow of ASCENT. Candidate questions from MedQA-USMLE and the HuatuoGPT-o1 SFT dataset were filtered and stepwise-annotated by experts, either directly or via DeepSeek-R1 with expert revision. The finalized questions were converted into stepwise diagnostic problems across clinical stages. b. The structure of ASCENT data. At each step, clinical findings are paired with a list of suspected disorders (Impression) and the corresponding rationale (Reason). As steps progress and new clinical information accumulates, the Impression is refined or updated to reflect the evolving diagnostic reasoning. In evaluations with ASCENT, each step is treated as a separate question, and models are prompted to generate either only the Impression or both the Impression and the corresponding Reason.

Figure 3: Expert assessment of stepwise rationales. The quality of model-generated rationales was assessed on three clinician-defined criteria: (1)Comprehensiveness & Relevance (Comp. & Relevance), (2)Clinical Validity, and (3) Soundness of Differential Diagnosis (Soundness of DDx ). Solid lines indicate sequential diagnostic steps.

CIs use 10,000 test-record bootstrap resamples (percentile method); within each resample, P, R, and F1 are computed from the same aggregated TP/FP/FN counts so the three values remain self-consistent. Bold marks the best value within each model category.

Table 2: Stepwise diagnosis performance of open-source and proprietary models on the ASCENT test set (n = 305), evaluated on two tasks: (1) generating impressions only (Imp) and (2) generating supporting rationales followed by impressions (Imp + Reason). Step columns report micro-F1 per stage (“Step3+” aggregates Step 3 onward); the “Overall” column reports micro-F1 across all steps. The “95% CI” column reports bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on Overall micro-F1, computed via 10,000 test-record resamples (percentile method); under Imp, the top reasoning cluster (o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1) is statistically separable from the lower cluster with non-overlapping CIs, whereas under Imp + Reason the second-tier models cluster more closely and several CIs overlap (notably Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct + SFT w/ ASCENT and DeepSeek-R1). Models are grouped by size and whether they are specialized in reasoning, with bold numbers indicating the best result within each model category.

Table 1: Comparison between datasets. Expert Review: Whether the dataset’s annotations were reviewed by medical experts. GT Rationale: Whether the dataset provides ground-truth explanations. Intermediate Target: Whether the dataset includes intermediate reasoning targets for sequential diagnostic evaluation. In the case of MedReason, △ under Expert Review indicates partial evaluation, where over 25 sampled questions across seven specialties were evaluated by directly comparing anonymized HuatuoGPT-o1 and MedReason Chain-of-Thought data.

Table 3: Inter-judge agreement between GPT-4.1 (Judge A) and GPT-5.2 (Judge B) on 313 impression-level pairs. The equiv-23 collapse merges Overly Specific and Overly Broad into a single granularity-mismatch class. Both settings show substantial agreement under quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ. The micro-F1 of GPT-5.2 was higher than GPT-4.1 by +0.08, but only 0.64% of pairs reverse direction (i.e., trend-reversing disagreements), indicating that residual disagreements concentrate at class boundaries rather than systematic inversions.

Table 8: Per-step and overall F1 for OpenAI o3-mini under mitigated (gold prior) and rollout (model’s own prior) protocols (Step 5 omitted, n = 2). Degradation worsens monotonically with step depth in both task modes. We focus the per-step analysis on o3-mini because it is the strongest model on ASCENT (Table 2) and therefore offers the most informative test of error propagation: if even the best evaluated model cannot recover under rollout, the collapse is unlikely to be an artifact of weak baseline capability. The corresponding overall rollout collapse for ours-32B is reported in the main text.

Table 10: Counterfactual perturbation of the most recent prior impression on a 75-case subset. Resilience is an auxiliary metric we introduce for this analysis: the fraction of cases in which the model still produces at least one correct impression somewhere in the diagnostic trajectory under the perturbed prior, complementing the per-step F1 column. o3-mini (gold-prior baseline F1 on this subset = 0.67) is broadly resilient, with all four variants staying within roughly 5 F1 points of baseline. ours-32B exhibits a striking asymmetry: collapse under overly broad priors (F1 = 0.15, far below its overall test-set F1 of 0.54 in Table 6) but robustness to irrelevant, overly specific, and order shift variants, consistent with content-based (rather than format-based) reliance on the prior impression.

Table 4: 4-class confusion matrix between GPT-4.1 (rows, Judge A) and GPT-5.2 (columns, Judge B). Class labels: 1 = Correct Match, 2 = Overly Specific, 3 = Overly Broad, 4 = Others. 95.9% of disagreements fall within two ordinal classes (|A − B| ≤ 2); strictly adjacent disagreements (|A−B| = 1, e.g., 1 vs. 2 or 2 vs. 3) account for 71.4%.
Table 7: Token-length ablation for OpenAI o3-mini on the full ASCENT test set (n = 305). Performance is approximately constant beyond 1,024 tokens.

Table 11: Edit distribution of physician revisions over the two draft sources used to construct ASCENT. “Major” is defined as similarity < 0.85 between draft and final. The reviewer protocol is described in Section 3.1.

Table 12: Ontology coverage of ASCENT ground-truth impression entities. The 117 unmatched UMLS entities are free-text terms. “via UMLS” indicates that mappings to SNOMED CT and ICD-10 were obtained indirectly, using each UMLS Concept Unique Identifier (CUI) as a bridge to the corresponding SNOMED CT and ICD-10 codes in the UMLS Metathesaurus (2025AA); we did not query SNOMED CT or ICD-10 directly. Consequently, SNOMED CT coverage is reported as a fraction of UMLS-matched entities, and the 401 ICD-10-linked entities span the full disease taxonomy (all 20 chapters).
Table 5: Confusion matrix after collapsing Overly Specific (2) and Overly Broad (3) into a single granularity-mismatch class.

Table 9: Recovery rate after first incorrect impression under rollout. Of the 275 o3-mini cases (90.2% of the test set) that produced a wrong impression at any step, none recovered at any subsequent step.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing a scene for physics simulation requires recovering its spatial layout and the support relationships that govern its behavior. We present Support2Sim, a Real2Sim system that reconstructs simulation-ready scenes from a single RGB image. Our design objective is to maximize source fidelity, support realization, and stability within a practical time budget for scene generation. Support2Sim infers a support graph, which a contact-guided pose initializer uses to propose poses for objects with multiple supports. The initializer generates and ranks candidates by geometric fit and source-image agreement. A coarse-to-fine refiner allocates a fixed search budget across supported objects and evaluates pose updates with physics rollouts. After an accepted update, it searches from the new pose at a finer translation and rotation scale. We benchmark our method on 50 scenes spanning four datasets. Compared with the strongest baseline, Support2Sim improves source-mask IoU after 10 seconds by 21.4 pp, realizes 87.1% versus 73.2% of intended supports, and reduces mean object drift from 79.6 to 45.3 mm. See our project page at https://support2sim.github.io for more details.
authors: Samarth Chopra, Ankit Prabhu, Akshayan Nagarajah, Sumer Murthy, Pratik Chaudhari, Vijay Kumar
bullets: Targets visually faithful Real2Sim reconstruction with reliable object supports and practical generation time.
Infers a support graph and uses contact-guided pose initialization for objects with multiple supports.
Refines object poses through coarse-to-fine search, geometric/image agreement, and physics rollouts.
Across 50 scenes from four datasets, it improves 10-second source-mask IoU by 21.4 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
It realizes 87.1% of intended supports and reduces mean object drift from 79.6 to 45.3 mm.

papers.abstract: Recently developed World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, providing predictive context for control. However, existing WAMs typically learn implicit attention allocation with limited explicit action-relevant attention guidance, leading to limited performance. To unleash strong capabilities of WAMs, we introduce explicit attention guidance as a unifying principle and propose our Attention-Guided WAM (AG-WAM), an end-to-end framework with three plug-and-play attention guidance modules that directly reformulate internal attention paradigm in WAMs: the Content-Adaptive Predictive Attention module, the Guidance-Point Visual Attention module, and the State-Conditioned Text Attention module. Without any external plugin module adopted, our end-to-end framework with the unifying principle of explicit attention guidance boosts the accuracy and efficiency of WAMs. Without using any private embodied training data, our AG-WAM establishes new state-of-the-art performance on multiple public robotic manipulation benchmarks including LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, significantly outperforming other methods, even those using massive private embodied training data by a notable margin, meanwhile notably improving training and inference efficiency.
authors: Hongcheng Zhang, Lei Sun, Songxuan Liu, Tengteng Pan, Yuqiang Zhai, Xianglong Xu, Jianya Guo, Xiao Song
bullets: Existing WAMs rely on implicit attention, limiting action-relevant prediction and control.
AG-WAM introduces three plug-and-play modules: content-adaptive predictive, guidance-point visual, and state-conditioned text attention.
The framework is end-to-end and requires no external plugin modules or private embodied training data.
It reports state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, with improved training and inference efficiency.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
authors: Itai Mizlish, Boaz Ben-Moshe
bullets: Quantising the transformer-based Depth Anything V2 directly causes severe information loss because many attention weights fall below int8 precision.
The proposed ResNet-34 U-Net student, distilled from Depth Anything V2-Large, runs at 27.1 FPS using 24.5M parameters.
Its int8 predictions closely match its float version (Pearson 0.99993) and achieve the best held-out simulated-yard accuracy among tested onboard models (AbsRel 0.269).
On 1,000 stereo-verified real-drive points, it performs comparably to the vendor’s Depth Anything V2-Small while running faster (27.1 vs. 21.6 FPS).
Integrated with mapping, planning, and SLAM, the system reaches goals without contact in most hardware-in-the-loop yard trials, though less often than with exact obstacle maps.

papers.selection_reason: Attention-free depth distillation enabling onboard robot navigation on low-power hardware; efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: An attention-free, distilled depth model enables real-time monocular obstacle ranging and navigation on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Hailo-8L hardware.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods rely on 2D foundation models applied to registered images captured alongside the 3D point clouds. However, such images may not be available in many cases, while direct 3D point cloud segmentation methods require semantic class supervision and are challenging to deploy in a zero-shot manner. To address these issues, we present SplatSeg3D, which segments a bare colored point cloud in an open-vocabulary manner without requiring the accompanying images, camera poses, class supervision, or instance mask proposals. To achieve this, we first surfelize the input point cloud and obtain oriented 2D Gaussians. We then render views of the scene by splatting, with a view selection strategy that maximizes scene coverage with as few views as possible. Next, we apply text-prompted segmentation on the rendered views, giving each 3D point a set of multi-view semantic cues, fused to produce a 3D segmentation of the scene. We evaluate SplatSeg3D on semantic segmentation and novel-class instance segmentation on 4 standard benchmarks: Scannet, Scannet++, Replica, and S3DIS. Our pipeline not only performs better or on-par with the state-of-the-art, but we also achieve these results efficiently across runtime and compute requirements. Code will be published.
authors: Sandeep Inuganti, Mahdi Chamseddine, Marcel Rogge, Martin R. Oswald, Didier Stricker, Jason Rambach
bullets: Addresses settings where registered images, camera poses, class supervision, or instance proposals are unavailable.
Surfelizes point clouds into oriented 2D Gaussians and selects a small set of coverage-maximizing splatted views.
Applies text-prompted segmentation to rendered views, then fuses multi-view semantic cues onto 3D points.
Evaluated on semantic and novel-class instance segmentation across ScanNet, ScanNet++, Replica, and S3DIS.
Reports performance on par with or better than state of the art while reducing runtime and compute requirements.

papers.title: SplatSeg3D: Efficient Zero-Shot 3D Segmentation via Point Cloud Surfelization and Splatting

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable simultaneous processing of egocentric video and textual target descriptions to produce action commands for embodied tracking platforms. However, these platforms rarely move exactly as commanded, in part due to unexpected environmental disturbances such as wind, unleveled terrain, and road bumps. Here we study how such models handle uncommanded egomotion. First, we explore performance across diverse disturbances by benchmarking three tracking VLAs on three datasets. We find that models differ in which environmental disturbances hurt them most, but all are sensitive to sudden target loss. Tracing egomotion from pixels to emitted actions, we identify two gaps. In representation, motion is reliably recovered through explicit relations between frames, but aggressive compression of past frames weakens small-motion readouts. In action, large rotations do reach the decision state, yet the decoded direction carries only a few percent of a mirrored rotation's effect on the turn. Targeting both gaps, we fine-tune one model, Uni-NaVid, on data amounting to just 1.7% of its original training set in a ladder of analysis-motivated variants. These gain 5-22 points after target-loss without degrading clean success; after a smooth loss, the best one improves success by 72% (relative), recovering 76% of its gap to clean. We also show that targeted fine-tuning improves recovery partly via a text-mediated action dependency, without new architecture, large-scale data collection or training from scratch.
authors: Dan Zlotnikov, Nadav Alali, Ohad Ben-Shahar
bullets: Benchmarks three tracking VLAs across three datasets and diverse disturbances.
All models are sensitive to sudden target loss, though disturbance susceptibility varies.
Explicit cross-frame relations recover motion, while aggressive frame compression weakens small-motion perception.
Large rotations reach the decision state, but their decoded turn direction has little effect relative to mirrored rotations.
Analysis-driven fine-tuning on 1.7% of original training data improves target-loss recovery while preserving clean performance; gains are strongest after smooth loss.

papers.abstract: In object pose estimation methods, predicted poses are expressed with respect to a canonical frame, defined by a reference model of that object. In learning-based methods, an arbitrarily chosen modeling convention defines this canonical frame, which is then used to generate the ground-truth pose-annotations for training. Object pose estimation methods are therefore bound to such arbitrary conventions, restricting generalization. In this work, we propose that such a canonical frame can instead be derived for any object, and present RestPose, an approach towards open object pose estimation that does not require reference models or canonical frame conventions during training. From a single input image, we generate an object mesh and canonicalize it through a geometric and physical analysis of the object, then use foundation model-based dense matching to estimate the pose. We choose category-level benchmarks for our experiments, which contain instances across various object categories and enable us to measure the effectiveness of our canonicalization. Across HouseCat6D, NOCS, and Omni6DPose datasets, we improve on the supervised state-of-the-art methods by 18.3 points in absolute metrics and 13.8 points in scale-agnostic metrics, without requiring task-specific training. Code will be published.
authors: Sandeep Inuganti, Weihang Li, Benjamin Busam, Didier Stricker, Jason Rambach
bullets: Addresses the dependence of pose estimation on arbitrary, object-specific canonical frames and reference models.
Generates an object mesh from one image, then canonicalizes it using geometric and physical analysis.
Uses foundation-model-based dense matching to estimate the object pose.
Evaluated on HouseCat6D, NOCS, and Omni6DPose, improving over supervised state-of-the-art methods by 18.3 absolute and 13.8 scale-agnostic metric points.
Scope: experiments focus on category-level benchmarks; code is planned for release.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview. RestPose computes a canonical frame from generated geometry. A masked reference view yields a generated mesh of a remote. In their native frames (middle) the two meshes (generated and GT mesh) lie along different axes. RestPose’s canonicalization F sets each mesh at rest in a common reference frame - allowing us to design an annotation-free and pose trainingfree method.

Figure 3. RestPose pipeline. Onboarding runs once per object. A mesh is generated from one masked view, with its depth in the RGB-D setting, in the generator’s native frame. one unique canonical frame is selected, and the azimuth is read from the radial profile, giving the canonical rotation. Inference runs per detection. Templates are rendered from cameras placed around the RestPose mesh, and reciprocal matches against each are counted. The template with most inliers wins, and its matches are lifted to a Sim(3) fit inside RANSAC. In case of insufficient inliers, the detection takes the boxed ICP branch instead. In the RGB-only setting onboarding uses no metric-scale sensor depth and the query’s predicted depth has arbitrary scale. Multi-view labelling runs post hoc on the per-frame outputs. Each frame’s estimate is first labelled jointly among the four flips, and the labelled poses then vote for a consensus.

Figure 7. Qualitative results. HouseCat6D and REAL275 rows show the query object, the generated mesh in its native frame and in RestPose’s frame, and the single-view pose, with the predicted 3D box in teal and the annotated box in dashed orange. Right: the single-view failure that remains, the family near-tie of Sec. 4.5. The generated box lies flat while the CAD stands on its end, each following its own source’s upright, so their frames sit a face apart. The two boxes coincide, but the predicted axes differ from the annotation’s by 169 to 180◦ in every one of the scene’s frames. Bottom: Results on ROPE evaluated by relative pose. Each example shows two views, which stay on the same parts of the object as it turns, and compares our relative rotation with the annotated one, which coincide at these errors.

Figure 6. Multi-view labelling and voting with VGGT-predicted cameras. Top: each frame’s single-view pose carries its own flip Φk, and one view has no evidence to prefer one, so most pairs through them disagree with the cameras’ relative rotation. Middle: the labelling of Eq. (11) chooses the flips jointly. Bottom: the V=16 object poses lifted to the world by the predicted cameras. Their chordal mean R̄wo is projected back into every view (Eq. (12)).

Figure 4. Physics under-determines the canonical. The rest-pose construction on an example bottle mesh. Top: the convex hull and the centre of mass ḡ, then the resting facets with their probabilities Pf , then the families they merge into. Bottom: the bottle at rest in each family. Lying on its front and on its back differ by only ∆P = 0.003, so stability alone cannot uniquely decide on a frame.

Figure 5. The azimuth from the radial profile, on two example meshes resting w.r.t their selected family, seen from above. Left: δr is each projected point’s distance from the footprint’s centre (the mean r̄). Middle: δr summed in 10◦ bins of θ (solid grey line) and its first two circular harmonics (Eq. (5)), each drawn at amplitude hk/π. Right: the mesh after Rhu = Rotz(−α), which puts the chosen direction on +x (red). Top: a spoon’s handle is an off-centre protrusion: h1 > h2, so α = argm1. papers.abstract: Neural networks in continual learning often lose plasticity: some neurons become inactive, while others fire almost constantly. This limits adaptation to shifting data and wastes capacity. Prior work mitigates this by periodically reinitializing low-utility units, but such resets can destroy previously learned features and do not proactively prevent low utility. We study a simple diagnostic measure: the firing rate of ReLU units, defined as the fraction of positive pre-activations. Low rates identify dead units, while very high rates indicate linearized, always-on units. Based on this view, we introduce a lightweight load-balancing mechanism that adjusts per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range. Across continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, firing-rate distributions explain differences in plasticity across a range of approaches, including well-known techniques such as L2 regularization and non-affine normalization, and load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on both benchmarks. The same mechanism carries over to reinforcement learning, improving Rainbow DQN on Atari over a LayerNorm baseline.
authors: Jan Robine, Marc H\"oftmann, Stefan Harmeling
bullets: Problem: Continual learning can produce dead or always-on neurons, reducing adaptability and wasting capacity.
Method: Adjust per-neuron activation thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range.
Finding: Firing-rate distributions serve as a diagnostic of plasticity across multiple continual-learning approaches.
Results: Load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, and improves Rainbow DQN on Atari over LayerNorm.
Scope: Demonstrated in supervised continual learning and reinforcement learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Continual ImageNet: Evolution of firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy with error bands (right), averaged over 10 runs. Standard training collapses neuron activity toward 0%, while BatchNorm, L2 regularization and CBP keep firing more balanced. The temporal alignment between balanced firing rates and rising accuracy is what connects the two; per-method findings are in the main text.

Figure 2: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy with error bands (right), averaged over 15 runs. Accuracy is relative to the from-scratch Resets baseline, which is the zero line. Continual training drives neurons gradually inactive, while resets and CBP keep firing patterns from collapsing, and accuracy follows those trends; per-method findings are in the main text.

Figure 13: Continual ImageNet: Effects of non-affine normalization on firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right). Non-affine BatchNorm + L2 clusters firing rate near 50%, while non-affine LayerNorm + L2 broadens the distribution across layers. Both configurations improve accuracy, with non-affine LayerNorm achieving the highest performance of all methods. Enforcing 50% via load balancing on top of non-affine LayerNorm tightens rates but lowers accuracy.

Figure 9: Continual ImageNet: Layer-wise firing-rate distributions over tasks. Rows correspond to methods, columns correspond to successive layers. Early layers stay active while later layers collapse in the baseline; CBP shows heterogeneous behavior; non-affine BN + L2 maintains near-balanced firing rates across layers.

Figure 7: Rainbow DQN: Human-normalized scores (0 = random, 1 = human) on 6 Atari games for four variants: the original baseline, a baseline with LayerNorm (LN), and load balancing at a 50% target and CBP instantiated on that LayerNorm agent (LB 50% @ LN and CBP @ LN). Curves show the mean over 5 random seeds and are smoothed with a time-weighted exponential moving average.

Figure 8: Rainbow DQN: Firing-rate distributions, one row per game and one column per agent, in the same order as Figure 7. The baseline collapses to very low rates in both games; LN lifts them part of the way; load balancing holds the hidden layers near the 50% target, with the residual mass at 0% and 100% coming from the value head, which is excluded by design. The contrast between the two games explains the accuracy result: LayerNorm alone already raises firing in BattleZone, leaving load balancing little to add, while in DemonAttack it does not.

Figure 4: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) for different load-balancing ranges, averaged over 15 runs with ±1 standard error bands; accuracy is relative to Resets. Loose bounds (5–95%) reproduce reset-like behavior with improved accuracy, while control near 50% yields further gains, surpassing resets and prior methods. The LB 50% panel concentrates nearly every neuron in a single bin, so it is dark apart from the line at 50%.

Figure 10: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Layer-wise firing-rate distributions over tasks. Continual training and CBP exhibit linearization in Block 2. Load balancing with a 95% upper limit prevents it, at the cost of some saturation at the limit in the early layers.

Figure 11: Continual ImageNet: From left to right: fraction of dormant neurons (threshold τd = 0.01), weight magnitudes, overall maximum spectral norm across layers, and effective rank (Lewandowski et al., 2025), over tasks. Dashed lines indicate variants built on a BatchNorm backbone (BN + L2, except L2 init + BN, which adds no further L2). Averaged over 5 runs with ±1 standard error bands.
Figure 19: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Layer-wise firing-rate distributions for all approaches.
Figure 15: Continual ImageNet: Test accuracy of additional baselines. Dashed lines indicate variants built on a BatchNorm backbone (BN + L2, except L2 init + BN, which adds no further L2).

Figure 12: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: From left to right: fraction of dormant neurons (threshold τd = 0.01), weight magnitudes, overall maximum spectral norm across layers, and effective rank (Lewandowski et al., 2025), over tasks. Averaged over 5 runs with ±1 standard error bands.

Figure 5: Entropy: Continual ImageNet (left) and class-incremental CIFAR-100 (right), with H(s), ∑ i H(si), and TC(s) computed on the test set, averaged over 3 random seeds. On continual ImageNet the three configurations are the Baseline, BN + L2, and BN + L2 with load balancing at 50% (“+ LB 50%”); on class-incremental CIFAR-100 they are the Baseline and load balancing at 5–95% and 50%.

Figure 6: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) for ReLU, LeakyReLU, and GELU, all based on the BN + L2 setup. In the right plot the dashed lines show the results for load balancing 50%.

Figure 3: Continual ImageNet: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) under BN + L2 with and without load balancing, averaged over 10 runs with ±1 standard error bands. Constraining neurons to intermediate regimes (40–60% or 50%) improves accuracy over both the unconstrained baseline and CBP.
Figure 18: Continual ImageNet: Layer-wise firing-rate distributions for all approaches.

Figure 14: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) under non-affine normalization and normalized skip connections; accuracy is relative to Resets, as in Figure 4. Both modifications steer firing rates toward balanced regimes and improve accuracy beyond resets and CBP.

Figure 17: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions of the first and second ReLU within all ResNet blocks. Left: Non-affine BatchNorm baseline; the second ReLU distribution is skewed. Right: Non-affine BatchNorm on the skip path before addition re-centers the second ReLU pre-activation, yielding a more symmetric distribution around 50%.

Table 4: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Final test accuracies averaged over tasks 15–20, with the standard error of the mean over 15 runs. The class order is drawn from the run’s seed and all methods use the same 15 seeds, so the last column reports the paired per-run difference against Resets — the from-scratch reference the accuracy panels are also plotted against. The gain from pairing is smaller here than on continual ImageNet (1.2–1.8× against 2–5×): that window is 100 nearly independent tasks, this one is 5 consecutive tasks whose difficulties are strongly correlated. Rows are ordered by accuracy, which is also the order of the paired difference. ∗ p < 0.05, ∗∗ p < 0.001, two-sided paired t-test, df = 14.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted to enhance the multimodal reasoning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods share a common limitation of Module-Level Credit Entanglement, in which the vision encoder, projector, and LLM modules are jointly optimized using the same advantage signals even when perceptual correctness and final-answer correctness differ. To address this limitation, we propose Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across model modules. Specifically, MSPO uses responses to perception checklists comprising auxiliary questions about visual information to derive an advantage for training the vision encoder. From these responses, MSPO computes the Confidence-aware Perception Reward (CaPR), using a perception sign obtained by thresholding checklist accuracy to determine reward direction and posterior confidence from a Beta distribution over latent perception accuracy to scale reward magnitude. We then derive the vision advantage through group-relative normalization of CaPR and scale it using main-task success rates. This advantage guides updates to the vision encoder, while the projector and LLM retain outcome-based GRPO updates. Extensive experiments on seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MSPO outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales.
authors: HuiSeong Cho, Jun Yeong Park, Yu Rang Park
bullets: Addresses module-level credit entanglement when visual perception and final-answer correctness diverge.
Uses auxiliary visual perception checklists to generate vision-training signals.
Computes confidence-aware perception rewards from checklist accuracy and Beta-distribution-based confidence.
Applies group-relative normalization and task-success scaling to form the vision advantage; projector and LLM use GRPO advantages.
Outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average across seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks at 3B and 7B scales.

papers.abstract: Robot teams can split workloads or combine complementary bodies, but only if each robot leaves the shared world in a state its teammate can use. Existing multi-robot benchmarks emphasize task allocation and skill sequencing, rarely testing whether the resulting physical states are usable. To evaluate collective physical capability, we introduce DeCoNav-Act, a benchmark for language-guided multi-robot mobile manipulation in a shared physics simulation. Its 350 homogeneous and 150 heterogeneous tasks, each verified by joint reference execution, span two coordination mechanisms: parallel workloads in shared space and physical dependencies in which one robot establishes a condition for a teammate to use. Beyond team success, DeCoNav-Act measures path efficiency and handoff coverage and success, and adds a diagnostic from verified pre-handoff states. Evaluating sensor-grounded adaptations of ASPIRE and RAX and our agent CoMoMa, we find that with GPT-5.6-luna no method completes a task, at most 8.8% of dependencies are reached, and even from pre-handoff states no handoff is completed; with GPT-6.1-sol, CoMoMa establishes the condition in 26.5% of trials, but only 4.1% succeed.
authors: Yunzi Wu, Sunyao Zhou, Xiaotao Zhang, Yucheng Deng, Yuehao Huang, Lin Qian, Xuanrui Cui, Xinhai Li, Chenjia Bai, Hongqing Chu, Xuelong Li

Measures team success, path efficiency, handoff coverage and success, plus verified pre-handoff-state diagnostics.
Evaluations show no complete tasks with GPT-5.6-luna; dependencies were reached in at most 8.8% of cases and no handoffs succeeded.
With GPT-6.1-sol, CoMoMa established dependency conditions in 26.5% of trials, but only 4.1% resulted in successful handoffs.

papers.abstract: High-resolution video matting requires accurate recovery of continuous alpha values, including fine hair, soft boundaries, and motion blur, yet dense alpha supervision remains scarce. Pretrained text-to-video diffusion transformers (DiTs) offer rich spatio-temporal priors, whereas existing generative video matting approaches typically route alpha predictions through RGB-trained VAE latents, which can attenuate fine details and introduce additional decoding overhead. We present TokenMatte, which adapts a pretrained video DiT into a single-pass, auxiliary-free RGB-to-alpha predictor with a pixel-native output interface. At its core is a single shared linear readout that maps each spatio-temporal token directly to its corresponding ($t \times p \times p$) block of alpha pixels, predicting spatial details and temporal variations within the same local video block. Tiling these blocks produces the full-resolution alpha sequence without a convolutional decoder or learned upsampling. The predicted alpha is supervised directly in pixel space, while the ground-truth alpha never enters the VAE, eliminating target-side alpha encoding and output-side VAE decoding. Leveraging the pretrained video prior, TokenMatte is trained using only existing public matting datasets, without additional data curation or auxiliary inputs at inference. Compared with a matched latent-output baseline, our pixel-native interface improves matting accuracy while achieving a 1.51$\times$ inference speedup. TokenMatte establishes a new auxiliary-free state of the art on VideoMatte, YouTubeMatte, and V-HIM60.
authors: Zanyi Wang, Dengyang Jiang, Fengfei Yu, Shilong Liu
bullets: Addresses scarce dense alpha supervision and detail loss from routing predictions through RGB-trained VAE latents.
Uses one shared linear readout to map each spatio-temporal token directly to a local block of alpha pixels.
Supervises alpha directly in pixel space, avoiding alpha VAE encoding, convolutional decoding, and learned upsampling.
Outperforms a matched latent-output baseline in accuracy and achieves a 1.51× inference speedup.
Reports auxiliary-free state-of-the-art results on VideoMatte, YouTubeMatte, and V-HIM60.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method Overview. From an RGB video, a frozen VAE encoder produces latent tokens and a pretrained T2V backbone runs one deterministic pass (τ = τ0, ϵ=0) to yield a spatio-temporal token field (Sec. 3.1). A shared linear head unfolds each token into its local block of alpha pixels (Sec. 3.2), supervised in pixel space with no alpha encoding or VAE decoding (Sec. 3.3).

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison with auxiliary-free and mask-guided methods. We compare TokenMatte with auxiliary-free RVM and GVM, and with mask-guided MatAnyone2 and VideoMaMa using SAM2 guidance. The SAM2 mask sequence is shown for reference, and colored boxes indicate the magnified regions on the right. While all methods recover the main foreground, RVM produces diffuse hair boundaries and the other baselines tend to smooth some thin strands. TokenMatte preserves finer and more separated hair structures without auxiliary mask guidance.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison with auxiliary-free methods. We compare TokenMatte with RVM and latent-based GVM across three video frames. The blue and orange boxes indicate regions magnified on the right. RVM produces diffuse alpha boundaries, while GVM exhibits over-smoothed predictions that blur fine structures and merge neighboring details. In contrast, TokenMatte preserves sharper boundaries and finer, more separated alpha structures without auxiliary inputs.

Figure 1. Latent-based vs. our native pixel-based training. (a) Latent supervision encodes the GT matte through a frozen VAE and supervises in latent space; the alpha target must survive a VAE round-trip, and the pixel objective only reaches the model through the decoder. (b) We never encode the alpha target: a readout module unfolds each token directly into pixels, supervised in pixel space. (c) Quality bottleneck—the GT matte incurs reconstruction error after a VAE round-trip, revealing an empirical ceiling for alpha reconstruction, especially on detail-heavy data (VideoMatte 3.50, V-HIM60 1.22, YouTubeMatte 0.54, MAD). (d) Speed bottleneck—removing the VAE-decode stage cuts per-clip latency from 576ms to 382ms, a 1.51× saving at equal depth.

Figure 7. Fast water spray. TokenMatte captures rapidly changing water structures and fine spray details from RGB input alone.

Figure 11. Complex foreground interaction. TokenMatte preserves the articulated foreground together with thin structures such as hair, ropes, and the moving weapon across temporally separated frames.

Figure 10. Soft emissive boundaries. TokenMatte captures the foreground together with soft, spatially varying alpha transitions around the glowing hand across frames.
Figure 9. Translucent tentacles. TokenMatte preserves thin tentacles and translucent structures across separated frames.

papers.title: TokenMatte: Unlocking T2V Diffusion Priors for Pixel-Native Video Matting

papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models has produced increasingly elaborate methods built on CLIP and on one shared principle: the zero-shot text classifier is the anchor, and labeled images only correct it. We argue that this principle reflects CLIP's visual features rather than a property of the task. We provide a simple Bayesian interpretation, in which a class name is worth exactly kappa = sigma^2 / tau^2 labeled images, the ratio between the visual spread of a class and the misalignment of its name. The Bayes classifier of this model counts text as kappa more samples. With modern frozen encoders, few-shot adaptation then reduces to a well-regularised convex probe. Specifically, we introduce TASP, a simple convex logistic regression on frozen features that incorporates class-name embeddings as weighted training examples and as a regularization prior. On the standard 11-dataset benchmark, TASP with frozen PE-Core-L features achieves 87.1% accuracy at 1 shot and 91.4% at 16 shots, outperforming state-of-the-art few-shot vision-language adaptation methods by 4.6 to 11.0 percentage points. While stronger representations explain much of this improvement, controlled comparisons on matched features show that existing frozen-encoder adaptation methods do not materially improve on this probe. We further find that the weight assigned to text matters more than how it is incorporated, and that combining self-supervised visual features with vision-language representations is most beneficial for weaker visual encoders. Together, these findings suggest that progress in few-shot vision-language adaptation depends more on representation quality and the appropriate use of text supervision than on increasingly complex adaptation mechanisms.
authors: Reda Bensaid, Ismail Ben Ayed, Fran\c{c}ois Leduc-Primeau, Vincent Gripon
bullets: Challenges the assumption that zero-shot text classifiers should always anchor adaptation; this may reflect CLIP’s visual features rather than the task itself.
Introduces a Bayesian view where text contributes an equivalent of κ = σ²/τ² labeled images, based on class variability and name misalignment.
Uses TASP: logistic regression on frozen visual features, incorporating class-name embeddings as weighted training examples and a regularization prior.
On an 11-dataset benchmark with frozen PE-Core-L features, TASP reaches 87.1% at 1 shot and 91.4% at 16 shots, outperforming prior methods by 4.6–11.0 percentage points.
Finds that text weighting matters more than its integration mechanism; gains rely substantially on representation quality, especially for weaker visual encoders.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a simple yet effective few-shot adaptation method for vision-language models, relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Text Is Just Another Shot in Vision-Language Models: Simple Probes on Frozen Encoders Do It
papers.tldr: TASP shows that few-shot vision-language adaptation can be reduced to a simple convex probe that treats class-name text as weighted additional examples, with strong performance from frozen encoders.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong results in arm-centric manipulation, yet humanoid whole-body control (WBC) requires dynamic balance and tightly coupled full-body coordination. Existing hierarchical humanoid VLAs typically decouple motion generation from physical execution, leaving tracking and balance errors unable to directly optimize the VLA generator. We propose DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T N1.7 with SONIC, a pretrained whole-body behavior foundation model. To enable execution-aware differentiable training, we replace the non-differentiable simulator with a learned, action-conditioned world model, allowing multi-step body-execution losses to backpropagate through the frozen whole-body controller and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T improves average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2% to 71.7%), demonstrating that execution-aware gradients effectively align high-level motion generation with closed-loop whole-body dynamics.
authors: Sichen Wu, Qian Sun, Mengfan Liu, Weikai Qin, Bike Zhu, Hesheng Wang

papers.abstract: Can artificial intelligence reproduce the economic dynamics that emerge as households, firms and governments interact and adapt through markets and institutions? To answer this question, we define an economic world model (EWM) as an agent's internal representation of how an economic system works, enabling counterfactual simulation and decision-making under resource constraints. We then propose a general framework for studying EWMs that links three tasks: simulating agent behaviour, learning economic transitions and systematically evaluating the dynamics. As an initial implementation, we learn household policies from microeconomic data and calibrate a structural economic transition model using macroeconomic data, linking individual decisions to aggregate dynamics. Our micro-to-macro evaluation framework compares simulated individual actions and group distributions with observed microdata and assesses macroeconomic dynamics through forecasting and counterfactual experiments. Results show that simulated and observed household consumption distributions overlap by 94.9%, while EWM forecasts closely track real GDP and several other aggregate levels. In government-borrowing counterfactuals, the EWM reproduces the benchmark life-cycle model's short-run transmission from borrowing to consumption. For ex ante planning, the EWM enables an LLM agent to achieve 10.29% higher simulated GDP under the epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions. This initial EWM is only a starting point. We invite economists and AI researchers to build a stronger EWM together. Economists can contribute richer economic models and knowledge, while AI researchers can develop stronger data-driven methods for simulating agent behaviour and learning economic transitions. Together, we aim not only to reproduce real economic dynamics, but also to discover and test new mechanisms that support better decisions and benefit society.
authors: Qirui Mi, Yujia Ming, Bo Li, Haifeng Zhang
bullets: Defines an EWM as an internal representation of economic systems that supports counterfactual simulation and resource-constrained decisions.

Simulated household consumption distributions overlap observed distributions by 94.9%, and forecasts closely track real GDP and other aggregates.
An LLM using the EWM achieves 10.29% higher simulated GDP under an epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions; the implementation is presented as an initial starting point.

papers.abstract: Deep search is a critical capability for agents tackling complex, open-ended tasks, where solving a problem requires iterative information gathering, query reformulation, and evidence-based verification rather than a single retrieval step. To address these requirements, we present Bathys 9B and 27B deep search agents built around a training framework that spans verifiable question synthesis, post-training, and online reinforcement learning (RL) under context compression. Our high-quality data construction ensures both search depth and reliability: each clue is reformulated as an indirect reference requiring independent retrieval, and retained evidence chains enable verification that the clues jointly determine a unique answer. Curated trajectories underpin a pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO), and Compaction-Managed Group Sequence Policy Optimization (CM-GSPO): SFT provides a stable foundation for tool use over long horizons and query reformulation; KTO uses binary feedback on trajectories to improve the selection of answers grounded in evidence; CM-GSPO optimizes execution sub-trajectories with length-normalized likelihood ratios on the recorded rollout contexts and reweights sub-trajectory advantages to correct the extra weighting introduced by independently averaging sub-trajectory losses. Bathys 9B and 27B attain 66.51% and 80.49% on BrowseComp, respectively, under an evaluation protocol with trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Shengyou Yuan, Nang Yuan, Ming Ma, Zelin Xiao, Lin Zhou, Siyuan Luo, Jiaqi Su, Chengrui Wu, Tiankuo Yao, Nairong Zheng, Cong Pang, Jiapeng Luo
bullets: Targets complex open-ended questions requiring multi-step search rather than one-shot retrieval.

Reports BrowseComp scores of 66.51% for Bathys 9B and 80.49% for Bathys 27B.
Evaluation includes trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.

papers.abstract: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.
authors: Wenjie Deng, Zijian Tu, Xueyin Zhou, Huayi Wang, Zhuoyun Du, Mingyu Chen, Haochao Ying, Jian Wu

Conditioned on the request and patient evidence, the reasoner selects or revises an action, which an independent geometry engine materializes and verifies.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.
authors: Hongjia Liu, Dacheng Zhou, Minghao Fu, Chuanjun Guo, Tianze Wang, Qingtao Liu, He Wang, Li Yi
bullets: Uses robot demonstrations to jointly learn an actor, action-conditioned world model, and bootstrapped critic.
Predicts endpoint visual latents, proprioception, reward, and continuation for action chunks, avoiding intermediate video-frame generation.
Adapts the world model and critic on real rollouts, then improves the actor with imagined-rollout PPO or critic-guided best-of-N selection.
Outperforms large-scale VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and reaches 75% average success on two real-world tasks versus 45% for π₀.₅.
World-model accuracy and speed, plus ablations, support jointly learning dynamics and value for better policies.

The backbone θ predicts visual latents and proprioception at the action-chunk endpoint, conditioned on the observed context and clean actions. papers.abstract: We were surprised to find that leading end-to-end driving models across major paradigms, despite scoring close to human drivers on NAVSIM, cannot reliably make a simple 90-degree turn in photorealistic closed-loop simulators. To investigate why, we build LaWanle, a benchmark of turns drawn from three such simulators. Driving each turn from several starts, we find that the same model passes it from one start and fails it from another, and that the two drives look alike until they enter the junction. Rotating the car by a few degrees at the junction entry can fail a turn it otherwise passes. Conversely, a slight heading correction to the plans can rescue about half of the failed turns we tested. Such errors arise when a model drives by itself, so we post-train an open-source lane-keeping model with closed-loop DAgger on its lateral path. Training 5% of its parameters is enough to raise its turn pass rate from 19% to 76%. The gain transfers to the two other benchmarks, where the policy also scores among the leading models. Further fine-tuning on recovery data repairs the deviations it is trained on but, against a control trained equally long, improves turns on none of the three benchmarks, and every variant stays far below a human driver.
authors: Chengzhi Gao, Junzhe Gao, Yongzhi Liu, Weichao Zhuang, Weilong Hu, Taonian Liang, Guodong Yin
bullets: Models that score near humans on NAVSIM often fail simple turns in photorealistic closed-loop simulators.
The same turn may pass or fail depending on the starting position, with failures emerging only after entering the junction.
Small vehicle rotations at junction entry can cause failure; slight plan-heading corrections rescue about half of tested failures.
Closed-loop DAgger on lateral paths raises an open-source lane-keeping model’s turn pass rate from 19% to 76% after training 5% of its parameters.
Recovery-data fine-tuning does not improve benchmark turns beyond a matched control, and all variants remain well below human performance.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.

papers.abstract: Complex cooperative tasks require coordinated multi-agent behavior. Offline generative policies learn expressive cooperative behaviors from trajectories but remain limited by fixed datasets. Online reinforcement learning can improve them through environment interaction. However, fine-tuning flow policies is difficult because action likelihoods are hard to compute. We propose TeamFlowRL, a two-stage framework that pretrains multi-agent flow policies offline and fine-tunes them online. We formulate team policy optimization over the complete denoising trajectories of decentralized flow policies, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. The resulting objective weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage and clips each ratio separately, aligning local policy updates with the common team return. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, TeamFlowRL improves every offline initialization, with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score. It also achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning across 6 bimanual tasks.
