papers.abstract: Dynamic obstacle avoidance is essential for safely deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments, where rapidly approaching objects require immediate evasive responses. Recent advances in reflexive evasion have focused primarily on quadrupeds, which typically rely on large-scale whole-body maneuvers. In contrast, humanoids can exploit their rich body articulation to evade through small, localized body adjustments. By moving threatened body regions without repositioning the entire body, these responses may require less execution time and less surrounding free space. However, local adjustments can alter mass distribution or support conditions, making it challenging to achieve rapid evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. To this end, we propose BARE (Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion), a humanoid reflexive evasion framework guided by human motion priors that enables rapid local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. A risk-guided motion adapter is designed to select reference motions from a retargeted human evasive motion library based on the threatened body region and to adjust their temporal phases based on collision urgency, allowing the robot to reach evasive postures before potential contact. Conditioned on the adapted reference and link-level collision risk, a reflexive evasion policy learns through reinforcement learning to coordinate local body adjustments with whole-body stabilization. We validate BARE in simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating its ability to perform targeted local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $\pi_{0.5}$. papers.abstract: Block floating-point (BFP) quantization is widely adopted for efficient low-bit large language model (LLM) inference, where the choice of block scales plays a critical role in quantization accuracy. HiFloat4 (HiF4) employs a hierarchical scale encoding scheme consisting of a global E6M2 scale and two levels of binary scale extensions. However, its conventional rounding rule and fixed scale extension thresholds may not fully capture the statistical characteristics of the quantized tensors in practice, leading to suboptimal scale representations. In this work, we propose HiCal, an offline calibration approach that improves HiF4 quantization accuracy by refining the encoding decisions across all three scale levels. Specifically, we introduce a calibrated rounding bias for the Level-1 E6M2 scale and optimize the scale-extension thresholds at Levels 2 and 3 based on the empirical distributions of local group magnitudes. The resulting calibration parameters are determined offline and remain fixed during inference, while the hierarchical encoding continues to adapt to individual blocks through their local values. This design eliminates the need for per-block multi-candidate scale search while preserving the original deterministic HiF4 encoding procedure. Experiments across five synthetic and real activation distributions show that the proposed method reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%-23.50% relative to the original HiF4 scheme, including a 13.00% reduction on real Qwen3-8B activations. End-to-end evaluations across six benchmarks further show average-score improvements of 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, without per-block multi-candidate search during inference.
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang, Yanzhao Li, Hui Dong, Sifan Cheng, Mingen Zheng, Hui Wang

Improves average end-to-end benchmark scores by 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively.

The three components highlighted in red—the E6M2 rounding rule and the Level-2 and Level-3 magnitude thresholds—are the parameters calibrated in this work; all other operations follow the original HiF4 procedure.

papers.abstract: Collecting diverse real-world manipulation demonstrations is costly, motivating the use of simulation to augment existing demonstrations for robot policy learning. When objects, layouts, or robots change, transferring motions from a source demonstration can produce behavior that is semantically implausible or physically infeasible in the new setting. We introduce RoboRecast, an agentic optimization framework that preserves the interactions required by the source task while jointly optimizing the simulated scene and robot motion to make those interactions executable in the target setting. When an interaction fails, the agent uses simulation feedback to diagnose the cause, revise the relevant scene or motion parameters, and test whether the revision resolves the failure. This flexibility allows RoboRecast to generate synthetic data from both human and robot demonstrations and to adapt them to new layouts, objects, and robot embodiments. When target demonstrations are available, adding RoboRecast data improves policy success on both real-world single-arm and simulated bimanual tasks. Even without demonstrations in the target configuration, RoboRecast adapts source demonstrations to support policy learning with new objects or robot embodiments.
authors: Yushi Long, Juzhan Xu, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Yin Chen, Sida Peng, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited diversity of real-world manipulation demonstrations when layouts, objects, or robots change.
Uses agentic, diagnosis-driven optimization to revise scene and motion parameters after failed interactions.
Generates synthetic data from both human and robot demonstrations across new layouts, objects, and robot embodiments.
Improves policy success on real-world single-arm and simulated bimanual tasks when target demonstrations are available.
Can support policy learning in new configurations even without target demonstrations.

papers.abstract: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight ($\sim$67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.

bullets: Targets unified parsing of text, tables, and formulas with high accuracy and throughput.
Uses bounded recursive self-improvement with external expert consensus, visual verification, and factorized synthesis to create reliable supervision.

Introduces PTPv2, a ~67M-parameter parallel draft module that preserves token-for-token equivalence with autoregressive decoding.
On OmniDocBenchv1.6, reports 96.45 overall and 98.57 formula CDM; PTPv2 provides up to 2.96× single-request speedup and 2.36× batched throughput on one H20 GPU.

papers.abstract: Virtual staining synthesizes special-stain images from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), extending the information available from an existing digital slide. However, a fixed inference rule can leave available real target-stain references unused, limiting query-specific correction of stain appearance at deployment. Test-time adaptation (TTA) provides a mechanism for this reference-guided, query-specific refinement without retraining the generator. We therefore propose FewRef-5, a reference-assisted TTA method for virtual staining built on StainPromptInversion. We extract tissue-masked optical-density means and standard deviations from five real Masson's trichrome (MAS) training patches and average them into a fixed stain target. A scheduled statistic-matching loss introduces this target into per-query visual-prompt optimization alongside our edge/Gram consistency penalties and the inherited reconstruction objectives. The target remains unchanged across queries, avoiding recursive dependence on earlier generated outputs while the pretrained generator stays fixed. On recorded H&E-to-MAS outputs for 1,989 queries, FewRef-5 reduces target-set FID from 183.201 to 166.904 and increases source-referenced SSIM from 0.92787 to 0.94996 relative to our Edge+Gram variant. Source PSNR and MS-SSIM decrease, showing an endpoint trade-off rather than uniformly better reconstruction.
authors: Wenxuan Wang, Liwen Wang, Mingmin Wu, Xingbo Dong, Zhe Jin
bullets: Addresses unused real target-stain references and limited query-specific correction in fixed-rule virtual staining.
Applies fixed-reference test-time adaptation on StainPromptInversion with tissue-masked optical-density statistics averaged from five MAS patches.
Optimizes per-query visual prompts using scheduled statistic matching plus edge/Gram consistency and inherited reconstruction objectives; the generator remains fixed.
Across 1,989 H&E-to-MAS queries, target-set FID improves from 183.201 to 166.904 and source-referenced SSIM from 0.92787 to 0.94996 versus Edge+Gram.
PSNR and MS-SSIM decrease, indicating a trade-off rather than uniformly improved reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Multi-vehicle collaborative perception can use observations from different perspectives to alleviate the problems of occlusion and limited sensing range. However, missing echoes and false echoes caused by bad weather will reduce the quality of single-vehicle features and affect collaborative detection. LiDAR provides richer geometric information, and 4D Radar has strong weather adaptability. The complementarity of the two provides the possibility to improve perception under degraded observations. However, how to adjust cross-modal repair according to the current observation conditions and how to reasonably integrate multi-vehicle features whose reliability still differs after repair are still problems that need to be solved. To this end, we propose CoReQ, a condition-aware repair and quality-guided collaborative perception framework. For the former, the condition-guided bidirectional cross-modal repair module (CBCR) extracts vehicle-level observation conditions from point cloud occupancy, density and feature statistics, and adjusts the bidirectional correction of LiDAR and Radar features accordingly. For the latter, we combine local reliability assessment with collaborative weighting: first, the task-aware quality estimation module (TaQE) uses the classification and positioning information of the EMA teacher to construct a supervision target and predict the spatial quality of the repaired features; then, the condition and quality guided fusion module (CoQF) matches the quality information with the content, and the observation conditions of both parties are jointly used for multi-vehicle feature weighted fusion. Experiments on V2X-R and V2X-Radar-C show that the framework is competitive under a variety of observation conditions, achieving significant gains in AP@0.7 on V2X-R under snowy conditions, and achieving the highest AP among the compared V2X-Radar-C methods.
authors: Ziwei Guo, Lingzhi Li, Jin Wang, Yunjiang Xu, Yupeng Ouyang, Benyuan Yang, Yujun Shi
bullets: Addresses missing and false echoes that degrade single-vehicle features and collaborative detection in adverse weather.
CBCR uses occupancy, density, and feature statistics to adapt bidirectional LiDAR–Radar feature repair to observation conditions.
TaQE estimates spatial quality of repaired features using task-aware teacher supervision from classification and localization information.
CoQF combines feature quality and observation conditions to weight multi-vehicle feature fusion by reliability.
On V2X-R and V2X-Radar-C, CoReQ is competitive across conditions, with significant snowy-condition AP@0.7 gains on V2X-R and the highest AP among compared V2X-Radar-C methods.

papers.abstract: A common occurrence in Large Language Models (LLMs) is the emergence of so-called massive activations. This phenomenon is well known in the literature and has been connected to attention sinks, representational compression, as well as signal propagation. However, the reasons and consequences for their appearance are not yet well understood. In this paper, we explain the role of massive activations in deep learning by showing that they are connected to the region migration phenomenon in delayed robustness. Under the spline theoretic interpretation of deep networks, we show that massive activations push the representations away from the nonlinearity boundaries of the network, decreasing the complexity of its input-output map around data points. Furthermore, we uncover for the first time that this phenomenon is not unique to transformers and actually appears in a number of common architectures performing simple supervised learning tasks. We validate this connection through extensive experiments on a diverse set of architectures including residual MLP, ResNet18, Vision Transformers and GPT and datasets including MNIST, CIFAR10, Imagenette and Shakespeare Text. We consistently observe that massive activations and region migration co-occur with adversarial robustness. Furthermore, we illustrate that this connection holds in the large-scale pretraining of LLMs by showing that the rise of massive activations in LLMs closely tracks the adversarial accuracy of the model under perturbations of the token embeddings.
authors: Tigran Fahradyan, Riccardo Ali, Sergio Calvo-Ordo\~nez, Jos\'e Miguel Hern\'andez-Lobato, Pietro Li\`o, \'Alvaro Arroyo
bullets: Connects massive activations in LLMs to region migration, a phenomenon associated with delayed adversarial robustness.
Uses a spline-theoretic view to explain how massive activations reduce local network complexity around data points.
Shows the phenomenon is not transformer-specific, appearing across residual MLPs, ResNet18, vision transformers, and GPT.
Experiments across image and language tasks consistently find co-occurrence between massive activations, region migration, and adversarial robustness.
During large-scale LLM pretraining, the growth of massive activations tracks robustness to perturbations of token embeddings.

papers.abstract: Adding compliance to robot hands results in higher grasp quality and robust contact with the environment. Soft hands are inherently compliant, but are typically more complex to control and model than rigid equivalents. We extend prior work on soft-rigid hybrid robot fingers into a five-fingered dexterous gripper --- an integrated tendon-driven hand that is highly compliant and controllable. Structural compliance combined with a rigid skeleton, when realized in a five-fingered hand, allow us to use linear control to achieve soft-grasping generality. We evaluate the use of this hand in a variety of teleoperated manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the overall mechanical design and control strategy. Our contributions include: (1) Mechanical design of the a five-fingered Soft-Rigid Hybrid Hand, composed of 12 active degrees of freedom, demonstrating a high degree on generalization enabled by the soft-rigid architecture, with our gripper, able to complete 28 of the 33 (84.8\%) grasp postures in the human range. (2) Precise, high bandwidth (up to 1432deg/s extension speed, compared with 700deg/s for the equivalent human joint). (3) Position and task space controllers for the soft-rigid hybrid finger and whole hand. (4) A teleoperation framework for control of this hand, as well as demonstrations of its efficacy in a variety of grasping and manipulation tasks Further tests illustrate the hand's advantages in completing non-rigid manipulation tasks, such as picking up thin deformable objects (such as a dollar bill or folding cloth) as well as in interfacing with soft or delicate targets.
authors: Chao Liu, Wil J. Norton, Brandon Romero, Daniela Rus
bullets: The hand uses a soft-rigid hybrid architecture to improve grasp compliance while retaining simpler linear control.
Its 12 active degrees of freedom reproduce 28 of 33 human-range grasp postures (84.8%).
Position- and task-space controllers support precise, high-bandwidth finger and whole-hand control, with extension speeds up to 1432°/s.
A teleoperation framework demonstrates grasping and manipulation across varied tasks, including thin deformable and delicate objects.
The abstract focuses on demonstrated task effectiveness; broader performance limits are not specified.

papers.abstract: Socially-aware robot person following (RPF) requires a mobile robot to follow a designated person in dynamic human environments while maintaining target identity, avoiding obstacles and pedestrians, and preserving socially comfortable formations. Existing benchmarks only partially evaluate this coupled problem: embodied visual tracking benchmarks emphasize target visibility with limited social interaction, person re-identification benchmarks study perception without closed-loop control, and motion-planning benchmarks often assume ground-truth target and pedestrian states. We introduce Follow-Bench 2.0, an end-to-end 3D benchmark for evaluating socially-aware RPF under coupled perception--planning challenges. Built in Unreal Engine, Follow-Bench 2.0 provides difficulty-leveled scenarios with diverse pedestrian flows, lighting and weather conditions, cluttered layouts, bottlenecks, queueing behaviors, distractors, and temporary target occlusions. The benchmark supports modular perception--planning pipelines, end-to-end visual policies, and foundation-model-based active trackers under a unified closed-loop protocol. It further evaluates both back- and side-following configurations and reports safety--comfort metrics covering task success, target visibility, target recovery, social-space intrusion, following formation, and motion smoothness. Experiments show that RPF-oriented modular pipelines substantially outperform current end-to-end visual policies on close and socially comfortable following, but also reveal that socially-aware RPF remains far from solved in interaction-heavy environments and especially in side-following. Follow-Bench 2.0 therefore provides a diagnostic platform for studying how perception errors, occlusions, crowd interactions, and following configurations jointly affect robot person following.

papers.abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale, Expert Parallelism (EP) becomes increasingly important for distributing experts across devices. However, the resulting token dispatch and combine operations can become a major bottleneck during inference. Overlapping these communication phases with computation is constrained by the sequential dependencies of standard MoE architectures. We introduce BRAID-MoE, an architecture that pairs laddered residual connections with early routing to relax these dependencies. Laddered residuals enable each expert combine to be deferred to the following block, while early routing computes the next routing decision from the pre-combine residual, with experts still receiving the updated post-combine hidden state. This creates an extended communication window in which the preceding combine and next dispatch can execute back-to-back on a dedicated communication stream, overlapping attention computation. On Qwen3-shaped MoEs with 0.4B-A0.1B and 2.5B-A0.5B parameters, BRAID closely matches sequential training at matched compute, with validation-loss increases of only 1% and 0.5%, respectively. We further demonstrate that existing MoE checkpoints can be adapted to BRAID with limited additional training, largely recovering their original accuracy. On a converted Qwen3-30B-A3B model, BRAID achieves speedups of up to 1.29$\times$ in prefill and 1.37$\times$ in decode, and at least 1.12$\times$ across diverse workloads and EP configurations on one or two four-H100 nodes. It outperforms competing overlap strategies in all tested settings, with the strongest gains when communication is a major latency bottleneck and its duration approaches the available computation window. These results demonstrate that early routing enables more effective communication-computation overlap in MoE inference at a modest cost in model quality.
authors: John Zarka (MLIA), Danyal Ahmed (MLIA), Eugene Belilovsky (DIRO, MILA), Edouard Oyallon (MLIA)
bullets: Targets token dispatch and combine bottlenecks caused by sequential dependencies in expert parallelism.

On converted Qwen3 models, reports up to 1.29× prefill and 1.37× decode speedups, with at least 1.12× across tested workloads and configurations.

papers.abstract: Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational drift provide limited insight into how these changes affect model decisions. We therefore evaluate latent knowledge stability across visual and linguistic elicitation conditions from two complementary perspectives: answer preference and internal support. Specifically, we devise the margin retention score (MRS), which measures the first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin over competing options across conditions and assesses how changes in latent knowledge representations affect this margin. We also present latent knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which evaluates reference-correct items by comparing internal support profiles constructed using the margin gradient under the reference condition, which jointly reflects changes in how internal support is distributed and changes in total support magnitude. We further construct MMStableBench, comprising 19,452 knowledge items (facts), each probing the same latent knowledge across varied image viewpoints, semantically equivalent question formulations, and answer-option permutations. Experiments across 15 MLLMs show that MRS and KSS reveal latent knowledge instability not captured by accuracy, while an MRS-inspired regularizer further improves the generalization of edited latent knowledge.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates. However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision-language-action (VLA) models. By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations. Specifically, a visual-action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution. To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent and uses it to query memory. The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence. MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0. Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks. The code will be made publicly available.

papers.abstract: Sol-Attn (Sparsifying online attention) combines sparse exact computation with low-cost representative approximation to accelerate training-free inference in diffusion video models. However, intra-block attention can focus on only a few tokens. While preserving these key interactions exactly, the block-level decision incurs the cost of evaluating many low-response members. We propose Sol$^{3}$, a training-free hierarchical sparse attention method that further refines how exact computations are allocated. First, we introduce Gaussian-guided hierarchical routing, which determines the scope of exact computation step by step, from blocks to tokens, using statistical thresholds at each level. Only a subset of members within Mixed blocks that require refinement is selected for exact computation, while representative terms approximate the remaining members. We further design heterogeneous routing statistics that combine block-center correlations with variations in Key and Value within blocks to identify blocks that are difficult to approximate. Among these Mixed blocks, we uniformly compare raw token relevance to select members requiring exact computation. Experiments on video generation, audio-video co-generation, and world simulation tasks demonstrate that Sol$^{3}$ achieves 86% attention sparsity and delivers a $3.07\times$ attention speedup while preserving quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/FofGofx/sol3.
authors: Guoxin Fan, Weilun Feng, Chuanguang Yang, Mingqiang Wu, Xiaokun Liu, Jitao Lu, Zhulin An, Libo Huang, Boyu Diao, Di Gao, Yongjun Xu

Experiments across video generation, audio-video co-generation, and world simulation report 86% attention sparsity and a 3.07× attention speedup while preserving quality.

papers.abstract: Segmenting a 3D object into semantically meaningful parts requires joint reasoning about geometric structure and semantic context. Pretrained 3D experts provide spatially grounded region proposals, while 2D experts provide semantic cues for identifying object parts. The challenge is to integrate these complementary capabilities into a framework that can both produce meaningful part segmentations and progressively refine them. We present PartAgent, a training-free agentic framework for 3D part segmentation built upon two complementary modules: (i) Structural-Semantic Expert Integration combines regions predicted by the 3D expert with multiview semantic evidence from the 2D expert through image-to-surface correspondences, constructing compositional part partitions at multiple granularities. (ii) Observation-Driven Closed-Loop Partition Refinement observes the current partition and its supporting evidence to select targeted inspection, evidence repair, composition, or reselection actions. It verifies proposed changes and uses the updated state and action outcomes to guide subsequent decisions. On PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT, PartAgent achieves 68.41 mIoU, outperforming the strongest competing method by 8.53 points. Across 3DCoMPaT200, PartNeXt, PartNetE, and PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartAgent achieves the highest mIoU on each dataset, averaging 69.36 across the four datasets, 7.28 points above the highest mean among competing methods.
authors: Yang Cao, Zhe Zhu, Yiheng Zhang, Zhengqiang Zhang, Haoyuan Li, Le Wan, Dan Xu
bullets: Combines spatially grounded 3D region proposals with semantic cues from 2D experts via image-to-surface correspondences.
Builds compositional part partitions at multiple granularities through Structural-Semantic Expert Integration.
Uses observation-driven actions—including inspection, evidence repair, composition, and reselection—to refine and verify segmentations.
Achieves 68.41 mIoU on PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT and the highest mIoU across four evaluated datasets, averaging 69.36.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of PartAgent. (A) Structural–Semantic Expert Integration (SSEI) uses multiview semantic evidence to refine 3D expert regions and combine them into candidate segmentations at multiple granularities, then selects an initial segmentation P0. (B) Observation-Driven Closed-Loop Partition Refinement (CLR) uses a VLM to examine the current segmentation and its supporting evidence and choose targeted actions. Proposed segmentation updates are verified before adoption, and feedback guides subsequent actions.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an agentic framework for 3D part segmentation that integrates 3D and 2D experts, relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial understanding for embodied agents.
papers.title: PartAgent: Agentic 3D Part Segmentation via Expert Integration and Closed-Loop Refinement
papers.tldr: PartAgent is a training-free 3D part-segmentation framework that integrates 3D geometry with multiview 2D semantics and iteratively refines partitions through closed-loop agentic actions.

papers.abstract: Text-to-motion generation has made great progress in capturing what action to perform, yet it remains limited in controlling how that action is executed. For example, when only the height word of a kick request changes, none of the tested state-of-the-art methods reaches all three of knee, waist and head height. The other words of a caption usually imply an attribute such as height, so neither the training loss nor the standard metrics require a model to use the word that states it. A model has to use this word only when it alone separates two otherwise identical captions. We introduce MinPair, which creates such caption pairs from real motion clips. It starts from rule-based motion descriptors that measure the 3D body motion of each clip. From these descriptors a language model writes MinPair captions, timed body-part captions that say how each body part moves. The same descriptors show in which attributes two clips of the same action differ. A measured minimal pair joins the true caption of one clip with an altered copy in which only one attribute takes the value measured in the other clip. A contrastive pair loss then requires a diffusion denoiser to reconstruct the clip more accurately from its true caption than from the altered copy. Training needs no synthetic motion and inference stays unchanged. Control is tested on 22 target tasks and on caption edits that each change one attribute. MinPair captions alone help motions reach their targets and improve the standard metrics M2M, R@3 and FID, yet a model trained on them still ignores most single-word edits. The pair loss raises the share of followed template edits from 11% to 60%, while the standard metrics do not improve further. With body-part captions, MinPair reaches more targets than state-of-the-art methods that were trained on up to 99 times more motion data.
authors: Lennart Schiweck, Crist\'obal Curio
bullets: Targets the gap between generating the correct action and controlling how that action is performed, such as kick height.
Builds minimal caption pairs from real motion clips using rule-based 3D motion descriptors and language-model-generated body-part captions.
Adds a contrastive pair loss that favors reconstructing motion from the true caption over a minimally altered caption; inference remains unchanged.
On 22 target tasks, the pair loss raises followed template edits from 11% to 60%, while standard metrics do not improve further.
Body-part captions reach more targets than prior methods trained on up to 99× more motion data.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. Top, training. (1) A script measures quantities in a real clip, here the left wrist height. A language model writes them into a timed part caption and a further call judges it against the measurements. (2) A template pair copies the true caption with the value of a partner clip of the same action, here hip height. A free-form pair rewords a short span after a measured difference such as the elbow bend and is checked against the measurements. (3) Both captions condition the same denoiser on the same noisy motion. The pair loss asks the true caption for the smaller error inside the caption’s time window (shaded). The curves in (3) are illustrative. Bottom, the part-track denoiser of Sec. 3.1, shown for frame u. Only the text encoders are frozen.

Figure 3. Caption edits. Each block changes one attribute in the part captions of a held-out test clip (blue to magenta) under the same sampling noise. Elbow and knee are free-form edits, the others template edits. Turn and tempo show the pelvis path, the numbers the measured value. Over all test edits of these six kinds MinPair follows 83, 49, 72, 53, 48 and 43%, FrankenMotion at most 3%. Each block shows a clean edit with a large requested change whose motions come close to the requested values.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses fine-grained control in text-to-motion generation using measured minimal pairs, a key challenge in robot learning and manipulation for precise action execution.
papers.title: MinPair: Measured Minimal Pairs for Fine-Grained Control in Text-to-Motion Generation
papers.tldr: MinPair improves fine-grained text-to-motion control by training diffusion models on measured minimal caption pairs, substantially increasing their ability to follow single-attribute edits.

papers.abstract: Aligning inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals with text enables zero-shot activity recognition across wearable devices. A worn device's signal depends on its setup, the combination of body site and mounting. Leading IMU-language models make their encoders invariant to the mounting, which also discards the device's orientation relative to the body, such as the direction of gravity that separates sitting, standing and lying. We introduce SetCon, which replaces full invariance with selective invariance. It estimates each device's mounting on its known body site from a few unlabeled windows and conditions its encoder on this estimate. Because the mounting stays nearly fixed while the device is worn, the moving body serves as a calibration target. Both calibration and representation learning are supervised by 3D human motion, since one movement can be simulated under many known sensor setups. At test time, a class is represented by its name or by an anchor, which averages the text embeddings of the name and of activity descriptions and needs no labeled window. A language model built on the frozen encoder also answers how and in what order a movement is performed. Trained only on IMU simulated from the same Nymeria motion capture as AnyMo, SetCon reaches 56.6% mean zero-shot accuracy on 13 real datasets with class names and 65.3% with anchors, against 41.8% and 46.7% for AnyMo.
authors: Lennart Schiweck, Alaa Saleh, Crist\'obal Curio
bullets: Mounting affects IMU signals and provides orientation cues important for distinguishing activities such as sitting, standing, and lying.
The method estimates a device’s mounting from a few unlabeled windows and conditions the encoder on this setup.
3D human motion supervises both calibration and representation learning by simulating movements under varied sensor setups.
Class representations use either activity names or label-free anchors combining names with activity descriptions.
On 13 real datasets, SetCon achieves 56.6% mean zero-shot accuracy with class names and 65.3% with anchors, compared with AnyMo’s 41.8% and 46.7%.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SetCon. The top row shows how the graph encoder, a spatio-temporal graph network over the body sites, reads a device. Every sample is rotated so that gravity points up and a calibrator estimates the setup reference Q̂ (orange) from unlabeled windows and the body site, so that the encoder also receives gravity in the segment frame. In the bottom row, stage 1 learns how a movement appears under a target setup and stage 2 aligns the encoder with captions under calibrator errors from an error bank. The weights stay fixed at test.

Figure 3. Embeddings of UCI-HAR. Each panel shows the first two principal components of one model’s embeddings of the scored windows, with the first seed in (c) and (d). Lying mixes with sitting in (b) and (c) but forms its own cluster in (d).
Table 2. Ablations. Mean-13 accuracy (%) with six random context windows (Tab. 1, third row). Mean ± sd over three seeds. Free answers are judged against the class names (Sec. 4.4).
Table 3. Accuracy per motion group. Mean class accuracy (%) with class names over Mean-13 classes, grouped by name. SetCon uses six random context windows (three seeds, mean ± sd).

Table 1. Zero-shot classification. Mean-13 accuracy and macro-F1 (%) with class names and anchors, plus the Mean-13 accuracy of the class-mean readout (Sec. 4.2). The calibrator estimates the reference from unlabeled context windows of each device, never scored. In the last row it chooses six of twelve context windows. The first three rows share their scored windows. On the last row’s scored windows, UniMTS reaches 41.4 and 43.2 and AnyMo 41.8 and 46.7 with names and anchors. papers.selection_reason: Proposes SetCon for setup-conditioned IMU-language learning using 3D human motion, directly addressing sensor setup invariance for embodied agents and learning from human video data.
papers.title: SetCon: Setup-Conditioned IMU-Language Learning from 3D Human Motion
papers.tldr: SetCon improves zero-shot IMU activity recognition by conditioning language-aligned representations on each device’s estimated mounting setup rather than enforcing full mounting invariance.

papers.abstract: Real-world generative problems in biology, medical imaging, or robotics, rarely come with perfectly paired source and target distributions. While unbalanced Optimal Transport (uOT) provides a robust framework to bridge unpaired datasets via minimum-length paths in probability space, existing formulations based on the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry introduce a structural bias toward high density regions, often triggering mode collapse. We introduce Contact unbalanced Optimal Transport (CuOT), a novel uOT formulation grounded in contact geometry that decouples density transport direction from mass growth to eliminate structural bias. This allows CuOT to adapt sampling steps to the local data structure, naturally reducing step sizes in high-density regions to prevent overshooting and ensuring stable convergence. The result is a stable, scalable path-length minimization solver that consistently outperforms WFR-based methods on biological dynamics reconstruction, unpaired image-to-image translation, and video generation.
authors: Andrea Testa, S{\o}ren Hauberg, Andras Gabor Kupcsik, Tamim Asfour, Leonel Rozo
bullets: Targets unpaired source and target distributions in biology, medical imaging, robotics, and related generative tasks.
Decouples transport direction from mass growth, avoiding the high-density bias of WFR-based formulations.
Adapts sampling steps to local data structure, using smaller steps in dense regions to prevent overshooting.
Provides a stable, scalable path-length minimization solver.
Reportedly outperforms WFR-based methods on biological dynamics reconstruction, unpaired image translation, and video generation.

papers.selection_reason: Unbalanced optimal transport generative formulation with demonstrated video-generation application is transferable to video generation research.
papers.title: Contact Geometry for Generative Models: An Unbalanced Optimal Transport Formulation
papers.tldr: CuOT uses contact geometry to improve unbalanced optimal transport for unpaired generative problems, reducing density-driven bias and improving stability.

papers.abstract: Vision foundation backbones are often treated as drop-in upgrades for improving region proposals in open-vocabulary panoptic segmentation (OVPS). Yet, improvements in backbones often fail to translate well into downstream cross-domain performance. Using ODISE, a diffusion-based OVPS model with a CLIP-based recognition branch, as a testbed, we replace its diffusion visual extractor with DINOv2, ConvNeXt, or DINOv3, and find that backbone upgrades can introduce a grouping-recognition mismatch: an alignment gap between dense-region features and CLIP text embeddings. Across source and near-domain, the newer DINOv3 variant improves source-domain performance but collapses on several cross-domain targets, whereas other baselines, interestingly, show the opposite. Stage-wise diagnostics, linear probes, and region-text alignment analyses indicate that DINOv3 embeddings retain semantic information but are geometrically incompatible with CLIP. We test adaptations, including text-side adapters, conformal mask retention (CMR), and a lean 2.7M-parameter visual-side LoRA, and find that text-side adaptation is more sensitive to vocabulary overlap. CMR provides only limited and target-specific gains, indicating that retention alone cannot resolve the full cross-domain failure. To understand why ADE20K resists improvement across all interventions, we evaluate OVSeg, CAT-Seg, and MaskCLIP. This separates two failure axes: a recoverable visual-to-CLIP interface gap that visual-side LoRA largely repairs, and a vocabulary-boundary limitation shared by the evaluated CLIP-based recognition systems that requires different remedies.
authors: Huy Hoang Nguyen, Oliver Zendel, Tobias Glueck, Minh Nhat Vu, Andreas Kugi
bullets: The study identifies a grouping–recognition mismatch between region features and CLIP text embeddings as a hidden cross-domain failure mode.
Replacing ODISE’s diffusion extractor with DINOv2, ConvNeXt, or DINOv3 produces divergent domain-transfer behavior; DINOv3 improves source results but collapses on several targets.
Diagnostics show DINOv3 preserves semantic information, but its embedding geometry is incompatible with CLIP.

A 2.7M-parameter visual-side LoRA largely repairs the visual-to-CLIP interface gap; text adapters are more sensitive to vocabulary overlap, while conformal mask retention offers limited, target-specific gains.
ADE20K failures persist across OVSeg, CAT-Seg, and MaskCLIP, revealing a separate vocabulary-boundary limitation in CLIP-based recognition systems.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the alignment gap between dense visual features and CLIP text embeddings in open-vocabulary panoptic segmentation, directly relevant to spatial intelligence and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Align or Fail: The Hidden Gap in Cross-Domain Panoptic Segmentation
papers.tldr: Upgrading vision backbones can improve source-domain OVPS while harming cross-domain performance when dense visual features become misaligned with CLIP’s text space.

papers.abstract: We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, co-ordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The deadline makes parallel work valuable when it increases the return earned before the cap. We train Avalon-M1-Mini (120B) across 147 environments. For the trained model, eight-hire organisational execution raises IMO-ProofBench-Advanced scores from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations achieve similar average scores at approximately one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution and just over half that of eight independent attempts followed by selection. The trained model also outperforms Nemotron 3 Super, post-trained from the same base model, across all evaluations when comparing each model's best tested configuration. On EdgeBench, organisations overtake the single agent after approximately 0.4 derived hours. Over the course of training, organisations develop hierarchies to manage communication costs, invest more in peer review, and alter how work is divided. Safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios. These results establish a shared-advantage baseline for studying organisational learning, performance-latency trade-offs, and collective oversight.
authors: Iliyan Zarov, Henry Course, Anthony Hartshorn, Ran Achiron, Louis Roche, Akshit Sinha, Chengxi Taylor, Ross Taylor
bullets: A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy and coordinate via a message board and workspace.
A common outcome-derived advantage rewards organisational strategies that increase returns before a deadline.
Eight-agent execution improves IMO-ProofBench-Advanced from 23.8% to 39.0% versus single-agent execution.
Across 12 benchmarks, organisations reach similar average performance at roughly one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution.
Training produces communication hierarchies and more peer review, but external reporting declines in two of three oversight scenarios.

Over training, CEOs hire lead roles more frequently, creating a middle-management layer. Left: share of hires with lead titles in the software-build training environments. Right: the same share on the EdgeBench evaluation. Bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over environments and tasks.

papers.abstract: Geospatial reasoning segmentation aims to localize geographic targets from language requiring semantic inference beyond direct visual perception. However, existing benchmarks often operationalize reasoning as category omission while overlooking attribute mixing, which neglects explicit-category reasoning, introduces perceptual shortcuts, and fails to precisely evaluate reasoning capability. To diagnose and address these limitations, we first reformulate geospatial reasoning segmentation along category expression (explicit vs. implicit) and attribute nature (perceptual vs. inferential), and audit 90,708 queries across existing benchmarks to reveal that pure explicit-inferential queries account for only 0.61% whereas 31.98% mix both attribute types. We then develop a three-stage pipeline that harnesses OpenStreetMap attributes while mitigating geometric and semantic noise to construct RSReasoner, a large-scale dataset of 106,610 images with 213,220 reasoning queries, and RSReasoner-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 75,400 queries across four canonical types and controlled variants. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSReasoner-Bench precisely evaluates model capability across multiple dimensions while exposing shortcut behaviors, and fine-tuning on RSReasoner boosts both reasoning and cross-type generalization. Our findings offer key insights for future geospatial reasoning research and benchmark design. Datasets and code will be released at https://github.com/Ricardo-XZ/RSReasoner.
authors: Xu Zhang, Xinpeng Zhang, Yunrui Zou, Hongliang Chen, Xiaotian Jiang, Yang Zheng, Kaitai Guo, Jimin Liang

papers.abstract: Training and evaluating robots across diverse tasks requires a supply of simulation environments suited to those tasks. While recent scene and task generators offer a promising way to expand this supply, delivering a usable task environment still faces two practical gaps: generated scenes that look plausible in appearance often fail to support the intended task interactions or remain physically stable in simulation, and generated scoring programs frequently attempt task conditions without implementing them faithfully. We present EmbodiedStudio, a task-driven simulation generation platform that bridges these gaps by jointly authoring scene, task, robot-behavior, and rubric programs under closed-loop simulation feedback and independent review. Crucially, as the coding agent iteratively debugs scenes, behaviors, and stateful rubrics in simulation, this closed-loop process natively yields both forward construction experience for learning to build environments and physical execution experience for policy learning, all bound to frozen environment revisions for repeatable evaluation. Across scene generation, rubric evaluation, ablations, and learning studies, EmbodiedStudio substantially improves task readiness and rubric faithfulness while improving physical stability and retaining actionable supervision signals for layout authoring and policy adaptation.

papers.abstract: General-purpose robotic manipulation requires task reasoning, failure recovery, and precise control, yet limited manipulation data make these abilities difficult to obtain from a single policy. Recent multimodal agents show promise in task reasoning and recovery but lack reliable fine-grained control and incur high inference cost, whereas learned policies provide efficient fine-grained execution but struggle beyond their learned skills. Although their complementary strengths suggest combining the two, doing so requires repeatedly deciding which executor should act as task demands change. Instead of relying on the agent for each decision, we present Next-Manip, an on-demand agent--policy collaboration framework that decouples executor allocation from costly agent inference. We propose an Agent Invocation Controller (AIC) that allocates control between the policy and the agent through a lightweight classifier of current execution demands. We further introduce Task Dynamics Context (TDC), which packages informative manipulation changes from in-context examples into compact task references to support both agent reasoning and executor allocation. Across two simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments, Next-Manip achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing agent inference costs.
authors: Jiayi Liu, Ke Ye, Jiaming Zhou, Yufei Huang, Haotian Liang, Kun-Yu Lin, Junwei Liang

Achieves state-of-the-art performance across two simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments while reducing agent inference costs.

papers.abstract: Learned driving planners keep being updated after deployment as new logs arrive, yet continual learning evaluations rarely ask whether an update improves on the deployed model, and their verdicts rest on unstated evaluation choices. We present ContinualDrive, a deployment-anchored benchmark for post-deployment continual learning of driving planners. It updates a deployed planner on real-world nuPlan logs one scenario-type group at a time, evaluates the same checkpoints in open and closed loop, makes four measurement axes explicit (evaluation loop, reference checkpoint, temporal aggregation and stream protocol), and anchors a three-valued release verdict to the deployed checkpoint. We study two planners (PlanTF and Diffusion Planner) under full fine-tuning and adapter or LoRA updates, with and without replay or gradient projection, in three task orders. Verdicts can reverse or vanish when one axis changes: open-loop ADE ranks the final PlanTF model above the deployed one in half of its core-suite runs, whereas every closed-loop score ranks it below; backward transfer misses this loss, which on average is already present when each group has just been learned; and regime rankings vary far less across training seeds than across task orders. In the core suite of full and adapter updates, no regime measurably improved on the deployed planner in closed loop; on a panel more than ten times larger every evaluated final checkpoint trails it, and joint training on all groups recovers much of the loss without exceeding its nuPlan closed-loop score. We distill these findings into a reporting contract and will release the code and all checkpoints.

papers.abstract: If Chinese had been Latinized, as the Latinxua Sin Wenz movement proposed, what would it have meant for Chinese NLP? Homophones and tone marking complicate the answer. We convert Chinese corpora to syllable-separated Pinyin and train superBPE tokenizers from scratch. The resulting Pinyin vocabularies not only exhibit expected homophone collisions, but also show approximately 10% higher fertility than characters. An alternative BPE configuration changes the relative fertility of the two representations. We further pretrain Llama-style models on Chinese characters and Pinyin. The Pinyin models perform worse on per-character perplexity, homophone disambiguation, and overall ZhoBLiMP minimal-pair accuracy. An exploratory phonological probe yields near-chance performance for both representations. The broader implication is that written input representations are not merely neutral encodings. Choices for representations affect language modeling and their downstream performances. Latinization never actually happened for Chinese, but other languages did, such as Hangul and Latin script replaced character in Korean and Vietnamese; the cost we measure is a guide to where modeling effort for those languages should concentrate.
authors: Zijie Zheng, Ej Zhou
bullets: Pinyin tokenizers show expected homophone collisions and about 10% higher fertility than character tokenizers, though results vary with BPE configuration.

A phonological probe is near chance for both character and Pinyin representations.
The findings suggest written representations are not neutral and may guide modeling choices for languages that underwent script Latinization.

papers.abstract: Visual-inertial-leg (VIL) state estimation offers cost-effective localization for legged robots, adding only a camera to the onboard IMU and joint encoders. However, learning-based leg odometry is limited by its supervision: networks trained in simulation suffer from the sim-to-real gap, while real-world labels require costly sensors or inherit the errors of visual estimates. To address this, we present AirLeg, a self-supervised VIL SLAM system in which vision and leg proprioception improve each other from training to deployment. We pre-train the leg odometry network in simulation and adapt it to the robot without ground truth through imperative learning, where multi-sensor bundle adjustment uses the leg odometry to refine the visual map, which in turn supervises the network. During deployment, the fused estimates adapt the network online. To improve both localization and this supervision, a dual-window estimator fuses vision, IMU, and leg odometry, relates loaded feet to the visually reconstructed terrain through a deformation-aware constraint, and weights the constraints by variance component estimation. AirLeg completes all 17 GrandTour sequences with the lowest average error (0.19 m) among 19 methods. On a low-cost quadruped, it achieves the lowest drift (0.6%) with only 0.5 h of unlabeled data, in real time on an embedded computer.
authors: Kuan Xu, Tianxin Hu, Ruofei Bai, Ruimeng Liu, Yuefan Hao, Zeyu Jiang, Zitong Zhan, Shenghai Yuan, Chen Wang, Lihua Xie
bullets: Addresses simulation-to-reality transfer and costly or inaccurate real-world supervision for learned leg odometry.
Uses imperative learning: multi-sensor bundle adjustment refines the visual map with leg odometry, which then supervises the network.
A dual-window estimator fuses vision, IMU, and leg odometry with deformation-aware terrain constraints and variance-based weighting.
Completes all 17 GrandTour sequences with the lowest average error among 19 methods (0.19 m).
On a low-cost quadruped, reaches 0.6% drift using 0.5 hours of unlabeled data and runs in real time on embedded hardware.

papers.abstract: Specialists post-trained from a shared checkpoint acquire complementary capabilities, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) can consolidate them into a single model. However, we find that existing consolidation methods, from weight merging to MOPD, fall short when specialists diverge substantially from the shared checkpoint, whereas prior studies mostly examine specialists that remain close to it. We present a unified recipe for multimodal MOPD that consolidates such specialists back into the single student they branched from. The recipe specifies initialization, data selection, balanced supervision across teachers, and preservation of existing capabilities for consolidation, together with a targeted refinement stage for capabilities that still lag behind their specialists. In an industrial setting with six specialists, the student closely approaches each specialist in its own domain and surpasses the perception specialist. It recovers 97.0% of their average gain, compared with 79.8% for IM-MOPD. In the fully open five-domain setting with Qwen3-4B, our method recovers 95.7% of the specialists' average gain after consolidation and 97.5% after refinement, compared with 94.1% for IM-MOPD. We further analyze the full pipeline through mechanism ablations and training dynamics, providing practical guidance for diagnosing incomplete consolidation. Code will be released.
authors: Zihan Liang, Zikun Qu, Ben Chen, Fan Yang, Wenwu Ou, Min Zhang, Zhongxiang Dai, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Addresses the failure of existing weight-merging and MOPD methods when specialists diverge far from their shared starting checkpoint.
Combines careful initialization, data selection, balanced multi-teacher supervision, and capability preservation.

With six industrial specialists, the student closely matches each domain specialist and surpasses the perception specialist.

Recovers 97.0% of specialists’ average gain in the industrial setting and 95.7% after consolidation—or 97.5% after refinement—in the open five-domain setting, compared with 79.8% and 94.1% for IM-MOPD, respectively.

papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient monocular 3D hand pose estimation is an important perception capability for embodied human interaction and dexterous manipulation. Recent diffusion-based methods model pose uncertainty by iteratively denoising 3D joint coordinates. However, directly diffusing the final joints requires the generative process to simultaneously explore plausible poses and recover precise coordinates, often relying on additional denoising steps or multiple hypotheses and consequently increasing inference cost. In this work, we propose DiffAnchor, a few-step anchor-space diffusion framework that diffuses anchors rather than joints. Our key insight is that stochastic exploration does not need to operate directly on the final output. Instead, diffusion searches for informative intermediate anchors that serve as local 3D regressors, while anchor-to-joint offset prediction and weighted aggregation complete precise joint localization. Specifically, fixed context anchors provide stable global references, whereas noisy dynamic anchors are iteratively refined toward informative joint regions. An importance-guided anchor selection and replenishment mechanism further retains useful anchors, removes ineffective ones, and explores insufficiently covered regions. This design reduces the precision burden of the diffusion process and enables accurate prediction using only a few denoising steps and a single hypothesis. Extensive experiments on HO-3D V2, NYU, ICVL, and InterHand2.6M demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the first three benchmarks and competitive performance on challenging interacting-hand estimation, while maintaining inference efficiency comparable to deterministic regression baselines.
authors: Changlong Jiang, Youci Tang, Haohong Kuang, Hang Xu, Jinghong Zheng, Ran Wang, Zhenghong Yu, Chen Feng, Xiaofeng Yue, Yang Xiao
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of joint-space diffusion, which must jointly explore pose uncertainty and recover precise coordinates.
Uses fixed context anchors and iteratively refined noisy dynamic anchors to locate informative 3D regions.
Predicts anchor-to-joint offsets and aggregates them with weights for precise joint localization.
Importance-guided selection and replenishment retain useful anchors and improve coverage.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on HO-3D V2, NYU, and ICVL, competitive interacting-hand performance, and efficiency comparable to deterministic regression baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of DiffAnchor. Given an input image, the image encoder extracts multi-scale visual features. Fixed context anchors provide stable global spatial references, while dynamic anchors are initialized from noise and iteratively refined in the anchor space. At each denoising step, the diffusion decoder predicts anchor-to-joint offsets and importance scores. Joint-specific informative anchors are selected for weighted anchor-to-joint aggregation, whereas highconfidence denoised anchors are retained and the remaining anchors are replenished with newly sampled candidates. After a few iterations, the final 3D hand pose is obtained from the anchor-to-joint ensemble.

Fig. 4. Architecture of the diffusion decoder. Anchor embeddings serve as spatial queries, while image features and diffusion-timestep embeddings condition anchor interaction and image-to-anchor feature aggregation.
Fig. 3. Architecture of the image encoder. Extracted pyramid image features are flattened, concatenated, and enhanced using deformable self-attention.

Fig. 1. The main idea of DiffAnchor. (a) A diffusion model with the diffusion process q and the reverse process pθ . (b) Diffusion model for image generation task. (c) Our anchor-to-joint paradigm with the denoised informative anchors from noisy anchors.

High-confidence denoised anchors are retained, whereas the remaining anchors are replaced by newly sampled candidates.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) planners inherit semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models, but their reasoning is rarely grounded in 3D scene structure and its evolution over time. We introduce GeoVLDrive, a geometry-grounded VLA framework for 3D spatiotemporal reasoning and planning. Multi-layer features from a 3D foundation model augment the vision-language backbone through gated cross-attention. A structured latent chain of thought (CoT) organizes future scene geometry, key-agent motion, and meta-actions into ordered, separately supervised latent states. An action expert generates trajectory proposals from these states and multi-layer scene features, and ranks them using scene-grounded, interacting score tokens. We also introduce NAVSIM 3DQA to train and evaluate metric 3D spatial and motion understanding. GeoVLDrive achieves 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. On NAVSIM 3DQA, the geometry-grounded backbone scores 89.2% overall, 4.6 percentage points above the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B baseline. On LingoQA, the backbone achieves 68.6% Lingo-Judge accuracy.
authors: JiaHui Huang, Songyan Zhang, Hanbing Li, Hanchao Leng, Kuiyuan Yang, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the lack of 3D spatiotemporal grounding in vision-language-action planners.
Uses gated cross-attention to integrate multi-layer 3D foundation-model features with a vision-language backbone.
Structures reasoning into supervised latent states covering future geometry, key-agent motion, and meta-actions.
Generates and ranks trajectory proposals with an action expert and scene-grounded interacting score tokens.
Reports 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 89.2% on the proposed NAVSIM 3DQA benchmark.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a serious competitor to gradient-boosted trees, predicting on a new table in a single forward pass by in-context learning. However, their attention is quadratic in the number of samples and features, which caps pretraining at small synthetic tables and forces inference on large ones to rely on chunking or subsampling. Row-compression models reduce the feature-wise cost, but only by discarding the cell-level representation, and remain quadratic in the number of samples. We introduce InducedTFM, which replaces both attention stages of a bidimensional TFM with the induced attention of the Set Transformer, preserving cell-level representations while making its cost linear in both samples and features. Under a training budget matched to a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation, InducedTFM matches its accuracy on TabArena and on a benchmark of larger datasets, and clearly outperforms a kernel linear-attention baseline of the same asymptotic cost. It overtakes TabICLv2 in inference time on narrow tables, reaching a 30x speed-up at 640K rows, although row compression remains preferable on wide tables.
authors: Salome Gobbi, Nicolas Atienza, Nicola Cancedda, Michael Arbel
bullets: Addresses the quadratic attention cost that limits TFM pretraining and inference on large tables.
Replaces both attention stages in a bidimensional TFM with Set Transformer-style induced attention.
Preserves cell-level representations while achieving linear cost in the number of samples and features.
Matches a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation on TabArena and larger-dataset benchmarks, and outperforms a same-cost kernel linear-attention baseline.
Provides up to a 30× inference speed-up at 640K rows on narrow tables; row compression remains preferable for wide tables.

papers.abstract: As the use of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes more widespread in cyber-physical systems, it becomes increasingly important to design RL agents that are able to adapt to changes in their environments in order to maintain safety and reliability. This paper addresses the question of whether different classes of RL algorithm are more robust against forgetting previously learned behaviours, a critical issue in continual learning, in non-stationary environments. We evaluate the robustness of representative examples of three important classes of RL algorithm in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment. These are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which is a model-free on-policy algorithm, Soft-Actor-Critic (SAC), which is a model-free off-policy algorithm, and Drama, which is a model-based algorithm. The agents must learn to successfully park in four different scenarios, which are presented successively, with parking spaces oriented at varying angles. We find off-policy algorithms appear to be more robust compared to on-policy algorithms due to their use of replay, while model-based algorithms do not appear to offer any direct advantage over model-free algorithms. These experiments also highlight the additional challenges of finding robust abstractions of the environment, and oversensitivity to hyperparameters.

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) delivery is an important application of the low-altitude economy, enhancing the flexibility and accessibility of last-mile logistics. Existing UAV delivery methods generally rely on precise terminal coordinates, predefined terminal specifications, or task-specific localization procedures, limiting the scope and flexibility of delivery. As UAV logistics becomes more intelligent, open-ended semantic descriptions offer a new paradigm for specifying terminal destinations. However, conventional aerial navigation methods have limited ability to generalize to delivery scenarios that require open-vocabulary terminal navigation. To enable this broader delivery paradigm, we propose CoFiNav, a VLM-guided coarse-to-fine UAV semantic navigation framework that progressively grounds relation-defined terminal destinations through hierarchical semantic search and active 3D observation. Given a task description, a coarse prior map from OpenStreetMap (OSM), and accumulated observations, CoFiNav uses a vision-language model (VLM) to determine which unresolved entity or spatial relation should be verified next. A geometry-aware module converts the semantic observation request into feasible viewpoints using RGB images and LiDAR, while conventional motion planning handles safe execution. Experiments across multiple urban environments show that CoFiNav outperforms representative adapted baselines in success rate while requiring shorter flight paths and fewer observations.
authors: Xuanpu Wang, Shun Hu, Bing Li, Rongqing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of delivery systems requiring precise coordinates, fixed terminal specifications, or task-specific localization.
Uses a VLM with an OSM-based coarse map and accumulated observations to select which entities or spatial relations to verify.
Converts semantic observation requests into feasible viewpoints using RGB imagery and LiDAR, then executes them with conventional motion planning.
Experiments across multiple urban environments report higher success rates, shorter flight paths, and fewer observations than adapted baselines.

papers.abstract: Composing an editable 3D scene from images requires an asset for each object and a layout that places the assets. 3D generation and CAD retrieval now supply the assets, but layout still lacks a general solution: scene generation methods couple it with generation, and pose estimators handle one object at a time and need true-size CAD models, depth, or iterative refinement. We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout separately from asset generation. Given one or more images of a scene, the object masks, and an asset for each object from any source, it jointly predicts the rotation, translation, and per-axis scale of all objects in a single forward pass of about one second. The key idea is to treat objects as views: renders of the assets are processed together with the scene images by a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-$\Omega$, and each object pose follows in closed form from the cameras predicted for its renders. Camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth are optional inputs. When the meshes produced by five scene generation methods are kept fixed and only their layout is replaced, the layouts of X-3DComposer are more accurate than the native layouts of these methods. Compared with the stand-alone layout model SceneMaker, it reduces the scene-level Chamfer distance by 52% on IndoorMix, our test set from six indoor datasets, and by 28% on 3D-FUTURE.

bullets: Separates scene layout prediction from asset generation, addressing a key limitation of existing 3D scene composition methods.

Processes asset renders and scene images together with a multi-view geometry model, deriving poses in closed form from predicted cameras.
Improves fixed-asset scene layouts over native layouts from five scene-generation methods; reduces scene-level Chamfer distance versus SceneMaker by 52% on IndoorMix and 28% on 3D-FUTURE.

papers.abstract: Driving world models anticipate action consequences through representations of how the world evolves. For autonomous driving, these representations must capture both the surrounding scene and the ego vehicle's motion under a candidate plan. We propose CodeWAM, a driving world model that incorporates executable code as part of its world representation. Code represents ego dynamics by expressing how the vehicle state evolves under plan execution, while a learned visual model captures scene-dependent consequences. Executing the code produces a candidate-conditioned motion sequence, which is evaluated relative to the prior plan and recorded motion history. The resulting execution consequences and learned scene outcomes jointly represent the candidate's future, enabling the planner to assess both what a plan may lead to and how the vehicle transitions into that future. The selected plan becomes part of the next decision's execution context, linking successive choices within the model. CodeWAM achieves 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD. Further experiments demonstrate improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training, supporting executable code as a complementary representation for driving world models.
authors: Zhisheng Chen, Jinpeng Wang, Beicheng Lou, Zhengwei Xie, Hao Wu, Rui Qian, Kun Wang, Vivian W. H. Wong
bullets: Addresses the need for driving world models to represent both scene evolution and the ego vehicle’s motion under candidate plans.
Uses executable code to generate plan-conditioned vehicle motion, while a learned visual model predicts scene-dependent consequences.
Combines execution outcomes with visual predictions and prior plan history to assess candidate futures across sequential decisions.
Reports 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD.
Shows improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich robotic manipulation, but existing visuo-tactile simulators trade physical fidelity for scalability, and benchmarks largely focus on two-finger grippers. We present ViTacLab, a framework comprising ViTacSim, ViTacBench, and ViTacPolicy. ViTacSim uses a tri-modal tactile primitive: a global sparse contact-force lattice, a local dense force array, and tactile images. Anchored to PhysX contact-solver outputs, it corrects normal inconsistency through local stiffness alignment and reconstructs tangential forces under decoupled slip-stick regimes while preserving GPU parallelism. A joint projection preserves the sparse wrench and enforces local friction cones. ViTacBench spans parallel grippers, dexterous hands, and bimanual systems, with tasks ranging from vision-dominant to tactile-dominant regimes. ViTacPolicy aggregates variable numbers of heterogeneous tactile inputs using spatial-pose embeddings and a Transformer, and aligns force-array and tactile-image modalities through a two-stream VQ-VAE with a shared codebook. Controlled Hertzian-reference indentation and real-sensor sliding tests reduce normal and tangential force RMSE from 2.31 and 1.85 N to 0.42 and 0.53 N, respectively. Throughput reaches 2,482.9 tactile-pipeline FPS at 256 parallel environments. Simulation and real-world experiments show gains on several contact-rich tasks, while low absolute success on tactile-dominant tasks highlights the remaining difficulty of purely tactile control.
authors: Linjing You, Zeming Yang, Zhenhao Shen, Shengqiang Xu, Guanda Li, Wenxuan Li, Jiyu Guo, Jasper Lu, Kyle Xu, Shawn Xie, Junjie Zhu, Siyu Wu, Jian Liu, Changhao Zhang, Rongchong Li, Zeyi Li, Hengshuang Zhao, Ruihai Wu

ViTacPolicy fuses heterogeneous tactile inputs with spatial-pose embeddings, a Transformer, and a shared-codebook two-stream VQ-VAE.
Reference and real-sensor tests reduce normal-force RMSE from 2.31 to 0.42 N and tangential-force RMSE from 1.85 to 0.53 N; tactile-dominant control remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.
authors: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu, Shengfeng He
bullets: Addresses the mutation or disappearance of moving objects after they leave and re-enter the camera view.
Couples perspective video generation with low-frame-rate panoramic evolution without auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs.
Uses Geometric Anchoring for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation for temporal aggregation.
Supports both latent-level and attention-level camera conditioning architectures.
Experiments on a new dynamic benchmark show gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

The two streams coordinate across space and time via dedicated learned feature projections to exchange complementary context. GeoAnch transfers spatially aligned features at synchronized timestamps, while TemComp aggregates features across neighboring timestamps for intermediate observations.
