papers.abstract: Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student rollouts using a frozen teacher that views high-resolution evidence crops. Yet our cross-scale diagnostics show that models retain over half of their full-image accuracy when local evidence is completely masked, indicating that single-image correctness does not guarantee reliance on local evidence, while the need for visual correction also varies across tokens with their spatial attention states. We propose STAR, a visual on-policy self-distillation framework combining independent counterfactual dual-world rollouts with spatial-attention-guided target reconstruction. Local image editing constructs paired worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but distinct answer-determining facts, where a shared student samples trajectories independently to expose contextual shortcuts under image-consistent prefixes. Within each world, the teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to determine the visual correction direction, while the divergence between student image attention and a teacher-centroid spatial reference adaptively controls token-wise target log-probability reconstruction. Without auxiliary attention losses or test-time tool overhead, STAR improves Qwen3.5 across scales by up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy over initialization across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD's final accuracy $4.7\times$ faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.
authors: Yi Zou, Zhuang Yan, Yudong Zhang, Xu Wang, Yang Wang
bullets: Models can preserve over half their full-image accuracy even when local evidence is masked, revealing shortcut reliance.
STAR creates counterfactual image worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but different answer-relevant facts.
A teacher compares real and mean-color crops to identify visual corrections, while spatial-attention divergence guides token-level target reconstruction.
STAR improves Qwen3.5 by up to 8.04 percentage points across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD’s final accuracy 4.7× faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.

Figure 2. Overview of STAR. (a) A shared student independently samples on-policy rollouts in original and counterfactually edited worlds, while a frozen teacher evaluates each rollout conditioned on its own prefix. (c) Real-versus-mean-color crop contrast and the calibrated strength jointly reconstruct the target distribution, which supervises the student through Jensen–Shannon distillation. papers.selection_reason: Presents a self-distillation method for vision-language models, directly relevant to multimodal large language models.
papers.title: STAR: Counterfactual Dual-World Rollouts and Spatial Target Adaptive Reconstruction for Visual On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: STAR improves visual reasoning by training models to rely on answer-determining local evidence rather than global-context shortcuts.

papers.abstract: Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time communication and live captioning. However, powerful pretrained offline models cannot be directly deployed in this setting, while existing online methods typically retrain the entire model on simulated streaming prefixes constructed from offline videos, incurring high costs. To address this challenge, we propose Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (BCP), a unified lightweight framework that converts pretrained offline methods into online counterparts for sign-to-gloss (S2G), sign-to-text (S2T), and sign-to-gloss-to-text (S2G2T). Specifically, BCP freezes the pretrained model and introduces a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained SLR model, without any human annotation. At inference, a Boundary-Controlled Wait-K Output Policy then decides what to commit via prefix voting, yielding adaptive burst commits while preserving the output progress of the base Wait-K schedule. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily across four offline methods show that BCP, with less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per offline method, achieves a strong quality-latency trade-off on S2T and remains competitive on S2G and S2G2T.
authors: Xiao Ma, Lin Li, Shiqing Wu, Wang Gao, Chuanbo Liu, Jianquan Liu
bullets: Targets real-time sign-to-gloss, sign-to-text, and sign-to-gloss-to-text streaming tasks.
Freezes the pretrained offline model and trains a boundary adapter supervised by CTC alignments, avoiding human boundary annotations.
Uses prefix voting with an adaptive Wait-K output policy to control when outputs are committed.
Evaluated across four offline methods on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily.
Adds less than 0.1% trainable parameters per offline method and achieves a strong quality–latency trade-off for S2T, while remaining competitive on S2G and S2G2T.

papers.selection_reason: Online sign language recognition/translation is a video-language understanding task; the lightweight streaming adaptation framework is transferable to video understanding.
papers.title: BCP: A Lightweight Boundary-Controlled Framework for Online Sign Language Recognition and Translation
papers.tldr: BCP efficiently converts pretrained offline sign-language models into online recognizers and translators using a lightweight, annotation-free boundary-control module.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often recognize fine-grained details more accurately in a relevant crop than in the full image. Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) methods exploit this by transferring the advantage of a crop-view teacher to a full-image student. However, their supervision relies on region-specific questions curated through an elaborate synthesis pipeline, which brings three weaknesses: (1) every region needs a question--answer pair written exclusively for it, locking training into costly QA curation that is hard to scale to unlabeled images; (2) all rollouts of a region answer the same question, so the teacher supervises only the details it asks about, leaving other visual elements in the region unsupervised; and (3) every question presupposes that its target exists, so the student becomes prone to answering even when the target is absent. In this paper, we study how to turn unlabeled images into broad visual supervision through multi-aspect self-description and privileged-view distillation, and propose CaptionOPD, which replaces tailored questions with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts, ranging from general descriptions to focused captions of parts, colors, counts, text, and layout. The rollouts of a region receive different prompts, so the teacher supervises various aspects of the region. Moreover, because caption prompts mask the model to describe what is visible instead of querying a specific target, they avoid presupposing what the region contains. Using the model itself as the crop-view teacher, CaptionOPD requires no questions, no answers, and no larger model annotations: only images and region boxes. Experiments show that, trained on the same images and regions, CaptionOPD outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks.
authors: Haozhan Shen, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Tiancheng Zhao, Jianwei Yin
bullets: Addresses costly, narrow, and target-presupposing QA supervision in multimodal on-policy distillation.
Uses fixed, image-agnostic caption prompts covering descriptions, parts, colors, counts, text, and layout.
Distills a model’s crop-view outputs into a full-image student using varied prompts across region rollouts.
Requires only images and region boxes—no questions, answers, or larger teacher model annotations.
Outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks when trained on the same images and regions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Caption Handoff. (a) Given a boxed full image, the student generates a general caption whose first sentence typically identifies the target object. (b) Standard distillation retains the box cues during training and supervises the entire caption, causing the student’s perception to rely on oracle boxes. (c) The proposed caption handoff removes the box cues from both the student’s image and prompt, while keeping the teacher’s cropped view unchanged. The first sentence serves purely as a textual anchor (masked from the loss), and only the remaining detailed description is supervised on the clean full image.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on questions with false premises. Each question presupposes an absent target: (a) a scooter rather than a bicycle, (b) a dog figurine rather than a real dog, and (c) a bowl of strawberries rather than oranges. QA-trained baselines (Vision-OPD, S2VOPD, and VAD) blindly follow the question’s premise and hallucinate the queried object, whereas CaptionOPD faithfully identifies what is actually present and rejects the false premise. All models are based on Qwen3.5-9B. More examples are shown in Appendix E.

Figure 1: Comparison of prompt construction and rollout allocation between previous fine-grained OPD and CaptionOPD. (a) Previous fine-grained OPD relies on a large VLM to synthesize a tailored question qi for every image–region pair and spends all K rollouts answering that same question qi, tying training to costly QA curation while supervising only a single queried detail per region. (b) Our CaptionOPD eliminates per-region QA generation by reusing a fixed, image-agnostic pool of caption templates (detailed in Section 3.1) across all images, assigning diverse prompts across the K rollouts to supervise multiple visual aspects of each region.

Table 2: Results on fine-grained perception benchmarks. Unlabeled Experience denotes learning without question–answer annotations, from images and region boxes only. Best and second-best scores within each model size are bold and underlined.

Table 5: Ablation of the prompt pool. Each row changes only the prompts assigned to the 8 rollouts of a region. Single repeats one focused template, sampled per region, for all 8 rollouts; Diverse assigns distinct focused templates; General only repeats general caption prompt for all 8 rollouts. General-caption rollouts use caption handoff as in the full method. All models use Qwen3.5-9B.

Table 4: Ablation of caption handoff and size-aware allocation. Uniform assigns two general-caption rollouts to every region; size-aware assigns one, two, and three to small, medium, and large regions (Section 3.1). All models use Qwen3.5-9B.
Table 1: Representative tasks from the caption prompt pool. Prompts are simplified for brevity; see Appendix F for the exact wording.

papers.selection_reason: Caption-driven distillation for fine-grained VLM perception, relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Describe, Don't Ask: Caption-Driven On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Visual Perception
papers.tldr: CaptionOPD improves fine-grained full-image perception by distilling diverse crop-based self-descriptions without requiring region-specific question–answer annotations.

papers.abstract: Visual decision-making demands accurate judgments and timely responses. Yet for multiple questions sharing the same visual input, autoregressive multimodal large language models generate answers token by token, accumulating sequential decoding costs as question count grows and delaying completion of the decision set. Their predictions can also vary with question order. We introduce ViDM, which transforms multi-question visual inference into parallel decisions in a single forward pass, improving both accuracy and inference efficiency. ViDM organizes shared visual context, multiple questions, and question-specific decision slots into one sequence, reusing the native language-model head to produce all answer distributions simultaneously. A Decision-Query Mask aligns each decision query's direct attention with shared context and its corresponding question, while case-balanced multi-order training strengthens robustness to question reordering. Across nine benchmarks spanning image, multi-image, and video tasks, ViDM improves Qwen3.5-4B's average accuracy from 73.49% to 77.55% while achieving 8.4x the baseline's average end-to-end throughput. On GQA, where each evaluated image has 11.4 questions on average, the end-to-end speedup reaches 20.3x. ViDM also improves mean and worst-order accuracy while reducing order-induced variation across multiple benchmarks, with further validation on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and InternVL3.5-4B.
authors: Xudong Tan, Peng Ye, Chenyu Huang, Yaoxin Yang, Huafeng Qin, Tao Chen
bullets: Addresses sequential decoding costs and sensitivity to question ordering in multi-question visual inference.
Organizes shared visual context, questions, and decision slots into one sequence for simultaneous answer prediction.
Uses a Decision-Query Mask to connect each decision with the shared context and its corresponding question.
Case-balanced multi-order training improves robustness to reordered questions and reduces order-induced variation.
Across nine benchmarks, ViDM raises average accuracy and achieves substantial throughput gains, including up to 20.3× speedup on GQA.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Architecture and training pipeline of ViDM. (Left and middle) Given an image, multiple images, or a video with K questions, ViDM feeds shared visual tokens, question tokens, and K decision slots into a Transformer decoder. A Decision-Query Mask restricts each decision query’s direct attention to shared context, its own question, and its own cue. A shared decision head reuses native LM-head rows to map decision states to K answer distributions in parallel, without autoregressive answer decoding. (Right) During training, the same question set is presented in M distinct orders, with predictions aligned to their question-specific labels. Case-balanced Multi-order CE averages cross-entropy over questions and orders within each case, then weights cases equally, encouraging order-robust decisions.

Figure 2. Question-order sensitivity in multi-question visual reasoning. (a–b) The same image and eight questions are presented in original and reversed orders. Despite unchanged visual evidence and question content, Qwen3.5-4B’s answers vary with question order, while ViDM produces more consistent decisions. Green checks and red crosses denote correct and incorrect answers. (c) Absolute original–reverse accuracy gaps (pp.) show that this sensitivity is not an isolated case: it occurs across tasks in both Qwen3.5-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-7B. ViDM reduces these gaps in most comparisons.

Figure 4. Attention allocation and order sensitivity. (a) At the decision layer (Layer 32) of the untrained, unmasked parallel model, decision-token regions (pink arrows) allocate substantial attention to other questions and earlier decision cues. V+S: visual/shared context; D: decision-cue spans. (b) Cyclically moving the same question to different positions changes answer confidence across K. Curves show mean absolute confidence changes from position 1, conditioned on preceding ground-truth answers.

Figure 6. Confidence-based decision reliability. Models answer all questions in cases across multiple datasets. R (%) denotes the fraction of answers retained in descending confidence order within each dataset. Error rates among retained answers are averaged equally across datasets. At the same R, lower error rates indicate more reliable high-confidence answers.

Figure 5. Efficiency and scalability. Performance and end-to-end throughput of ViDM and autoregressive Qwen3.5-4B on GQA and TempCompass. (a–b) ViDM’s throughput advantage widens as the question count K increases. (c–d) With K = 4, ViDM maintains higher throughput across visual-token budgets, demonstrating the persistent efficiency benefits of parallel decisions.

Figure 1. ViDM: efficient parallel decisions for multiple questions. (a) Given shared visual input and K questions, ViDM predicts all answer distributions in a single forward pass. (b) Autoregressive MLLMs generate answers token by token through multiple forward passes. (c) ViDM achieves higher throughput than Qwen3.5-4B across benchmarks spanning image, multi-image, and video tasks (q/s, logarithmic scale).

papers.selection_reason: Improves multimodal large language models for visual decision-making, directly fitting the MLLM subtopic.
papers.title: ViDM: Efficient and Order-Robust Parallel Visual Decision Making
papers.tldr: ViDM enables robust, parallel answers to multiple visual questions in one forward pass, improving both accuracy and inference speed.

papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop is readable through the shared language-model head. Post-training them is hard. Reward-only reinforcement learning needs a verifier and learns from one sparse signal per response; spreading the reward over loops collapses the entropy of every loop; and cross-loop self-distillation, as in LoopOPD, can only teach intermediate loops, because the last loop cannot learn from its own frozen copy: the loss is zero at initialisation. We observe that a looped model already contains a policy that decodes better than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELPSD (Extrapolated-Loop Policy Self-Distillation) turns this distribution into a self-distillation target: a frozen copy of the model computes it, and the model's own last loop is distilled towards it on its own rollouts, using the exact reverse KL at every visited prefix. Teacher and student are the same model, so ELPSD needs no reward, no external teacher and no privileged context, and it leaves rollouts and decoding unchanged. We show that the objective pulls the last loop towards the base model's last loop with weight 1+w and away from the base model's first loop with weight w, and that the teacher must stay frozen, since an idealised teacher recomputed from the current model extrapolates without bound. We evaluate ELPSD on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking across five math benchmarks against the base model, GRPO, RLTT and OPSD. Without any reward, ELPSD raises the average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69 and is the best method on all five benchmarks, ahead of GRPO (62.32), which uses a verifier, and the self-distillation method OPSD (61.77), which needs reference solutions.
authors: Linghua Zhang
bullets: Looped models reuse one transformer stack across multiple loops, but standard post-training struggles with sparse rewards and cannot self-distill the final loop from itself.
ELPSD uses a frozen model copy to extrapolate the next-token distribution from the first loop through the last and applies reverse-KL distillation on the model’s own rollouts.
The method requires no verifier, reward signal, external teacher, privileged context, or rollout/decoding changes.
The frozen teacher is essential: recomputing the extrapolated teacher from the current model can cause unbounded extrapolation.
On Ouro-1.4B-Thinking across five math benchmarks, ELPSD raises average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69 and outperforms GRPO and OPSD.

figures.caption: Table 1: Post-training methods for looped language models. “Loop 2” is LoopOPD’s intermediate student loop k = 2; “last loop” is loop T , the loop used at deployment.
Table 3: Settings shared by all trained systems.
Table 2: avg@8 on five mathematics benchmarks (Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, step 100, 4 loops, 8 samples, temperature 0.6). Avg. is the unweighted mean. Best per column in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Self-distillation method for looped language models directly concerns LLM post-training and policy improvement.
papers.title: The Teacher Is Already Inside: Self-Distilling Looped Language Models Beyond Their Last Loop
papers.tldr: ELPSD improves looped language models by distilling the model’s own extrapolated early-to-late-loop policy into its final loop, without rewards, external teachers, or changed decoding.

papers.abstract: Pansharpening aims to fuse a single observed image pair, comprising a low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) image and a panchromatic (PAN) image, to obtain a high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) image. Recently, deep learning-based methods have achieved significant performance due to their strong capability of extracting nonlinear features. However, distribution shifts between training data and test images can degrade the performance of pretrained pansharpening networks, limiting their generalization in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose an instance-specific test-time adaptation framework that uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair to select and update only a subset of the pretrained network's parameters. Specifically, the framework uses cross-scoring to identify parameter groups whose updates improve reconstruction across image patches. It then updates the selected groups by minimizing a loss that combines a spectral consistency term with a newly designed spatial consistency term. Experiments show that the adapted networks perform better than their pretrained counterparts and outperform representative state-of-the-art pansharpening methods on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView series datasets.
authors: Jin-Liang Xiao, Liang-Jian Deng, Yu-Xuan Zhang, Hua Meng, Zhengchun Zhou
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by distribution shifts between training and real-world test images.
Uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair and cross-scoring across patches to identify parameter groups worth updating.
Optimizes selected parameters with spectral and newly designed spatial consistency losses.
Experiments on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView datasets show improvements over pretrained networks and representative state-of-the-art methods.

This observation motivates the selective adaptation of the most beneficial parameters rather than indiscriminately updating the entire network.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an instance-specific test-time adaptation framework, directly fitting the test-time learning subtopic.
papers.title: Which Parameters to Update? An Instance-Specific Adaptation Framework for Real-World Pansharpening
papers.tldr: An instance-specific test-time adaptation method improves real-world pansharpening by selecting and updating only the most useful pretrained parameters for each observed image pair.

papers.abstract: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.
authors: Akshata A Bhat, Daman Deep Singh, Niyati Chhaya
bullets: Introduces intent-aware OCR, which jointly reasons over document content and visual cues such as arrows, strikethroughs, carets, and insertions.
Presents DocIntent, a dataset of 1,600 financial documents with more than 5,700 annotated intent cues and corrected OCR targets.
Introduces IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark for evaluating robustness to diverse annotation conditions.

papers.abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).
authors: Joonghyuk Shin, Alex Trevithick, Katar\'ina T\'othov\'a, Liyuan Zhu, Shengyu Huang, Jaesik Park, Shalini De Mello, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Riccardo de Lutio, Haithem Turki
bullets: Video world models often lose long-term visual consistency, while explicit 3D worlds lack photorealistic appearance.
M2R stores rendered features on mesh surfaces in each object’s coordinate frame and retrieves them by rasterizing visible surfaces.
This makes appearance move with objects, persist across revisits, and remain shared among observing agents, with memory tied to surfaces rather than frames.
Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and coding-agent-authored worlds.
It more than doubles object permanence, nearly doubles cross-agent consistency, and renders 720p video at 40 FPS.

When agent B encounters the same surfaces, it retrieves and renders them as agent A saw them (a). We train our renderer on rollouts that revisit earlier views. With a one-chunk window, it must render each revisit from the memory it wrote, supervised by a frozen teacher that sees the full past (b).

papers.abstract: Long-horizon panoramic video wandering aims to continuously synthesize scene-consistent $360^\circ$ observations along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial equirectangular projection (ERP) panorama. Existing panoramic video models have achieved promising results in camera-controlled generation, while recent 3D-guided approaches further provide geometric guidance for improving scene consistency. However, stable long-horizon wandering remains challenging due to diverse motion--orientation relationships and imperfect memory guidance induced by accumulated generation artifacts and depth inaccuracies. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PVWander}, a 3D-memory-guided framework that accumulates generated observations into an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide subsequent generation, with two complementary designs: \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} for motion--orientation alignment and \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} for adaptive memory guidance. \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} exploits the horizontal cyclic symmetry of ERP panoramas to uniformly align each clip's ERP orientation with its principal translation direction, yielding more consistent, forward-like relative motions while preserving the prescribed camera path. \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} exploits the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion denoising to adaptively regulate reprojected memory guidance through timestep-dependent channel-wise gates, preserving its structural benefits while mitigating visual artifacts from imperfect projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVWander achieves improved long-horizon generation quality, while ablations validate the effectiveness of both designs.
authors: Chuanxin Song, Xiaodong Wang, Shijie Chen, Junliang Xie, Zhanmi Zhong, Suiying Wu, Peixi Peng
bullets: Targets scene-consistent panoramic video synthesis along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial ERP panorama.
Accumulates generated observations in an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide future frames.
Path-Facing canonicalization aligns ERP orientation with the principal translation direction while preserving the camera path.
Timestep-aware gating adaptively controls memory guidance during diffusion denoising to reduce artifacts from imperfect projections.
Experiments and ablations report improved long-horizon generation quality and validate both design components.

papers.abstract: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.
authors: Yoonki Cho, Youngju Na, Taegeun Yang, Jinhwan Seo, Sung-Eui Yoon
bullets: UME models embed heterogeneous multimodal inputs in a shared space for similarity-based tasks.
HEME addresses the risk that candidate-conditioned representations overfit to or collapse toward the candidate.
A hindsight teacher uses masked, mismatched-candidate conditioning and query-token alignment to learn query-grounded representations.
A standalone student distills the teacher’s representations and similarity distributions, requiring no candidate conditioning or teacher at inference.
Experiments on MMEB-V2 and selected MMEB-V3 tasks demonstrate effectiveness and more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-based methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of HEME. (a) Hindsight teacher training. The candidate and query passes encode their inputs independently, while the hindsight pass conditions the query on its matched candidate by reusing the candidate KV cache. The hindsight mask allows candidate context to influence the embedding only through query content tokens. Together with mismatched-candidate conditioning and query-token alignment, this encourages the hindsight representation to remain grounded in the query. The mismatched-candidate hindsight pass is omitted for clarity. (b) Learning from hindsight. The frozen hindsight teacher supervises a standalone student through embedding and similarity-distribution matching, while the student is also trained with standard InfoNCE. Distribution matching aligns the teacher and student similarity distributions over the same in-batch candidates, using their respective candidate embeddings (c̄ and c). At inference, only the standalone student embedder is used.

Figure 3. Query-grounded hindsight and its transfer to inference. (a) For a target C+ and a challenging near-miss C−, the hindsight pass shows larger query-token shifts on words that distinguish the two candidates; at inference, HEME exhibits stronger target–near-miss separation in the illustrated examples. (b) For a single page C+ answering two different questions, conditioning on the same answer produces question-specific hindsight rankings; from the question alone, HEME exhibits corresponding retrieval behavior.

Figure 1. Reasoning at test time vs. hindsight during training. (a) Reasoning-driven UME approaches generate additional context through intermediate reasoning at test time. (b) HEME instead uses the matched candidate as privileged context during training: a hindsight teacher produces a candidate-conditioned hindsight representation, which is distilled into a standalone embedder. At test time, HEME encodes queries and candidates independently without the hindsight teacher or additional reasoning steps.

papers.abstract: Video foundation models have emerged as powerful generators of dynamic visual content, exhibiting remarkable capabilities in synthesizing complex actions and interactions. We argue that these models have also become excellent motion generators, with motion priors that are richer and more general than those learned by dedicated motion models. Their advantage extends beyond visual realism and is manifested in two important aspects: motion naturalness, including coherent body coordination, physical plausibility, and realistic interactions with objects and the environment; and motion scope, encompassing a much broader range of activities and semantic coherence, particularly uncommon, complex, and compound actions. To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that compares video and dedicated motion models through three complementary settings: text-only motion generation, reconstruction of video-generated motion from sparse keyframes, and video-based enrichment of motion-model outputs. By converting all outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation, we evaluate motion naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical motion characteristics, and fidelity to motion constraints. Our results suggest that video foundation models can generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. Moreover, we investigate motion-conditioned generation through loose skeletal control, finding that dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion, while video models can enrich skeletal animations using sparse motion guidance. Our findings suggest a shift in the role of specialized motion models, from generating complete animations to guiding and controlling the richer motion capabilities already embedded in video foundation models.
authors: Kian Izadpanah, Ali Mahdavi Amiri, Daniel Cohen-Or, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Andreas Aristidou
bullets: They offer richer motion priors, producing more natural coordination, physical plausibility, and object-environment interactions.
Their motion scope covers a broader range of activities with stronger semantic coherence, particularly for uncommon or complex actions.
A unified framework compares both model types across text-to-motion, sparse-keyframe reconstruction, and video-based motion enrichment.
Outputs are converted to a shared 3D skeletal representation and evaluated for naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical characteristics, and constraint fidelity.
The findings reposition dedicated motion models primarily as guides or controllers for video models rather than standalone animation generators.

papers.abstract: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.
authors: Chenrui Fan, Qiyang Hu, Luca Scharr, Paolo Favaro
bullets: Generated videos often contain subtle deformations and sliding that undermine 3D reconstruction and are difficult to label manually.
The method pairs real clips with keyframe-conditioned re-creations, then measures each pixel’s deviation from rigid-scene behavior along the generated camera path.
The released dataset contains 871 real-generated video twins, with construction code and an official benchmark test split.
NRG-PD predicts per-pixel rigidity-violation angles from RGB alone and achieves 0.85 AUROC, outperforming seven existing consistency or motion-segmentation methods.
Its predictions improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction for videos containing generated content.

papers.abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.
authors: Mohamed Eltahir, Manar Eyad, Yara Alzahrani, Fatimah Albesher, Duaa M. Tahir, Tanveer Hussain, Naeemullah Khan
bullets: Addresses the slowdown, accuracy loss, and context-window limits of one-pass long-context inference.
Uses training-free block-sparse attention to read local and strided spans from a single KV cache in one batched forward pass.
Employs a stair position schedule to keep spans within the model’s trained position range.
Matches grid probing’s accuracy and reach across long video, long-text inference, and image grounding while using a fraction of its cost.
Reports up to roughly 10-point gains over single-pass inference, finds information beyond the context window, and can be as fast as one-tenth of grid probing.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/Recurrent-DLLM/
authors: Linhao Zhong, Bozhen Fang, Xuehao Wang, Zekai Luo, Liyang Li, Hourong Li, Chenchen Jing, Hao Chen
bullets: MDLM hidden states exhibit layer-wise and cross-step refinement dynamics.
Deeper layers are more predictive, while removing transformer blocks gradually degrades representations.
Final hidden states remain strongly aligned across consecutive denoising steps.
Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR) transfers hidden-state information between steps.
Experiments show CSRR improves text generation quality.

papers.abstract: Temporal localization in long videos is challenging because brief, question-relevant events are dispersed among extensive redundant content. Limited visual budgets increase the risk of omitting these events or their temporal context, undermining reliable reasoning. Existing frame selection methods emphasize semantic relevance or temporal coverage, often overlooking the complementary evidence needed to locate related events and establish their temporal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TESS, a training-free framework for query-guided temporal event-structured frame selection. TESS selects frames that jointly show the reference event and the event asked about, in the required temporal order. Leveraging frozen vision-language representations, TESS integrates soft temporal gating, role-aware budget allocation, and within-role redundancy suppression to preserve complementary event evidence. Extensive experiments across four long-video understanding benchmarks and three multimodal backbones demonstrate that TESS consistently outperforms the strongest compared baseline by 4.0-5.5 percentage points under a fixed frame budget. Further analyses reveal greater improvements on longer videos and robust performance under tighter visual budgets, while independent evidence annotations confirm enhanced event and temporal-relation coverage. These findings establish explicit temporal evidence organization as an effective training-free strategy for preserving event relationships and supporting efficient temporal reasoning over long videos. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TESS_code.
authors: Qi Lu, Shiyan Tong, Shujie Li, Sen Li, Likun shi, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Yao Hu
bullets: Targets the omission of brief, related events and their temporal context in long videos.
Uses frozen vision-language representations with soft temporal gating, role-aware budget allocation, and redundancy suppression.
Selects complementary frames showing both the reference event and the queried event in the required order.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.0–5.5 percentage points across four benchmarks and three multimodal backbones.
Shows larger gains on longer videos and under tighter frame budgets, with improved event and temporal-relation coverage.

papers.abstract: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Jyotirmoy Nath, Neeraj Kumar, Brejesh Lall
bullets: Global freezing thresholds can prematurely remove small or slowly converging edits in multi-edit instructions.
TIDE localizes each instruction part using the editor’s attention and unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models.
It freezes tokens based on part-relative prediction drift, estimates their endpoints, and sparsely computes only active tokens.
On FLUX.2 Klein, TIDE reduces dropped edits by up to 77% at matched or higher speed and achieves up to 4.89× acceleration with 5.3× fewer TFLOPs.
It also performs fastest on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 across the reported benchmarks, though results are limited to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.
authors: Jiewen Hou, Guanxiang Qi, Meina Kan, Shiguang Shan, Xilin Chen
bullets: Problem: VLN agents may mistake off-route observations for progress, advancing their internal instruction stage and making recovery difficult.
Method: A verifier detects cross-modal evidence mismatches in VLM residual representations and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms.
Recovery: When a mismatch is detected, a contextual bandit selects how far to rewind instruction progress before steering onward.
Evaluation: Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show improved reliability across multiple state-of-the-art VLN methods at test time.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of our PHAR framework. (a) Probe-Based Verifier: a temporal probe aggregates VLM states vt into a probe state ht to score a proposed STOP; the calibrated threshold τ determines whether to raise an alarm. (b) Adaptive Progress Steering Module: upon an alarm at the step Tk, LinUCB selects an appropriate progress steering operator Sρjk using the probe state hTk and remaining step budget.

Figure 5. Test-time Recovery with PHAR framework. The heatmap shows sub-instruction attention pt,j , and the red curve traces the instruction progress pointer µt.The agent initially grounds its current observation in a later sub-instruction S4, advancing µt beyond the actual task stage. PHAR Steers µt toward the correct stage S2, enabling the agent to resume navigation and reach the goal.

Figure 6. Recovery requires an appropriate steering strength. (a) Instruction progress distribution pt (defined in Sec. 3) under different steering strengths: ρ = 0.2 triggers another STOP, ρ = 0.8 redirects attention toward S3 and enables recovery, while ρ = 1.0 shifts attention back to S1 and leads to unsuccessful exploration. (b–d) Sampled observations and maps show the initial failed execution and recovery attempts with different steering strengths ρ. Orange and blue paths indicate the original and recovery trajectories.

Figure 2. Instruction progress and progress hallucination. (a) Progress distribution pt (heatmap) and pointer µt (red curve) along a successful trajectory. (b) Failed trajectories achieve less spatial progress than successful trajectories at comparable µt. Spatial progress is 1 − dt/d0, where dt and d0 are the current and initial goal distances.

Figure 3. Investigating the cause and mitigation of progress hallucination. (a) Each point shows pointer rewind ∆µt under gray-image replacement of off-route history. Steps are normalized from deviation onset to termination. (b) Early-history truncation induces pointer rewind ∆µT (left axis) and changes predicted actions from STOP to movement (right axis).

Figure 7. Real-world recovery with PHAR. (a) NaVILA prematurely stops near the wrong green chair; our verifier detects the unreliable termination (sT = 0.9545). (b) Our Adaptive Progress Steering Module redirects instruction progress, enabling the robot to complete the missed right turn and reach the target chair, where termination is accepted (sT ′ = 0.5614). (c) Instruction progress distribution pt and pointer µt (red curve; see Sec. 3) illustrate the effect of steering; the dashed line marks the intervention. (d) Schematic layout showing the two chairs, the passage between bookshelf segments, start and goal, and illustrative failed (red) and recovery (blue) routes.

Table 1. Comparison with existing methods on the R2R-CE [14] and RxR-CE [15] benchmarks. ∗ denotes methods based on the waypoint predictor from [11]; † denotes our reproduction results. Shaded rows show our results for NaVILA [7], NaVIDA [37], and AwareVLN [9]. The best and second-best results in each metric column are bolded and underlined, respectively.
Table 2. Ablation study on probe-based verifier. Failure precision (P) and recall (R) use successful val-seen calibration at αcal = 0.03. All metrics are percentages.
Table 3. Ablation study of Adaptive Progress Steering Module on R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen splits.

Table 4. Navigation recovery under different steering strengths ρ. Each steering operator Sρ is applied independently to the same termination states of 100 failed trajectories. Union counts distinct trajectories recovered under at least one steering strength.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time recovery framework for continuous vision-and-language navigation directly targets VLN.
papers.title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: PHAR improves test-time recovery in vision-and-language navigation by detecting hallucinated progress and adaptively rewinding instruction progress after route deviations.

papers.abstract: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal. We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.
authors: Omar Emara, Nan Lu, Dima Damen, Hazel Doughty
bullets: Standard contrastive learning assumes co-occurring audio and video are equally aligned, but off-screen sounds can violate this assumption.
CGAAL uses modality-specific captions to estimate audio-video semantic agreement.
Agreement scores weight positive pairs, with warm-up and gradual thresholding to introduce alignment-aware training progressively.
Applied to three contrastive baselines, CGAAL consistently improves audio-visual retrieval performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our caption-guided alignment-aware learning (CGAAL). As in standard contrastive learning, we (a) learn a shared space for audio-visual retrieval where audio and video encoders project each modality into a shared embedding space where we measure their similarity. Rather than treating all co-occurring pairs as equally positive, we instead use (b) modality specific captions to estimate the alignment of each positive pair. After first warming up the representation with all positive pairs, CGAAL uses the estimated alignment scores to weight positive pairs in a contrastive loss (c). A gradually increasing threshold introduces the alignment scores gradually so that the weakest correspondences are down-weighted first. This produces a shared embedding space in which proximity better reflects audio–visual correspondence, rather than co-occurrence alone.

Figure 1: Alignment in audio-video contrastive learning. Standard contrastive methods assume strong semantic correspondence between modalities of a given sample, encouraging alignment even when the modalities share little semantic content. This can encourage the model to associate audio and visual content that does not correspond. We thus propose CGAAL which determines how strongly to pull the modalities’ embeddings of a sample according to a pair’s semantic agreement.
Figure 7: Performance vs. alignment score. The relative improvement of our method compared to CLIP and CoMM increases with alignment score.

Figure 3: Alignment score estimation. We prompt the LLM to predict the alignment score by: (1) setting the criteria for measuring the semantic alignment with clear inputs (modality captions) and the output (alignment score); (2) providing examples with different alignment strength alongside an explanation to calibrate the scores across various examples; and (3) providing the vision and audio caption pair for which a score needs to be predicted.

Figure 4: Examples of modality-specific captions with varying semantic alignment. We show high (top), moderate (middle) and weak (bottom) alignment examples. High (row1,col1): vision shows cooking on stove while audio has distinct sizzling sound. Moderate (row2,col3): walking is not evident from the audio. Weak (Row3 col 3): no evidence of golfing in the audio.
Figure 8: Qualitative Results for A2V over different alignment levels. Our retrieved videos show better fine-grained semantic correspondence with the audio query.

Figure 5: Impact of Synthetic Misalignment on Training Set. We show the distributions of caption-based alignment scores for the full pretraining set (left) and the 15% of the samples selected for audio shuffling (right). The original pretraining set (blue) already contains many low-scoring pairs, suggesting substantial natural variation in audio–visual correspondence. Adding synthetic misalignment (orange) shows a clear shift towards lower scores.
Figure 6: Reliability of Alignment Scores. Captionbased LLM scores closely agree with human ratings of audio–visual correspondence.
Table 2: Zero-Shot Retrieval. Adding CGAAL improves a model’s ability to generalise to unseen datasets, particularly with increased misalignment in training.
Table 6: Cross-modal embedding similarity across alignment levels. Mean (± standard deviation) audio–video cosine similarity on test set, grouped by alignment score.
Table 3: Model Ablation. Alignment weighting contributes most to our performance. Gradual thresholding gives a further gain with synthetic misalignment, while warm-up improves without it.
Table 5: Robustness to LLM Choice. CGAAL benefits from LLM-based alignment scoring without relying on a particular LLM.
Table 1: Comparative Results. Combining our approach with standard contrastive baselines (SLIP, CMC and CLIP) improves retrieval performance both with and without synthetic misalignment.

Table 4: Alignment Weighting vs. Filtering. Filtering removes training pairs with alignment scores below threshold T . CGAAL improves retrieval in both settings, whereas filtering at either threshold reduces performance relative to CLIP.

papers.selection_reason: Caption-guided alignment-aware contrastive learning for audio-visual representations is transferable to multimodal foundation model training.
papers.title: Not All Pairs Align: Caption-Guided Audio-Visual Contrastive Learning
papers.tldr: CGAAL improves audio-visual contrastive learning by weighting paired examples according to caption-estimated semantic alignment.

papers.abstract: A faithful 4D reconstruction should capture both the shape and motion of objects, even when they disappear from view. Existing methods preserve previously observed geometry and extend motion through occlusion using local spatial and motion associations. However, treating short-term contact or shared motion as sufficient evidence of persistent rigidity can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort overall reconstruction. To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework that identifies reliable rigid relations and uses them to maintain spatial consistency through occlusion. PRC4D combines 3D contact and relative motion consistency with sequence-level verification to distinguish persistent couplings from transient interactions. The resulting graph guides observed-pose refinement and motion propagation from visible to occluded components without altering reconstructed geometry. Experiments on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy, reduced relative pose errors, and more consistent object configurations under changing visibility.
authors: Junho Kim, Hyunyoung Choi, Jiseok Kim, Seongwon Lee
bullets: Addresses incorrect rigidity assumptions caused by transient contact or shared motion.
Combines 3D contact, relative-motion consistency, and sequence-level verification to identify persistent rigid relations.
Uses a relation graph to refine observed poses and propagate motion to occluded components without changing reconstructed geometry.
Experiments on real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations show improved accuracy, lower relative pose errors, and more consistent configurations under changing visibility.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PRC4D. Geometric contact and relative motion provide candidate rigid relations, which are verified through sequence-level persistence reasoning. The resulting graph refines observed component poses and guides motion propagation through occlusion.

Figure 4. Persistent and transient physical relations. In MultiObj2, PRC4D distinguishes persistent rigid relations between reconstructed book fragments from transient contacts and co-motion during robot interactions. Solid and dashed edges indicate persistent and transient relations, respectively.

Table 2. Quantitative comparison on the multi-object reconstruction benchmark. We report F-score (↑) for each scene, along with mean F-score, precision, and recall. Best and second-best results among non-oracle methods are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively. The last-view oracle uses only the final-frame pointmap and is excluded from the ranking.

Table 5. Ablation of physical-relation graph construction. We evaluate reconstruction quality and rigid-relation inference as temporal verification and graph-level consistency checks are progressively introduced.
Table 4. Comparison with alternative approaches. We compare our physical relation-constrained reconstruction with temporal SE(3) smoothing and rigid relations derived from 4DPM grouping.

Table 3. Ablation study of pose refinement and motion propagation. We independently evaluate the two modules using the same initial reconstruction and inferred relations. Original denotes the 4DPM motion extension. Best results are in bold and secondbest results are underlined.

papers.selection_reason: Physical relation-constrained 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes; fits 3D vision.
papers.title: PRC4D: Physical Relation-Constrained Persistent 4D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: PRC4D improves persistent 4D reconstruction by using verified physical relations to propagate reliable object motion through occlusions.

papers.abstract: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). Under leak-free 10-fold CV across four zero-scaler-byte non-linear benchmarks, FNS with an INT8 readout surpasses 0-hidden Linear-INT8 by +3.6 to +10.8 pp while delivering 10.7x-129x total Flash reduction (725x-2,773x hidden reduction) relative to converged Float32 MLPs (90.30% Ionosphere in 285 B; 97.22% Optical Digits in 2,598 B; 97.90% PenDigits in 2,598 B; 87.00% Satimage in 1,570 B).
authors: Volkan Dagli, Zerrin Dagli, Daghan Dagli
bullets: Addresses the O(W) Flash cost of explicitly stored neural-network parameters on resource-limited microcontrollers.
Derives hidden-layer weights procedurally from a constant-size seed near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary, using smooth escape dynamics and geometric sampling schemes.
The bifurcation-boundary representation preserves local continuity and effective rank across magnifications, unlike Fourier/lattice-noise bases and SHA-256 PRNGs evaluated in the abstract.
With an INT8 readout, FNS outperforms a zero-hidden Linear-INT8 baseline by 3.6–10.8 percentage points across four benchmarks while reducing Flash substantially versus Float32 MLPs.
Reported accuracies range from 87.00% to 97.90%, with total Flash reductions of 10.7×–129× relative to converged Float32 MLPs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: End-to-end Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS) pipeline. A 24-byte coordinate tuple Θ = (cx, cy, ℓ) ∈ F3 64 drives the lookup-free quadratic kernel fc(z) = z2 + c (R = 256) along ∂M, sampled through four geometric apertures into a boot-time volatile SRAM buffer supporting either 0-byte procedural Mode I reflexes or compact FP32/INT8 Mode II readouts.

Figure 6: Systems profiling from Experiment 4 (H = 256, Intel64 host). (a) Persistent hidden-layer Flash (24 B constant FNS seed vs. O(dH) FP32/INT4 MLPs, 725×–2,773× reduction). (b) Warmed-up boot-time amortization (τboot/Ncycles + τSRAM,b=1) using apples-to-apples single-sample SRAM inference.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving language models can continuously acquire useful experience through test-time interaction, reflection, and prompt optimization, yet turning such experience into model itself to ensure self improvement remains challenging. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides a natural mechanism for internalizing test-time information into model parameters, yet it largely assumes that the gener- ated experience is worth learning. We show that this assumption does not always hold: experiences that improve test-time performance may provide limited or even harmful training signals. To better characterize which experience should be inter- nalized, we systematically analyze diverse mutated experiences across multiple tasks and reflection models, and find that gradient-based alignment is a more reli- able indicator of downstream distillation gains than immediate test-time improve- ment. Based on this finding, we propose E2L, a self-evolution framework that iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their esti- mated training utility. E2L closes the loop between experience generation and parameter learning, enabling agents to autonomously produce experience suitable for self-improvement.
authors: Haoyuan Li, Gangyi Zhang, Dong Wang, Yang Liu, Daoxuan Liu, Jiancan Wu, Shiu-hong Kao, Wu Liu, Yicong Li, Yongdong Zhang
bullets: Problem: Test-time experiences that improve performance may still provide weak or harmful signals for parameter learning.
Finding: Gradient-based alignment more reliably predicts downstream distillation benefits than immediate test-time improvement.
Method: E2L iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their estimated training utility.
Contribution: A closed-loop framework for producing experiences specifically suited to model self-improvement.

papers.abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.
authors: Songtao Jiang, Yuan Wang, Fucheng Niu, Hualiang Wang, Jian Wu, Zuozhu Liu
bullets: Scalar fitness-only search discards diagnostic failure information; the proposed loop analyzes structured errors and tests falsifiable architectural hypotheses.
Under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, agents use counterfactual controls to convert validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules.

The loop finds that shifting computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin boundaries while reducing cost, while support-confined region contrast helps separate nested compartments.
LeanNeXt reaches 0.78× nnU-Net MACs and 0.92× training-step time, with a +1.63 Dice-point gain on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation.
Trigger-routed LeanNeXt+ improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and surpasses the larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30× its parameter count.

papers.abstract: Automatic visual story generation using diffusion-based models has become an increasingly important research direction in generative artificial intelligence. However, maintaining character identity consistency across consecutive frames remains an open challenge, as existing models often produce significant variations in facial traits, clothing, visual style, or anatomical proportions. This paper proposes a modular pipeline to improve character identity consistency in multi-frame visual story generation using Stable Diffusion XL alongside additional conditioning and automatic selection mechanisms. The proposed system integrates LoRA fine-tuning for character personalization, ControlNet for pose-based structural control, and IP-Adapter for visual identity transfer. Furthermore, a reranking mechanism based on Best-of-K candidate selection and persistent identity memory is introduced to automatically select the most visually consistent generated images. The work also includes integrating and extending the StoryDiffusion framework into a reproducible local workflow, along with improvements for generated frame selection. Performance evaluation uses automatic metrics such as CLIP image similarity, DINO similarity, and CLIP text-image alignment. Experimental evaluation was conducted on a custom benchmark of multiple characters and visual stories organized into difficulty levels (easy, medium, and difficult). Both progressive variants of the proposed pipeline and extended versions of StoryDiffusion were evaluated, including SDXL baseline, Best-of-K, Identity Memory, and the Full Pipeline. Results show that reranking, identity memory, and visual conditioning reduce identity drift across frames and improve the overall coherence and stability of generated visual stories.
authors: Maria-Emilia Grigore, Stelian Sp\^inu
bullets: Addresses identity drift in facial features, clothing, style, and anatomy across consecutive generated frames.
Combines LoRA character personalization, ControlNet pose control, and IP-Adapter identity transfer.
Uses Best-of-K reranking and persistent identity memory to select more consistent frames automatically.
Evaluates progressive pipeline variants and StoryDiffusion extensions on a custom benchmark spanning easy, medium, and difficult stories.
CLIP, DINO, and text-image alignment results indicate improved identity consistency and story coherence, though the evaluation is limited to the custom benchmark and tested configurations.

papers.abstract: Large language models can write competent robot navigation code, but not only does the research on the topic advance, a model may also, due to the volume of findings, fail to recall relevant findings and apply them to the task at hand. In this work, we test whether providing particular research papers as context improves the LLM-written navigation code for the Go2 quadruped, with the LLM (Claude Opus 5) and locomotion policy frozen. Specifically, we compare the navigation controllers the LLM writes when provided with and without particular papers across three settings: behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, 2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This difference appears only under physics: in an idealized kinematic simulator, the controllers written with and without the paper are indistinguishable. We hypothesize that an LLM provided research papers as context tends to overweight both their content and their goals -- in this case, the efficiency of incremental replanning -- negatively affecting the fulfillment of the main task and leading to less robust code.
authors: Barnabas Juhasz, Rolf Pfister
bullets: The study tests whether selected research papers improve LLM-written quadruped navigation code with the model and locomotion policy fixed.
Controllers are compared with and without paper context across behavior trees, shared-base edits, and from-scratch implementations.
With an incremental-replanning paper, fewer context-conditioned controllers completed all blocked-maze trips under Isaac Sim physics: 2/8 versus 7/8 without context.
This difference was absent in an idealized kinematic simulator, suggesting sensitivity to physical realism.
The authors hypothesize that paper context can cause the LLM to overemphasize the paper’s objectives, such as replanning efficiency, at the expense of robust task completion.

papers.abstract: In streaming video understanding, the evidence needed to answer a question may have already left the recent-frame window. Keeping all frames does not scale with video length, while dropping older frames limits the model's ability to reason about the past. We propose Visual-State Graph (VSG), a training-free memory that stores the state of a stream rather than the raw sequence of frames. VSG represents the stream as a graph of objects and their relations, together with a log of events; similar to a dynamically evolving scene graph. An object observed repeatedly is represented by one persistent node, with a timestamped history of how its state changes. To determine whether a newly mentioned object already exists in the graph, we compare the relations it takes part in with those of stored objects. We build this memory as the video arrives, before the questions are known. When a question arrives, we retrieve relevant objects and events alongside recent frames under a fixed input budget. Our evaluation spans four streaming-video benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models ranging from 7B to 32B parameters. Under matched input budgets, VSG improves reasoning about the past while preserving real-time understanding.
authors: Ailar Mahdizadeh, Pritam Sarkar, Xiangteng He, Leonid Sigal
bullets: Addresses the loss of long-term evidence when streaming systems retain only recent frames.
Builds a dynamically updated graph of persistent objects, their relations, and timestamped state histories, plus an event log.
Matches newly observed objects to existing graph nodes using their relational context.
Constructs memory online before questions are known, then retrieves relevant objects and events with recent frames.
Evaluated on four streaming-video benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models; improves past reasoning while preserving real-time understanding under matched budgets.
