papers.selection_reason: Presents a novel LLM pretraining architecture with a separate control channel for steerability, constituting an architectural advance fitting large language models.
papers.title: Steerable by Design: Conditional Pretraining for Robust Control of Language Models
papers.tldr: Conditional pretraining with a dedicated, non-writable control channel makes language models more steerable and resistant to counter-steering.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes from RGB video requires reasoning about both 3D geometry and motion across viewpoints, yet existing methods either split reconstruction and tracking into fragmented pipelines or face prohibitive dense spatiotemporal decoding costs. We introduce MoGe-4D, a feed-forward framework that unifies geometry and motion prediction via ordered queries of paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps. Each query maps source pixels to a target time simultaneously in both camera frames, resolving relative camera pose in closed form while flexibly serving depth, dynamic registration, and dense 3D tracking. For efficient dense querying, MoGe-4D decouples scene modeling from query decoding: a high-capacity context encoder caches coarse global spatiotemporal features once, while a lightweight query encoder rapidly decodes dense point maps at flexible resolutions. Furthermore, as supervising dense 4D queries demands continuous 3D correspondences whose raw trajectory storage is prohibitive, we introduce RigIDTrack, a synthetic data pipeline and dataset that compresses surface dynamics into rigidity-regularized affine bodies, recovering exact arbitrary-frame 3D trajectories with $\sim15\%$ storage overhead over RGB-D video. Across diverse benchmarks, MoGe-4D achieves state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, matches dedicated 3D foundation models in reconstruction, and runs substantially faster than prior 4D baselines.
authors: Ruicheng Wang, Linlin Xin, Sicheng Xu, Jianfeng Xiang, Zelong Lv, Yu Deng, Yue Dong, Guangzhong Sun, Tong Zhang, Jiaolong Yang
bullets: Predicts paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps to jointly model geometry, motion, camera pose, depth, registration, and tracking.
Uses cached global spatiotemporal features plus a lightweight query encoder for efficient dense decoding at flexible resolutions.
Introduces RigIDTrack, a synthetic pipeline and dataset that represents surface dynamics with rigidity-regularized affine bodies and compact trajectory storage.
Reports state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, reconstruction performance matching dedicated 3D foundation models, and substantially faster inference than prior 4D baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of the MoGe-4D framework. Left (unification): querying paired allocentric and egocentric point maps unifies 4D geometry, motion, and camera pose. Middle (flexibility): on-demand query compositions adapt to diverse reconstruction and tracking tasks. Right (efficiency): a dual-encoder architecture decouples global spatiotemporal reasoning from lightweight query decoding for high-throughput inference. ∗Measured on an NVIDIA A100 GPU with 32 frames at 518× 336 resolution (Fig. 11).

Figure 3 MoGe-4D architecture. A high-capacity context encoder processes the input sequence once at coarse resolution and caches multi-layer features. For each query (i, j), a lightweight query encoder re-encodes source image i at flexible resolution, attending to bridged source and target context tokens via conditioned attention blocks. Convolutional heads then decode point maps and auxiliary maps, while MLP heads predict scalars from special context tokens.

Figure 5 RigIDTrack data pipeline. Dynamic scenes are procedurally assembled from 3D asset pools with animation, physics simulation, and collision-aware camera paths. Affine-body motion compression groups motion-consistent mesh faces into shared transformation trajectories, from which dense 4D supervision is recovered via per-frame depth, body-ID maps, and body transforms.

Figure 7 Long-horizon feed-forward camera trajectory comparisons on Oxford-Spires. Each method processes 500 frames in a single feed-forward pass without sliding windows. papers.abstract: Video recasting aims to transform the entities and environments of existing videos into new visual worlds while preserving their essential actions and interactions. However, achieving coherent transformations remains challenging, as coordinated edits can disrupt the original event structure. In this paper, we introduce RecastAgent, an experience-guided agentic framework for source-conditioned video recasting that operates under frozen model weights. Our framework employs an Experience-Guided Planner to choose edit prompts and input video states under qualitative visual critique, allowing the agent to build upon partial progress or backtrack to preserve source structure. Across tasks, an Experience Accumulation module distills completed trajectories into conditional, evidence-linked principles that record both an editing strategy and its scope of validity. We additionally construct a benchmark of 67 source videos with 134 paired-specification tasks across six creative categories for evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that RecastAgent outperforms single-pass and agentic rewriting baselines across Bernini and Ditto. Furthermore, accumulated experience improves performance on held-out test videos and transfers zero-shot to external benchmarks like FiVE-Bench and VE-Bench.
authors: Shiying Zhang, Yuxia Zhu, Huaze Xue, Shengqi Dang, Yizhen Wu, Yijie Li
bullets: Addresses incoherent transformations caused by coordinated edits that disrupt source event structure.
Uses an Experience-Guided Planner to select prompts and video states, enabling refinement, continuation, or backtracking under qualitative critique.
Distills successful trajectories into conditional, evidence-linked editing principles with defined validity scopes.
Introduces a benchmark of 67 source videos and 134 paired-specification tasks across six creative categories.
Outperforms single-pass and agentic rewriting baselines, with experience improving held-out performance and enabling zero-shot transfer to FiVE-Bench and VE-Bench.

papers.abstract: Recovering articulated robot state from video supports metric spatial sensing for manipulation, scene reconstruction, and action planning. Yet the problem is ill-posed: different intrinsics, camera-to-robot poses, and joint angles can explain similar observations. Prior task-specific regressors typically assume known intrinsics, fit one robot through laborious data collection and robot-specific training, and still transfer poorly across scenes. Foundation models apply to any robot zero-shot, but their estimates have large errors. We present OVOK (One Video to Kinetics), a recursive self-improving agentic framework for this task. Under a human-authored protocol, an agentic initializer constructs robot-specific OVOK-4k; a proposer--executor--verifier loop then jointly evolves tools and executable workflows from feedback. Updated tools and workflows are accepted only when the verifier judges a positive improvement. The retained workflow is frozen for accurate inference. Experiments demonstrate that the evolved workflow achieves state-of-the-art results on DREAM-V and RoboKeyGen-V, delivering robust and accurate estimates.
authors: Cheng Dai, Renkai Luo, Guanfeng Tang, Siming Li, Hao Zhao

Accepts updates only after verified improvement, then freezes the resulting workflow for inference.

papers.abstract: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.
authors: Jiawei Gu, Linjie Li, Yiming Liu, Yunzhuo Hao, Huichen Wang, Guanzheng Chen, Zhichao Peng, Luxin Xu, Xinyu Zhang, Li Luo, Disen Lan, Zican Hu, Mingyang Song, David Valente, Alex Jinpeng Wang, Yafu Li, Ganqu Cui, Zhengyuan Yang, Qizhe Xie, Yejin Choi, Ranjay Krishna, Yu Cheng

Adds automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning.

papers.abstract: Geometric rotary position encodings (RoPE) incorporate 3D camera geometry into multi-view attention by rotating token features according to viewing rays, depths, and reprojected image coordinates. Each coordinate is rotated across a progression of frequencies--its frequency band--yet existing implementations leave this band to inherited defaults, either retaining standard 2D RoPE's top frequency or letting the frequency span grow exponentially with the attention head dimension. We show that this unstandardized setting can reverse benchmark rankings. In novel view synthesis on RealEstate10K, RayRoPE matches the strongest baseline in the 47M model (144-channel heads), yet trails by 1.2 dB in the 25M model (48-channel heads), and exhibits the same reversal when varying head size alone at fixed model width. Populating a 243x range with four frequencies instead of the 3x default at 48 channels recovers 0.9 dB of that gap. Across view synthesis and two-view depth estimation, overly narrow bands consistently blur correspondence, whereas all three projection-based encodings perform reliably when their top frequency lies within 0.3--3 rotations per 8-pixel patch (10--90 rotations across 256x256 RealEstate10K). At the opposite extreme, overly wide bands degrade RayRoPE through a forward-backward asymmetry: averaging rotations over a predicted depth interval damps high frequencies in the forward pass, yet leaves their gradients with respect to predicted depth undamped. Blocking only those high-frequency depth gradients recovers 90--93% of the lost PSNR, showing that forward smoothing does not guarantee backward stability. Guided by this analysis, we distill practical guidelines--setting bands in image coordinates, populating spans in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping--and advocate reporting and matching frequency bands in future multi-view benchmarks.
authors: Seonghyun Jin, Youngmin Kim, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Unstandardized frequency bands can reverse benchmark rankings across model head sizes.
Narrow bands blur correspondences; reliable performance occurs when top frequencies span roughly 0.3–3 rotations per 8-pixel patch.
Very wide bands destabilize RayRoPE because high-frequency depth gradients remain undamped despite forward-pass smoothing.
Expanding a 48-channel band from a 3× to 243× span recovers 0.9 dB of a reported performance gap.
The study recommends image-coordinate band selection, denser frequency population in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping.

figures.caption: Figure 7. Why overly wide bands harm RayRoPE (47M models; high frequencies: > 1 rotation/patch). (a) Uniform averaging over [µ −∆, µ +∆] damps the forward output |Φ| as 1/ω, but shifting µ leaves boundary changes undamped (Eq. (4); dashed: its envelope), unlike a smooth Gaussian window. (b) Zeroing single high frequencies on keys at test time barely changes rendering error (top), yet they carry on average one third of RayRoPE’s summed per-frequency depth-gradient norms (bottom; 311: mean and min–max across three runs). (c) Share of the 311→243× PSNR gap recovered by each intervention on 47M RayRoPE (white dot: second seed).

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison on RealEstate10K (full-view PSNR below each crop). Narrowing RayRoPE’s band to 3× blurs fine detail, whereas widening it to 311 introduces colored streaks and blurred texture that disappear when high-frequency depth gradients are stopped.

Figure 3. Default frequency bands and spatial selectivity. (a) Image-plane bands assigned by each released rule at d = 48 and 144 (Gray shown with its RayRoPE host; shading: RayRoPE’s plateau). (b) Unweighted positional kernel K(δ) (Eq. (2)) across patch offsets for four frequency ranges. (c, d) Single-ray RayRoPE with 16- vs. 8-px patches (47M) (c) and on two-view depth (d).

Figure 2. From discrete patch indices to continuous projected segments. (b) Across cameras, geometric RoPE projects a token’s 3D viewing ray into the other view: the reprojected position is continuous, and unknown depth spreads it along a segment. (c) Target crop around the projected segment (0.45 patches, red) for a ±15% depth interval of the marked source pixel, overlaid with the top frequency of three bands: 3× barely varies across patches, 243× separates sub-patch offsets, and 311 turns ∼300 times inside the segment (drawn 77× coarser).

papers.abstract: Generative reward models (GRMs) make language-model evaluation more explicit by generating critiques, rubrics, or intermediate analyses before predicting a final preference. However, explicit evaluation does not necessarily imply a reliable evaluation process: under outcome-only supervision, a model may reach the correct final preference while producing weak or unsupported intermediate judgments, turning the evaluation into a post-hoc rationalization. We introduce STEP-GRM, a framework that directly supervises the intermediate evaluation process of rubric-based GRMs. In addition to conventional preference supervision, STEP-GRM provides structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments, encouraging the model to learn not only the correct final preference but also a more reliable process for reaching it. Extensive experiments show that STEP-GRM achieves strong performance on standard reward-modeling benchmarks while improving the consistency and correctness of intermediate evaluations. Moreover, reward signals produced by STEP-GRM lead to better downstream policy optimization, demonstrating that more reliable evaluation processes can translate into practical gains beyond reward-model accuracy.
authors: Qiyuan Chen, Yuze Zhao, Jiahe Chen, Hongsen Huang, Hongxia Xu, Yingda Chen, Jian Wu
bullets: Outcome-only supervision can produce correct preferences with weak, unsupported, post-hoc rationales.
STEP-GRM adds structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments.
Experiments show strong benchmark performance and more consistent, correct intermediate evaluations.
Its reward signals also improve downstream policy optimization, extending benefits beyond reward-model accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of STEP-GRM. (A) Structured preference data are constructed and partitioned for probe training, cold-start SFT, and RL. (B) A single-criterion probe is trained to independently judge response pairs under individual criteria and is frozen thereafter. (C) STEP-GRM is initialized with SFT and subsequently optimized with process supervision: privileged rubric self-distillation Lpriv guides the evaluation structure, the frozen probe provides criterion-level reward Rcrit, and outcome and format rewards Rout and Rfmt supervise the final preference and output structure, respectively. (D) At inference time, only STEP-GRM is retained, constructing its own rubric, producing criterion-level judgments, and predicting the final preference without reference rubrics or the probe.

Figure 4: STEP-GRM judge system prompt. The generative reward model first proposes a rubric of instancespecific criteria, each tagged [Hard Rule] or [Principle] and labelled with the response it favors in isolation, and then aggregates these criterion-level judgments into the final preference.

Figure 7: Single-criterion probe system prompt. The probe judges the two candidate responses under a single criterion in isolation and outputs a reason together with a three-way verdict (A, B, or tie).

Figure 3: Training dynamics of process supervision. Left: Removing Rcrit preserves outcome reward growth but leads to a sharp collapse in criterion-level agreement, illustrating post-hoc rationalization drift. Right: Privileged guidance maintains a stable KL divergence with a sparse gate activation ratio of ≈ 27–28%.

Figure 1: Making evaluation explicit is not enough. Outcome-only supervision can yield the correct final preference while leaving intermediate criterion-level judgments unsupported, allowing the generated evaluation to become a post-hoc rationalization. STEP-GRM supervises both rubric construction and criterion-level judgment, turning the evaluation process itself into a direct object of learning.

Figure 6: Teacher user prompt. Used for privileged rubric self-distillation: the self-teacher is conditioned on the reference rubric and re-evaluates the two responses, verifying each expert-labelled criterion and aggregating the labelled criteria into the final preference.

papers.abstract: Existing clip-based soccer commentary models often produce delayed, repeated, or poorly synchronized narration on untrimmed full-match videos. Recent streaming video-language models make low-latency full-match narration feasible, but they often favor general descriptions rather than professional, event-grounded soccer commentary. They may describe nearby actions while failing to mention key events such as goals, cards, substitutions, and offsides correctly and on time. In this paper, we present SoccerNarrate to bridge low-latency streaming narration with event-grounded professional soccer commentary across data, training, and evaluation. First, we construct SoccerNarrate-Data, a large-scale time-anchored dataset with word-level ASR alignment, quality filtering, and entity calibration. Second, we perform macro-window preference alignment (MWPA), which aligns the model with complete event-level commentary semantics by comparing causal multi-step rollouts from the same streaming prefix while keeping second-level inference unchanged. We further use event-mismatched human commentaries as counterfactual negatives to emphasize event semantics over commentary style. Third, we introduce SoccerNarrate-Eval, an event-centric benchmark based on temporally constrained event entailment. Full-match experiments show that SoccerNarrate improves event coverage and event-aligned precision over strong offline and streaming baselines. Code and models are released at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/SoccerNarrate.
authors: Zihan Jia, Zhilin Dai, Zhengming Zhang, Min Yang, Zhenpeng Huang, Jiaqi Li, Caixia Sun, Xi Chen, Liang Li, Junlan Feng, Gangshan Wu, Limin Wang
bullets: Targets delayed, repetitive, poorly synchronized, and overly generic commentary in existing systems.
Introduces SoccerNarrate-Data with time-anchored annotations, word-level ASR alignment, quality filtering, and entity calibration.
Uses macro-window preference alignment to compare multi-step streaming rollouts and emphasize complete event-level semantics.
Adds event-mismatched human commentaries as counterfactual negatives and proposes the event-centric SoccerNarrate-Eval benchmark.
Full-match experiments show improved event coverage and event-aligned precision over strong offline and streaming baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 4: SoccerNarrate-Data curation pipeline. Starting from SoccerNet videos, we extract word-level ASR transcripts from match audio, filter noisy or irrelevant commentary, and normalize entity mentions using match metadata. The output is a clean, time-anchored, and entity-grounded text stream for streaming SFT, macro-window preference construction, and event-centric evaluation. The bottom example shows how a commentary sentence is converted into timestamped word tokens.

The Noisy Text (top) contains multiple error types highlighted in red, including phonetic entity errors (e.g., "Daicha"), word fragmentation (e.g., "coa- ch"), token repetition, and irregular punctuation. The Corrected Text (bottom) displays the final output with all restored and normalized segments highlighted in green, verifying the model’s robustness in simultaneously performing de-duplication, de-fragmentation, and entity correction.

Figure 5: Overview of Macro-window Preference Alignment (MWPA) and counterfactual hard-negative construction. Given the same streaming prefix and video window, MWPA compares two human commentary trajectories from the same match. The preferred trajectory Y + k matches the target event, while the rejected trajectory Y − k is sampled from a type-mismatched event as a counterfactual hard negative. This provides event-level preference supervision while preserving micro-step streaming inference.

papers.abstract: Evaluating the physical plausibility of generated videos is critical for reliable robotic planning with world models. These videos inform action proposal and assessment before real-world execution, so undetected physical violations can lead to erroneous assessments of action feasibility and safety. Yet current video generators often produce physically implausible interactions. Detecting such violations directly with vision-language models (VLMs) remains challenging as physical verification requires evidence-grounded spatiotemporal reasoning beyond high-level semantic understanding. We develop five law-specific metrics for evaluating physical plausibility by combining spatiotemporal evidence from segmentation, tracking, 3D geometry, or appearance comparisons with targeted VLM reasoning: Contact fidelity, Object persistence, Solidity, Robot deformation, and Object deformation. Building on this metric suite, we introduce RoboProbe, an agentic evaluation framework that coordinates metric execution and selectively refines evaluations through constrained actions. To evaluate the physical plausibility of robot world models, we further introduce RP-Bench, with 761 human-labeled generated videos and 130 real demonstrations of 239 manipulation tasks from 12 robot datasets. On RP-Bench, all five metrics achieve AUROCs above 0.85 and outperform the evaluated learned judges, prior evaluators, and a frames-only Gemini baseline. Applying these metrics to five video generators reveals distinct patterns of physical violations across models, in both violation types and frequencies.
authors: Zhuoying Yang, Jiachen Ni, Yichen Guo, Xiaoshan Wu, Mengyu Wang
bullets: Motivation: Physically implausible generated videos can cause unsafe or incorrect robotic planning decisions.
Method: Combines segmentation, tracking, 3D geometry, and appearance evidence with targeted VLM reasoning across five law-specific metrics.
Framework: RoboProbe is an agentic evaluator that coordinates metrics and selectively refines assessments through constrained actions.
Benchmark: RP-Bench contains 761 human-labeled generated videos and 130 real demonstrations covering 239 manipulation tasks from 12 robot datasets.

Results: All five metrics exceed 0.85 AUROC and outperform the evaluated learned judges, prior evaluators, and a frames-only Gemini baseline; analyses of five generators reveal distinct violation patterns.

papers.abstract: A learned critic can improve a pretrained flow-matching policy by steering sampled actions toward higher predicted value. However, even a critic that fits the behavior data well can provide misleading action gradients. Gradient components pointing away from the data-supported region are weakly constrained by behavior data and can lead guidance to exploit critic extrapolation errors. We introduce RetraQ (Retraction-based Q-guidance), which uses geometry encoded by the pretrained flow to constrain both the direction and the destination of critic guidance. A single velocity evaluation of the frozen flow defines a denoising map. RetraQ filters the critic gradient with the map's Jacobian and applies the map itself to correct the updated action. Our analysis characterizes when these operations approximate tangent filtering and retraction onto the behavior manifold. The same update guides actions at test time and provides targets for policy distillation and online reinforcement learning. In controlled studies, RetraQ improves true return while keeping refined actions close to the data-supported region, and its distillation targets remain more stable than those of raw critic ascent. In offline-to-online training on LIBERO and OGBench, RetraQ achieves higher mean final success than the evaluated critic-guidance baselines. On a real-world plug-insertion task, test-time RetraQ improves the success rate of a behavior-cloned $\pi_{0.5}$ policy from 55.0% to 76.7%. Online training further increases success to 98.3% in only 30 minutes and 100% within one hour. Project page: https://2027ICLR.github.io/retraq/
authors: Xuanzhuo Liu, Wu Chen, Ruixiang Wu, Shuai Yuan, Chuankang Li, Tongxin Li, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Critic gradients can exploit poorly constrained regions outside the behavior-data manifold.
RetraQ filters critic gradients using the frozen flow’s Jacobian and retracts updated actions with its denoising map.
The same geometry-aware update supports test-time guidance, policy distillation, and online RL.
Controlled studies report higher true return, closer adherence to data-supported actions, and more stable distillation targets.
On plug insertion, success improves from 55.0% to 76.7% at test time, reaching 98.3% after 30 minutes and 100% within one hour of online training.

papers.abstract: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.
authors: Xiangwei Wang, Jianyuan Lin, Peng Wang, Saman Halgamuge
bullets: Standard ES/ARS for VLMs can overfit patch-grid artifacts and catastrophically forget general or OOD capabilities.
It extracts a contrastive visual basis from paired cross-grid views to focus perturbations on shared spatial signals.
A soft subspace prior anchors shallow visual-fusion layers while allowing deeper reasoning layers to adapt.
Paired-view scoring filters view-fragile perturbations during top-k ARS selection.

On Qwen3-VL-8B, it reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO and maintains OOD performance, achieving 75.41% average single-view micro accuracy across seven benchmarks versus 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO.

papers.abstract: Latent reasoning and key-value communication store intermediate information in continuous representations, limiting direct inspection of model behavior. Existing activation readers trade the low cost of task-specific probes against the flexibility of language-model decoders. We propose the Calibrated Latent Reader, CLR, a compact transformer that predicts reasoning outcomes and message content through task-conditioned interactions between states and candidate answers. Source adapters support transfer across models, while conformal calibration provides coverage and false-alarm guarantees under exchangeability. On two CODI models, CLR improves accuracy over MLP and attention probes by 4-18 percentage points for final-answer prediction and reference-value membership. On CODI-GPT-2, it achieves accuracy comparable to a 1.7B LatentQA-based verbalizer using 437-648 times fewer inference FLOPs. On synthetic Qwen3-4B communications, comparing decoded facts with public commitments detects 93.1% of message substitutions at a nominal 5% false-positive rate.
authors: Zixi Wang, Gaohao Zhou, Yubo Huang, Xin Lai, Yushe Cao, Jingzehua Xu, Shuai Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of inspecting intermediate information stored in continuous representations.
Uses task-conditioned interactions between model states and candidate answers, with source adapters for cross-model transfer.
Applies conformal calibration to provide coverage and false-alarm guarantees under exchangeability.
Improves final-answer and reference-value prediction accuracy by 4–18 percentage points over MLP and attention probes on two CODI models.

Achieves comparable accuracy to a 1.7B LatentQA verbalizer with 437–648× fewer inference FLOPs, and detects 93.1% of message substitutions at a nominal 5% false-positive rate in synthetic Qwen3-4B communications.

papers.abstract: In embedding-based video anomaly detection (VAD), normal clips can have high similarity to anomalous descriptions, an anomaly bias that leads to false positives. Methods such as PRISM mitigate this bias by measuring deviations from a normality reference along anomaly directions. Both the normality reference and the anomaly directions are derived from text and shared across videos, although normal activity and the appearance of anomalies vary across scenes. The resulting scores are also sensitive to prompt selection. To address these limitations, we propose Visual Intrinsic Distribution Estimation (VIDE), a training-free framework that adapts text-derived scoring to each test video using frozen clip embeddings. VIDE estimates normal scene content from clips with low initial anomaly scores and uses this estimate to partially correct the textual reference. It then rescales category responses, penalizes clips with strong responses across categories, and refines the anomaly directions using high-scoring clips. VIDE averages scores across prompt views to reduce sensitivity to prompt selection and fuses scores from two frozen encoders. With both encoders, VIDE improves AUC over the best PRISM result by $1.5$, $1.9$, and $3.5$ points on UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, respectively, and AP by $6.5$ points on XD-Violence and $9.3$ points on MSAD. VIDE yields the highest AUC among the compared training-free methods on all three benchmarks and the highest reported AUC among all compared methods on XD-Violence and MSAD. Our code is included in the supplementary material and will be made publicly available.
authors: Kevin D. Nguetche, Atif Belal, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli
bullets: Addresses false positives caused when normal video clips resemble anomalous text descriptions.
Estimates normal scene content from low-scoring clips and uses it to correct textual references.
Refines anomaly directions with high-scoring clips, rescales category responses, and penalizes broadly activated clips.
Averages scores across prompt views and fuses two frozen encoders for greater robustness.
Improves over PRISM across UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, achieving the best reported AUC among compared methods on XD-Violence and MSAD.

papers.abstract: Large language models have shown strong capabilities on complex tasks, yet how to control their reasoning effort remains a significant challenge for practical deployment. This paper provides a systematic investigation of reasoning-effort training, contrasting reinforcement learning (RL) with on-policy distillation (OPD). We find that compressing reasoning and separating effort tiers are governed by different signals. Length-penalized RL reliably compresses a single policy, reducing thinking on AIME25 by 70\% without accuracy loss, but collapses the tiers when they are trained jointly. Multi-teacher OPD separates them: across 33 benchmarks, low and medium use 58\% and 43\% fewer thinking tokens than high, while high improves on the reference policy by 3.1 points. We trace this difference to the training signal. A sequence-level reward cannot tell tier-specific behavior from shared behavior, whereas OPD supplies a tier-specific target at every visited state, including the decision to stop. Building on this analysis, we show that a single token-level KL anchor on the high tier is sufficient to learn separated tiers within one RL stage, and that natural-language effort instructions make this separation emerge from the start of training, yielding a policy competitive with multi-teacher OPD at matched thinking length. Finally, the separation built by dense targets holds only on the states seen in training: it does not carry over to unseen agentic tasks, where effort acts mainly through the number of interaction turns, whereas the compression induced by sequence-level rewards does.
authors: Tianliang Lv, Hao Li, Xinchao Xu, Zhengkun Zhang, Ju Huo
bullets: Length-penalized RL reduces AIME25 thinking by 70% without accuracy loss, but jointly trained effort tiers collapse.
Multi-teacher on-policy distillation separates tiers: low and medium use 58% and 43% fewer thinking tokens than high, while high improves over the reference policy by 3.1 points across 33 benchmarks.
The difference arises because sequence-level rewards do not provide tier-specific guidance, whereas distillation supplies state-level targets, including when to stop reasoning.
A single token-level KL anchor on the high-effort tier enables tier separation in one RL stage; natural-language effort instructions help separation emerge from training start.
Dense-target separation is limited to training-seen states and does not transfer to unseen agentic tasks, where effort mainly changes interaction turns.

papers.title: Rethinking Reasoning Effort Training in Large Language Models: On-Policy Distillation or Reinforcement Learning?
papers.tldr: The paper shows that reinforcement learning compresses reasoning effectively, while on-policy distillation better separates reasoning-effort tiers, and proposes a hybrid RL approach that achieves both within one stage.

papers.abstract: Episodic-memory embodied question answering enables agents to answer questions based on previously recorded visual observations of the surrounding scenes. However, growing observation histories, varying observation quality across viewpoints, and limited computational resources make it challenging to construct and maintain compact visual memories while retrieving sufficient evidence for question answering. To address these challenges, we introduce CoverMem, which incorporates three key components: (1) a coverage-constrained memory construction method that selects a compact set of informative full frames satisfying object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements; (2) a coverage-preserving incremental maintenance strategy that locally reselects only the affected frames to satisfy updated coverage requirements as observations arrive; and (3) a budgeted complementary frame selection method that balances question relevance, additional support for question requirements, and redundancy with selected frames within a fixed budget. Experimental results on three benchmarks covering diverse environments and question types demonstrate that CoverMem improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets.
authors: Ruijie Ma, Haoyue Liu, Mingda Zhang, Dongxu Yue, Xiaoying Tang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining sufficient visual evidence from growing, variable-quality observation histories with limited computation and memory.
Constructs memories by selecting informative full frames that satisfy object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements.
Incrementally updates memories by locally reselection affected frames as new observations arrive, preserving coverage efficiently.
Selects complementary frames based on question relevance, additional requirement support, and redundancy within the budget.
Improves embodied question-answering performance on three benchmarks spanning diverse environments and question types under limited visual budgets.

papers.abstract: Switching scenes while preserving the original subject in streaming video generation exposes a conflict: cached history helps maintain the subject but also sustains old-scene objects that should disappear. Through controlled interventions on text conditioning, denoising steps, the local window, and the attention sink, we identify how cached visual history keeps this obsolete content. When the original frames remain in the cache, KV flush and sink recomputation still leave old-scene objects in the generated videos. Replacing this history with target-scene history largely removes those objects, but also changes the subject, reducing face similarity to the pre-switch subject. We then propose Molt Forcing, a training-free method that rebuilds scene history from a cold-start target scene while selectively retaining subject tokens from the original cache. Across 16 scene families, Molt Forcing removes old-scene objects at least as reliably as an Echo-Forcing hard cut while keeping the subject much closer to its pre-switch appearance.
authors: Hao Zhou, Ziyang Xu, Chenhan Jin, Hao Qin, Shengze Xu, Tieyong Zeng
bullets: Cached visual history preserves old-scene objects even after KV flushing and attention-sink recomputation.
Replacing the cache with target-scene history removes stale objects but alters the subject.
Molt Forcing rebuilds history from a cold-start target scene while selectively retaining subject tokens.
Across 16 scene families, it matches or exceeds Echo-Forcing’s old-object removal while better preserving subject similarity.

papers.abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving, all-weather physical scene understanding across darkness, smoke, and walls. However, standard instruction tuning treats continuous radar streams as static text-like tokens, causing near-random global radar-to-text retrieval and severe physical drift under sensor blackouts. Conversely, coupling pairwise contrastive losses (e.g., SigLIP) directly into the shared backbone improves retrieval but injects $O(B^2)$ repulsive gradients that fracture continuous coordinate manifolds ($R^2 Rollout) and sample-axis Batch-VICReg to predict +3.0 s physical states; a stop-gradient alignment head then maps frozen prompt states onto the text hypersphere with false-negative masking. On a 4,541-window tri-domain suite (77/60.25/60 GHz) against 10 baselines, freezing the physical backbone and training only the decoupled head lifts R->T R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% and improves MedRank from 107.0 to 60.0 while preserving identical physical readout: 3.37 deg ($R^2=+0.961$) blackout +3.0 s torso tilt, 1.89 m ($R^2=+0.679$; 1.19 m/+0.863 at the RF front-end) cluttered UAV altitude, 2.04 m ($R^2=+0.461$) behind-wall NLOS range, 0.9976 virtual-RIS invariance, and 100% fall recall. Across five 0.5B-1.8B LLM families (15 zero-overhead models), World-JEPA improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in 10/10 runs and blackout tilt in 4/5 (Span-Euc), 2/5 (Scatter), and 5/5 (per-family best) over SFT.
authors: Yicheng Huang, Feng Ke, Linhan Chen, Ziyi Jiang, Xiu Yin Zhang
bullets: Addresses static text-like tokenization and backbone damage from direct contrastive alignment of continuous radar streams.
Uses a frozen physical world model with Batch-VICReg temporal prediction and a stop-gradient alignment head with false-negative masking.
On a 4,541-window, tri-domain suite, R→T R@10 increases from 5.95% to 15.01% and MedRank improves from 107.0 to 60.0.
Preserves physical readouts for blackout tilt, cluttered UAV altitude, behind-wall range, virtual-RIS invariance, and fall detection.
Across five LLM families, improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in all 10 runs, with blackout-tilt gains varying by model family.

papers.abstract: Bimanual manipulation requires each arm to perform distinct motions while coordinating with the other. Common flow-based robotic policies combine both arms' actions into one token per future timestep, giving attention distinct positions across time but not across arms. We introduce Duo, a simple but effective design that models spatial and temporal dependencies within one shared action head. Specifically, Duo separates both arms into two action tokens per timestep, allowing each arm's motion to interact via cross-arm attention during flow matching. On RoboTwin 2.0, Duo improves the overall success of all four base policies, from 0.45B to 3.62B parameters, with gains of 12.55 and 9.02 percentage points for FLOWER (0.89B) and $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.62B), respectively. Despite its compact size, FLOWER-Duo achieves the best randomized-generalization, precision, and memory scores on RoboDojo. In real-world tasks, it outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in both success rate and execution speed, while scaling effectively with increasing training data. To provide deeper insight into the design of Duo, we conduct systematic ablations on inter-arm coordination, action grouping, and token granularity, confirming that cross-arm attention drives the improvement while arm-wise interaction offers the best accuracy-compute trade-off.
authors: Zhimu Zhou, Yuqi Yang, Yixin Lin, Junsen Zhang, Jian Zhao, Jiayu Zhong, Jiaxun Sun, Bingxin Wang, Binhua Zuo, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limited inter-arm modeling of flow-based policies that use one combined action token per timestep.
Separates the two arms into distinct tokens, allowing their motions to interact through cross-arm attention during flow matching.
Improves all four evaluated base policies on RoboTwin 2.0, including gains of 12.55 points for FLOWER and 9.02 points for π₀.₅.
FLOWER-Duo achieves top randomized-generalization, precision, and memory scores on RoboDojo, and outperforms π₀.₅ in real-world success and speed.
Ablations indicate that cross-arm attention drives gains, while arm-wise interaction provides the best accuracy–compute trade-off.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents translate user instructions and screenshots into executable actions. To learn executable actions, existing approaches often rely on explicit reasoning during training, which encourage over-reliance on specific reasoning patterns rather than generalizable action-relevant information. In this paper, we propose an implicit framework, RISE, which integrates action-relevant reasoning into implicit state representations to guide GUI action prediction. To this end, action-relevant reasoning is captured through three complementary supervision objectives: full-CoT state alignment preserves information across the reasoning process, action-distribution alignment encodes action preferences, and reasoning-to-action boundary alignment captures the representation immediately before action generation. In this case, our RISE effectively learns informative implicit representations, thereby improving the accuracy of next-action token prediction. RISE achieves 70.6\% accuracy on OSWorld-G, establishing state-of-the-art performance among compared 8B models with a 4.3-point gain over its backbone. Results across two distinct backbones and six diverse benchmarks further demonstrate its effectiveness in GUI grounding and action prediction. Our code is available on our project page.
authors: Enqi Liu, Zhi Gao, Liu Liu, Lifeng Fan, Liyuan Pan
bullets: Targets the limited generalization of GUI agents trained with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning.
Uses three supervision objectives: full-CoT state alignment, action-distribution alignment, and reasoning-to-action boundary alignment.
Learns implicit representations that preserve reasoning information and encode action preferences before action generation.
Reaches 70.6% accuracy on OSWorld-G, with a 4.3-point gain over its backbone and state-of-the-art results among compared 8B models.
Effectiveness is supported across two backbones and six diverse benchmarks for GUI grounding and action prediction.

papers.abstract: Text-to-scene methods turn a short instruction into a furnished 3D room, but the room that a particular person wants rarely comes across fully in words: many preferences surface only when the person sees a concrete room and can point to what they like and dislike in it. We therefore study personalized indoor scene synthesis under hidden user preferences: over several turns, a system shows a 3D scene, and the user, who sees only rendered images of the scene, replies with brief free-form feedback and a satisfaction score. The system must therefore bring the whole room toward the user's preferences from feedback that comments on only part of it at a time. It must also be able to change every part of the room, because a preference concerns not only single objects but the look and atmosphere that surfaces, lighting, textiles, furniture and their arrangement create together. We present PreferenceScene, in which a large language model keeps an explicit estimate of the user's preferences for every design attribute of the room and, after each turn, infers the taste behind the feedback and revises the whole estimate, including the parts that the feedback does not mention. A scene instantiation module builds every estimated value as its own part of the room, so that each of these parts can follow the user's preferences. We evaluate on the test set of a benchmark with 320 instances in ten room types, with a simulated user and a render-based evaluator. PreferenceScene matches the hidden preferences better than five published text-to-scene baselines adapted to the same interaction, and its match rises with every turn. It even surpasses them when they are given the preferences directly, and a vision-language model rates its scenes as the most realistic and functional.
authors: Seongrae Noh, RyunHa Lee, HyeongYeop Kang
bullets: Addresses the gap between text instructions and preferences that emerge only after users view concrete rooms.
An LLM maintains and updates explicit preferences for every room design attribute, including unmentioned aspects.
A scene instantiation module applies these preferences across objects, lighting, textiles, surfaces, furniture, and layout.
On a 320-instance, 10-room-type benchmark with simulated users, preference matching improves over interaction turns.
It outperforms five adapted text-to-scene baselines and receives the highest realism and functionality ratings from a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents translate screenshots and user instructions into executable actions. Most existing approaches rely on vision-language models to generate actions as text, often leading to substantial inference latency due to autoregressive decoding. To address this inefficiency, we propose GUI-PRISM, a hybrid action decoder that directly predicts action types and structured arguments while retaining language generation for open-ended text. Unlike existing spatial decoding methods that primarily focus on target localization, GUI-PRISM extends direct prediction to action types and their associated arguments, enabling complete GUI action prediction. Specifically, GUI-PRISM employs field-specific queries to extract action-relevant semantic and spatial information from a shared multimodal feature bank. It further models dependencies among action components through conditional queries. Gated residual cross-attention refines these predictions using fine-grained multimodal information. GUI-PRISM achieves 95.1\% accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2, outperforming the strongest head-based spatial decoding method by 2.0 percentage points while delivering a 3.8$\times$ inference speedup over the baseline. On AndroidControl-v2 and MM-Mind2Web-v2, it improves complete-action accuracy by 4.8 and 0.7 percentage points while achieving 2.7$\times$ and 3.9$\times$ inference speedups over the baseline, respectively. Our code is available on our project page.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large vision-language models (LVLMs) by calibrating quantization parameters on a small dataset without retraining. However, despite increasingly sophisticated calibration strategies, prior methods suffer substantial performance degradation under low-bit weight--activation quantization. To understand this degradation, we locate where quantization error is concentrated and examine the corresponding weight and activation distributions. We observe that a few outliers dominate the ranges shared by per-channel (PC) weights and per-token (PT) activations, leaving insufficient resolution for most values and mapping many of them to zero. These findings motivate a shift in focus from calibration refinement to the underlying quantization representation. We therefore present Rotate-and-Refine Quantization (RRQ) as a simple, effective baseline for LVLM PTQ, combining local Hadamard transforms with group quantization and efficient group-aware execution. Across 8 multimodal tasks and diverse quantization settings, RRQ substantially outperforms baselines while reducing inference time and memory usage. At W4A4, it retains over 96\% of full-precision performance on 8B models and over 99\% on a 32B model, compared with less than 8\% for these baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/kmc3661/RRQ

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.

Patient-relative direction reasoning is especially difficult: 27 of 32 open models score below 40%.
Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K improves two MLLMs by 16–20 points, while supplied 3D maps are largely ignored.
GeoJeV enables explicit 3D scene reconstruction and operations, achieving the highest accuracy among evaluated models and narrowing the physician gap.

papers.abstract: Robot-programming agents improve executable control policies through repeated testing and repair, yet binary success saturates while execution risk persists across unseen scenes. We introduce MARGIN, a risk-aware agent that converts successful robot rollouts into actionable evidence for program refinement. Its near-miss margin measures the fraction of the execution budget remaining in the slowest successful development rollout. The agent uses this signal to prioritize fragile programs, guide targeted repairs, and select revisions that preserve development success while increasing execution headroom. An exact safe-racing rule accelerates success-based candidate evaluation. We evaluate MARGIN across LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-90, and Robosuite. In our 80-task LIBERO-Pro reproduction, 78 programs attain perfect development success while accounting for substantial failures on unseen seeds. The near-miss margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774, and low-margin programs exhibit 2.97 times higher failure risk. Across two independent evaluation rounds spanning 37 unique LIBERO-Pro tasks, MARGIN reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0%, with reductions of 18.0-20.0% on LIBERO-90 and Robosuite. Safe racing reduces fixed-sequence candidate-evaluation episodes by 53.5% while retaining identical selections, and paired execution probes improve acceptance decisions by identifying hidden regressions. Together, these results establish near-miss evidence as an effective basis for risk-aware, budget-efficient robot program refinement.

The risk trigger allocates repair budget B; a complete development sweep recomputes S(P ′) and m(P ′), and the controller accepts only success-preserving, margin-improving audited revisions. papers.abstract: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence misalignment through MemPath, an interventional framework that diagnoses failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose BiDE-Mem, which represents questions as typed demands and uses them to guide retrieval and evidence organization. We formalize demand--evidence support; in the evaluated compact path, it is conveyed through provenance-aware evidence organization and Reader guidance rather than a separate generative four-state verification step. On LoCoMo, BiDE-Mem improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis; on LongMemEval, it achieves 91.80%, with strong multi-hop and temporal performance. Supplementary Qwen-Reader evaluations place it first among seven systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S under two judging protocols. Ablations and evidence-level analyses show that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute to answer quality.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences. Misleading or adversarial guidance in source trajectories can corrupt these experiences, allowing harmful instructions to persist across tasks and influence future agent actions. Assessing the risks of potentially corrupted experiences poses three challenges: (1) modeling provenance and execution dependencies before experience reuse, (2) learning task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and (3) repairing risky experiences at online inference. To address these challenges, we present ExpGuard, a framework for retrieval-triggered experience risk assessment and online repair. Specifically, to tackle challenge (1), ExpGuard integrates experience semantics with provenance and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risks before experience reuse. To enable task-conditioned risk supervision and tackle challenge (2), we conduct matched counterfactual replays of each original experience and its minimally neutralized counterpart from the same task and environment checkpoint, deriving separate risk labels from differences in attack success and legitimate task completion. To tackle challenge (3) at inference time, ExpGuard repairs candidate experiences flagged as high-risk by the graph-based predictor at retrieval and re-predicts their risks before they enter the agent's active experience context. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpGuard in identifying risky experiences and defending agents against experience corruption.

papers.abstract: The widespread deployment of latent generative models (LGMs) makes generated image source attribution essential for copyright auditing and data governance, yet practical attribution should remain reliable under common post-processing and platform-induced processing. Existing reconstruction-based attribution methods summarize an image's reconstruction response to a single global scalar, such as the reconstruction error or the ratio of two consecutive errors. These summaries discard channel-frequency structure, allowing image content and post-processing variation to obscure source evidence and making attribution after spreading difficult. We instead uncover a more stable source-discriminative cue under post-processing: the frequency-resolved evolution of residual energy across repeated applications of the same reconstruction operator. Motivated by this insight, we characterize a phenomenon we term Spectral Contraction and use it to build SpCon, a source-attribution framework that accesses only the target model's VAE. SpCon obtains adjacent residuals through two deterministic reconstructions, builds a spectral-contraction representation from their frequency-resolved relative energy change, and aggregates Student-t response densities for each source-condition pair over a finite set of fitted reference components. The same representation supports three settings according to non-belonging reference availability: none (Target-Only, TO; belonging references only), external out-of-domain sources (External-Reference, ER), or known in-domain competitors (Known-Reference, KR). Across seven LGMs, TO, ER, and KR attain average AUROC/AP of 0.8786/0.6344, 0.9404/0.7886, and 0.9652/0.8626 over the 35 conditions, all outperforming the strongest baseline (0.8154/0.5277), and achieve 0.8581/0.5507, 0.9369/0.7549, and 0.9734/0.8773 on the three social platforms.
authors: Chao Wang, Zijin Yang, Yaofei Wang, Yuang Qi, Weiming Zhang, Kejiang Chen
bullets: Existing methods reduce reconstruction behavior to a single scalar, losing frequency-specific source evidence.
SpCon uses two deterministic VAE reconstructions to measure frequency-resolved relative changes in residual energy, termed Spectral Contraction.
The framework supports target-only, external-reference, and known-reference attribution settings.
Across seven latent generative models and 35 conditions, all settings outperform the strongest baseline; performance remains strong on three social platforms.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on source attribution for generated images using spectral contraction. While a forensic task, it deals with the properties of generative models (Latent Generative Models) and their outputs.
papers.title: Not the Scalar, but Its Evolution: Robust Source Attribution for Generated Images
papers.tldr: SpCon improves generated-image source attribution by modeling how reconstruction residual energy evolves across frequencies, making attribution more robust to post-processing and platform processing.

papers.abstract: We propose LoopDVR, a framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Rather than reducing the network width or depth directly, LoopDVR reuses Transformer blocks across layers in both the ViT backbone and Transformer decoder, reducing the number of parameters while retaining the original computational structure. However, naively sharing parameters can disrupt the distinct transformations learned at different depths. To address this challenge, we identify suitable sharing groups based on inter-layer representation dissimilarity and keep the final backbone block independent for multi-scale feature construction. We then initialize each shared backbone block with the pretrained weights of its group's terminal layer to better preserve the learned representations. An independent Loop Adapter at each layer further helps retain depth-specific transformations within shared blocks. Subsequently, we distill visual representations into the looped backbone and integrate it with a looped decoder for task-specific training. Experiments demonstrate that LoopDVR achieves the best accuracy--parameter trade-offs across dense recognition tasks. Compared with the reference models, it reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy. Notably, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 box AP with only 7.0M parameters, highlighting its effectiveness in compact models.
authors: Sirui Liang, Xuanlong Yu, Longfei Liu, Xiaodong Cun, Xi Shen
bullets: Targets parameter reduction in dense visual recognition without directly shrinking network width or depth.
Shares Transformer blocks across selected layer groups in both the ViT backbone and decoder, while keeping the final backbone block independent for multi-scale features.
Uses representation-dissimilarity-based sharing groups, terminal-layer initialization, and per-layer Loop Adapters to preserve depth-specific transformations.
Applies visual representation distillation before task-specific training with the looped decoder.
Reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy; LoopDet-S reaches 50.9 box AP with 7.0M parameters.

papers.selection_reason: LoopDVR reduces parameters in dense visual recognition by reusing Transformer blocks (looping). This parameter sharing strategy aligns with Token Pruning and Eviction for efficiency.
papers.title: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition
papers.tldr: LoopDVR converts pretrained Transformer-based dense vision models into compact looped networks by reusing blocks while preserving accuracy through structured sharing, adapters, and distillation.

papers.abstract: Open-weight LLMs are competent software engineers, but they sometimes fail at tasks they are otherwise able to do. Often it is not a failure of reasoning. It is a few small missteps over a long trajectory (repeating a step that has already failed, or declaring the task done while a requirement is still unmet) that make the difference. Correcting this calls for a surgical weight update that steers the model toward the right actions without interfering with its reasoning. Such updates, typically learned with LoRA adapters, are often too small to survive merging into a released checkpoint. In our BF16 release, the median weight change is only 1.5% of a single rounding step, and merging loses roughly two thirds of the update's norm. When the same adapter is merged into the mixed FP8/NVFP4 release of the same model, 93% of the update disappears. Instead of increasing the size of the update, we directly train on the surviving part. We introduce merge-aware fine-tuning. Standard LoRA rounds the merged weights to the storage format only at export, so the loss never sees the rounded weights. We instead round the sum of base weights and adapter update to the release format at every training step, keeping the vendor's quantization scales, and compute the loss on these weights. The forward pass matches the serving engine numerics, and the gradient passes straight through the rounding, so the model we train is the model we ship. The loss optimizes only the model's actions and keeps its reasoning close to the base model. Applied to Nemotron-3.5, the recipe improves agentic coding in both the BF16 and the NVFP4 release, by up to 8.4 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and we publicly release both models.
authors: Sandeep Singh Sandha, Prann Bansal, Arvind Sundararajan
bullets: Targets small action-level mistakes in software-engineering trajectories rather than broad reasoning failures.
Standard LoRA updates can largely disappear when merged into BF16 or mixed FP8/NVFP4 releases.
Trains with the merged weights rounded to the deployment format at every step, matching serving-time numerics.
Applied to Nemotron-3.5, it improves Terminal-Bench 2.1 performance by up to 8.4 points across BF16 and NVFP4 releases.
The authors publicly release both resulting models.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Learning curves. Training is a single pass, so each step’s rows are unseen when they are scored; every point is a held-out measurement (10-step mean). (a) Action gain: the drop in negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the teacher’s actions relative to the base, per action token. Gains appear after about 60 steps, once the served model has moved enough (ρ ≳ 1.5 × 10−5, fig. 3a). NVFP4 with format-aware learning rates (orange) learns as much as BF16 (blue); an NVFP4 run that adapts only the BF16 latent projections (gray) learns 0.4× as much. (b) The thinking drift penalty k3 against the base stays at 1 to 6× 10−6, which corresponds to a mean log-ratio of about 0.0015 to 0.0035 nats per thinking token, since k3(R) ≈ R2/2: actions improve while the reasoning stays in place.

Figure 1: Merge-aware fine-tuning. Left: standard LoRA trains W + sBA and ships Qfmt(W + sBA), so most of a small update is rounded away (section 2). Right: we compute the loss through the served weight W ′ = Qfmt(W + sBA) and pass the ordinary LoRA gradient straight through the rounding. Only action tokens receive a likelihood term. Thinking tokens are held near the frozen base by a sequence-level KL-style (k3) penalty, and context is masked. The shares kept on the left are for our released BF16 adapter merged by plain rounding (table 1). The dashed arrow is the gradient, which passes the rounding unchanged. Bottom right: the released weights are exactly those the loss was computed on, and the served change is held to a small fixed target (section 3).

The trajectory explores, edits, tests, cleans up, checks the staged diff, re-runs the suite, and submits with the exact protocol. 18 of its 21 assistant turns are supervised; the first three stay in the context without loss. Figure 3: Served change during training. Both panels are measured every five optimizer steps (one step is one update on 24 rows; 158 steps are one pass over the data) by merging the current adapter into the release format. (a) How far the served weights moved, ρ. It grows smoothly in both formats and crosses the range of our best checkpoints (shaded) near step 100, the step we released in both cases. (b) Share of the trained update that survives the merge, κ. BF16 weights keep about a third at the released step, whether in the BF16 run (blue) or in the BF16 latent projections of the NVFP4 run (green); the NVFP4 run as a whole (orange), mostly FP8, keeps about 16%, so it needs a larger learning rate on its FP8 modules to reach the same ρ.

papers.selection_reason: Merge-aware fine-tuning of frontier LLMs, directly relevant to LLM training and release.
papers.title: Fix How It Acts, Not How It Thinks: Surgical Fine-Tuning of Frontier LLMs
papers.tldr: Merge-aware fine-tuning preserves surgical LoRA behavior after quantized checkpoint merging, improving agentic coding while keeping the base model’s reasoning largely unchanged.

papers.abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.
authors: Junsoo Oh, Jihun Yun, Junhyuck Kim, Hanbaek Lyu
bullets: Linear attention avoids growing key-value caches but can lose information through fixed-size memory collisions.
The method uses a delta state for current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of past delta states.
An adaptive readout combines both states to retrieve information across multiple timescales.
A chunkwise parallel formulation supports hardware-efficient training.
Experiments report improved performance across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation, alongside evaluations of efficiency and memory use.

papers.title: Integral DeltaNet: Improved Linear Attention with Adaptive Memory Integration
papers.tldr: Integral DeltaNet improves linear attention by combining fast-changing and long-term recurrent memories for better long-context information retention.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) strengthens model capabilities through feedback from humans and environments. However, emerging evidence suggests that reward optimization can produce outputs whose errors are harder for humans to detect. To address this issue, we construct ITHV (the Image-Text Hallucination Verifiability Dataset), comprising 2,728 visually grounded instances that distinguish between obvious hallucinations, which humans readily detect, and elusive hallucinations, which humans struggle to identify. We then propose DAPO-V, an extension of DAPO that maximizes correctness subject to a budget on verifiability-aware risk. Specifically, DAPO-V combines a verifiability-aware reward with adaptive dual control, where larger penalties are assigned to incorrect responses on questions with lower human verification accuracy. An adaptive multiplier further adjusts the penalty strength according to risk-budget violations. Across three MLLM base models, DAPO-V improves overall accuracy while substantially improving accuracy on elusive hallucination questions by 5.78--9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO. We further test DAPO-V with a blinded human study, which shows that hallucinations are more readily detected in DAPO-V than those of the base model.
authors: Jianhong Pang, Ziyi Ye, Qiuxia Hou, Yanhao Zhang, Zuxuan Wu
bullets: RL can increase capability while making errors harder for humans to recognize.
ITHV contains 2,728 visually grounded instances distinguishing obvious from elusive hallucinations.
DAPO-V combines verifiability-aware rewards with adaptive dual control under a risk budget.
Across three MLLM base models, it improves elusive-hallucination accuracy by 5.78–9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO.
A blinded human study found DAPO-V hallucinations easier to detect than those from the base model.

papers.abstract: Surgical scene understanding is constrained by data scarcity and long-tail class imbalance, as annotating surgical videos demands scarce clinical expertise while rare procedural events remain underrepresented. We tackle this through data generation and propose SurgGenesis, a generative surgical world model that learns future surgical state transitions in a latent space from visual observations and textual procedural descriptions, serving as a scalable surgical data engine. To adapt a large-scale video diffusion model to the data-scarce surgical domain without catastrophic forgetting, we introduce a three-stage progressive LoRA strategy that incrementally injects endoscopic visual priors, procedural semantics, and spatial motion cues. Rather than judging generation by visual fidelity alone, we validate SurgGenesis along two axes that separate a world model from a generic generator: (i) future-awareness, by comparing predicted futures against the real future through a GT-latent prediction gap and temporal-horizon analysis, and (ii) action-faithful usefulness, by checking that generated clips contain the commanded surgical triplet and that using them to rebalance long-tail events and drive downstream understanding (segmentation, triplet recognition, 3D reconstruction) yields action-specific gains. Conditioned futures therefore complement conventional long-tail sampling. Code: https://zh-qr.github.io/SurgGenesis
authors: Qirui Zhong, Quande Liu, Yang Chen, Cheng Xue
bullets: Learns latent future surgical state transitions from endoscopic observations and textual procedural descriptions.
Uses a three-stage progressive LoRA adaptation to inject visual, procedural, and spatial-motion knowledge into a video diffusion model.
Evaluates both future awareness against real future states and whether generated clips follow commanded surgical actions.
Generated data supports long-tail rebalancing and improves downstream segmentation, triplet recognition, and 3D reconstruction.
Scope: designed for data-scarce surgical video understanding, with usefulness assessed through action-specific downstream gains.

papers.abstract: World-action models connect visual prediction with executable robot control. We present EffectWAM, which develops this connection through three complementary components: Effect, camera positional encoding (CaPE), and Action Grounding. Effect represents visual change as the difference between independently encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor. CaPE conditions endpoint pooling on relative camera pose when reliable extrinsics are available, while sharing the same learned parameters with pose-free pooling for uncalibrated trajectories. Action Grounding trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. An exponential moving average of the observation encoder supplies Effect targets. A shared generation expert learns to jointly predict Effect and an executable action chunk through flow matching, and reuses the sampled pair to generate future video on demand. This allows the controller to execute actions without waiting for video synthesis. We train on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, excluding unused chain-of-thought data, and accommodate dataset-specific joint, end-effector, and hand-pose representations. Our evaluation uses the Small (8B) configuration on all five benchmarks and additionally evaluates the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. Experiments examine closed-loop manipulation across complementary benchmarks, and comparisons across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from Action Grounding.

papers.abstract: In-context segmentation (ICS) uses one or a few annotated reference images to specify what to segment in a target image. Existing training-free ICS approaches typically rely on manually designed inference procedures, which may limit how flexibly reference information is combined. Learned in-context inference offers an adaptive alternative, but acquiring this capability through segmentation-specific training can compromise generalization to unseen domains. We therefore ask: can a pretrained in-context learner infer what to segment from annotated references without segmentation-specific training? We introduce SegPFN, a training-free framework that reformulates ICS as tabular classification over frozen visual features. A frozen tabular prior-data fitted network (PFN) uses labeled reference patches as context to classify patches in the target image. We comprehensively benchmark SegPFN against major existing ICS methods across 11 datasets spanning semantic, part, and personalized segmentation. SegPFN improves overall mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) by 4.7 points over the strongest overall baseline and achieves the highest average mIoU in four of five task-shot settings. Further analyses show that hard-negative reference patches improve fine-grained target discrimination, while joint conditioning enables SegPFN to use multiple references effectively. These results show that SegPFN offers a simple and effective paradigm for training-free in-context segmentation.

papers.abstract: LiDAR reconstruction supports closed-loop autonomous driving simulation, but hours of per-scene optimization make large asset libraries costly to build and maintain. We present Instant LiDAR, a feed-forward pipeline that reconstructs multiple LiDAR scans as reusable Gaussian assets in minutes without per-scene optimization. LiDAR measurements provide strong geometric priors, but directly initializing Gaussians from them yields poor reconstruction due to nonuniform sampling and a limited field of view. Sparse returns leave surface gaps, while combining scans expands coverage but introduces redundant primitives. To address these challenges, Instant LiDAR combines measurement-anchored Gaussian prediction, sampling-aware Gaussian scales, and multi-frame consolidation. The predictor refines attributes anchored to recorded returns, while the scales adapt spatial support to LiDAR sampling. Multi-frame consolidation merges overlapping predictions into a compact asset spanning the driving log. Compared with NuRec, Instant LiDAR reconstructs scenes approximately 46 times faster on Physical AI (PAI) and 70 times faster on Waymo. It also achieves comparable downstream 3D detection accuracy on Waymo.
authors: Xin Kang, Jiahui Huang, Jiawei Ren, Sipeng Zhang, Yu Chen, Weihua Zhang, Junjie Lai
bullets: Eliminates costly per-scene optimization, reducing reconstruction to minutes.
