papers.abstract: Continued fractions have been shown to be a function class capable of constructing expressive yet parameter-efficient neural networks. These neural networks are not only effective for supervised learning, but also for training LLMs. However, the rational form of this function class introduces poles when the denominator approaches zero, which prior work has avoided by enforcing a small positive (non-smooth) lower bound. We show that performance and training stability can be highly sensitive to the choice of this lower bound. In this work, we introduce a novel transformation of the partial denominators, inspired by its connection to the Green's function in physics, that mitigates the above issue elegantly by constraining the spectra of the constructed tridiagonal Hamiltonian. Our approach further eliminates the need for incremental training used by previous works for stability, thus avoiding involved modifications to standard pre-training procedures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our reparameterization by replacing FFNs with a previously proposed continued fraction architecture for both language and image generative modeling. Across diverse models, such as GPT-2 XL, (nano) Llama-MoE, and Granite, we show that our proposed method achieves performance comparable to the original (FFN-based) architectures while maintaining ~30%-50% parameter savings as before, and in most cases even outperforms the more complicated incremental training baseline. We further demonstrate, for the first time for continued fraction networks, that their effectiveness also carries over to image generative modeling, that utilize diffusion objectives. On a state-of-the-art Diffusion Transformer, we show that our approach again achieves performance comparable to the original FFN-based models with ~30% parameter savings and significantly outperforms the previous incremental training approach.
authors: Soumyadeep Pal, Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Dennis Wei, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy
bullets: Continued-fraction neural networks are expressive and parameter-efficient but can become unstable when denominators approach zero.

It removes the need for incremental training and its modifications to standard pretraining procedures.
Experiments replacing FFNs in language models and diffusion transformers show performance comparable to FFN baselines, often surpassing incremental training.
The approach extends continued-fraction networks to image generative modeling for the first time, with similar parameter savings.

papers.abstract: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) achieves linear computational complexity through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism, particularly for long-context workloads with small batch sizes or limited head-level parallelism per GPU. We present FlashQLA, a context-parallel execution framework for GDN that exposes additional sequence-level parallelism while reducing boundary-state preprocessing overhead. FlashQLA reduces boundary-state preprocessing overhead through decay-aware preparation and extends sequence parallelism across GPUs with Dual CP, which shares summary computation across parallelism levels. Workload-adaptive Auto CP and CP-aware kernel co-design further improve execution efficiency. FlashQLA achieves $1.7\times$-$3.1\times$ forward speedup and up to $4.4\times$ backward speedup over Flash Linear Attention (FLA) on a single GPU. On eight GPUs with context lengths up to 1M tokens, Dual CP achieves up to $4.8\times$ forward speedup and $4.4\times$ speedup for combined forward and backward execution over FLA KCP.
authors: Xi Lin, Chengruidong Zhang, Huiqiang Jiang, Xiao Li, Zekun Wang, Junda Feng, Yunfei Mao, Siqi Zhang, Siyu Wang, Man Yuan, Rui Men, Bo Zheng, Dayiheng Liu, Bohan Zhuang, Jianwei Zhang

Adds workload-adaptive Auto CP and context-parallel-aware kernel co-design for improved efficiency.
Reports 1.7×–3.1× forward and up to 4.4× backward speedup over FLA on one GPU.
Across eight GPUs and up to 1M-token contexts, Dual CP reaches up to 4.8× forward speedup and 4.4× combined forward/backward speedup over FLA KCP.

papers.abstract: Self-attention over tens of thousands of tokens dominates the generation time of video diffusion transformers, because its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. The FP4 matrix products of modern GPUs can speed up attention, but the 4-bit rounding of the queries Q and the keys K introduces large errors. We show that the exponential in softmax amplifies the error of their product QK, which therefore dominates the attention error. We propose DeCo-Attention, a co-design of algorithm and system for low-precision attention. DeCo-Attention is training-free and compensates the rounding error of Q and K along a few principal directions found by a per-head eigendecomposition. The lightweight compensation terms are appended to Q and K as extra channels, so the FP4 matrix product corrects its own rounding error while it computes the attention scores. Once the products run in FP4, the softmax bounds the kernel, and we optimize the softmax so that the gain of FP4 computation translates into realized speedup. With QK in FP4, we implement DeCo-Attention with the rest of attention in FP8 on GB300 and VR200 and in FP4 on RTX PRO 6000. On Wan2.2, these kernels run 2.13x, 2.49x, and 2.82x faster than BF16 attention, and the whole generation runs 1.55x, 1.68x, and 1.80x faster. On four video generation models, the FP8 configuration achieves LPIPS comparable to prior 8-bit QK methods, and the fully FP4 configuration lower LPIPS than prior fully 4-bit kernels.
authors: Yuhang He, Harrison Zhang, Fanrong Li, Chang Liu, RuQing G. Xu, Perkz Zheng, Zhenhua Wang, Rajeev Rao, Mengdi Wang, Sharan Chetlur, Jun Yang
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost of attention over tens of thousands of video tokens.
Uses per-head eigendecomposition to identify principal error directions in quantized queries and keys.
Appends compensation channels to Q and K, allowing the FP4 matrix product to correct its own rounding error.
Combines FP4 QK with optimized softmax and lower-precision attention components for practical speedups.
Reports 2.13–2.82× faster attention and 1.55–1.80× faster generation on Wan2.2, with competitive or improved LPIPS versus prior low-precision methods.

An eigendecomposition (EVD) of the Gram matrices of 1/256 of the tokens gives the 32 principal directions 𝐵. The projections of the residuals and of the quantized operands onto 𝐵 are appended as NVFP4 compensation channels, so 𝑄′ and 𝐾 ′ have 192 channels. 𝑉 is smoothed by subtracting its block means 𝑉 and quantized to 𝑉 . The block means are added back, the softmax rescales lazily, and 𝑂 is finally divided by ℓ.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DeCo-Attention, a training-free method to compensate for low-precision (FP4) errors in video diffusion transformers. This directly addresses efficient attention mechanisms in video generation models.
papers.title: DeCo-Attention: Decompose to Compensate for Low-Precision Attention
papers.tldr: DeCo-Attention makes long-context video diffusion attention faster in FP4 by correcting QK rounding errors with lightweight, training-free compensation.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D garments for digital characters requires preserving a reference design while adapting the garment to the target body's shape and pose. Sewing-pattern methods can struggle to reproduce unfamiliar designs and fine details, while image-to-3D generators offer rich shape priors but typically lack explicit 3D body context. We present \textbf{BodyWeave}, a framework that unifies garment generation and fitting through native 3D body conditioning. Building on 3D generative priors, BodyWeave uses the body as a spatial reference throughout geometry generation: a \textbf{Global Body Adapter} guides garment placement and extent in the shared coordinate frame, while \textbf{Local Body Attention} guides surface refinement using nearby body geometry. A \textbf{Surface Penetration Loss} supervises decoded surfaces to reduce body intersections, and the resulting geometry conditions material synthesis to produce garments with physically based rendering attributes. To support learning across designs and wearers, we construct \textbf{GarmentWeave3D} with 293K aligned garment--body observations, including 114K same-design cross-body pairs. Evaluations on out-of-domain \textbf{Artist-Created Garments} demonstrate high geometric fidelity and low body penetration. Cross-body evaluations demonstrate accurate adaptation to new wearers with consistent garment--body spacing, while appearance comparisons show faithful fabric reproduction. Additional results and resources are available at https://gavin-jy.github.io/bodyweave-page/
authors: Junyi Zhang, Yuanchuan Wang, Qichao Wang, Wenzhe Qian, Shizhuo Cheng, Min Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of preserving unfamiliar garment designs while adapting them to different body shapes and poses.
Uses a Global Body Adapter for garment placement and extent, plus Local Body Attention for nearby surface refinement.
Introduces a Surface Penetration Loss to reduce intersections between garments and bodies.
Builds GarmentWeave3D with 293K aligned garment–body observations, including 114K same-design cross-body pairs.
Reports high geometric fidelity, low penetration, accurate cross-body adaptation, and faithful fabric appearance on artist-created garments.

papers.abstract: Occupancy world models predict future 3D scenes conditioned on ego actions, yet their predictions may not faithfully follow the specified trajectory under counterfactual actions. Because driving datasets provide sparse coverage of alternative trajectories for each scene, existing models learn the spatial effect of ego motion implicitly from observed scene--trajectory combinations, which may entangle action effects with scene--trajectory correlations. We propose ReCast, an ego-trajectory-guided transformer that grounds future prediction in action-induced geometric correspondence across ego-centric frames. ReCast decouples historical encoding from future decoding and aligns deformable interactions using relative ego transformations, while retaining flexibility for non-rigid scene evolution. We also introduce a counterfactual action-faithfulness benchmark covering in-distribution, tail, and out-of-distribution trajectories. On Occ3D-nuScenes, ReCast achieves competitive standard forecasting performance while improving counterfactual forecasting, with particularly clear gains under out-of-distribution trajectories.
authors: Jongseong Bae, Ha Young Kim
bullets: Existing models can entangle action effects with scene–trajectory correlations because driving data sparsely covers alternative trajectories.
ReCast uses an ego-trajectory-guided transformer with relative ego transformations to align future predictions across ego-centric frames.
The model separates historical encoding from future decoding while preserving flexibility for non-rigid scene changes.
The proposed benchmark evaluates counterfactual action faithfulness on in-distribution, tail, and out-of-distribution trajectories.
On Occ3D-nuScenes, ReCast maintains competitive standard forecasting and improves counterfactual forecasting, particularly out of distribution.

papers.abstract: The realistic rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has drawn interest from real-time applications that require maps to be built online. This led to coupling 3DGS with SLAM, providing camera poses and initial Gaussians for the map. However, the map is still optimized with designs inherited from conventional SLAM, which train only on keyframes selected for localization and regularize geometry with uncertain frontend depth. These designs overlook the model complexity of a 3DGS map: with millions of parameters but few views of each region, the map overfits to sparse inputs. Resolving this is challenging, as every view and Gaussian added to the map competes for the same real-time budget. We close this gap from both sides. To add views while keyframes preserve the structure of the map, we progressively admit non-keyframe images as mapping updates complete and allocate the limited updates across different groups of frames according to the supervision each group provides. To control the model complexity of the map, edge-guided initialization places new Gaussians where image detail requires them. To complement the uncertain frontend depth, Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization (SOR) uses accumulated rendering evidence, at no extra rendering cost, to suppress the opacity of Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of a map-derived surface reference. Together, these designs improve both the appearance and the geometry of online maps within the real-time budget.
authors: Dong Hwi Kim, Park Sangwon, Chaehyeon Song, Ayoung Kim
bullets: Online 3DGS maps can overfit because millions of parameters are optimized from sparse views under a real-time budget.
Non-keyframe images are progressively admitted after mapping updates, with updates allocated according to each frame group’s supervision value.
Edge-guided initialization adds new Gaussians where image detail requires greater representation capacity.
Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization suppresses Gaussians that persistently appear in front of a map-derived surface reference, complementing uncertain frontend depth.
The combined approach improves online-map appearance and geometry while preserving real-time constraints.

papers.abstract: AI-generated music has become common on music streaming platforms, and listeners often cannot distinguish it from music made by humans. AI-music detection is therefore needed, but detectors trained on a fixed set of generators often fail on unseen generators. As new generators emerge frequently, updating a universal detector, a single model for all generators, typically requires substantial training data and computation, while risking performance degradation on previously learned generators. We therefore introduce IncrementDET, a detector that learns each new generator by a process called enrollment. For each generator, IncrementDET trains one linear classifier, which we call a needle, to separate samples of that generator from a fixed set of human reference tracks. Enrolling a new generator adds one needle while the previously constructed needles remain unchanged. A Sidak correction keeps the overall false-positive rate at its target as needles are added. To compare detectors under these conditions, we define the task of continual AI-generated music detection and introduce a benchmark in which generators arrive one at a time. The benchmark measures the accuracy of a detector before and after each update and the cost of each update. For this benchmark, we also construct EvoMusicFake-17K, a dataset of instrumental music from six recent generators and four human music platforms. Compared with SpecTTTra, a state-of-the-art universal detector, IncrementDET learns a new generator more accurately from only a few samples, generalizes better to unseen generators and better preserves detection performance on previously learned generators, at a substantially lower update cost. The structure of IncrementDET can also be applied to the detection of generated images and video, where new generators are released just as frequently.
authors: Runbao Du, Wei Li, Qile He
bullets: Addresses the failure of fixed-generator detectors and the high cost and degradation risks of updating universal detectors.
Enrolls each generator with a linear “needle” classifier trained against fixed human reference tracks; existing needles remain unchanged.
Uses Sidak correction to maintain the target overall false-positive rate as more needles are added.
Introduces continual AI-generated music detection and the EvoMusicFake-17K benchmark covering six generators and four human platforms.
Reports better few-shot learning, unseen-generator generalization, retention of prior detection performance, and lower update cost than SpecTTTra under the benchmark setting.

papers.abstract: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their specialties but hard to unify: their training data are often private, and independently developed specialists cannot be assumed to share an architecture. Deploying these large models separately is costly. We present HuluOPD, an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies heterogeneous specialists into one lightweight VLM using only unlabeled prompts, without requiring reference answers or the specialists' training data. The lightweight model answers each prompt, and the specialist of the prompt's modality supervises its response; a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss makes this possible even when they differ in architecture and tokenizer. We apply HuluOPD to five specialists, for ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography, and dental imaging. To distill and evaluate them, we build HuluOPDCorpus, 914k unlabeled prompts, and HuluOPDBench, 47k held-out test items, from over 90 public datasets, and score all models under one protocol on 132k test items, including third-party benchmarks. A single model with 10% of the five specialists' combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance, and one with 2% retains 89%. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of unifying heterogeneous medical specialist VLMs without requiring their training data or a shared architecture.

Models using 10% and 2% of the specialists’ combined parameters retain 94% and 89% of their question-answering performance, respectively.

papers.abstract: Latent action models (LAMs) learn action-like latents from unlabeled video by coupling frame-pair inference with latent-conditioned prediction, enabling policy and world-model pretraining. However, what the latent must explain depends on the representation space used for action inference and transition prediction. When this space entangles the agent's evolving physical state with visual context, such as background and persistent agent appearance, inferred latents can encode information unrelated to the agent's actions. To address this challenge, we propose Agent-State LAM, which jointly learns a compact agent-state representation and latent actions modeling its transitions. The compact state aggregates dense visual features into a shared space for both action inference and forward prediction. To guide what this state retains, we introduce spatially matched temporal discrimination (SMTD), which trains the state to distinguish its source frame from nearby frames through spatially flexible matching with frozen local visual features. Rather than comparing global frame representations, SMTD scores each frame by emphasizing its strongest local feature matches across spatial locations. This scoring allows background and persistent agent appearance to remain matched across frames despite displacement, making these shared cues less informative for identifying the source frame and encouraging the representation to capture the agent's evolving physical state. Extensive experiments on distracting control tasks and six real robot video datasets demonstrate improved action recovery, downstream control, and world-model prediction. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mid-Push/Agent-State-LAM.
authors: Shaoan Xie, Fan Feng, Peiyuan Zhu, Peter Spirtes, Kun Zhang
bullets: LAMs can encode background and persistent appearance when action inference and prediction use entangled visual representations.

papers.abstract: Agentic harnesses enable frontier vision-language models (VLMs) to manipulate robots through perception, planning, and control tools, yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging. We present RoboHarness-RL, an agentic reinforcement learning framework for improving VLM-based robot manipulation through tool calls. Starting from supervised fine-tuning on successful teacher demonstrations, the VLM further improves through multi-turn reinforcement learning with task-outcome rewards, without relying on vision-language-action models or world action models. To support efficient multi-turn training, we develop LiteHarness, which uses hierarchical memory to keep interaction contexts compact while preserving task performance. With Qwen3.5-9B, RL raises success from 31.2% to 44.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 and from 57.8% to 73.3% on LIBERO-Pro; these gains extend to randomized RoboTwin scenes unseen during training (26.4% to 38.0%). Behavioral analysis further shows that RL reduces repetitive-call rates by up to $4\times$, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback. RL reduces repetitive tool calls, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback.

papers.abstract: Promptable video trackers such as SAM2 achieve accurate and robust performance through strong temporal consistency, making them important foundations for downstream video understanding and tracking applications. As their use continues to expand, understanding their robustness to adversarial perturbations becomes increasingly important. Existing attacks on SAM2 largely focus on local mask degradation and short-term temporal feature disruption, leaving its longer-term dynamics and competing object interferences (Distractors) insufficiently explored. We observe that SAM2 itself exposes useful distractor cues when tracking becomes uncertain. Based on these observations, we propose DistractAttack, a white-box attack that uses background distractors to disrupt target tracking persistently. Its core procedure, Counterfactual Distractor Search (CDS), propagates clean and attacked trajectories in parallel to discover plausible competing regions and identify those that become increasingly effective under perturbation. The discovered evidence is accumulated over time to weaken target support and promote recurrent alternatives or disappearance predictions. Extensive experiments under video-level and one-shot perturbations across Visual Object Tracking and Video Object Segmentation demonstrate strong attack effectiveness, raising DRE to $4.4\times$ and NRE to $7.3\times$ their nearest baselines under video perturbation, while transferring effectively across model scales and tracker variants in black-box settings. papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) requires choosing both a batch size and a parallel configuration. Existing systems make these decisions in isolation, tuning parallelism for throughput and batch size for convergence, but neither objective alone determines training efficiency. We present LIBRA, a lightweight runtime framework that co-tunes batch size and parallel configuration to minimize end-to-end time. LIBRA treats throughput and convergence as two noisy objectives and searches their joint space using parallel noisy expected hypervolume improvement (qNEHVI). To make this runtime search efficient, we propose hierarchical pruning, which removes infeasible and low-throughput parallel configurations through system-level performance estimation and then narrows batch-size candidates through critical-batch-size-aware convergence monitoring. We further design acquisition-guided parallel evaluation (AGPE), which evaluates surviving candidates concurrently across GPU groups in order of their acquisition values. On clusters of up to 256 GPUs, LIBRA reduces time-to-convergence by 31.1% on average over state-of-the-art methods, while runtime tuning accounts for only 0.3-3.5% of overall time.

papers.abstract: Latent world models learn compact recurrent dynamics from offline trajectories, yet deployed simulators can retain backdoor triggers or stale transitions from outdated physical regimes. Existing unlearning methods fail in autoregressive physics: gradient updates distort latent manifolds and compound rollout drift, naive output zeroing suppresses valid control responses on trigger onset, and single-step deletion leaves corruption inside recurrent hidden states. We propose Analytical Dynamics Excision (ADE), a deterministic, zero-training closed-form unlearning algorithm for latent world models. Using only cached pretraining moments, ADE recovers retain covariances via single-pass matrix downdating without raw retain data and cascades closed-form edits across the input bottleneck, hidden states, and downstream heads. Pairing orthogonal excision with whitened recurrent damping and mean-preserving affine calibration neutralizes out-of-manifold backdoors and realigns in-manifold shifts without variance collapse. Across four regimes on three MuJoCo benchmarks, ADE outperforms seven tuned baselines on DreamerV1, eliminating HalfCheetah and Hopper velocity-flip triggers $4.4\times$ faster than fine-tuning, and transfers zero-shot to DreamerV3.
authors: Sirui He, Chi Zhang
bullets: Targets trigger-induced backdoors and outdated physical regimes in autoregressive latent simulators.
Uses cached pretraining moments to perform closed-form covariance downdating without raw retain data or training.
Edits the input bottleneck, recurrent hidden states, and output heads using orthogonal excision, recurrent damping, and affine calibration.
Evaluated across four regimes and three MuJoCo benchmarks, outperforming seven tuned baselines on DreamerV1.
Removes HalfCheetah and Hopper velocity-flip triggers 4.4× faster than fine-tuning and transfers zero-shot to DreamerV3.

papers.abstract: Comparing two entities in an image, multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) often answer wrongly. We find that the answer bias enters not when the model sees, but when it decides with the image in view: the model's own descriptions of the two entities often already hold the right answer. We therefore propose D$^3$ (Describe, Don't Decide): the model describes each entity alone, decides from these descriptions without the image, and merges this decision with its direct answer. Without any training, D$^3$ improves all 79 model-benchmark pairs across ten benchmarks and eight 7-9B MLLMs. On held-out GQA comparison questions, the mean accuracy of these models rises from 72.4% to 83.2% (up to +21.5% per model), higher than that of Qwen2.5-VL-32B answering directly (82.8%). Code will be available at https://github.com/paul-swu/describe-dont-decide.
authors: Shuwei Wu, Longin Jan Latecki
bullets: MLLMs often identify the correct comparison evidence in their descriptions but make errors when deciding with the image visible.
D³ has the model describe each entity independently, compare the descriptions without the image, and combine that decision with its direct answer.
The training-free method improves all 79 model–benchmark pairs tested across ten benchmarks and eight 7–9B MLLMs.
On held-out GQA comparison questions, mean accuracy increases from 72.4% to 83.2%, with gains up to 21.5% per model.
The approach is evaluated for image-based comparison questions; the abstract does not establish broader task coverage beyond these settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. D3 describes with the image in view and decides without it. Left: the direct answer. Given the image and the original question, the MLLM answers wrongly; pimg (orange) is its probability for each option. Right: the three steps of D3; in the first two, the MLLM takes the box on its left and returns the one on its right. Describe Each Entity Alone: the two entities and the aspect (yellow) are read from the question, and each entity is described in its own call, with the image but not the original question, giving d1 and d2 (green). Decide Without the Image: given only d1, d2, and the original question (the text-only call), the MLLM gives the description-based decision pdesc (purple). Merge at Equal Weight: the output is the option y with the larger (1 − λ) pimg(y) + λ pdesc(y), where λ = 1 2 (Eq. 1). The snowflake marks the frozen MLLM, the same in every call. Example: Qwen2.5-VL on one GQA question.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a training-free inference strategy to correct answer bias in multimodal LLMs, directly relevant to multimodal foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Describe, Don't Decide: Correcting Answer Bias in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: D³ reduces answer bias in multimodal LLMs by making them describe image entities separately before deciding between them.

papers.abstract: Even when multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer incorrectly, their internal cues often point to the relevant region. A widely used remedy re-presents the cue-selected region as an enlarged crop to supply finer detail. However, we find that much of its gain requires no new detail: it largely survives when the crop comes from the already-seen low-resolution input, and partly even when the region's cached tokens are merely copied. Part of re-presentation's gain thus comes from drawing attention to evidence the model already holds. We propose InCue, a test-time framework that makes better use of this evidence without additional visual input. InCue treats visual attention and predictive-entropy gradients as Internal Cues, couples them into a spatial target, and optimizes only an offset on the existing visual tokens to steer attention toward it. Under matched visual-token budgets, InCue achieves state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming recent test-time methods and improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V$^*$ and 23.4% on its hard samples. Its gains carry over to eight general benchmarks. Code will be available at https://github.com/paul-swu/InCue.
authors: Shuwei Wu, Siyue Yu, Longin Jan Latecki
bullets: Re-presenting cropped regions helps partly by highlighting evidence the model has already seen, not only by supplying finer detail.
InCue combines visual-attention and predictive-entropy gradients to identify a spatial target.
It optimizes an offset over existing visual tokens, avoiding additional visual input while preserving matched token budgets.
The method reportedly achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V* and 23.4% on hard samples, with gains across eight general benchmarks.
Scope: InCue is a test-time framework and relies on internal cues available from the MLLM.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of InCue. The MLLM stays frozen, and the only free variable is an additive offset ∆U on the cached visual tokens U0. SCC couples the read-out attention cue A with the sensitivity cue S, obtained by backpropagating the predictive entropy H(p), into the joint response J . RCR amplifies J inside the best-scoring window W ⋆ to form the spatial target T . Test-time optimization then updates ∆U to increase the overlap between the current attention A(k) and T (k). The cues and the target are refreshed at every step k, and the answer is read out after K steps (Output): here it changes from (C) pink to the correct (D) black.

Heat maps show attention over visual tokens, green boxes the ground-truth targets, and top-left labels the predictions (green correct, red wrong). Bottom-left numbers give the correct-answer margin (correct minus strongest wrong option logit), and bottom-right numbers the attention in the boxes relative to step 0. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a test-time optimization framework that steers MLLM visual tokens using internal cues, fitting both test-time learning and multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: InCue: Making Better Use of What Multimodal LLMs Already See at Test Time
papers.tldr: InCue improves MLLM test-time reasoning by steering attention toward internally identified evidence already present in the input, without adding visual information.

papers.abstract: Recently, physics-inspired neural networks have gained widespread attention due to their interpretability. The closed-form, frequency-time decoupled solution of the wave equation offers linear complexity and allows different frequency components to evolve independently, making it a potential alternative solution for efficient image super-resolution. Therefore, a physics-inspired wave evolution attention framework is proposed, namely WaveSR. The WaveSR framework involves two key modules, i.e., wave evolution attention (WEA) and Frequency-Adaptive Feed-Forward Network (FA-FFN). The WEA module achieves feature interactions through the analytical solution of the 2D wave equation in the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) domain, enabling independent evolution of different frequency components with learnable wave speed \(c\) and damping coefficient \(\alpha\). The FA-FFN module realizes adaptive frequency feature selection through learnable spectral modulation, effectively enhancing feature representation capability. Subsequently, we employ a two-stage training strategy with a hybrid objective that combines a spatial-domain pixel loss and a frequency-domain loss to improve reconstruction quality. Our method provides a preliminary exploration of physics-inspired neural networks for efficient image super-resolution.
authors: Xiaoyan Lei, Biao Luo, Wenlong Zhang, Tingwen Huang, Chunhua Yang, Weihua Gui
bullets: Targets efficient image super-resolution using the closed-form, frequency–time-decoupled wave equation.
Wave Evolution Attention performs FFT-domain feature interactions with independently evolving frequency components.
Frequency-Adaptive Feed-Forward Network selects and enhances frequency features through learnable spectral modulation.
A two-stage training strategy combines spatial pixel loss with frequency-domain loss to improve reconstruction quality.
The work is presented as a preliminary exploration of physics-inspired neural networks for efficient super-resolution.

papers.title: WaveSR: Physics-Inspired Wave Evolution Attention for Efficient Image Super-Resolution
papers.tldr: WaveSR uses wave-equation-inspired frequency modeling and adaptive spectral filtering to pursue efficient, high-quality image super-resolution.

papers.abstract: Can a language model work in the weight space of a policy network for a repeated game? We put four questions to a mid-size open model, on recurrent networks of 1{,}218 weights with exactly checkable answers. Given a population of opponents described in English, write a policy that is optimal: its value is a finite computation over the agent's information state, so a submitted network has an exact gap from the optimum. Given a network's weights, report its action after each of fifteen opponent histories; recover the state machine it implements, judged on every opponent sequence to depth ten; or repair a network whose output was altered in one place and say which round first goes wrong. The model recovers the program in 62 of 66 replies, reports all fifteen behavioral entries correctly in 34 of 36, and attains the optimum in 20 of 20 when it states a policy the evaluator compiles. Repair is the exception: 4 of 18 repaired, 5 of 18 diagnosed, with a median patch covering one of the two entries needed.
authors: Ancil Crayton
bullets: Tests four tasks on recurrent policy networks with 1,218 weights and exactly checkable answers.
Writes optimal policies from English descriptions of repeated-game opponents; all 20 compiled policies attain the optimum.
Recovers implemented state machines in 62 of 66 replies and predicts 15-step behavior completely in 34 of 36 cases.
Repair is substantially weaker: 4 of 18 repairs succeed and 5 of 18 faults are diagnosed.
The study evaluates exact policy values, action sequences, state machines, and first-failure rounds.

papers.selection_reason: Studies LLM capabilities for reading, writing, and repairing policies in weight space, relevant to language foundation model research.
papers.title: Reading, Writing and Repairing Game-Theoretic Policies in Weight Space
papers.tldr: A mid-size language model can read, write, and often recover recurrent game policies directly from their weights, but struggles to repair damaged ones.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.
authors: Chenru Wang, Shengwei An
bullets: Addresses the cost of training looped diffusion transformers from scratch by distilling an existing non-looped teacher.
Shares one block across depth and trains each loop output toward the teacher using a fixed-point, ODE-inspired distillation process.
Supports variable loop counts at inference without retraining and applies higher-order ODE solvers along the depth dimension.
Introduces loop guidance using outputs from different loop counts to improve samples with little extra computation.

On SD3-medium, a student with about 37% of the teacher’s parameters matches average evaluation quality with two to four loops; two loops use about 58% of teacher compute, while loop guidance improves the reported four-step score average from 88.2 to 99.2.

(c) Each round combines the previous hidden state and the output of the looped blocks with weights 1−∆sk and ∆sk, where ∆sk = sk − sk−1. All rounds share Rθ , conditioned on sk, and all per-loop outputs share Q. The output after every round is regressed to its per-round target of Eq. 5, which mixes the stop-gradient previous output and vT with weights 1 − ak and ak, where ak = sk−sk−1

papers.abstract: Modeling 4D hand-object interaction (HOI) is fundamental to understanding manipulation. This requires physics, since hands move objects only by touch and each material responds differently. Yet existing methods ignore this physics or simulate only a narrow range of matter. Programs can instead describe any matter with its physics, but coding agents omit the hand that drives the interaction. We close this gap with CodeHOI, to our knowledge the first agentic framework that writes physically plausible 4D HOI as programs. To write one, an Object Agent first builds each object with the physics of its matter. An HOI Agent then specifies the hands by their contacts and simulates each kind of matter with an established physics solver. Finally, an Evaluator Agent checks each result against physical laws. We also introduce CodeHOI-Bench with 100 reconstruction and generation tasks across four kinds of matter. With off-the-shelf frontier models, CodeHOI writes interactions that are plausible for every kind of matter and remain so when transferred to an independent physics engine. It thereby enables coding agents to write physically plausible HOI across diverse matter.
authors: Seonghwan Park, Inho Chang, Min-Gyu Park
bullets: Addresses the lack of physics and hand modeling in existing 4D hand-object interaction methods.
An Object Agent models each object’s material physics, while an HOI Agent defines hand contacts and interactions.
An Evaluator Agent validates generated interactions against physical laws.
Introduces CodeHOI-Bench with 100 reconstruction and generation tasks spanning four material types.

papers.abstract: Cross-lingual transfer is uneven across tasks, succeeding for natural language understanding but often failing for mathematical reasoning. We argue that this asymmetry is governed by the geometry of parameter space. Specifically, cross-lingual generalization is determined by whether English and target-language LoRA adapters share a low-error basin. To test this, we use linear mode connectivity (LMC) between English and target-language adapters, evaluating on three tasks. We find that NLI and QA model-language pairs are mostly linearly connected, whereas mathematical reasoning (Math) pairs are not, indicating that basin geometry is task-dependent. Such disconnection in Math is ``local'' rather than global. A small target-language task sample, applied only to the English adapter's language encoding or semantic composition layers, is enough to repair it. Cross-lingual generalization is also factorizable into language-specific encoding and language-agnostic composition, each supplied separately from a cheaper signal. English task data routed to the composition layers and an unlabeled target-language corpus routed to the language encoding layers each alleviate it on their own for nearly every pair. Composition is the more influential of these, and it needs no target-language data. Together, these results suggest that cross-lingual generalization decomposes into language-specific and language-agnostic components in parameter space. This decomposition offers a practical route for low-resource cross-lingual adaptation.
authors: Yeoreum Lee, Jaeseong Lee, Seung-won Hwang
bullets: NLI and QA adapters are usually linearly connected across languages, while Math adapters often occupy disconnected low-error basins.
Mathematical disconnection is local: updating language-encoding or semantic-composition layers with a small target-language sample can repair it.
Transfer decomposes into language-specific encoding and language-agnostic composition components.
English task data can improve composition, while unlabeled target-language data can improve encoding; composition is more influential and needs no target-language data.
The findings suggest a low-resource adaptation strategy based on selectively supplying these two components.

papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) accelerates autoregressive decoding through block-wise prediction, but remains vulnerable to error accumulation across sequentially generated blocks. To investigate this limitation, we analyze the distinction between block-wise and sequence-level cumulative information loss (CIL). Specifically, when the model generates using its own previous outputs without access to reference answers, the input-conditional gap equals the cross-block dependence of the reference targets. To improve prediction when these generated prefixes are imperfect, we propose Dual-MTP, which supervises shared prediction heads under full and randomly masked contexts. Together, complete-prefix supervision and context perturbations provide complementary training signals while retaining the MTP architecture. To characterize this training objective, we use the normalized dual loss to bound the divergence between the model's predictive distributions under full and masked contexts. Experiments across five backbones and six tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and GLUE understanding show that Dual-MTP achieves the highest average task score on four of five backbones, with gains of up to 2.46 points over MTP. On mathematical reasoning tasks, Dual-MTP also achieves 1.4 to 1.9 times the decoding throughput of the NTP reference. Together, these results show that dual-context supervision can improve prediction accuracy while retaining efficient multi-token decoding.
authors: Tangyu Jiang, Zhanke Zhou, Haodi Wang, Yiu-ming Cheung, Xiaohua Jia, Bo Han
bullets: MTP suffers from cumulative information loss when generated prefixes contain errors and differ from reference contexts.
The paper distinguishes block-wise from sequence-level loss and links the input-conditional gap to cross-block dependence in reference targets.
Dual-MTP applies shared prediction heads with full-prefix and randomly masked-context supervision.
A normalized dual loss bounds divergence between predictions under full and masked contexts.
Across five backbones and six tasks, Dual-MTP improves average scores on four backbones, with gains up to 2.46 points; reasoning-task throughput is 1.4–1.9× NTP.

papers.abstract: Hybrid physics-neural simulators embed neural networks in partial differential equation (PDE) solvers to model unresolved subgrid dynamics while preserving resolved physics and conservation laws. Because closure outputs feed back across time steps, single-step offline regression does not directly minimize multi-step rollout error, motivating online trajectory optimization. Solver backpropagation through time (BPTT) is the standard online solution when solver derivatives are available, yet many operational Fortran and C/C++ simulators expose only non-differentiable, forward-only interfaces. We introduce FORGE (Forward-Only Response and Gauss-Newton Estimation), an online framework that trains embedded networks from forward runs alone by decoupling exact network derivatives from black-box simulator dynamics. Stage I warms up the rollout via a low-dimensional Gauss-Newton step along output-orthonormal weight directions, canceling multi-layer feature drift via a final-layer correction. Stage II perturbs spatial output fields to fit a gain-bounded causal linear response operator across rollout steps, solves for regularized target outputs, and updates all weights via network backpropagation. Across five 2D and 3D benchmarks spanning phase separation, reaction-diffusion, fluid and MHD turbulence, and ocean circulation, FORGE outperforms gradient-free, reinforcement-learning, and emulator-based baselines, cutting coarse-solver test mean squared error (MSE) by 50%-96% in 2D and 70% in 3D, outperforming the strongest forward-only baseline by 16%-69%, and recovering 88%-98% of Solver BPTT's gains. Code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/FORGE.
authors: Ruiqi Shu, Tianrun Gao, Haomin Wen, Xiaomeng Huang
bullets: Addresses multi-step rollout optimization when operational Fortran/C/C++ simulators expose only forward, non-differentiable interfaces.
Uses a two-stage approach: low-dimensional Gauss–Newton warm-up with final-layer correction, followed by response-operator fitting and network backpropagation.
Evaluated on five 2D/3D benchmarks covering phase separation, reaction-diffusion, turbulence, and ocean circulation.
Reduces coarse-solver test MSE by 50–96% in 2D and 70% in 3D, recovering 88–98% of BPTT’s gains.
Scope: targets embedded neural closures in PDE-based hybrid simulators with forward-only access.

papers.abstract: Generating videos with physically plausible dynamics remains challenging despite advances in visual quality. Latent world models offer predictive signals for evaluating physical plausibility, but higher agreement between predicted and observed features may reflect easier-to-predict scene content rather than more plausible dynamics. We propose \textbf{S}elf-Referenced \textbf{P}hysical \textbf{A}lignment \textbf{R}ewards (\textbf{SPAR}), a framework that uses world-model predictions for inference-time physical alignment. SPAR compares each video's prediction error with that of static clips constructed by repeating its own frames, providing a content-matched reference for evaluating generated dynamics. To account for the uneven spatial and temporal distribution of physical interactions, we introduce a unified \textbf{spatiotemporal reward refinement} strategy. \textbf{Spatial refinement} emphasizes localized prediction discrepancies, while \textbf{temporal refinement} moderates brief error peaks and supplements prediction errors with agreement between predicted and observed feature changes. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SPAR improves the physical plausibility of both \textbf{text-to-video generation} and \textbf{image-to-video continuation}, bringing generated dynamics into closer alignment with the physical regularities governing real-world events. Additional results and resources are available at https://gavin-jy.github.io/spar-page/
authors: Junyi Zhang, Qichao Wang, Wenzhe Qian, Yuanchuan Wang, Min Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that world-model prediction agreement can reflect predictable content rather than physically plausible dynamics.
Compares a video's prediction error with static, frame-repeated clips from the same video to create a content-matched reference.
Uses spatial refinement to focus on localized interactions and temporal refinement to reduce sensitivity to brief error spikes.
Adds agreement between predicted and observed feature changes to complement prediction-error signals.
Evaluations across multiple benchmarks show improved physical plausibility for both text-to-video and image-to-video generation.

papers.abstract: Advancing surgical automation requires a comprehensive spatio-temporal understanding of how instruments act on tissue throughout an action. Existing surgical benchmarks, however, largely define supervision through task-specific targets, leaving the relationships between action semantics, instrument motion, and tissue interaction incompletely specified. To address this limitation, we introduce TACTUS (Tool, Action, Contact and Trajectory Understanding in Surgery), a new dataset and benchmark that establishes a unified annotation framework for complete surgical actions. The framework jointly specifies tool and action identities, nested action and interaction windows, instrument-specific landmark trajectories, and tissue-region tracks. To construct these annotations at scale, we develop a two-tier pipeline combining human annotation, point tracking, and model-generated spatial prompts. Using this pipeline, we re-annotate 141 videos from five public sources, producing 22,995 action clips spanning 2.9 million frames. The dataset comprises 15,668 Gold clips with human spatial prompts followed by review and re-checking, and 7,327 Silver clips combining human semantic and temporal annotations with model-generated spatial prompts. We further introduce TactusNet, the companion reference network, to benchmark semantic, temporal, and spatial prediction from shared video features. Across TactusNet and 13 published baselines, tool-action accuracy reaches 95.8% with per-head encoder fine-tuning, while the best temporal recall and contact Dice reach 46.6% at temporal IoU 0.7 and 0.351, respectively. Moreover, adding Silver improves the default TactusNet's pair accuracy from 93.8% to 95.5%. Together, these contributions establish a foundation for learning and evaluating the instrument-tissue interactions underlying future surgical automation.
authors: Lurui Wang, Hao Ding, Chenhao Yu, Chenyan Jing, Jiru Xu, Ruoqi Zuo, Liwei Mei, Chang Liu, Lalithkumar Seenivasan, Mathias Unberath
bullets: Introduces a unified framework for complete surgical actions, linking tools, actions, interaction windows, trajectories, and tissue-region tracks.
Uses a two-tier annotation pipeline combining human labeling, point tracking, and model-generated spatial prompts.
Re-annotates 141 videos from five public sources into 22,995 clips spanning 2.9 million frames, with Gold and Silver annotation tiers.
Provides TactusNet and 13 baselines for semantic, temporal, and spatial prediction; reported tool-action accuracy reaches 95.8%.
Establishes a foundation for modeling and evaluating instrument–tissue interactions in surgical automation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $\tau$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $\tau$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.

Evaluations across VLA models, simulation benchmarks, and two real robots show effective speedups with near-baseline success rates.

papers.abstract: A driving planner needs both scene semantics, which vision-language models (VLMs) provide, and spatial structure, which geometric foundation models recover from visual history. We present VLG-Drive, which keeps both models frozen and trains only a fusion interface and a planner from trajectory labels. At each camera-grid cell, the interface fuses the paired VLM and geometry features into one joint token through a geometry-anchored residual, and a command-conditioned planner reads these tokens to predict the ego trajectory. VLG-Drive achieves 31.78 EPDMS on NavHard under perturbed initial states, the highest among the compared methods, and 88.27 PDMS on NavTest from cameras alone. Pointwise fusion outperforms independent VLM and geometry streams on both benchmarks. In closed-loop driving on 420 HUGSIM scenarios, VLG-Drive outperforms all compared planners. These results indicate that a lightweight planner trained on fused features of frozen vision-language and geometric foundation models is an effective alternative to adapting either model for planning.
authors: Junge Zhang, Jie Zhu, Yanqi Jia, Xiangyu Xu, Zixun Huang, Wenbin He, Xin Li, Jiachen Li, Liu Ren

Fuses paired features at each camera-grid cell using a geometry-anchored residual interface.

Pointwise fusion outperforms using independent VLM and geometry streams; the approach avoids adapting either foundation model.

papers.abstract: Hands grasp objects with soft skin. A fingertip flattens against a mug, and a palm curves around a bottle. Yet hand-object datasets and estimators represent the hand as a rigid articulated mesh, which hovers above or penetrates the object where skin would press against it. Existing refiners keep the mesh rigid and adjust only the pose, trading pose accuracy for physical plausibility. We ask whether a rigid hand can instead touch the object as skin does while staying close to its original pose. We lift annotated or estimated rigid hands to contact-consistent meshes through an optimization that (i) slightly adjusts the joints and wrist to bring the fingers onto the object, (ii) deforms the skin so that penetrating regions settle onto the surface, and (iii) keeps this deformation consistent over time. Since deformation reaches only skin already near the object, we further train a lightweight head on the lifted annotations to predict where an estimated hand should touch and steer the deformation there. Unlike existing refiners, the lift more than doubles the skin lying on the object surface for three published estimators while barely changing the pose. Guidance from the learned head further improves grasp stability by closing contact gaps that the estimate leaves open. Existing hand-object datasets and estimators can thus adopt contact-consistent hands without changing the hand model or retraining the estimators.
authors: Seonghwan Park, Min-Gyu Park
bullets: Rigid hand meshes often hover above or penetrate objects instead of modeling soft-skin contact.
The method jointly makes small joint/wrist adjustments, settles penetrating skin onto object surfaces, and enforces temporal consistency.
A lightweight learned head predicts likely contact regions to guide deformation of estimated hands.
The lifted meshes more than double skin coverage on object surfaces across three published estimators with minimal pose change.
The approach improves grasp stability and works with existing hand models and estimators without retraining them.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models enable action- and camera-controlled exploration, yet struggle to maintain consistent spatial geometry and appearance when revisiting previously explored locations. Historical KV caches help auto-regressive video diffusion models maintain long-term consistency, but their retrieval and attention computation introduce substantial latency as history grows. We propose DraftKV, a training-free framework that retrieves historical KV caches based on geometric grounding and query-conditioned relevance, while combining CPU offloading with tile-wise streaming attention to reduce GPU memory usage and inference latency. Theoretically, we show that draft relevance reproduces the mean branch of full-resolution block relevance exactly, so its deviation is confined to the $\beta$-weighted max branch, and we bound retrieval utility loss in terms of the measured Top-K selection overlap. We further show that draft relevance cannot distinguish blocks with similar pooled descriptors regardless of camera pose, motivating geometric grounding before refinement. Then, we introduce streaming CG-Attention, which overlaps CPU-to-GPU KV transfers with attention computation through tile-wise streaming, hiding transfer latency while maintaining bounded GPU memory usage. Experiments across diverse model families show that DraftKV achieves superior generation quality and consistency while achieving $3.27\times$ end-to-end speedup and 42.2% peak GPU memory reduction over other CPU-offloaded KV cache retrieval methods. Notably, DraftKV enables high-quality interactive world generation with historical KV retrieval on a single H100 GPU using SolarWM-33B.
authors: Xiaoling Zhou, Haopeng Li, Yufa Zhou, Rui Ding, Yu Li, Jun Lin, Enze Xie, Chunhua Shen, Xuan Shen
bullets: Addresses spatial and visual inconsistency when revisiting locations, while reducing the latency and memory cost of growing KV histories.
Uses geometric grounding and query-conditioned draft relevance to retrieve the most useful historical KV cache blocks.
Introduces tile-wise streaming attention with CPU offloading to overlap KV transfers and computation under bounded GPU memory.
Reports 3.27× end-to-end speedup and 42.2% lower peak GPU memory than other CPU-offloaded retrieval methods.
Supports high-quality historical-KV world generation on a single H100 GPU with SolarWM-33B.

papers.abstract: For latency-constrained candidate ranking, we propose a similarity-identity decoupling framework that separates target-history compatibility from target-only information. We study two orders for computing pooled similarity, similarity-then-pool and pool-then-similarity, and identify linearity of the similarity operator in its history argument, for each fixed target, as sufficient for their equivalence, justifying the cheaper pool-then-similarity form. We instantiate the framework as multi-head efficient lightweight operator for decoupling identity and similarity (MELODI), whose similarity branch combines target-conditioned multi-head history pooling with a single residual-free cross layer that is linear in its pooled-history input and whose identity branch is problem-dependent. On public benchmark datasets, MELODI matches or surpasses the evaluated target-aware and target-agnostic baselines. On two large-scale industrial datasets, its area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), normalised discounted cumulative gain (NDCG), and recall values are equal to or higher than those of the evaluated target-aware baselines. Processor measurements show lower latency than the evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts, further reduced by request-local history reuse.
authors: Quoc Phong Nguyen, Vuong Le, Volodymyr Vaskovych, Julien Monteil
bullets: Separates target-history compatibility from target-only information for latency-constrained ranking.
Shows that pool-then-similarity is equivalent to similarity-then-pool when the similarity operator is linear in the history input.
Uses target-conditioned multi-head history pooling and a residual-free cross layer for its similarity branch, with a problem-dependent identity branch.
Matches or surpasses evaluated baselines on public benchmarks and achieves equal or higher reported AUPRC, NDCG, and recall than target-aware baselines on two industrial datasets.
Has lower measured latency than evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts; request-local history reuse reduces latency further.

papers.title: MELODI: Similarity-Identity Decoupling for Lightweight Ranking
papers.tldr: MELODI decouples target-history similarity from target identity to enable lightweight, low-latency candidate ranking without sacrificing evaluated ranking quality.

papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop can be read out through the shared language-model head. Post-training them with verifiable rewards is hard: the outcome reward carries one bit per response, spreading it over loops trains intermediate loops on tokens sampled from the last loop, and distillation needs either a teacher that ignores the reward or an external, larger model. We observe that a looped model already contains a teacher stronger than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELGO (Extrapolated-Loop Group-relative Optimization) adds to GRPO a dense per-token distillation term towards this distribution. The teacher is computed from an anchor copy of the model, which stays frozen and is replaced by the current model once the student's KL to the teacher falls below a threshold, so the teacher improves with the student without chasing its own extrapolation. The outcome reward splits probability between correct and incorrect responses, and the teacher decides which tokens are preferred inside a response. Between refreshes the objective is KL-regularised RL anchored at the teacher, whose optimum tilts the teacher by the reward. On Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, ELGO raises the average avg@8 over five math benchmarks from 62.32 with GRPO to 64.20 and is the best compared method on every benchmark, while spreading the reward over loops falls below the base model.
authors: Linghua Zhang
bullets: Looped models reuse one transformer stack across multiple loops, but outcome-only rewards provide too little supervision for intermediate loops.
ELGO extrapolates the model’s next-token distribution from the first through the final loop to form a stronger internal teacher.
A frozen anchor teacher is periodically replaced as the student approaches it, enabling improvement without unstable self-chasing.
The method combines GRPO with token-level distillation and KL-regularized reinforcement learning.
On Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, ELGO improves average avg@8 from 62.32 with GRPO to 64.20 across five math benchmarks; directly spreading rewards over loops underperforms the base model.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ELGO. The anchor copy θ̄ reads out loops 1 and 4 on every rollout prefix and extrapolates them into the teacher πT. The anchor starts at the initial model, stays frozen between refreshes, and is set to the current parameters when the dense loss falls below κ. The trained model samples rollouts from its last loop πθ, as in GRPO. The verifier gives one sparse advantage Âi per response; the teacher gives a dense log-ratio δi,j per sampled token. The loss is LGRPO + β LKD.

Figure 1: Left: GRPO gets one bit per response; RLTT trains intermediate loops on last-loop samples and their entropy collapses; LoopOPD has no reward. Right: ELGO extrapolates loop 1 to loop T of an anchor copy of the model, refreshed when the student has absorbed it, into a dense target for the last loop, next to the outcome reward.
Table 2: Settings shared by GRPO, RLTT, OPSD and ELGO.

papers.selection_reason: Post-training RL method for looped language models; relevant to LLM optimization.
papers.title: Beyond the Last Loop: Reinforcement Learning with a Teacher Extrapolated from the Model Itself
papers.tldr: ELGO improves reinforcement learning for looped language models by using a self-extrapolated, progressively updated teacher to provide dense token-level guidance.

papers.abstract: Comparing language-model checkpoints requires estimating performance differences, yet evaluation pipelines can pay to score responses whose contributions cancel from those differences. We introduce Contrast-Aware Feedback Acquisition (CAFA), a sampler-agnostic method that identifies which scores a requested linear report needs before acquiring feedback. CAFA groups identical scoring inputs and aggregates their report coefficients, removing queries beyond ordinary caching while preserving the fully scored result. For a fixed response bank and an otherwise unrestricted scalar scorer, we characterize necessary and sufficient query sets for exact recovery of sample means, either alone or jointly with ordinary sample covariances. On controlled updates, CAFA removes 55.8% and 90.1% of the scoring inputs remaining after caching for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, respectively, averaged over four generation repetitions. Across three online group relative policy optimization (GRPO) trajectories, Independent Star sampling with CAFA achieves 46.1-51.3% lower recorded generation-plus-feedback cost than independent autoregressive sampling with caching at a common empirical precision threshold (RMS MCSE $\leq 0.04$). This is a post hoc comparison of completed runs on a fixed budget grid. All 504 evaluated report cells reproduce the fully scored means and covariances to numerical precision. We provide a modular implementation supporting existing response banks, versioned caches and external scorers.
authors: Hui Zhang, Haoda Yue, Bicheng Deng, Yuanchao Zhu, Jun He, Rui Qian
bullets: Targets redundant scoring when contributions cancel in checkpoint-difference reports.
Groups identical scoring inputs and aggregates report coefficients before requesting feedback.
Characterizes necessary and sufficient query sets for exact sample means and joint covariances under an unrestricted scalar scorer.
Removed 55.8%–90.1% of post-caching scoring inputs in controlled updates and reduced recorded generation-plus-feedback cost by 46.1%–51.3% in three GRPO trajectories.
Reproduced all 504 evaluated report cells to numerical precision; comparisons were post hoc on completed runs and a fixed budget grid.

The vertical axis is the fraction of deduplicated inputs avoided. Left: individual base-relative gains at steps 2, 8 and 32. Right: all three gains, with and without the base mean. papers.abstract: Shape decomposition represents 3D objects as a compact set of geometric primitives for interpretable modeling and simulation. However, existing decomposition methods are trained primarily for geometric fidelity, without explicit constraints on physical plausibility, and can therefore produce disconnected parts or physically unstable reconstructions. We present PhysDec, an agentic framework that draws on a pretrained vision-language model's semantic understanding and commonsense reasoning to predict material-aware primitive decompositions from a few images. Within this framework, PhysDec-Loop is an agentic pipeline that reasons about part structure and materials, using a reference 3D point cloud for geometric feedback and physical verifiers to guide iterative refinement. Through self-evolution, we further develop another agentic pipeline, PhysDec-Evolved, which learns from prior corrections to predict primitive decompositions from images without point-cloud feedback or a correction loop at inference. Experiments show that PhysDec-Loop improves geometric fidelity, physical plausibility and visual quality over geometry-focused baselines, while PhysDec-Evolved approaches its performance at substantially lower inference cost.
authors: Wenchao Ma, Rui Yu, Fan Zhu, Jiachen Liu, Sharon X. Huang
bullets: Targets failures of geometry-only decomposition, such as disconnected or physically unstable parts.
PhysDec-Loop combines semantic and material reasoning with point-cloud feedback and physical verifiers for iterative refinement.
PhysDec-Evolved learns from prior corrections to work without point-cloud feedback or an inference-time correction loop.
Experiments report improved geometric fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality over geometry-focused baselines, with PhysDec-Evolved achieving similar performance at lower inference cost.

papers.abstract: Affordance grounding localizes where an agent should interact with an object to perform a task. Many everyday manipulation tasks, however, require bimanual affordance, in which two hands assume complementary and cooperative roles to accomplish a shared goal. Existing 3D affordance datasets primarily ground single interaction regions, and manually annotating dual-hand, cooperative contacts does not scale. To address this gap, we introduce DUALingo, a large-scale dataset for task-conditioned, role-aware bimanual 3D affordance grounding on diverse everyday objects. DUALingo represents each task as two cooperative, hand-agnostic roles, each grounded as a heatmap on the object surface. It contains 271K free-form tasks on 71K objects, generated by a fully automated pipeline of open-weight foundation models without human labeling. Expert ratings and a validated LLM judge confirm the quality of the resulting annotations. Trained on DUALingo, existing 3D affordance models learn to ground both cooperative roles from natural-language instructions, with the best-performing model achieving a more than threefold improvement in aIoU over the zero-shot baseline, from 10.3 to 37.8. Robotic manipulation demonstrations illustrate the actionability of the predicted bimanual affordances in performing cooperative tasks. These results position DUALingo as a scalable foundation for learning everyday bimanual affordances. Project page: https://nycu-pair-labs.github.io/DUALingo/
authors: Ming-Lun Lee, Yi-En Li, Feng-Dian Su, Ming-Han Lee, Kun-Ru Wu, Krzysztof Czarnecki, Yu-Chee Tseng
bullets: Targets bimanual affordance grounding, where two hands interact with complementary regions to complete a shared task.
Represents each task as two role-aware, hand-agnostic surface heatmaps on an object.
Provides 271K free-form tasks across 71K everyday objects without human labeling, using open-weight foundation models.
Expert ratings and a validated LLM judge support the quality of the generated annotations.
Models trained on DUALingo improve aIoU from 10.3 to 37.8 over zero-shot performance; robotic demonstrations show practical actionability.

papers.abstract: Latent world models learn representations by predicting future states in an abstract embedding space rather than reconstructing raw pixels. When training across multi-frame sequences, however, not all frames and spatial regions are equally informative or predictable. We argue that forcing a world model to minimize every prediction error may be unnecessary and harmful. Under standard $L_2$ loss, unbounded gradients force the encoder and predictor to overfit noisy or transient frames at the expense of core physical structure, while amplifying gradient conflict with representation regularizers. Conversely, $L_1$ loss bounds large gradients, but its constant gradient magnitude near zero disrupts the local smoothness required for planning. We resolve this tension with \textbf{ReJEPA}, a bounded predictive regulation principle that combines bounded gradients for large errors with smooth quadratic behavior near zero, instantiated simply via the element-wise $\log\cosh$ loss. As a drop-in training replacement across Temporal Straightening, LeWorldModel, and V-JEPA~2.1, $\log\cosh$ consistently outperforms $L_2$, a curvature-matched quadratic control, $L_1$, and Smooth-$L_1$ baselines without altering architectures or inference procedures. Notably, the gains grow with environmental complexity, scaling from simple navigation to contact-rich manipulation and real-world autonomous driving on NAVSIM. Probing and geometric analyses confirm that relaxing the penalty on extreme errors yields representations that better capture physical states and align with the true planning cost landscape.
authors: Fangzhou Lin, Yuping Wang, Shuo Xing, Yang Chen, Yuwen Heng, Xin Li, Wenbin He, Yuhan Yao, Zhengzhong Tu, Liu Ren
bullets: Motivation: Penalizing every future-state prediction error equally can overfit transient frames and conflict with representation regularization.
Method: Replace standard predictive losses with element-wise log-cosh, combining bounded gradients for large errors with quadratic smoothness near zero.
Scope: A drop-in training change evaluated across Temporal Straightening, LeWorldModel, and V-JEPA 2.1 without architectural or inference modifications.
Results: The method consistently outperforms L2, curvature-matched quadratic, L1, and Smooth-L1 baselines, with larger gains in more complex environments.
Analysis: Probing and geometric results indicate improved physical-state representations and better alignment with planning costs.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models (VLMs): even when their coordinate predictions are incorrect, they can describe visual evidence worth inspecting. We introduce \textbf{SPARK}, \textit{\textbf{S}emantic \textbf{P}robe-guided \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{R}egion see\textbf{K}ing}, a training-free framework that turns this semantic guidance into targeted visual observations. Exploration probes describe relevant context and distinguishing target details, while verification probes identify evidence needed to assess emerging hypotheses. Their spatial attention guides view placement, contextual responses determine crop extent, and observation history encourages complementary inspection. The resulting predictions are combined through uncertainty-weighted voting. On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and UI-TARS, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Consistent gains across four additional benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse interfaces and grounding tasks. These results establish semantic probing as an effective mechanism for turning a frozen VLM's understanding of what to inspect into more accurate GUI grounding.
authors: Ruixiao Shi, Fu Feng, Yucheng Xie, Jing Wang, Xin Geng
bullets: GUI grounding benefits from additional views, but effective inspection must balance fine detail with contextual meaning.
SPARK uses exploration probes to identify relevant context and target details, then verification probes to test emerging localization hypotheses.
Spatial attention guides where to look, probe responses determine crop extent, and observation history promotes complementary views.
Uncertainty-weighted voting combines observations into final predictions.
On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves single-view accuracy by 13.9–25.2 percentage points across three VLM backbones and also gains on four additional benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SPARK. (a) Probe-guided adaptive focusing translates contextual and local-detail attention into view placement and context-dependent crop extent. The resulting localization predictions are passed to the aggregation module. (c) Uncertaintyweighted voting accumulates entropy-based prediction weights within spatial clusters and returns the medoid of the highest-scoring cluster as the final location.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models need to continually acquire new manipulation skills while retaining the ability to follow previously learned instructions. Experience replay (ER) can mitigate catastrophic forgetting, but retaining only a small number of historical expert frames per task leaves many old-instruction responses without direct supervision. Under limited replay, we observe a structured failure mode in which an earlier instruction can trigger a subsequently learned, competing goal. To address this gap, we propose Cross-Instruction Anchoring (XIA), which supplements expert replay with instruction-conditioned response preservation. At each task boundary, XIA freezes the previous policy as a teacher and matches its responses to old instructions paired with current observations. This extends supervision beyond stored historical examples without requiring additional expert replay data. Experiments across multiple VLA architectures and three LIBERO suites demonstrate improved success rates and reduced forgetting compared with ER under identical historical expert-data budgets. Additional RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support the effectiveness of XIA.
authors: Ziyang Chen, Dehua Chen, Shaoguang Wang, Xu Yan, Hao Huang, Tao Chen
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when continual VLA learning uses only small historical expert-data budgets.
Identifies a failure mode where old instructions trigger newly learned, competing goals.
Freezes the previous policy as a teacher and matches its responses to old instructions under current observations.
Improves success rates and reduces forgetting versus experience replay across multiple VLA architectures and three LIBERO suites.
RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support its effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of Cross-Instruction Anchoring (XIA). XIA combines two supervision paths under a limited historical expert replay budget. Both objectives jointly update the student without additional historical expert demonstrations.

papers.title: Beyond Expert Replay: Cross-Instruction Anchoring for Continual Vision-Language-Action Learning
