papers.abstract: Flow-based policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. In online actor-critic learning, off-policy value estimates can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, where expressive policies may shift probability mass toward critic-favored actions. We propose MIFLOW, which calibrates online flow-policy learning with a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions. Inspired by canalization as a qualitative analogy for path-dependent stabilization, we use the prior as a moving density reference for value-guided policy improvement. MIFLOW uses the approximate recent-action log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets. This correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, MIFLOW achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks. In a Walker2d-v4 case study, MIFLOW shows a lower proportion of actions assigned low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. Prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and prior-defined diagnostics. These results support dynamic recent-behavior priors for reference calibration in the evaluated settings. The diagnostics measure how sampled actions align with the learned reference. True action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured in these experiments.
authors: Chenhao Wang, Haonan Ma, Wenjie Zhang, Yifan Wang, Mingbin Gao, Yuan-Ye Zhang, Wenjing Hong
bullets: Targets unreliable off-policy value estimates in action regions with limited behavioral coverage.
Fits a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior to recent actions and uses its dimension-normalized log-density in actor updates and critic targets.
Across six MuJoCo tasks and five seeds, it shows competitive learning curves and higher late-training mean returns than evaluated baselines on several tasks.
In a Walker2d-v4 case study, sampled actions—including high-Q actions—were less often assigned low density by the learned reference.
Prior-defined diagnostics do not measure true action support or critic extrapolation error; results are limited to the evaluated settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of MIFLOW. Recent executed actions are stored in a sliding prior buffer and used to train a recency-adaptive flow-matching behavior prior. The prior provides an approximate recent-action log-density that acts as a dynamic reference in path-density actor-critic updates. Low-prior-density actions remain selectable but receive an additional cost during critic-guided policy improvement. The upper panel provides a qualitative analogy for pathdependent adaptation; the algorithm itself is defined by the learned prior and reference-calibrated objectives.

Fig. 2. Main performance comparison on six MuJoCo-v4 continuous-control tasks. Curves show smoothed mean episodic return over environment steps, and shaded regions denote standard deviation across five seeds. These curves provide descriptive comparisons and do not indicate formal statistical significance.

Fig. 3. Walker2d-v4 diagnostic case study. Bars report mean ± SEM over five random seeds. SACFlow denotes the no-prior path-density flowpolicy baseline, and SACFlow-GP denotes the learned Gaussian-prior variant. OOS Rate is prior-defined: it counts policy actions whose action-dimensionnormalized log ρϕ(a) falls below the 20th percentile of recent-buffer actions under the same learned prior. HQ/LP Cond is the fraction of top-20% clippeddouble-Q policy actions that also lie in this low-prior region. MIFLOW has the lowest reported mean for both prior-defined diagnostics in this case study.

papers.title: MIFLOW: Dynamic Recent-Behavior Priors for Reference-Calibrated Online Flow-Policy Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: MIFLOW stabilizes online flow-policy reinforcement learning by using a recent-action density prior to discourage poorly supported, critic-favored actions while preserving exploration.

papers.abstract: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.
authors: Kai Zeng, Ruichuan An, Zhen Fang, Xi Fang, Han Lyu, Moran Li, Yingchen Yu, Yifan Dai, Bohan Zeng, Quanqing Xu, Zhengzhou Zhu, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Addresses missing factual, visual, and temporal information in knowledge-intensive video prompts, plus weak credit assignment in agent training.
Builds evidence-grounded temporal prompts with retrieved text and reference images.
Introduces Rubric-Based Credit (RBC) to score intermediate search and planning steps before video rendering.
Uses RBC-SFT and RBC-GRPO to incorporate step-level quality signals without rendering videos during reinforcement learning.
Improves evaluation across three video generators; MiniMax-H3’s overall score rises from 32.80 to 70.67, with further gains on scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents can iteratively self-improve robot manipulation skills in simulation benchmarks, yet real-world tasks provide neither ground-truth success scorers nor resettable practice environments. Our key observation is that a single real demonstration simultaneously specifies scene geometry, defines the terminal success criterion, and serves as a physical reference trajectory for verifying world fidelity---all decoupled from the source robot's kinematics. We present {RESET}: we reconstruct a contact-rich world and derive a frozen read-only criterion from one demonstration ({R}ebuild); check that world against the demonstration by open-loop replay and silhouette consistency ({E}xamine); evolve modular white-box task graphs and skill code from per-node failure evidence ({S}elf-improve); deploy frozen code on real robots with zero runtime LLM calls ({E}xecute); and share the verified world and criterion with unseen robots without new demonstrations ({T}ransfer). On 8 manipulation tasks, each rebuilt from one real demonstration, RESET achieves 97% average success on unseen layouts in simulation, whereas zero-shot code reaches 27%, per-task fine-tuned pi0.5 policies 31%, and Diffusion Policy 50%; injecting reconstruction defects shows that practice tolerates many reconstruction errors, that geometric errors can still stall or mislead it, and that the check flags most of them while physical randomization covers the rest. Without any target demonstrations, 3 heterogeneous robots acquire the same task skills in the shared world: a robot with similar arms copies 95% of its skill functions unchanged from the source robot, while robots with different arms and hands write their own. In real-robot experiments, the resulting programs run on 4 robots and succeed in 80% of 280 trials.
authors: Zheng Sun, Zhuo Li, Zhihao Li, Hengyi Sim, Ge Wang, Ziyue Zhu, Mingkai Jia, Fei Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of success scorers and resettable practice environments in real-world robot learning.
Rebuilds scene geometry and a frozen success criterion, then validates fidelity through open-loop replay and silhouette consistency.
Self-improves modular task graphs and skill code using per-node failure evidence before deploying frozen programs.
Achieves 97% average simulation success on unseen layouts across 8 tasks, compared with 27% for zero-shot code and 50% for Diffusion Policy.
Transfers skills to 4 heterogeneous robots, reaching 80% success over 280 real-world trials; geometric reconstruction errors remain a limitation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Demonstrated tasks, their rebuilt worlds, and autonomous real-robot execution. (a) Top: the eight tasks, each demonstrated once on the source robot xTrainer. Bottom: the world rebuilt from each demonstration, rendered from the demonstration camera. (b) The final programs running on four robots without human intervention. For each robot we show four of the tasks it ran (all results are in Tab. 5), each in action and at the end. Franka, LIFT2, and G1 received no demonstration.

papers.abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
authors: Jian Yang, Zhizhuo Kou, Qiyuan Zhu, Han Chen, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Persistent clean-KV updates can dominate runtime once denoising is accelerated, while stale-cache reuse increases later denoising work.
SAMR combines motion-aligned historical KV with in-flight KV, using calibrated affine correction and selective true $t=0$ refreshes.
Tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels implement the reconstruction efficiently without retraining the frozen video DiT.
On LongLive-1.3B, it cuts DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7%, while improving final-quarter PSNR over token reuse.
It transfers to Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B, reducing reuse-induced step inflation and improving late-stage PSNR, with calibration further recovering diagnostic quality.

papers.abstract: Training capable omni video agents requires more than diverse question-answer pairs: agents must learn to reliably find, connect, and correct task-relevant evidence in omni-setting. However, we argue that existing data pipelines provide limited control over task-relevant evidence and weak supervision for these capabilities. In this work, we present Open OmniCoach, a new framework for evidence-seeking omni video agents. It contains a high-quality dataset, OmniCoach-240K, and a new agentic reinforcement learning (RL) method, Step-Level Evidence-Guided Policy Optimization (SEPO). For the former, OmniCoach-240K comprises 248.2K interaction trajectories, including 230.7K multi-span trajectories and 17.4K reflection trajectories. We design a three-stage data pipeline by leveraging both fine-grained omni-evidence and the agent's own errors. Meanwhile, compared with other RL baselines, SEPO provides turn-level credit based on improvements in evidence coverage and temporal localization. Applying both trajectory data and the SEPO method, we obtain Open OmniAgent models. The resulting models outperform the baselines across multiple video and audio-visual understanding tasks by significant margins, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Open OmniCoach framework. In particular, Open OmniAgent-30B improves average accuracy over Qwen3-Omni by 6.3 percentage points across nine benchmarks, with gains of 12.2 and 13.3 points on LVOmniBench and LVBench, respectively.
authors: Weisong Liu, Xiangtai Li, Haochen Wang, Haiquan Wen, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses limited control over task-relevant evidence and weak supervision in existing omni-video agent data pipelines.
Introduces OmniCoach-240K, containing 248.2K interaction trajectories, including multi-span and reflection trajectories.
Uses a three-stage data pipeline built from fine-grained omni-evidence and agents’ own errors.
Proposes SEPO, which assigns turn-level credit based on improvements in evidence coverage and temporal localization.
Open OmniAgent models outperform baselines across multiple video and audio-visual tasks; the 30B model improves average accuracy over Qwen3-Omni by 6.3 percentage points across nine benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.
authors: Shanmuga Venkatachalam, Quinn Jacobson, John Paul Shen
bullets: Uses temporal coding with at most one spike per input line and multi-segment dendritic neurons.
Learns all 4-bit integer weights through local reward-modulated STDP, avoiding backpropagation through time; inference uses comparisons and additions.
Achieves 78.6% on CREMA-D with 2.34M synapses and 98.82% on UrbanSound8K-AV with 1.38M synapses.
Reports 23–106× lower weight memory and two- to three-orders-of-magnitude lower measured synaptic energy than spiking baselines.
Supports single-pass learning on CREMA-D and rapid continual adaptation to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.

papers.abstract: Video understanding depends not only on how models reason about visual evidence, but also on which evidence they observe. Fixed observation policies determine this evidence in advance; agentic harnesses allow models to seek further observations as their understanding develops. This shift creates an opportunity to realize capabilities that fixed inputs leave untapped, yet the ability to request observations does not ensure their effective use. We investigate when and why video harnesses improve understanding, examining how task demands and models' capacity for interaction jointly shape their benefits. Using Video-Relook as an experimental framework, we let models adapt their temporal and spatial observations from a common default configuration, and analyze performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks. Adaptive observation yields substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2. Even under the same observation interface, gains differ substantially across models; interaction traces reveal corresponding differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision. The benefits also vary across tasks for the same model, ranging from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions. Together, these findings support an account in which harness effectiveness depends on the alignment between opportunities for informative observation and the model's ability to turn interaction into reliable revisions. They motivate video harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning, matching observational autonomy to task demands and model capabilities.
authors: Luoyuan Zhang, Xuanyu Zheng, Yancheng Long, Haoyang Xu, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao
bullets: Fixed observation policies may miss useful visual evidence, while agentic harnesses let models adapt temporal and spatial observations.
Using Video-Relook, the study analyzes performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks from a shared default configuration.
Adaptive observation produces substantial gains in fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2.
Gains vary across models and tasks, reflecting differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision.
The findings motivate harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning rather than assuming observation autonomy alone is sufficient.

papers.abstract: Old and new document embeddings coexist during incremental gallery re-encoding. RELAY trains a new query encoder with a learned projection against the original gallery, then freezes both to train the new document encoder. The same query vector scores both document versions throughout a single re-encoding pass. After backfill, optional query refinement drops the projection and reuses the stored document vectors. Across three text-to-image retrieval upgrades on COCO and Flickr30K, RELAY improves Recall@1 on untouched galleries by 8.66-10.23 percentage points over the original systems. For direct re-encoding, RELAY ranks first in both Qwen-to-Qwen upgrades and second in CLIP-to-Qwen by area under the Recall@1 curve, under both native scoring and matched calibration. With embeddings held fixed, calibrating scores separately for each document version can reduce drops in Recall@1 during backfill and change which method achieves the highest backfill AUC. After query refinement, final Recall@1 is within 0.97 percentage points of conventional joint training in all three upgrades.
authors: Yu Wang, Chuan Qin, Qiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses compatibility between old and new document embeddings during gallery backfill.
Trains a projected query encoder against the original gallery, then freezes it to train the new document encoder.
A single query representation scores both document versions during one re-encoding pass; optional refinement later removes the projection.
Across three COCO and Flickr30K text-to-image upgrades, it improves untouched-gallery Recall@1 by 8.66–10.23 points over the original systems.
Final Recall@1 after refinement is within 0.97 points of conventional joint training; calibration can affect backfill performance and rankings.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a method for learning compatible representations during incremental re-encoding, relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: RELAY: Learning Compatible Representations One Encoder at a Time
papers.tldr: RELAY enables incremental document re-encoding while keeping new queries compatible with both old and new embeddings, achieving near-joint-training final retrieval quality.

papers.abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.
authors: Saraswathy Amjith, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba, Yoon Kim
bullets: A topic or animal preference can be distilled between vision-language models via number sequences.
The transferred animal preference affects image generation and representations, but color and style preferences do not.
A constant component of the student’s parameter change explains much of the shift toward the transferred trait.
The effect depends on how concepts are distributed across prompt tokens: whole-prompt traits transfer more readily than single-token attributes.
The proposed weight lens detects subliminal traits in nearly every trained student, including traits absent from generated images.

papers.abstract: Robots must often keep working after the world changes, as when a block moves or the camera shifts while the robot still acts on what it saw before. Recent work showed that one change during a task lowers success for every policy tested, but did not separate the effect of its timing from the cost of the changed world, or measure what it costs afterwards. We introduce CALVIN-MAX, a benchmark of 7,828 cases on CALVIN's five-instruction chains, each with one change to the objects, the camera, the robot, or the instruction. Each case compares three runs that are identical until the affected instruction begins: one without the change, one with it in place from that moment, and one in which it arrives while the robot is moving. The second run against the first gives the cost of the changed world, and the third against the second the effect of meeting it mid-motion. On 1,526 held-out cases per policy, with hypotheses fixed in advance, each of ten released policies loses 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction over the eight core changes. Whether timing matters depends on the change: one that alters what the robot sees costs 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start, whereas a change to the scene itself or to the robot shows no detectable effect. Rewinding the robot to the start of the instruction removes the benefit for every policy; the stricter test we fixed in advance, that the rewound run then matches the second run, passes for three. The cost also outlasts the affected instruction: the change stays in place, and a policy that still completes that instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.
authors: Sajjad Pakdamansavoji
bullets: Evaluates 7,828 cases across object, camera, robot, and instruction changes in five-instruction CALVIN chains.
Separates the cost of a changed world from the additional effect of encountering it while moving.
All ten policies lose 4.4–9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction across eight core changes.
Timing matters for visual changes, which cost 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start; scene and robot changes show no detectable timing effect.
The impact persists: completing the affected instruction is followed by a 5.0–16.8-point lower chance of completing the next one.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark analyzing how mid-execution changes affect robot policies; fits robot manipulation and visuomotor control.
papers.title: CALVIN-MAX: When Does a Mid-Execution Change Hurt a Robot Policy?
papers.tldr: CALVIN-MAX shows that mid-execution changes hurt robot policies, with effects depending on the change and often persisting into the next instruction.

papers.abstract: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose humanoid control through pretraining on large-scale behavioral data. However, their proficiency in whole-body coordination does not readily extend to scene interaction, which requires adapting motion to scene-dependent geometric constraints and contact dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce Ada-BFM, a post-training framework that adapts pretrained BFMs for humanoid scene interaction. Ada-BFM augments the original architecture with a lightweight adapter, enabling interaction-specific adjustments while leveraging pretrained control capabilities. Rather than producing a separate controller for each task, the framework yields a shared model for each interaction domain, supporting diverse tasks involving terrain or object interaction. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate that Ada-BFM enables diverse scene interaction behaviors, accelerates learning compared with training from scratch, and largely preserves pretrained behavioral competence. These findings establish Ada-BFM as an effective and efficient approach to extending the capabilities of BFMs beyond their pretraining settings while retaining their strengths in general whole-body control.
authors: Furui Xu, Weishuai Zeng, Zirui Wang, Kangning Yin, Jiacheng Bao, Huayi Wang, Yingying Qin, Yufei Xue, Yang Tang, Zenghao Tang, Kailin Li, Jingbo Wang, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting general-purpose BFMs to scene-specific geometry and contact dynamics.
Adds a lightweight adapter through post-training rather than building a separate controller for each task.
Produces a shared model for each interaction domain across diverse scene-interaction tasks.
Simulation and real-world experiments show diverse behaviors, faster learning than training from scratch, and largely preserved pretrained competence.

papers.abstract: Large-scale pretraining provides embodied models with general capabilities, but reliable task execution still requires post training. In multitask settings, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) faces distribution mismatch between training and deployment, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) is limited by sparse rewards and uneven learning progress across tasks. Multi-teacher on policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates expert capabilities through dense supervision on the model's own trajectories, but achieving performance beyond the teachers remains challenging. We propose a two-stage post training framework for flow-based embodied models, constructing distillation objectives from the velocity regression formulation of conditional flow matching. Stage 1 efficiently consolidates expert capabilities through MOPD. Stage 2 combines RL with teacher distillation that weights velocity errors according to the sampling noise, where distillation is restricted to failed trajectories to supplement sparse rewards with dense guidance without directly constraining successful behaviors. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that the framework outperforms joint SFT and exceeds the corresponding teachers' aggregate success rates. Sample efficiency comparisons show higher success rates than direct RL with fewer environment interactions.
authors: Jiaming Zhang, Yao Lyu, Haoning Wang, Yongjun Chen, Liping Zhang, Shengbo Eben Li
bullets: Addresses SFT distribution mismatch and RL’s sparse rewards and uneven multitask learning.
Stage 1 uses multi-teacher on-policy distillation to consolidate expert capabilities on the model’s own trajectories.
Stage 2 combines RL with noise-weighted flow-matching velocity distillation on failed trajectories only.
Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks outperform joint SFT and exceed teachers’ aggregate success rates.
Achieves higher success rates than direct RL with fewer environment interactions.

papers.abstract: Visual self-models learn from images how a robot moves under motor commands. Continuum robots need them even more, as they bend continuously without measured joint angles or fixed link geometry. Existing continuum self-models predict point clouds, image-space curves, or future images, but not the next 3D shape, appearance, and tip pose together from an observed body. 3D Gaussians offer a renderable representation of shape and appearance, yet articulated Gaussian self-models rely on joint angles to drive deformation. In this work, we propose BendGS, which uses a virtual backbone estimated from observation to drive command-conditioned Gaussian deformation, enabling next-state prediction for continuum robots without measured joint angles. In Gaussian modeling, a feed-forward network reconstructs the robot as 3D Gaussians from multi-view images, and the backbone, a chain of coordinate frames, is fitted to back-projected depth points to estimate the bending state. In transition, a network predicts its change under a relative motor command to deform the bound Gaussians. The deformed Gaussians render the next images and the 3D shape, and the distal frame gives the tip pose. Training losses use RGB-D images and masks, without bending or tip labels. On simulated and real robots, BendGS achieves the lowest Chamfer distance, best image quality, and lowest tip errors among the compared methods.
authors: Jeong Woon Lee, Doungjun Kim, Namho Kim, Seungheon Chae, Jongwoo Kim, Hyoseok Hwang
bullets: Addresses self-modeling for continuum robots, which lack fixed link geometry and joint-angle measurements.
Reconstructs the observed robot as 3D Gaussians and estimates a virtual bending backbone from multi-view RGB-D observations.
Predicts backbone changes under relative motor commands to deform the bound Gaussians and render the next state.
Uses RGB-D images and masks for training, without bending-state or tip-pose labels.
On simulated and real robots, reports the best Chamfer distance, image quality, and tip errors among compared methods.

papers.abstract: Reactive robotic manipulation is acutely sensitive to simultaneous sensing noise, measurement dropouts, joint execution errors, and contact parameter variations. While single-frame frameworks like Domain-Randomized Instance Set (DRIS) achieve strong robustness under isolated uncertainties (86.4%), they degrade severely when perception and actuation uncertainties co-occur (27.6% across 10 coupled stress scenarios) due to memoryless encoding and fixed high-stiffness PD control. We propose Co-DRIS + SuperMimic, a perception-action co-design framework coupling: (i) an inertial world-frame physics-informed world model combining exact ballistic kinematics with a zero-initialized contact residual to roll forward missing observations and accelerate training via zero-cost counterfactual dropout consistency; (ii) an action-conditioned dual-stream causal GRU belief encoder resolving the denoising-vs-lag deadlock; and (iii) phase-aware variable-impedance soft-catching that transitions the 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm into an overdamped regime (zeta/zeta0 ~ 2.26x) at the torque layer. Under unbiased 3-seed tail evaluation on unseen throws (15,360 throws/scenario), our method achieves 89.6 +/- 0.4% on standard benchmarks (+10.5% on 4-sigma noise to 70.5%) and 66.6 +/- 0.5% across 10 coupled/dropout stress scenarios (+39.0% over DRIS; +30.4% on 50% dropout). We further validate impedance decoupling, causal contact triggering under +0.65 s flight-time shifts, and cross-task transfer to steel-plate ping-pong bouncing (87.5% to 100.0%) and FR3+Hand catching (+8.4% under 4x noise with 6-13% lower peak impact force).
authors: Yonglong Zhang
bullets: Addresses the severe degradation of memoryless, fixed-stiffness catching under coupled uncertainties.
Uses a physics-informed world model to predict missing observations and generate dropout-consistent counterfactuals.
Combines an action-conditioned dual-stream causal GRU with phase-aware, variable-impedance soft catching.
Achieves 66.6% across 10 coupled/dropout stress scenarios, a 39.0-point improvement over DRIS, and 89.6% on standard benchmarks.
Transfers to bouncing and hand-catching tasks, while reducing peak impact force under high sensing noise.

papers.abstract: Where a person looks indicates their focus of attention, and how their gaze shifts between targets reveals how that attention responds to a changing scene. Existing gaze target estimation methods largely operate frame by frame and do not model these shifts. Gaze shifts are often driven by dynamic changes in the scene, which is the kind of information world models are designed to encode. This relationship is subtle, however, since an event far across the frame may produce only a slight movement of the person's head or eyes. We therefore introduce the Gaze World Model (GWM), which co-trains latent scene prediction with person-conditioned gaze supervision on a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; in our ablations, the latent prediction objective improves both shift detection and gaze localization. Given a video clip and the person's head box, GWM estimates gaze locations and detects gaze shifts in the observed clip, and forecasts future gaze and shifts from predicted scene features. To train and evaluate these tasks, we augment VideoAttentionTarget and ChildPlay with event-level gaze-shift annotations. GWM achieves state-of-the-art shift detection on these benchmarks, about 10 points higher in four-class AP than the strongest baseline, while remaining comparable to the strongest image-based models in gaze target estimation, and outperforms the compared baselines on future gaze localization and shift forecasting.
authors: Jiawen Zhang, Houze Yang, Xu Cao, Yifan Shen, Zhongyi Zhou, Steve Wong, Ismini Lourentzou, Inki Kim, James M. Rehg
bullets: Addresses the limitation of frame-by-frame gaze estimation, which misses attention shifts caused by scene changes.

Adds event-level gaze-shift annotations to VideoAttentionTarget and ChildPlay.
Achieves state-of-the-art shift detection, comparable gaze localization, and stronger future gaze and shift forecasting than compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods achieve high returns in robotic control, yet trained actors exhibit high-frequency action oscillations. Most smoothness methods constrain the actor, whereas PAVE regularizes the critic by separately penalizing action-gradient variation and encouraging negative action curvature. The same gradient change, however, moves the critic's preferred action farther where the critic is flat, and separate penalties do not measure this motion. We characterize this motion through the greedy shift, which approximates greedy-action displacement across state transitions to first order under local concavity. Since displacement alone does not reflect its critic-value consequences, the analysis further shows that the shift's curvature-weighted energy approximates the value lost by retaining the previous greedy action to second order. Based on this relationship, POISE regularizes the curvature-weighted energy along temporal and spatial state displacements. It employs a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling while leaving the actor unchanged. On six continuous control tasks with TD3, POISE reduces the smoothness score on every task by $5.9\times$ on average ($4.5\times$ geometric mean), compared with $2.2\times$ ($1.9\times$) for the strongest baseline, and achieves the lowest score on five tasks. Paired return intervals include zero on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.
authors: Jeong Woon Lee, Namho Kim, Hyoseok Hwang
bullets: Motivation: Standard actor-critic policies can produce high-frequency action oscillations, while existing critic regularization does not capture how gradient changes move preferred actions through flat regions.
Method: Estimate greedy-action displacement across state transitions and regularize its curvature-weighted energy, using a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling.
Scope: The actor remains unchanged; POISE is evaluated with TD3 on six continuous-control tasks.
Results: POISE reduces the smoothness score by 5.9× on average (4.5× geometric mean), versus 2.2× (1.9×) for the strongest baseline, and performs best on five tasks.
Return impact: Paired return intervals include zero on four tasks; returns increase 14% on Ant and decrease 11% on Hopper.

papers.abstract: Pretrained antipodal grasping networks generalize well to canonical shapes but frequently fail zero-shot on novel objects with irregular mass distributions, thin rims, or unfamiliar handles. While episodic experience memory adapts a frozen base policy without retraining, naive retrieval suffers from visual appearance bias, negative transfer from overriding working base grasps, and degenerate closed-loop acquisition. We present VG-GP, a plug-and-play Visuo-Geometric Gaussian Process memory framework for closed-loop $SE(2)$ residual grasp transfer. First, we fuse color-invariant surface-normal DINOv2 features, canonical $SE(2)$ gripper-aligned 3D local heightmaps, and contact-geometry descriptors under a product kernel with Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) lengthscales learned strictly on source objects. Second, we model the joint posterior over the base grasp and candidate $SE(2)$ alternatives, overriding the base policy only when the joint-covariance Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) clears a risk-sensitive threshold. Third, an online counterfactual curation gate using single-record necessity and sufficiency interventions quarantines source experiences causing negative transfer. Fourth, we close the acquisition loop via Bayesian Expected Improvement (EI) over equal-budget $SE(2)$ probes. Across 42 disjoint YCB objects in ManiSkill3 (20 source, 12 development, 10 held-out test), VG-GP wraps a pretrained GR-ConvNet base policy and raises physical lift rate across all 22 unseen objects from 38.6% (34/88) to 53.4% (47/88) with zero regressions (+13 rescues, 0 losses; object-clustered 95% CI [+6.8%, +22.7%], exact McNemar $p = 0.00024$). On the 10 held-out objects, EI active acquisition reaches 45.0% (18/40 vs. 32.5% base, 5/7 of oracle headroom), achieves 55.0% probe divergence over passive fallback, and monotonically reduces epistemic uncertainty.
authors: Yonglong Zhang
bullets: Addresses failures caused by irregular mass distributions, thin rims, unfamiliar handles, visual bias, and negative transfer.

Uses Bayesian Expected Improvement to select equal-budget closed-loop probes and reduce epistemic uncertainty.
Across 22 unseen objects, lift rate increased from 38.6% to 53.4% with zero regressions; on 10 held-out objects, active acquisition reached 45.0% versus 32.5% for the base policy.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generators for robot control by jointly predicting future camera frames and actions, transferring physical priors learned from video into manipulation policies. However, generating future frames before every action makes test-time inference too slow for closed-loop control, while most existing policies remain restricted to short observation histories. Building on Fast-WAM, which showed that video prediction shapes policy representations during training so that future frame synthesis can be skipped at deployment, we present G0.7, a generalist world action model scaled along two axes: extending the context window from a single observation to up to five minutes of history, and scaling pretraining to a large-scale corpus of robot teleoperation and human egocentric (ego) video. Across public simulation suites and real-robot deployments, direct action decoding (Fast mode) matches imagine-then-act (IDM) inference from the same checkpoint while running in 60 ms per 16-step action chunk on a single RTX 5090 (7.6x faster than IDM) and supporting pause-free real-time chunking. Performance scales consistently with pretraining data, with human ego video driving the largest gains in out-of-distribution generalization: G0.7 achieves a 70.8 mean score across five simulation benchmark suites, 48% and 54% zero-shot pick-and-place success on Galaxea R1 Pro and R1 Lite, 96.7% in-distribution and 93.3% out-of-distribution success on video-conditioned in-context learning tasks, and 86.9% mean task progress across seven real-world post-training tasks including multi-minute box folding, drink preparation, and product bagging.

papers.abstract: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.
authors: Niranjan Rajesh, Meenakshi Khosla
bullets: Introduces a representation-level Fisher-like matrix to rank hidden directions by their influence on downstream computation.
Across pretrained vision networks, a small task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance and is often more compact than geometry-based alternatives.
The compressed subspace is more robust to adversarial attacks targeting the full network.
Functionally distinct directions, such as shape- and texture-sensitive subspaces, can be separated and selectively ablated.
These subspaces support continual learning and expose task-dependent inter-model alignment that full-space comparisons miss.

papers.abstract: Released autonomous-driving models achieve strong benchmark performance, yet deploying them on a new real vehicle remains challenging. We study this deployment gap and find that released models can remain coupled to assumptions from their source sensing, data, and execution processes even after conventional adaptation. We introduce Released-to-Real (R2R), a deployment-localization methodology that identifies such source-system coupling and corrects only the affected components while preserving the released model. For data and behavior adaptation, we find that the mismatch between trajectory-level optimization and receding-horizon execution enters through the ego state rather than the observation, and introduce Human-Anchored Reinforcement Learning (HA-RL), which corrects it on recorded target driving without the costly rollouts of generative closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). For physical sensor adaptation, R2R localizes and corrects source-dependent spatial and temporal representations with frozen perception weights, requiring neither target annotations nor retraining. HA-RL improves the closed-loop success rate of a released diffusion-based planner from 82.2% to 95.2%, while sensor adaptation across multiple released detectors and three real sensor rigs improves the vehicle mean average precision (mAP) of a released multi-camera detector from 0.041 to 0.420 on a five-camera target rig. These results provide a practical path for preparing released models before deployment on new real vehicles. Our project page is publicly available at https://released-to-real.github.io.
authors: Morui Zhu, Deyuan Qu, Qi Chen, Qing Yang
bullets: Released models may retain assumptions about their original sensors, data, and execution process, creating a deployment gap.
R2R corrects only the affected components while preserving the released model.
HA-RL adapts trajectory-level behavior to receding-horizon execution using recorded target driving, avoiding costly generative closed-loop RL rollouts.
Sensor adaptation corrects source-dependent spatial and temporal representations with frozen perception weights and no target annotations or retraining.
HA-RL raises closed-loop success from 82.2% to 95.2%, while sensor adaptation improves detector mAP from 0.041 to 0.420 on a five-camera target rig.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing the 3D poses of hands and objects from a single image, together with the contact between them, is fundamental to understanding manipulation. To be practical, the reconstruction must generalize to unseen objects, and the contact must be localized precisely. Yet joint feed-forward estimators often rely on predefined object sets, while contact is typically predicted from image features alone, without the explicit geometry needed to localize it. To address both limitations, we present HORCRUX, a unified feed-forward transformer with coarse-to-fine contact estimation. For unseen objects, a frozen foundation model encodes the object from a given or image-reconstructed mesh rather than from object-specific knowledge. A shared transformer then reasons jointly over the object and one or two hands to keep them aligned. For precise contact, coarse per-joint predictions from latent features are resolved over finer hand regions using the reconstructed geometry. Across seven benchmarks, HORCRUX achieves state-of-the-art object and hand pose accuracy among joint estimators and outperforms a dedicated contact estimator in fine-grained contact. These results suggest that contact is best estimated jointly with reconstruction, whose geometry directly localizes it.
authors: Seonghwan Park, Yong-Hoon Kwon, Min-Gyu Park
bullets: Addresses two limitations: dependence on predefined object sets and imprecise contact prediction from image features alone.
Uses a frozen foundation model to encode given or image-reconstructed object meshes for unseen-object generalization.
A shared transformer jointly reasons over the object and one or two hands to maintain alignment.
Refines coarse per-joint contact predictions over fine hand regions using reconstructed geometry.
On seven benchmarks, achieves state-of-the-art joint hand/object pose accuracy and outperforms a dedicated contact estimator in fine-grained contact.

A shared transformer reasons jointly over these tokens to keep the hands and object aligned, and heads decode their poses and coarse per-joint contact. The latter resolves this contact over finer hand regions using region distances from the reconstruction.

papers.title: Generalizable Feed-Forward 3D Hand-Object Reconstruction with Coarse-to-Fine Contact Estimation

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models generate navigable worlds frame by frame, but a persistent world requires previously observed scenes to remain recoverable as users move away and return. Existing memory evaluations, however, often focus on seen-view revisits and full rollouts, leaving cross-view scene recovery underexplored while entangling memory with trajectory-following errors and accumulated generation degradation. We introduce SceneMemBench, a benchmark for scene memory in interactive video world models. It evaluates two complementary dimensions: seen-view recall versus novel-view recovery, and controlled diagnosis versus end-to-end interaction. We introduce Continued Rollout from a shared ground-truth observation history, alongside Full Rollout over complete model-generated interactions. SceneMemBench contains 600 controlled trajectories across 33 Unreal Engine scenes and 60 Full Rollout cases, covering eight representative open- and closed-source models. We evaluate scene recovery along subject consistency, appearance fidelity, and geometric consistency. Results show that novel-view recovery is generally more challenging than seen-view recall, while model profiles under controlled histories can differ markedly from those observed in full interaction. Together, these findings reveal complementary failure modes obscured by seen-view revisits or end-to-end rollouts alone.
authors: Yuheng Si, Linye Lyu, Jiawei Zhou, Lingyi Du, Nanfei Ye, Aobo Liu, Yu Liu, Yu Li, Cheng Zhuo
bullets: Addresses gaps in existing evaluations that overlook cross-view recovery and conflate memory with trajectory or generation errors.
Measures seen-view recall versus novel-view recovery, and controlled diagnosis versus end-to-end interaction.
Introduces Continued Rollout from shared ground-truth histories and Full Rollout over complete model-generated interactions.
Covers 600 controlled trajectories across 33 Unreal Engine scenes and 60 full-rollout cases spanning eight models.
Finds novel-view recovery is generally harder, and that controlled-history model profiles can differ substantially from full interactions.

papers.abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.
authors: Yaswanth Chittepu, Raghavendra Addanki, Anup Rao, Branislav Kveton, Scott Niekum
bullets: Full interaction histories often retain irrelevant observations and actions, creating unnecessary input overhead.
The paper defines a sufficient state abstraction by preserving task performance of a fixed reference agent, rather than exactly matching its behavior.
Deterministic recursive programs are searched using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm.
On ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, abstractions maintain near-reference success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively.
The learned programs explicitly show what information is retained, updated, and discarded.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the genetic search procedure. Parent programs are selected for mutation or crossover and an LLM proposer generates a child. The child is evaluated and, when infeasible, iteratively revised using feedback from a reflector for at most three repair attempts. Only the highestfitness candidate from the resulting repair trajectory is added to the population.

Figure 1: (a) A standard LLM agent conditions on the full context ct, the concatenation of all observations and actions, which grows with the interaction. (b) The abstracted agent maintains a recursive state. At each step, ϕ combines the previous state st−1 with the preceding action at−1 and current observation ot to produce st, which is then provided to the policy. The raw interaction history is not retained.

papers.abstract: We compare a MEGABYTE-style byte-patch Transformer with a 64-byte sliding local decoder (local64) to a matched byte-level 8k BPE decoder (BPE-8k) under identical raw bytes, document order, and approximately matched bytes per optimizer step: 350M parameters and 10 billion training bytes. Under matched-span document sliding (identical scored byte ranges), BPE-8k leads with relative gaps of -5.2%, -4.9%, -9.3% and -6.1% in bits per byte (overall, text, code, math; paired bootstrap). Downstream, CharBench equal fine-tuning favors local64 (53.7% vs 40.0%), fact200 favors BPE-8k (16.5% vs 7.0%), and PIQA (raw and length-normalized) and ARC-Easy length-normalized favor BPE-8k after Holm correction at alpha = 0.05; remaining tasks are ties. Evaluation pitfalls that changed conclusions include context-length extrapolation past the BPE training context, bits per token reported as bits per byte, and inconsistent byte denominators. Unlike controlled tokenizer studies that vary the subword tokenizer under a fixed token budget, or FLOP-controlled byte-model scaling studies, we hold the raw bytes, their order and the optimizer recipe fixed and ask whether a fixed-patch byte model can replace the tokenizer at all. Limits: one size, one seed, one 8k vocabulary fixed before the runs, and a known difference in embedding initialization between the twins.
authors: Asadullah Maliyawala, Andrej Lisal
bullets: Both models use the same raw bytes, document order, optimizer recipe, and approximately matched bytes per step over 10B training bytes.
Under matched-span evaluation, BPE-8k leads in bits per byte overall, text, code, and math.
Equal fine-tuning favors local64 on CharBench, while BPE-8k leads on fact200, PIQA, and length-normalized ARC-Easy; other tasks are ties.
Evaluation choices that affected conclusions included context extrapolation, confusing bits per token with bits per byte, and inconsistent byte denominators.
Scope is limited to one model size, one seed, one fixed 8k vocabulary, and differing embedding initialization between the twins.

papers.abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.
authors: Xinhe Wu, Yicheng Ye, Yadong Jin
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering machine-readable measurements embedded in compound scientific figures.
Combines figure localization, panel decomposition, OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided MLLM reconstruction.
Adds batch processing, caching, and structured logging for high-throughput repository-scale extraction.
Applied to 605 toxicology/pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle articles, producing 468 and 242 tabular outputs, respectively.
Links reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata for downstream AI4Science applications.

papers.abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation relies on multimodal inputs that capture visual context and non-visual physical interaction cues for precise and coordinated control. To address the challenge of effectively integrating these modalities for policy learning, we propose HiMoDex, a two-stage framework centered on hierarchical multimodal world-state representations. In Stage 1, we pretrain a hierarchical representation network on the collected dataset of 1.19 million synchronized multimodal time steps. The network integrates visual context with tactile, force-torque, and audio cues into unified world-state embeddings. In Stage 2, we freeze the pretrained network and use its embeddings to condition a shared world-action transformer. The transformer jointly learns action generation and action-conditioned future-state prediction. Experiments across five real-world tasks show that HiMoDex achieves an average success rate of 78.7\%, representing an absolute improvement of 32.0\% over the strongest evaluated baseline. Extensive ablations validate the benefits of hierarchical representation learning and two-stage training. Failure analysis helps explain performance differences across variants. Code, data, and demos will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/research-website-BAB4/.
authors: Jin Yang, Youlin Wang, Ping Wei
bullets: Addresses multimodal integration for precise, coordinated bimanual control.
Pretrains hierarchical embeddings from 1.19 million synchronized multimodal time steps.
Freezes the representation network and conditions a shared world-action transformer on its embeddings.
The transformer jointly generates actions and predicts action-conditioned future states.
Across five real-world tasks, it achieves a 78.7% average success rate, 32.0 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.

papers.abstract: Converting pretrained softmax Transformers to efficient attention often causes substantial performance degradation, while recovery typically requires costly fine-tuning. We propose ET (Efficient Transfer), a framework for high-fidelity attention conversion with minimal optimization cost. ET combines exact local and shared-key softmax attention with a mean-anchored, scan-free global linear correction and adaptive gating, achieving linear complexity in sequence length. To preserve pretrained knowledge, ET freezes pretrained weights and calibrates only newly introduced parameters through alternating least squares on a small set of unlabeled samples, without gradient updates. On ImageNet-1K, ET achieves 79.64% and 81.55% top-1 accuracy on DeiT-S and DeiT-B, respectively, within 0.25 percentage points of their softmax teachers. At $768\times768$, ET outperforms T$^5$ by 3.59 percentage points at comparable inference FLOPs, without gradient-based fine-tuning. On DiT-XL/2, ET achieves an FID-50K of 2.59 with only 250 LoRA updates. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, ET matches the teacher's GenEval score at 1K resolution with just 0.73 A100 GPU-hours of gradient-free conversion and a 1.39$\times$ inference speedup.
authors: Guangfu Guo, Xiaoqian Lu, Linsey Pang, Weiran Yao, Haolin Chen, Long Cheng, Kunpeng Liu
bullets: Addresses the performance loss and costly fine-tuning typically associated with efficient-attention conversion.
Combines exact local/shared-key softmax attention with a mean-anchored, scan-free global linear correction and adaptive gating.
Freezes pretrained weights and uses alternating least squares on a small unlabeled sample set to calibrate added parameters.
On ImageNet-1K, remains within 0.25 percentage points of DeiT-S and DeiT-B softmax teachers; also improves over T$^5$ at comparable FLOPs.
Demonstrates gradient-free conversion for diffusion models, matching Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium's GenEval score with faster inference.

papers.abstract: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.
authors: Yizhak Ben-Shabat, Jiahao Zhang, Joseph Liu, Seonghyeon Moon, Young-Yoon Lee, Haomiao Jiang, Oren Jacob, Mubbasir Kapadia
bullets: Addresses limited scale, coarse captions, and insufficient hand articulation in existing datasets.
Provides ~542K in-the-wild sequences with 884 hours and 95.5M frames, filtered for complex bimanual motion.
Pairs each clip with five captions spanning global semantics to atomic finger states in a hierarchical taxonomy.
Introduces a 393-D bimanual representation adapted to the high-DoF kinematics of hands.
Benchmarks diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive models, exposing a trade-off between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility.

papers.abstract: As live video streams grow longer, repeatedly encoding and processing their full histories becomes increasingly costly. Answering questions as they arrive therefore calls for visual memory built in one pass before future questions are known. Existing methods mainly keep tokens that differ from earlier ones or match surrogate queries fixed in advance. Without modeling world dynamics, these criteria struggle to tell subtle surprising details from expected change. We introduce Dreamcatcher, a training-free framework and, to our knowledge, the first to use predictive signals from an independently pretrained, frozen video world model for online memory formation in streaming video question answering. Conditioned on recent history, the world model predicts incoming features using learned world priors. Its normalized prediction errors yield temporal and spatial surprisal signals that guide online segmentation and the retention of a frozen Video-LLM's native visual tokens, balancing surprising details with broad visual coverage under budgets that decay with segment age. At query time, an evidence gate admits a segment from a similarity-based shortlist only when the Video-LLM judges that it adds evidence for the question beyond the current view. We evaluate Dreamcatcher on three streaming and three offline long-video benchmarks. On OVO-Bench, Dreamcatcher achieves the highest overall accuracy among the compared training-free methods for each of four frozen Video-LLMs, reaching 78.9% with Qwen3.8-27B. With the three Qwen Video-LLMs, it also reduces average input tokens for answer generation by more than 80% relative to their base models at 1 fps.
authors: Jinxi He, Ce Zhang, Wenhe Liu, Jianshu Zhang, Katia P. Sycara, Yaqi Xie
bullets: Addresses the cost of repeatedly processing full histories in long, streaming videos.
Uses a frozen video world model to derive temporal and spatial surprisal signals for online memory formation.
Retains frozen Video-LLM visual tokens through adaptive segmentation and age-decayed memory budgets.
Uses an evidence gate to admit shortlisted segments only when they add question-relevant evidence.
Achieves the best accuracy among compared training-free methods on OVO-Bench and cuts answer-generation input tokens by over 80% for three Qwen Video-LLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Dreamcatcher. (a) World-Model Surprisal uses frozen V-JEPA 2 to predict block features from a sliding history window. Normalized prediction errors yield spatial scores pooled onto the reader’s token grid and block-level scores for online segmentation. (b) The Online Budget Allocator sets each segment’s budget by a retention ratio r(a) that decays with segment age toward the floor ρ. Ii combines coverage and surprisal to retain native visual tokens under budgets, while keeping the current anchor Wt in full. (c) The Evidence Gate shortlists segments by PE-Core [6] similarity to the question. The reader scores each candidate for evidence beyond the current view in a separate pass, reusing the cached anchor Wt as a shared prefix. Admitted segments (here S3 and S4) meet threshold τ and join Wt for answering. Snowflakes denote frozen models. Snowflakes denote frozen models.

papers.abstract: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) enable dense reconstruction in a feed-forward pass, yet their effective span is limited by cross-view attention. Local consistency has been expanded through geometric alignment of video chunks and recursive updates of an implicit memory, and large-scale scenes with pose graphs. However, both strategies are prone to drift, largely due to the lack of metric-scale observability from monocular geometry. We present Xtream,a hybrid streaming pipeline that maintains an explicit metric state through a factor graph over keyframes, while using a 3DFM as a geometric front end. Xtream incorporates metric information in two ways: through metric scale predictions from 3DFMs; or through inertial measurements if available. Across the large-scale benchmarks of VBR, Oxford Spires and KITTI, Xtream achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3DFM-based online reconstruction, reducing average absolute trajectory errors compared with published baselines and concurrent work. https://ernestolozano.github.io/xtream
authors: Ernesto Lozano, Alberto Jaenal, Javier Civera
bullets: Addresses drift in long-range reconstruction caused by limited cross-view attention and unobservable monocular metric scale.
Uses a 3D foundation model as a geometric front end within a streaming pipeline.
Maintains an explicit metric state over keyframes using a factor graph.
Incorporates metric scale from 3D foundation models or inertial measurements when available.
Evaluated on VBR, Oxford Spires, and KITTI, with lower average absolute trajectory errors than published baselines and concurrent work.

papers.tldr: Xtream enables drift-resistant large-scale streaming 3D reconstruction by combining a 3D foundation model with an explicit metric factor-graph state.

papers.abstract: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) have grown with the models' capabilities, notably for images far larger than those seen in training, where downscaling loses small details. Most of them wrap the VLM in a fixed procedure, such as a zoom tree, that decides in advance where it looks and how the evidence is combined. These procedures make up for the weaknesses of older models by keeping them on a task-specific path, but with frontier models that reliably plan and use tools, they can lower accuracy. We propose RVLM-X, a task-generalizable recursive VLM harness that runs unchanged across photographs, charts and maps. Following the recursive inference of Recursive Language Models, the VLM programmatically controls its own visual context in a code REPL that holds the full-resolution image and calls itself recursively on regions that it chooses. With a cost-efficient frontier model as the base of every method, RVLM-X is more accurate than a single call on all 7 public benchmarks and has the highest pooled accuracy. Because existing benchmarks mostly test whether a model finds one small detail, we also introduce MapGenBench, procedurally generated maps whose questions combine fine-detail perception with multi-step reasoning. There, RVLM-X answers 71.4% of held-out questions against 55.5% for the strongest baseline. Overall, our findings suggest that as VLMs plan and use tools more reliably, letting the model write its own visual search works better than fixing one in advance.
authors: Aadi Palnitkar, Dmytro Kurdydyk, Xiaomin Lin
bullets: Fixed zoom procedures can constrain frontier VLMs that are capable of planning and tool use.
RVLM-X uses a code REPL containing the full-resolution image, enabling recursive self-selection of regions and context.
The same harness operates across photographs, charts, and maps without task-specific changes.
It outperforms a single full-image call on all seven public benchmarks and achieves the highest pooled accuracy.
On the introduced MapGenBench, RVLM-X reaches 71.4% accuracy versus 55.5% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Expert pruning reduces the memory footprint of mixture-of-experts language models, but retaining model quality depends on which experts are removed. Frequency- and magnitude-based scores measure the expert in isolation and overlook how normalization consumes its contribution: subtracting one expert changes both the direction of the residual stream and the scale applied to what remains. We propose FN-Prune, a training-free criterion that compares the next RMSNorm outputs before and after subtracting each router-weighted expert contribution, holding original routes and weights fixed. Squared differences are averaged over all calibration tokens in one pass; low-scoring experts are physically deleted at uniform per-layer ratios, and inference reroutes among survivors. At 50% expert removal, FN-Prune achieves lower WikiText-2 perplexity than the best published methods on Qwen3, ERNIE, and OLMoE, including a 32% reduction on OLMoE. At the same budget, GSM8K accuracy improves over the best published methods by 7.5 and 7.0 percentage points on Qwen3 and ERNIE, respectively, while multiple-choice gains remain task-dependent.
authors: Zeyan Li, Jianfeng Xu
bullets: Targets MoE expert pruning while preserving model quality and reducing memory.
Scores each expert by the change in the next RMSNorm output when its routed contribution is removed.
Uses one-pass calibration with original routes and weights fixed, then uniformly deletes low-scoring experts per layer.
At 50% pruning, reports lower WikiText-2 perplexity on Qwen3, ERNIE, and OLMoE, including a 32% reduction on OLMoE.
GSM8K accuracy improves over prior methods on Qwen3 and ERNIE; multiple-choice results are task-dependent.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. However, it remains unclear which future representations a policy actually needs and how compactly they can be represented. Our probing study shows that complementary future representations can be compressed into a few tokens while retaining most of their action-decoding performance. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. With 1.4B parameters and no large-scale embodied pretraining, LeanWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, 12.3--41.5$\times$ faster than representative WAMs. These results demonstrate that compact predictive supervision can transfer video priors to robust and efficient control.
authors: Shaolong Li, Hongze Fu, Joyce Chai, Yinpei Dai
bullets: WAMs can retain most action-decoding ability using only a few compressed future-representation tokens.
A two-stage pipeline transfers priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy.
The method uses 32 predictive tokens plus complementary hidden-state world tokens, shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision.
LeanWAM outperforms strong VLA and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0.
It predicts action chunks in 25.1 ms on an A100, reported as 12.3–41.5× faster than representative WAMs.

papers.abstract: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time frequency scaling, which inevitably comes at the cost of either throughput or accuracy. To address this tightly coupled challenge, we propose GreenDynaMix, the first runtime system to jointly integrate a DVFS-based thermal manager with a dynamic precision-tuning throughput compensator. A sensitivity-aware allocator leverages intrinsic importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to assign higher precision to critical experts, preserving accuracy. Experiments on server, desktop, and embedded platforms demonstrate that GreenDynaMix reduces the temperature-induced aging rate of GPUs during LLM inference by 25-33%. Without offline profiling or model retraining, it recovers throughput at a perplexity cost of 0.9-1.6% with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.
authors: Han-Yi Lin, Kieran Griperay, Qiang Zhou, Xiangyu Zhou, Nate Bonacci, Zinachidi Achikeh, Li He, Shaofei Qi, Hongqiang Wang, Jeff Zhang, Tianlong Chen, Pi-Cheng Hsiu, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Targets thermal stress from sustained LLM inference, which can accelerate GPU aging and reduce reliability.
Combines DVFS-based thermal management with runtime dynamic precision tuning as a throughput compensator.
Uses MoE router importance signals to assign higher precision to more critical experts.
Across server, desktop, and embedded platforms, reduces temperature-induced GPU aging rates by 25–33%.
Requires no offline profiling or retraining; incurs 0.9–1.6% perplexity cost with 8/4-bit precision and 9.4% when memory constraints require 4/2-bit precision.
