papers.abstract: Understanding a group conversation means deciding, from video and audio, who is speaking and to whom. Leading systems treat these tasks offline on single-channel clips and align models with a self-evaluation reward. We propose BEARING, a geometry-first alternative built on one measured signal: the direction from which a microphone array beside the camera hears a sound. A label-free calibration learned from the stream registers this direction into the camera image, and an online registry of faces, voices and directions needs no enrollment. The registered direction serves as (i) a visual prompt for a vision-language model, a marker on the speaker or an arrow toward an off-screen source; (ii) one input of a reliability-weighted fusion with visual active-speaker detection, for speakers in the same direction from the array; and (iii) a verifiable reward for alignment: the named speaker must sit where the sound comes from, the confidence must match that check, and always answering "group" earns nothing. Every decision is online, with the lookahead as an explicit parameter. On 9,498 addressee-labelled utterances from three AMI sites and egocentric EasyCom, the direction prompt raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74%; addressee accuracy moves by about two points, because telling one addressee from the group depends on the words more than on where people are. For co-located speakers on AVDIAR, visual active-speaker detection holds 95% where direction alone falls to 59%. The verifiable reward beats self-evaluation under GRPO, reward-ranked fine-tuning and DPO; shrinking the lookahead from 5 s to 0.5 s costs 4.5 DER points on AMI, and learning the registration online costs a dip in the first two minutes before the system overtakes vision alone. Code and evaluation protocols will be released.
authors: Nader Lobandi, Lombe Chileshe, Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, Mohammad H. Mahoor
bullets: Calibrates microphone-array sound direction to the camera image without labels, while tracking faces, voices, and directions online without enrollment.
Uses the registered direction as a visual prompt, fuses it with visual active-speaker detection, and provides a verifiable alignment reward for model training.
Raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74% on AMI and EasyCom; addressee accuracy improves by only about two points because addressee identification depends more on language.
For co-located speakers, visual active-speaker detection reaches 95% accuracy versus 59% for audio direction alone on AVDIAR.
Performance depends on temporal lookahead and online calibration: reducing lookahead to 0.5 seconds costs 4.5 DER points, with an initial calibration dip.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Online latency–accuracy on AMI and VoxConverse (0 s collar, overlap scored, so not comparable to published leaderboards; lower DER is better). (b) The policy samples several answers (speaker, addressee, confidence). papers.abstract: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.

bullets: Targets recognizable, recurring stuck states in robot foundation models rather than random failures.

Reversed and random edits support that improvements came from the intended corrective behavior.

papers.abstract: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/
authors: Jiaqi Yin, Baoyue Zhang, Jiyuan Zhang, Wenxuan Liu, Zhaofei Yu, Yue Deng, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses the latency–accuracy trade-off in manipulating moving objects: prediction time can let the scene change before action execution.
Uses role-aware 4D modeling: metric SE(3) trajectories for the target, sparse 3D flow for surroundings, and the current frame for static content.
Runs in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10× faster than video world-action baselines.
Introduces OnTimeBench, which evaluates policies while scenes continue moving during computation.
Achieves 82.1% success on OnTimeBench and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: A language-model robot agent must decide whether to execute, question or refuse an instruction, and an unsafe execution costs far more than an unneeded question. No prior robot gate derives all its thresholds from error costs or acts on calibrated probabilities, and none was fitted in one domain and evaluated unchanged in another. We propose CATWAY, a cost-sensitive three-way decision gate: a loss matrix over four instruction conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe) fixes execute, ask and refuse regions on the probability simplex, the question being the information-gathering step. Its probabilities fuse a ten-sample vote with graded scores of ambiguity, infeasibility and risk by logistic regression. Fitted on household instructions and frozen, CATWAY was tested on text-level decisions of three small models in-domain, in two new robot domains and on the external TRUST-NAV benchmark. At eleven generations per decision against one, it was significantly cheaper than a direct prompt, a cost-aware prompt and an unguarded agent in all 18 household comparisons (mean loss per item 0.28 against 0.57-0.83), in 9 of 18 in the new domains and in 10 of 18 on TRUST-NAV (Holm per set), and never significantly costlier. It executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions. On a unanimous vote, the minimum-expected-loss rule reduces calibration to one loss-derived threshold, so for two of six model configurations a gate on the vote alone never executed a clear instruction, costing 0.49 per item on TRUST-NAV against CATWAY's 0.13 and 0.09; the fused estimate avoided this on every set.
authors: Erik Derner
bullets: Uses a loss matrix over clear, ambiguous, infeasible, and unsafe instructions to define execute/ask/refuse regions.
Fuses ten-sample voting with graded ambiguity, infeasibility, and risk scores via logistic regression.

Was significantly cheaper than comparison approaches in all household comparisons, most cross-domain comparisons, and never significantly costlier.
Executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions; fused probabilities outperformed vote-only gating on clear-instruction handling.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation requires predicting how robot-object interactions evolve over time, encompassing both visual appearance and scene geometry. In multi-camera settings, such predictions need to capture the evolving 3D scene consistently across viewpoints, while supporting controllable generation under different robot actions and camera configurations. Existing video generation models provide strong priors for visual appearance and motion but typically lack explicit geometric modeling. Meanwhile, recent advances in geometry-aware and multi-view generation have explored joint appearance-geometry modeling and cross-view consistency, yet generating temporally coherent appearance and geometry across multiple viewpoints under robotic manipulation conditions remains challenging. In this work, we propose GeoMVGen, a framework for joint multi-view RGB and pointmap video generation in robotic manipulation. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework employs modality-specific adaptation modules to capture the distinct characteristics of appearance and geometry, while using cross-modal residual connections to facilitate information exchange between the two modalities. To establish geometric correspondences across viewpoints, we further introduce a cross-view projection mechanism with complementary geometric supervisions, combining pointmap consistency with geometry foundation model-guided feature alignment. These designs enable controllable generation of temporally evolving multi-view observations with coherent appearance and geometrically consistent scene structures. Extensive experiments on 4D video generation dataset comprising simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios demonstrate that GeoMVGen outperforms state-of-the-art methods in video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency.
authors: Qiaoqiao Jia, Guile Wu, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting evolving 3D robot–object interactions consistently across viewpoints and under controllable actions and camera configurations.
Uses a video diffusion transformer with modality-specific adaptation modules for RGB appearance and pointmap geometry.
Connects modalities through cross-modal residuals and enforces cross-view correspondence with projection and geometric supervision.
Evaluations on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios report improved video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. But are LLMs truly location-aware, able to reliably interpret and precisely answer location queries involving real-world coordinates, points of interest (POIs), and geospatial distances? To answer this concretely, we present LimoBench, a street-level benchmark of 82 natural-language location queries over seven canonical spatial operations: geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, directionality, range search, $k$-nearest-neighbor search, and spatial join. The queries are grounded in real map data of West Lafayette, Indiana, and are graded by location and semantic complexity. They are designed to probe LLMs' street-level spatial awareness, from simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning. We also present Limo, an approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enhances the location awareness of LLMs. Limo grounds LLMs in PostGIS-backed spatial data through a compact set of tools. We find that ungrounded models mostly achieve single-digit accuracy (3.1% for GPT-6 Luna) across different spatial operations. In contrast, the same models achieve near-perfect accuracy (99.3% for GPT-6 Luna) when given access to Limo's spatial tools through MCP. Current LLMs thus have limited and unreliable street-level spatial knowledge, while grounding provides accurate answers at modest overhead (+0.2 s latency, 7.7$\times$ tokens, and 2.2$\times$ cost for GPT-6 Luna). We release the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code to encourage the community to evaluate their own location-aware LLM approaches.
authors: Gautam Choudhary, Jack Peng, Udesh Kumarasinghe, Rachel Rafik, Yousef Hammad, Ahmed Samy, Walid G. Aref
bullets: Benchmarks 82 natural-language queries across seven spatial operations, including geocoding, routing, range search, and spatial joins.
Uses real map data from West Lafayette, Indiana, with queries spanning simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Gradient-based actor optimization is central to deep reinforcement learning. However, conventional first-order optimizers do not explicitly exploit the local curvature of neural actor losses. We propose EQUIP (Curvature-Equilibrated Gradients for Policy Search), a novel approach that seeks to balance local contraction and expansion of the actor parameter space by equilibrating positive and negative curvature. EQUIP constructs a trajectory-informed search subspace and uses the projected Hessian of actor loss to build a bounded local metric for curvature equilibration. First-order loss matching preserves the approximated first-order decrease in actor loss. Meanwhile, gradient mixing and curvature-based gradient selection adjust the gradient applied for actor optimization. We establish the geometric properties of curvature equilibration, derive bounds on gradient alignment and magnitude, and identify conditions for improved actor loss reduction and convergence toward stationarity under direct gradient updates. We integrate EQUIP into Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) without modifying its actor loss, critic learning, or replay mechanism. Experiments on 6 MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks show that the resulting EQUIP-SAC algorithm achieves higher mean sample efficiency than SAC and two second-order policy optimization baselines. Ablation studies further highlight the benefits of curvature equilibration and trajectory-informed geometry for policy training.
authors: Gang Chen
bullets: Addresses the limited use of local loss curvature in conventional first-order policy optimization.

Provides geometric analysis and convergence-related bounds for direct gradient optimization.

papers.abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.
authors: Tongxiao Hu, Yikai Zhao, Qiyan Zhao, Xiaosong Yuan, Xuhang Chen, Pengzhou Cheng, Xiaofeng Zhang
bullets: High-confidence token commitments are often insensitive to image evidence, limiting confidence-based decoding.
Degenerate and hallucinated outputs show increased entropy in deep-layer attention organization.
CD-APC adjusts candidate scores using visual evidence within a base-supported pool.
Dual gating and an inverse-window mechanism adapt commitment decisions to acceptability and decoding difficulty.
The method consistently improves results across two backbones and five benchmarks.

papers.title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: CD-APC is a training-free decoding method that uses visual evidence to reduce image-insensitive commitments and improve multimodal diffusion language model outputs.

papers.abstract: Differentiable simulation enables gradient-based optimization in learning and control problems involving collisions, but its gradients are least reliable at the moment of impact, when the velocities jump. A fixed-step simulator detects a collision only after the bodies overlap, and some differentiable simulators correct for this with a linear estimate of the time of impact. In this paper, we study impacts between ellipsoids. We show that the gradient error of this estimate grows with the obliqueness of the collision, the curvature at contact, and the time step, and that ignoring spin adds a further error. Subsequently, we find the time of impact with continuous collision detection on the Perram Wertheim contact function and differentiate through the touching condition rather than the search. This gives exact gradients at any step size. We demonstrate our method on an optimal control problem and a system identification problem. In both, exact gradients recover the optimal control and the true parameters, while the linear estimate does not, even when it accounts for spin.
authors: Shamak Dutta, Biswadip Dey
bullets: Linear impact-time estimates become less accurate with oblique collisions, high contact curvature, larger time steps, and ignored spin.
The method uses continuous collision detection with the Perram–Wertheim contact function.
It differentiates the ellipsoid touching condition directly, avoiding differentiation through the collision search.
In optimal control and system identification, exact gradients recover the optimal control and true parameters, unlike the linear estimate—even with spin.

papers.selection_reason: Provides exact collision gradients in differentiable simulation, a technically meaningful contribution for gradient-based robot learning and control.
papers.title: Exact Collision Gradients for Ellipsoids in Differentiable Simulation
papers.tldr: A continuous-collision method computes exact gradients for ellipsoid impacts, improving optimization and system identification over linear time-of-impact estimates.

papers.abstract: Conversational assistants compact older messages into short notes and evict the originals. When the note's language requires a distinction that English leaves open, such as Spanish adjective gender (agotado vs. agotada), messages that omit or explicitly state that attribute can yield the same note. After eviction, later turns cannot tell them apart: taking the inflected form literally asserts an attribute the user never gave, whereas discounting it as routine grammar discards one the user did give. We propose a training-free repair across writing, pre-eviction verification and reading. The writer marks unstated attributes with paired forms (e.g., agotado/a), a likelihood check before eviction rewrites unsupported single forms into paired ones, and the reader trusts remaining single forms as stated facts. On five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models, eviction cuts recall of stated attributes from 90% to 34% in question answering (QA); our repair raises F1 (which penalizes both errors) on every model, by 9-53 points in QA and 12-40 points in agent handovers.
authors: Ian Miao, Fangrui Zhu, Bowen Jiang
bullets: Problem: Compacted notes can conflate omitted and explicitly stated attributes when the target language encodes distinctions English leaves ambiguous.
Method: Writers mark unsupported attributes with paired forms, pre-eviction checks repair unsupported single forms, and readers treat remaining single forms as stated facts.
Result: Eviction reduced stated-attribute recall from 90% to 34% in QA; repair improved F1 across all evaluated models.
Scope: Evaluated on five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models in question answering and agent handovers.
Contribution: A training-free repair spanning note writing, pre-eviction verification, and reading.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory compaction/eviction in conversational LLM assistants and a training-free repair for provenance loss, directly relevant to LLM memory and language model behavior.
papers.title: Provenance Loss and Repair in Multilingual Compaction
papers.tldr: A training-free multilingual compaction repair preserves whether attributes were explicitly stated, substantially improving later recall after message eviction.

papers.abstract: Although radiance fields provide detailed scene representations for robotics, they remain underexplored for trajectory planning, without a widely agreed-upon way to translate learned spatial primitives into reliable collision criteria. To bridge this gap, we introduce Collision Rendering, the first trajectory planning framework on sparse voxel radiance fields (SVR), which supports GPU-accelerated, risk-bounded collision checking and a differentiable collision cost. Our key insight is that the structured volumetric density of SVR allows its rendering pipeline to serve as a fast numerical approximator of collision probability. We approximate the robot with collision spheres and place a coinciding spherical camera at each sphere. Under a probabilistic collision model, we derive an upper bound on each sphere's maximum directional collision probability from the camera's rendering pipeline. Evaluating this bound on the GPU yields a modular collision checker that integrates with established sampling-based planners without an auxiliary geometric map or changes to the learned representation. We further compute a collision cost and its gradients from rendered opacities through the same pipeline, extending the framework to trajectory optimization. Experiments demonstrate millisecond collision checking time on a consumer-grade GPU and collision-free trajectories in all queries, outperforming other radiance field-based planners.
authors: Byoungkwon Yoon, Han Gyeom Lee, Hojun Lee, Yuseop Sim, Daniel Sungwoo Bae, Martin Byung-Guk Jun
bullets: Addresses the lack of reliable collision criteria for planning directly in radiance fields.
Models the robot with collision spheres and uses coinciding spherical cameras to estimate directional collision-probability bounds.
Runs GPU-accelerated collision checking without an auxiliary geometric map or changes to the learned representation.
Provides differentiable collision costs and gradients for trajectory optimization, while integrating with sampling-based planners.
Reports millisecond-scale checking on a consumer GPU and collision-free trajectories across all queries in experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. Collision checker (green, Sec. (a) Per-ray error: the rendered pixel opacity sums the density at discrete samples (red dots) along the pixel ray r(t), and the quadrature error in each voxel is bounded using its ray Lipschitz constant Lray and segment length. (b) Angular error: voxels between neighboring pixel rays (red) can be missed by the sampled rays (green). The angular error bound covers the density over the cone of half-angle δb around the bin ray rb(t), using the voxels in each radial shell.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a learned radiance-field-based trajectory planning and collision-checking framework, directly relevant to learning-based robot navigation.
papers.title: Collision Rendering: GPU-Accelerated Trajectory Planning on Sparse Voxel Radiance Fields with Risk-Bounded Collision Checking
papers.tldr: Collision Rendering uses sparse voxel radiance-field rendering to enable fast, risk-bounded collision checking and differentiable trajectory optimization for robotics.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.
authors: Javier Movellan, Manjot Bilkhu, Young-mok Jung, Sirajul Salekin, Henry Tran, Zhao Huang
bullets: Models each chunk’s answered queries with a mixture of von Mises–Fisher components anchored at its embedding, plus a time-varying latent utility.
Provides a closed-form online filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates from curator feedback.
Unifies several existing retrieval-feedback methods as special cases under fixed or simplified assumptions.
Matches prior methods on unchanged-query settings but outperforms them when new chunks make old ones obsolete.
On a nine-month personal-agent memory, improves Recall@5 from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little effect on never-queried chunks.

papers.selection_reason: Bayesian retrieval model for long-term memory with online utility updates, relevant to LLM memory and online adaptation.
papers.title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: BRAG is a Bayesian online retrieval model that adapts to changing chunk utility and improves long-term memory retrieval, especially when newer information supersedes older content.

papers.abstract: Pretrained latent diffusion models are effective priors for transfer learning, from geometry estimation to physics simulation. Existing approaches fine-tune the diffusion backbone but freeze the encoder of the VAE to preserve the latent distribution. However, a frozen encoder may miss salient details in non-RGB inputs and is limited to three channels. We introduce Diffusion Prior Anchoring (DPA), a regularizer applied during VAE fine-tuning that uses a score-distillation update to steer latents toward the high-density manifold on which the pretrained diffusion model denoises accurately. We validate DPA across three image and video models (FLUX 3, LTX-Video, Wan2.2) and four tasks: monocular depth estimation, MRI reconstruction, wind-flow simulation, and surface normal estimation, where DPA lowers the prediction error by 7.5% relative to the frozen VAE, 4.9% to decoder-only fine-tuning, and 4.0% to unanchored VAE fine-tuning. Its gain grows the further the target data lies from the RGB training distribution, from 3.3% on monocular depth estimation to 7.2% on complex-valued MRI. DPA also applies to modified VAEs, including pruned and multi-channel variants. With a four-channel VAE that encodes depth and surface normals, it lowers depth estimation error by 9.3%.
authors: Rafael Bischof, Dominik Narnhofer, Julius Erbach, Michael Kraus, Konrad Schindler, Bernd Bickel
bullets: Frozen VAE encoders preserve the latent distribution but can miss task-specific details and are restricted to three channels.
DPA regularizes VAE fine-tuning with score-distillation updates that steer latents toward the diffusion model’s high-density denoising manifold.
Across three image/video models and four tasks, DPA reduces prediction error by 7.5% versus a frozen VAE.
Benefits increase as data departs from RGB, reaching 7.2% on complex-valued MRI; DPA also supports pruned and multi-channel VAEs.
A four-channel VAE for depth and surface normals achieves a 9.3% reduction in depth-estimation error.

papers.abstract: Two wiring diagrams now cover the whole central nervous system of an adult fruit fly: one female, one male. Can such a diagram, run as a network of spiking neurons, drive a body? And if we swap the body's muscles for engineered actuators, what survives? We ran both connectomes, BANC and MaleCNS, as leaky integrate-and-fire networks of about 160,000 neurons each, and closed the loop through simulated sensors, actuators and bodies for walking and flight. The actuators are port-Hamiltonian, so energy is audited at every step, and swapping one for another changes only a configuration file. Null networks shuffled at five levels, from the whole nervous system to synapse counts, test whether a result depends on the wiring. The wiring produced specific functions: sugar on the labellum drove the proboscis motor neuron, leg joints resisted imposed movement, leg circuits oscillated, a looming disc drove a take-off signal on its side (in MaleCNS), and descending neurons throttled and steered flight. The resistance reflex survived 20 of 20 actuator settings in MaleCNS and 19 of 20 in BANC, including a Hill-type muscle pair and a geared DC motor; the actuator set walking speed and energy cost instead. Coordinated six-leg walking, flight stability and the correction of perturbations did not emerge. Each needed a labelled engineered stand-in, which the connectome could command. Such stand-ins can also manufacture an apparent dependence on wiring: in a rebuild of a published closed loop, odour navigation came from a hand-written rule, and the network entered only through one valence number. The two animals differed on some functions, and the differences traced to wiring, such as a haltere drive of the flight power muscles found only in MaleCNS. A whole-CNS connectome, embodied, gives reflexes, rhythms and command signals, but not the coordination that turns them into behaviour.
authors: Mauricio Mu\~noz Arias
bullets: BANC and MaleCNS connectomes were simulated as ~160,000-neuron spiking networks controlling embodied walking and flight models.
Wiring generated specific responses, including proboscis activation, resistance reflexes, leg oscillations, take-off signals, and flight steering.
The resistance reflex persisted across nearly all tested actuator configurations, while actuators changed speed and energy use.
Coordinated six-leg walking, stable flight, and perturbation correction did not emerge without labelled engineered stand-ins.
Null-network tests and a published-loop rebuild showed that stand-ins can create apparent wiring dependence; some behavioral differences traced to connectome-specific wiring.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Parallel block drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE propose a whole block in one forward pass, but they lose the dependence between tokens in the block; DSpark restores part of it with a lightweight correction head that runs sequentially. Measuring DSpark, we find that this head overrides the base prediction on most slots, so the expensive base readout through the target's full lm_head mostly provides a seed. We therefore propose Wavefront, which follows a simple principle: shrink the base and strengthen the correction head. Wavefront replaces the full lm_head with a learned low-rank base, conditions the correction head on the whole drafted prefix within the same block, and resolves it with a few parallel Jacobi passes. A fixed pass budget makes the draft step free of data-dependent control flow, so we capture it as a single CUDA graph in vLLM with fused kernels. On Qwen3-8B, Wavefront improves throughput over xPress, DSpark and DFlash by 2.6%, 10.7% and 23.6% on average across math, code, chat and agentic benchmarks, and by 9.6%, 14.3% and 28.9% on SPEED-Bench long-context prompts. On Qwen3.8-27B it leads DFlash2, DSpark and xPress by 7.6%, 10.6% and 5.0%, and by 7.4%, 5.8% and 6.0% on the same long-context prompts. The gains persist as serving load grows to concurrency 32.
authors: Huy Huu Nguyen, Xin Huang
bullets: Targets the limited within-block token dependence of parallel drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE.
Uses a learned low-rank base, a correction head conditioned on the full drafted prefix, and fixed-budget parallel refinement.
Implements the draft step as a single CUDA graph with fused kernels in vLLM, avoiding data-dependent control flow.
Reports throughput gains over prior drafters across math, code, chat, agentic, and long-context benchmarks on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.8-27B.
Gains remain as serving load increases to concurrency 32.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.
authors: Haoqun Cao, Tengyang Xie
bullets: Long reasoning traces degrade as context grows, limiting effective reasoning horizons.
A separate summarizer is trained with Delta-KL from token-level predictions on sampled local continuations.

Under fixed token budgets, gains reach 7.7 points and 12 points over vanilla and an untrained summarizer; at 128k tokens, it gains 10 points on AIME 2024–2026.

papers.abstract: Reliably evaluating the capabilities of advanced AI systems is critical for safe development and deployment, yet such evaluations may be undermined by sandbagging, a situation in which a model strategically suppresses capabilities it possesses. Existing work has developed controlled sandbagging settings and methods for detecting or eliciting hidden capabilities, but comparatively little is known about how a model's internal neural computation changes when its capabilities are suppressed. In this work, we study sandbagging through the lens of internal functional organization. Inspired by network neuroscience, we construct functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions while holding the model architecture and weights fixed. Surprisingly, across model architectures and community detection methods, we find a consistent structural signature in which sandbagging is associated with reduced functional connectivity within detected communities. We further demonstrate that this reorganization can guide capability elicitation. Ablating attention heads that exhibit the largest connectivity changes substantially recovers suppressed performance while largely preserving performance under honest behavior. Moreover, incorporating these structural signals further improves existing inference-level and weight-level elicitation methods. Together, our results show that sandbagging is accompanied by systematic reorganization of internal computation and demonstrate that functional network structure can provide both a mechanistic lens for understanding capability suppression and a practical signal for recovering hidden capabilities.
authors: Manzi Fabrice Niyigaba, Ishan Verma Prasad, Sansheng Cao, Zheng Huang, Yujun Yan
bullets: Sandbagging may hide a model’s true capabilities, complicating reliable safety evaluations.

papers.abstract: Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are increasingly able to do substantial reasoning without a monitorable chain of thought, chains of thought are becoming less legible, and are often monitored asynchronously to reduce cost. With the future of chain of thought monitoring unclear, it may be necessary to design LLMs with monitorability in mind. We propose a modification to existing LLM architectures based on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and similar methods to compartmentalize dangerous capabilities so that their use, especially in combination with dangerous reasoning types that may indicate strategic adversarial use, can be monitored more cheaply than chain of thought in a way that might outlast monitorable chain of thought. We propose several variants of this architecture designed to balance tradeoffs and discuss other benefits, such as capability removal.
authors: Jake Watts, Joel Sokol
bullets: Motivated by increasingly opaque and asynchronously monitored reasoning in frontier models.
Builds on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and related architectural methods.
Separates dangerous capabilities and reasoning types to enable cheaper monitoring of their use in combination.
Presents several architecture variants intended to balance monitorability and other tradeoffs.
Also discusses potential capability-removal benefits; the abstract does not report empirical results.

papers.abstract: Object detectors often transfer poorly to specialized domains, where box annotations are scarce and deployment requires compact, real-time models. Large vision foundation models can provide offline supervision, but their zero-shot predictions may be poorly aligned with the target domain. We present an adapt-label-distill pipeline that uses limited target annotations to specialize a foundation teacher and transfer its supervision to compact detectors. We adapt SAM3 on the labeled subset, generate pseudo-labels for the remaining unlabeled images, and train YOLOv11 students with confidence-guided supervision. Teacher confidence weights pseudo-label losses, while zero-gating retains uncertain hypotheses during assignment without applying their associated training losses. Experiments across six target domains and three student capacities show substantial gains in several domains, while revealing limited or negative transfer in others. Teacher comparisons under a common hard-label training recipe support the choice of SAM3, and comparisons with an EfficientTeacher adaptation provide additional evidence against an online SSOD baseline. With YOLOv11m, our pipeline improves over STAC-style self-training by up to 15.3 AP and reaches 51.6 AP on Garbage, compared with 54.1 under full supervision. On NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the deployed student achieves 188 FPS versus 2.9 FPS for SAM3, benefiting from foundation-model supervision without incurring the teacher's deployment cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zk2172-columbia/ProjectAdaptLabelDistill_ObjectDetection.
authors: Zhengye Yang, Anthony Wang, Yuyang Li, Mehmet Kerem Turkcan, Beizhan Yan, Zoran Kostic
bullets: Addresses poor cross-domain transfer, scarce box annotations, and the deployment cost of large vision foundation models.
Adapts SAM3 with limited labeled target data, generates pseudo-labels for unlabeled images, and trains YOLOv11 students with confidence-guided supervision.
Confidence weights pseudo-label losses, while zero-gating retains uncertain hypotheses without using their losses for training.
Across six domains and three student capacities, results show substantial gains in some domains but limited or negative transfer in others.
YOLOv11m improves over STAC-style self-training by up to 15.3 AP, reaches 51.6 AP on Garbage, and runs at 188 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin versus 2.9 FPS for SAM3.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed pipeline. A vision foundation model is fine-tuned on the small labeled set Dl and then applied once, offline, to the unlabeled set Du. Its raw predictions are filtered by confidence thresholding and non-maximum suppression, and the confidence score of every surviving detection is retained alongside its box and class. The compact student is trained on Dl with groundtruth annotations and on Du with pseudo-labels, where each pseudo-label contributes to the loss in proportion to the teacher’s confidence in it and uncertain pseudo-labels contribute nothing. The teacher is used only to produce the annotation set and is absent at deployment.

Figure 1. Cross-domain accuracy and deployment efficiency. Each spoke reports mAP50:95 using the dataset-specific scale shown at its boundary. Our method and the STAC-style baseline use only 5% labeled target data, while the gray polygon denotes fully supervised YOLOv11m trained with 100% labels. The adapted SAM 3 teacher uses the same 5% labeled subset. Solid curves denote deployable YOLOv11m students (188 FPS), whereas dashed curves denote the offline SAM 3 teacher (2.9 FPS), measured on NVIDIA AGX Orin.

Figure 1. Joint sensitivity to the unlabeled loss weight λu and zero-gating threshold η. Results are mAP50:95 on Garbage Classification for three student capacities. The initial retention threshold is fixed at τ = 0.25. The black star marks the shared configuration used in the main experiments, (λu, η) = (0.5, 0.5).

Figure 4. Zero-gating versus high-threshold filtering. Thresholding discards uncertain pseudo-labels and may turn real objects into background negatives. Zero-gating keeps these hypotheses for assignment but sets their loss weight to zero.

Figure 3. Effect of target-domain teacher adaptation. Performance of zero-shot and adapted SAM 3 on the test split of each target dataset. The teacher is adapted using only the limited labeled subset Dl available to the student, requiring no additional annotations. Adaptation substantially improves performance across diverse domains, particularly where zero-shot transfer is poorly aligned with the target data.

Table 4. Comparison with EfficientTeacher [26] adapted to YOLO11n. All methods use the same student architecture and labeled-data split. The adapted-SAM3 student uses hard pseudolabels without confidence weighting or zero-gating. Results are held-out test AP (%).

Table 3. Roadmap of the proposed method on Garbage Classification. Results use YOLOv11n with the same 5% annotation budget throughout. Starting from STAC-style self-training, we successively replace the self-teacher with SAM 3, adapt the teacher to the target domain, and add confidence-aware student training. All variants have identical deployment cost. The adapted-teacher baseline in this ablation uses the unweighted variant of our confidence-aware training recipe, whereas Tables 4 and 5 use the native YOLO hard-label loss.

Table 3. YOLO11 student augmentation policy.

papers.abstract: Learning spatial representations often relies on explicitly predicting geometric quantities, but how physical geometry is organized within learned representations remains less understood. We ask whether 3D structure can emerge from learning relations across 2D observations, without 3D prediction targets. We introduce RePT, which learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction. The learned relation space develops a geometric organization in which magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes without refitting (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78). The ARKitScenes-trained checkpoint also retains strong geometric organization on ScanNet++, showcasing generalizability. In controlled comparisons, distinct-point relational prediction consistently yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning. This organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context, and higher point-transfer accuracy does not by itself produce stronger organization. More broadly, our results suggest that 3D geometry need not be an explicit prediction target and can instead emerge as a structural property of representations trained to relate 2D observations, pointing to relational prediction as a complementary route to learning the representations that spatial intelligence builds on.
authors: Xize Duan, Binke Hou, Xingqiao Huang, Xinyuan Guan, Jiaxin Huang, Kaiyuan Hu, Zipeng Sun, Hong Kang, Meng Bi, Xue Liu, Yili Jin
bullets: Learns compact relations between distinct physical points using cross-view 2D point prediction.
The resulting representation organizes magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods according to physical 3D displacement.
A linear readout trained on 16 scenes generalizes to 39 held-out scenes, recovering displacement length and angle (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78).
Geometry remains organized across ARKitScenes and ScanNet++, and distinct-point relational prediction outperforms matched same-point correspondence learning in controlled comparisons.
Organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context; point-transfer accuracy alone is insufficient.

papers.abstract: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable. We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly backpropagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation rendering. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT's relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer. Project website: https://jmarangola.github.io/one-phase-visual-rl/
authors: John Marangola, Antonia Bronars, Younghyo Park, Stephen Andrews, Kushal Kedia, Pulkit Agrawal
bullets: Addresses the poor performance and inefficiency of distilling privileged-state RL teachers into vision-based students.
Uses frozen pretrained foundation vision encoders so RL learns only task control from test-time image observations.
Avoids costly vision-backbone training and supports transfer from fast, rasterized simulation to real robots.
Outperforms two-phase distillation by 58.8% in average real-world success across three manipulation tasks.
Shows increasing advantage under distribution shifts, with over 61% relative improvement in simulated OOD settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. One-phase visual RL closes the realizability gap, generalizes better outside of the training distribution and exhibits superior transfers to the real-world over two-phase approaches. Policy learning paradigm schematics above; Push-T results below: (a) full-pipeline L40S-equivalent GPU hours, with a 2-hour EMA half-life per seed; (b) Out of distribution evaluation (OOD) in simulation; (c) real-world transfer. Curves show threeseed means ± one standard deviation; OOD bars show three-seed means; real-world bars show separately evaluated policies (30 trials each). Dotted line: privileged teacher performance.

Fig. 7. One-phase visual RL transfers better to unseen real-world objects than two-phase distillation. Policies are trained in simulation on a single black 4,cm cube and evaluated zero-shot on four unseen objects over 20 real-world trials each. Both methods achieve 100% success on the training object, while DRIFT retains substantially higher success on objects with novel appearance and geometry.

Fig. 5. One-phase visual RL retains higher success under distribution shifts. In-distribution (In-distr.) and selected out-of-distribution (Out-of-distr., hatched) success for 1-Phase Visual RL and 2-Phase Distillation (DAgger with a frozen encoder). Object mass and scale use 4× mass for both tasks and 1.2× tee and goal scale for Push-T. Initial-state shifts use a 2 cm goal-position ring for Push-T (training jitter ±1 cm), a 10 cm box-position ring for Peg-Insertion (training range ±5 cm), and peg-start offsets in (1, 1.25] times the training half-range; rings use the maximum absolute axis offset. Viewpoint shifts use a 24 px image translation for Push-T and 0.85× camera field of view for Peg-Insertion. Force perturbations are Push-T only: 0.2 s pushes of 80 N on the gripper or 3 N on the tee. Success is episode-weighted within each selected sweep, then averaged equally across sweeps within each task and across tasks where available. Bars show means over three paired training seeds; error bars show ±1 standard error of the mean. Top-row images are illustrative examples.

Fig. 2. DRIFT learns visual policies directly from task rewards. Simulation provides privileged state information, such as object poses and velocities, that is not directly available at deployment. Two-phase approaches use this information to train a teacher, then train a visual student to imitate its actions (left). We instead optimize the visual policy directly with RL, using a frozen pretrained vision encoder to make training efficient (right).

Fig. 8. DRIFT real-world latents remain more consistent with simulation. Mean standardized latent log-likelihood over 30 real-world episodes per policy. Scores are standardized using each policy’s mean and standard deviation across completed held-out simulation rollouts. Shading denotes pointwise 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over real-world episodes. DRIFT (blue) exhibits a smaller standardized likelihood deficit than twophase distillation (gold), consistent with its real-world latents remaining closer to its simulation distribution throughout rollout.

Fig. 6. One-phase RL generalizes over a wide range of goals. Simulation success for Push-T goal positions (top) and Peg-Insertion box positions (bottom), comparing 1-Phase Visual RL (left) with 2-Phase Student Distillation using DAgger with a frozen encoder (right). Each panel subsamples a 5× 5 grid of 2 cm evaluation cells at the labeled offsets; numbers show mean success (%) over three training seeds and 100 episodes per seed and cell. Black squares mark the displayed offsets within the training range (±1 cm for Push-T; ±5 cm for Peg-Insertion), represented by the center cell in each panel.

Fig. 9. Not all frozen visual representations are equal for transfer. Frozen visual encoder ablation on Peg-Insertion for seven selected encoders in simulation (left), and for the best three encoders in the real world (right). DINOv3-S/16 outperforms all other representations by a small margin in simulation, and by a significant margin in the real world.

Fig. 3. Frozen ViT features and rasterization substantially increase training throughput. Visual RL breakdown per training hour on Peg-Insertion. Bar length gives physics steps collected per hour; segments show the fraction of timed training spent in simulation (including rendering), the neural-network forward pass, and backpropagation. Fractions are re-normalized over these three components; evaluation and un-timed overhead are under 2%. Rows compare rasterization with ray tracing and a frozen with an unfrozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 encoder. Ray tracing makes simulation dominate; unfreezing the encoder makes backpropagation dominate.

Table 3: One-phase visual RL network architecture. Policies trained with one-phase RL and with two-phase distillation use the same visual actor architecture. Self-attention is bidirectional for all transformers.

Table 1: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer. DRIFT achieves slightly higher success in simulation, but substantially better real-world performance across all three tasks, resulting in markedly smaller sim-to-real degradation than two-phase distillation. For each method, we report the seed with the highest real-world success. Simulation success is evaluated over 1,024 episodes per checkpoint, and throughput measures successful task completions per minute of rollout time.

Table 2: One-phase visual RL training hyperparameters. Settings used for all visual RL policies. Pick-Cube policies were trained on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU; all other policies were trained with distributed training using 4 L40S GPUs.

papers.tldr: DRIFT enables efficient one-phase sim-to-real visual RL by freezing pretrained vision encoders and learning control directly from images.

papers.abstract: Fabric manipulation challenges robot policies with changing geometry, self-occlusion, and contact, yet standardized evaluation remains focused on rigid objects. We introduce FabricBench, a benchmark for bimanual fabric manipulation with six tasks spanning garments, silk, and bags, 10,000 simulation-ready assets, and controlled tests of configuration and appearance generalization. Built on an open-source solver in Newton, our simulator enables stable bimanual grasping, holding, and release through contact forces, without artificial attachment. Redesigned cloth-rigid contact and bidirectional force coupling support interactions among robot arms, fabric, and free rigid objects, allowing a bag to support its contents and transmit their weight to the grippers. In a controlled grasp-hold-release evaluation, our solver succeeds in all 45 trials, compared with none for the tested baseline configurations. Evaluating six representative policies, including vision-language-action models and world action models, reveals substantial remaining challenges: the best policy achieves 77% average success, while no policy exceeds 36% on long-horizon T-shirt folding. Under the most deformed initial T-shirt configurations, success falls to 6-14% across policies, with larger drops than under the evaluated appearance shifts. Zero-shot deployment of $\pi_{0.5}$ on a real robot largely preserves task difficulty ordering across six tasks (Spearman $\rho=0.94$). These results establish FabricBench as a reproducible testbed for measuring fabric-manipulation capabilities and exposing limitations in configuration generalization. The project website is available at https://fabricbench.github.io/.
authors: Wenkang Hu, Haoran Wang, Liu Liu, Wenchao Huang, Yiji Chen, Mengao Zhao, Xincheng Tang, Zhengjie Shu, Lai Jiang, Wei Li, Zhendong Wang, Zhizhong Su, Huamin Wang, Ruigang Yang
bullets: Covers six bimanual tasks involving garments, silk, and bags, with 10,000 simulation-ready assets and tests of configuration and appearance generalization.
Uses a Newton-based deformable simulator with redesigned cloth–rigid contact and bidirectional force coupling, without artificial attachments.
The simulator succeeds in all 45 controlled grasp–hold–release trials, versus none for tested baseline configurations.
Across six representative policies, the best averages 77% success, while no policy exceeds 36% on long-horizon T-shirt folding.
Performance drops to 6–14% on highly deformed T-shirts; real-robot zero-shot evaluation largely preserves task difficulty ordering (Spearman ρ=0.94).

papers.selection_reason: Presents a standardized benchmark for bimanual fabric manipulation, directly relevant to robot manipulation and policy evaluation with a novel deformable simulator.
papers.title: FabricBench: A Standardized Policy Benchmark for Bimanual Fabric Manipulation with a Contact-Driven Deformable Simulator
papers.tldr: FabricBench is a standardized benchmark and contact-driven simulator that exposes major weaknesses in current bimanual fabric-manipulation policies, especially under deformation and long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Cognitive neuroscience learned that an activation map is not a map of necessity. Regions that light up during a task are not always needed for it, and only lesions reveal which ones are. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) vision-language models come with an activation map for free, since the router records which experts respond to image and text tokens, and recent work reads modality-specialized experts off this map. We bring the lesion. In Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, Kimi-VL-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3 to 12% of the experts are vision-exclusive: image tokens route to them at up to five times the uniform rate and text tokens almost never. In Qwen3-VL they receive a quarter of all image-token routing, and lesioning all of them costs less than one percentage point on average over eight perception benchmarks and free-form OCR, no more than lesioning a random set of the same size. In Kimi-VL and Gemma-4 the lesion also costs no more than a random set. Scoped lesions, which remove an expert set only at image positions or only at text positions, then show where the models do depend on their experts. In Qwen3-VL, silencing every expert at every image position costs 3 points, against 45 at text positions, where the dependence sits in dual-use experts that text-only tasks need as well. Across models the image-side dependence is 2 to 3 points in Qwen3-VL and Kimi-VL and 26 in Gemma-4. Reading text in images is the one ability that needs image-position experts in every model. The exclusive experts receive informative patches, produce outputs of ordinary size, and stay inert under sensory deprivation: text-only training recruits them only when load balancing forces it. In Kimi-VL the balancing bias itself manufactures most of them. Load balancing draws the modality map in the part of the computation the models depend on least. Expert selection, pruning and skipping should follow the lesion, not the map.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Kexin Geng, Wei Qiu
bullets: Across Qwen3-VL, Kimi-VL and Gemma-4, 3–12% of experts are vision-exclusive and can receive substantial image-token routing.
Removing vision-exclusive experts usually performs no worse than removing an equally sized random expert set.
Scoped lesions reveal stronger dependence on text-position experts than image-position experts in Qwen3-VL, while image-side dependence varies substantially across models.
Reading text in images is the only capability consistently requiring image-position experts across all three models.
Exclusive experts process informative patches but remain inactive under text-only inputs; load balancing may create many of them, especially in Kimi-VL.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Experts matter at text positions, not at the image positions that define the modality map. (A) Top: the two parts of Qwen3-VL’s image top-16 set and the cost of removing each. Below: the 424 dual-use experts removed at all positions, at image positions only and at text positions only, over nine probes and greedy TextVQA, with paired 95% intervals, next to every expert silenced at image positions. Over the eight image probes they cost 31.5, 1.0, 30.0 and 3.6 points: the dual-use cost is at text positions, and every expert at image positions can be silenced for a few points, except for reading text in images. (B) Five-probe mean cost of removing an expert set at image positions or at text positions, for the three models. Image-side dependence is 3, 2 and 26 points, while text-side dependence on the whole expert population is 37 to 45 points in every model.

Figure 4. The vision-exclusive experts take informative patches, produce ordinary outputs, and are still dispensable. (A) One V∗ item. Load of each patch on the vision-exclusive experts and on the dual-use part of the image top-16 set: the share of its expert selections that go to the set, as a multiple of the share under uniform routing, averaged over layers. Intact, the model answers the question correctly with probability 1.00. Without the 727 vision-exclusive experts it still does. Without the 424 dual-use experts it answers wrongly. (B) Load by patch position relative to the V∗ target box, and by patch-detail quintile over all 600 images. (C) Expert output statistics on image tokens.

Figure 5. Text-only training neither recruits the vision-exclusive experts nor damages vision through them. (A) Text load on the vision-exclusive experts, four-probe vision accuracy, and held-out text NLL over 1,200 steps of deprivation (text-only training on UltraChat) and 400 steps of re-exposure (caption training on COCO), for seven balancing conditions and the undeprived control. Diamonds give the load of the bias conditions re-measured with the bias active. In re-exposure the bias is removed at update rate 0.001 and kept at 0.02. (B) Image load on the vision-exclusive and dual-use experts under bias balancing, with the bias active and removed, at matched image budgets. (C) Vision accuracy relative to the control after deprivation and after re-exposure.

Figure 1. Experts that image tokens prefer are not the experts that vision needs. (A) Cognitive neuroscience separates an activation map (where does a region respond?) from a lesion (is it needed?), and degeneracy makes the two disagree. A MoE router gives the activation map for free, and expert ablation is the lesion. Brain adapted from NIH BioArt [25]. (B) Routing map of Qwen3-VL: all 48 layers by 128 experts, sorted within each layer by the fraction of text tokens among the selections of each expert after balancing the token mix. The 983 experts at the left are used almost only by image tokens, 89 at the right almost only by text. (C) Lesion test. Each line is one perception probe, intact to lesioned. Removing every vision-exclusive expert costs at most 1 point on average, no more than a random set of equal size (2.4 and 1.0). Silencing every expert at every image position costs 3.0 points in Qwen3-VL and 25.5 in Gemma-4. Removing the dual-use experts at text positions costs 34.8 and 10.2. Kimi-VL (omitted for space) gives +1.8, −2.0 and −1.3 points.

Figure 6. Kimi-VL’s native balancing bias creates most of its vision-exclusive experts and changes no behavior. (A) Fraction of image routing covered by the top-k experts per layer with and without the native bias, and the number of vision-exclusive experts in each regime. (B) Lesions in both regimes.

papers.abstract: Early exit neural networks reduce average inference cost by terminating once sufficient confidence is reached. On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly matched to LUT fabrics, consuming resources that could otherwise support the main datapath. We present ExitLUT, which replaces softmax-style exit decisions with learned Boolean functions mapped directly into FPGA LUTs. In our CNN evaluation, fpgaConvNet is the static spatial-dataflow baseline, while ATHEENA is its softmax-based early exit extension. ExitLUT reduces ATHEENA's exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58$\times$ over the softmax path and eliminates decision-path DSP usage, while preserving accuracy and exit behavior. Rerunning design-space exploration reinvests these savings into the datapath, improving throughput by up to 4.08$\times$ over fpgaConvNet and 1.82$\times$ over ATHEENA. For LUT-based NNs, embedded ExitLUT exits achieve 1.41-1.89$\times$ average time-to-decision speedup over static NeuraLUT-Assemble designs with under 1% LUT overhead.
authors: Oliver Cassidy, Marta Andronic, George A. Constantinides
bullets: Targets FPGA neural-network inference, where conventional confidence-based exits consume resources poorly matched to LUT fabrics.
Learns Boolean exit functions that map directly to FPGA LUTs, eliminating DSP usage on the exit decision path.
Reduces exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58× versus the softmax path.
Reinvesting saved resources improves throughput by up to 4.08× over fpgaConvNet and 1.82× over ATHEENA.
For LUT-based NNs, achieves 1.41–1.89× average time-to-decision speedup with under 1% LUT overhead.

papers.title: ExitLUT: Boolean Early Exits for Efficient FPGA-Based Neural Network Inference

papers.abstract: While recent vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate 3D geometry, how to effectively exploit it for precise and generalizable action prediction remains a central challenge. We introduce Hi3R-VLA, a 3D policy that grounds heterogeneous modalities - vision, language, and action - in explicit 3D geometry for robotic manipulation. Our model integrates spatially-aligned visual features and language conditioning into point cloud representations, enriching scene geometry with fine-grained, task-relevant semantics. It then anchors low-level control commands in the same 3D coordinate frame and uses 3D-RoPE enhanced action-to-point attention over coarse-to-fine point features to model geometric relationships between action targets and observed points. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of semantic fusion within 3D and spatial alignment between observations and actions. With fewer than 250M trainable parameters, Hi3R-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa, RLBench, RoboTwin2, DexJoCo and DexSuite across diverse manipulation tasks and embodiments, from single-arm and dual-arm grippers to dexterous hands. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate its effectiveness in the physical world. The model, code and dataset are publicly released at https://cshizhe.github.io/projects/hi3r_vla.html.
authors: Shizhe Chen, Paul Pacaud, Cordelia Schmid
bullets: Addresses the challenge of effectively using 3D geometry for precise and generalizable action prediction in vision-language-action models.
Fuses spatially aligned visual features and language conditioning into point-cloud representations with task-relevant semantics.
Anchors low-level control commands in the same 3D frame and applies 3D-RoPE action-to-point attention over coarse-to-fine features.
Analysis highlights the importance of 3D semantic fusion and spatial alignment between observations and actions.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across five manipulation benchmarks and effectiveness in real-robot evaluations, using fewer than 250M trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for mappings between function spaces, but their reliability cannot be characterized by the performance of a single trained model. Existing neural operator uncertainty quantification approaches often characterize predictive uncertainty without separately identifying the contributions of individual sources of epistemic uncertainty. Finite sampling of the training function space, output discretization, and model initialization can produce substantial variation among learned operators even when the underlying physical problem is deterministic. We systematically investigate these sources of epistemic uncertainty across a diverse set of operator learning architectures. Across our experiments, we train approximately 46,000 neural operator models and construct ensembles over training datasets, model initializations, and output discretizations to characterize distributions of relative $L_2$ error rather than individual trained realizations. We find substantial architecture-dependent differences in epistemic uncertainty, with model initialization often accounting for the largest proportion of variance in relative $L_2$ error. The ranked performance of neural operator architectures can invert as the number and spatial distribution of output samples change, with the best architectures under sparse or randomly sampled observations differing from those at higher-resolution or structured discretizations. Furthermore, ensembles that reliably characterize aggregate operator error can provide unreliable estimates of error quantiles for individual test functions. These results highlight the importance of distinguishing the sources of epistemic uncertainty when evaluating neural operator reliability and establishing robust benchmarking practices.
authors: Tian Yu Yen, Yucheng Fu, Pratanu Roy, Guang Lin, Michael Penwarden
bullets: Single-model performance does not capture the full epistemic uncertainty of neural operators for deterministic problems.
The study ensembles models across training datasets, initializations, and output discretizations, analyzing distributions of relative L2 error.
Across architectures, initialization often contributes the largest share of error variance.
Changing the number and spatial arrangement of output samples can reverse architecture rankings.
Ensembles may estimate aggregate operator error well while poorly estimating error quantiles for individual test functions.

papers.selection_reason: Epistemic uncertainty analysis for neural operators; relevant to reliable world-model prediction.
papers.title: Diagnosing Epistemic Uncertainty in Neural Operators: Effects of Initialization, Discretization, and Function Sampling
papers.tldr: A systematic study shows that neural-operator reliability depends strongly on initialization, training-function sampling, and output discretization, with uncertainty varying substantially by architecture and evaluation setup.

papers.abstract: Initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA) aims to jointly recover camera poses and scene structure without requiring an initial global estimate. It is a very challenging problem, especially compared to traditional BA where a good estimation is assumed. While recent methods optimize surrogate Object Space Error (OSE) objectives from random initialization, a low objective value does not necessarily yield an accurate reconstruction, revealing a gap between optimization and reconstruction. We show that existing InitFree BA pipelines struggle to produce accurate 3D reconstructions on modern SfM benchmarks, and demonstrate that incorporating learned metric depth substantially improves their practical feasibility. We introduce InitFree-SfM, a complete initialization-free SfM pipeline combining learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent track construction, and joint metric refinement. Within this framework, we propose a simple depth-augmented OSE (dOSE), which complements the directional constraints of OSE by constraining landmark positions along their viewing rays. Our approach substantially outperforms existing InitFree BA methods and achieves competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on challenging low-overlap image collections. Importantly, our analysis challenges the prevailing emphasis on surrogate objectives in previous InitFree BA research, revealing that geometric constraints play a central role in accurate reconstruction, while OSE-based optimization provides further improvements.
authors: Simon Weber, Mateo de Mayo, Je Hyeong Hong, Carl Olsson, Daniel Cremers, Ronald Clark
bullets: Addresses the gap between low surrogate-objective values and accurate 3D reconstruction in initialization-free bundle adjustment.
Combines learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent tracks, and joint metric refinement.
Introduces depth-augmented OSE (dOSE) to constrain landmark positions both directionally and along viewing rays.
Substantially outperforms prior initialization-free BA methods and reaches competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on low-overlap image collections.
Finds that geometric constraints are central to reconstruction accuracy, while OSE optimization provides additional gains.

Overall, our simple yet effective pipeline offers a new perspective on initialization-free BA, highlighting the central role of geometric constraints beyond surrogate objective optimization.

papers.tldr: InitFree-SfM makes initialization-free structure-from-motion practical by combining learned depth and correspondences with geometry-aware bundle adjustment.

papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth models are trained with truncated backpropagation, yet it remains unclear why this works. We show that input injection, commonly used in recurrent-depth models, is exactly Halpern iteration, and that a slowly vanishing stepsize provably converges with a backpropagation window polylogarithmic in the depth. The guarantees require a Lipschitz operator, which for SwiGLU leads to a weight constraint in both row and spectral norm, while only a row norm constraint for gates. Based on these constraints, we develop an optimizer tailored to each parameter group, Sparrow, which provides a drop-in replacement of Muon/MuonH with no overhead, that speeds up training even beyond recurrent models.
authors: Thomas Pethick
bullets: Input injection is identified as Halpern iteration, clarifying why truncated backpropagation can work.
With a slowly vanishing stepsize, convergence is provable using a backpropagation window that grows polylogarithmically with depth.
The theory requires Lipschitz operators; for SwiGLU, this implies specific row, spectral, and gate-norm constraints.
Sparrow applies tailored optimization to different parameter groups and is a no-overhead drop-in replacement for Muon/MuonH.
The abstract reports faster training, including beyond recurrent models, but gives no quantitative results or experimental details.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit near-zero forgetting in specific continual learning settings with experience replay. However, robustness to domain shift of learned tasks remains unexplored. In this work, we study the robustness of Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under out-of-distribution (OOD) data using the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. While the in-domain (ID) setup achieves near-zero catastrophic forgetting, OOD performance on previous tasks quickly collapses. Specifically, we show that during the continual learning process, the OOD capabilities of the model degrade, following a shared representational pattern across domain shifts, which is also visible behaviorally in the two simpler suites. Representational analysis shows that drift concentrates in the multimodal and action features. Linear probes indicate that OOD features still retain task-relevant information, but appear unreadable, consistent with representation misalignment. These findings suggest that even when ID stability remains intact, severe OOD forgetting can still occur, accompanied by representational drift during continual learning.
authors: Adri\`a Ruiz, Bart{\l}omiej Twardowski, Tinne Tuytelaars, Sergi Masip
bullets: Studies Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under continual learning on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus.
Finds that OOD performance on previously learned tasks rapidly collapses despite stable in-domain performance.
Identifies shared representational drift across domain shifts, concentrated in multimodal and action features.
Linear probes show OOD features retain task-relevant information but become difficult to read, suggesting representation misalignment.
Shows that ID stability alone is insufficient for assessing continual-learning robustness.

papers.abstract: Representation quality in pretrained text foundation models is not concentrated at the final layer, yet practitioners routinely probe it there because layer selection without labels has remained an open problem. We present a large-scale empirical study of where layer quality lives across 25 models spanning four architectural families and four pretraining strategies, evaluated on 13 datasets across classification, pair classification, semantic textual similarity, and multiple-choice question answering. Peak probing layers depend systematically on pretraining strategy and architecture: masked encoders peak in late-middle layers, sequence-to-sequence models shift their peak with task type, contrastive sentence encoders concentrate signal at the final layer under CLS and last-token readouts but peak early under mean pooling, and decoder-only models exhibit distinct phase structure tied to depth. We distill these findings into the Stable Geometry Index (SGI), a closed-form, fully label-free selector with no fitted coefficients combining power-law fit quality, effective-rank capacity, spectral stability, and a weak depth prior. Across 383 evaluation groups SGI improves over the last-layer baseline and lifts Hit@3 from 0.39 to 0.52, recovering 40% of the gap to the oracle without using any labels, and exceeds a supervised ELMo-style layer mix on the matched subset despite using strictly less information. Our ablations also reverse a common assumption in the spectral-decay literature: power-law fit quality is a stronger predictor of layer quality than the exponent's proximity to one.
authors: Arnesh Batra, Aniket Khandelwal, Arush Gumber, Krish Thukral, Kushagra Agrawal, Dev Sharma
bullets: Study spans 25 models, four architectural families, four pretraining strategies, and 13 datasets covering four task types.
Best layers depend systematically on architecture, pretraining strategy, task, and representation readout.
SGI combines power-law fit quality, effective-rank capacity, spectral stability, and a weak depth prior without labels or fitted coefficients.
Across 383 evaluation groups, SGI raises Hit@3 from 0.39 to 0.52 and recovers 40% of the oracle gap.
Power-law fit quality predicts layer quality better than the exponent’s proximity to one, challenging a common spectral-decay assumption.
